        • Root Container (UID 0) vs Non-Root Container
        • runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser: 1000

        • Default capabilities (~14) vs drop ALL
        • Dangerous: CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW
        • anihpj: Zero capabilities needed (drop ALL)

        • EncryptionConfiguration YAML structure
        • API Server flag: --encryption-provider-config
        • Rotating existing secrets after enabling
      • 19.3 Encryption Providers — Which to Use
        • identity: No encryption (dangerous default)
        • aescbc: AES-CBC, 32-byte key
        • aesgcm: AES-GCM, better performance
        • secretbox: XSalsa20 + Poly1305
        • kms: External Key Management (AWS/GCP/Azure)

        • Traditional runc: shared kernel, no isolation

        • Kata Containers: lightweight VM, ~20% overhead
        • Comparison: Isolation, Performance, Startup, Memory

🛡️ Kubernetes CKS — Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist

Complete Learning Guide with anihpj Django Project (jobpost app)

From complete beginner to CKS-certified Kubernetes security specialist. Learn cluster hardening, system hardening, minimizing microservice vulnerabilities, supply chain security, monitoring, logging, runtime security, and incident response — all through hands-on examples with a real Django application.

🟢 Beginner Friendly ☸️ Kubernetes v1.31+ 🐍 Django / Python 🔴 38 Chapters ⏱️ ~50 Hours 🎓 CKS Exam — 100% Coverage 📋 9 Appendices

🚀 Your CKS Learning Journey

🎯 Welcome! This guide takes you from complete beginner to CKS-certified Kubernetes security specialist. Every concept is explained with real examples using the anihpj/jobpost Django project — you'll learn by doing, not just reading. Covers all CKS exam domains: Cluster Setup (10%), Cluster Hardening (15%), System Hardening (15%), Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities (20%), Supply Chain Security (20%), and Monitoring, Logging & Runtime Security (20%).

✅ Before You Begin — CKS Readiness Checklist

🔴 MUST HAVE (Non-Negotiable)
  • Active CKA certification
  • kubectl: get, describe, apply, exec, logs
  • Write Pod, Deployment, Service YAML from memory
  • RBAC basics: Role, ClusterRole, Binding
  • Linux: systemctl, journalctl, ps, netstat, ss
📚 SHOULD KNOW (Recommended)
  • TLS basics: certificates, private keys, CAs
  • Docker: build, push, run; Dockerfile structure
  • Basic networking: TCP/IP, ports, DNS, firewalls
  • Linux file permissions: chmod, chown, setuid
  • OWASP Top 10 or general security concepts

📜 The Evolution That Led to Kubernetes Security

Understanding the journey from bare metal to security-orchestrated containers

2000s
🖥️
Bare Metal

No isolation. App compromise = server compromise. Physical security only.

2010s
💻
Virtual Machines

VM-level isolation. Still heavy OS per VM. Patching = slow.

2015
🐳
Docker Containers

Fast, lightweight — but shared kernel. Container escape = node compromise.

2019
🛡️
CKS Created

CNCF creates CKS. Security becomes a career. Falco, OPA, cosign emerge.

Today
🔐
Zero-Trust Era

mTLS everywhere, SBOM required, SLSA for builds. CKS certifies you for this.

🎯 CKS Exam Strategy EXAM PREP

First 5 Minutes — Setup Ritual

When your CKS exam terminal opens, the first 5 minutes are the most important. Run these commands immediately to save 10-15 minutes during the exam:

⚡ CKS EXAM TERMINAL SETUP — Run This First
~/.bashrc
# ═══ 1. SPEED ALIASES (save keystrokes) ═══
alias k=kubectl
alias kgp='kubectl get pods -o wide'
alias kgs='kubectl get svc'
alias kgn='kubectl get nodes'
alias kd='kubectl describe'
alias kaf='kubectl apply -f'

export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"
export now="--force --grace-period=0"

# ═══ 2. CKS SECURITY ALIASES (exam-specific) ═══
alias kauth='kubectl auth can-i'
alias kaudit='cat /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml'
alias kfalco='systemctl status falco'
alias kcerts='openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -text -noout'
alias kctx='kubectl config current-context'

# ═══ 3. VERIFY YOUR CONTEXT ═══
kubectl config current-context
kubectl config get-contexts

# ═══ 4. SAVE THESE BOOKMARKS ═══
echo "kubernetes.io/docs" > ~/bookmarks.txt
echo "falco.org/docs/rules" >> ~/bookmarks.txt
echo "cisecurity.org/benchmark/kubernetes" >> ~/bookmarks.txt
💡 Why This Matters

These aliases save you from typing full commands under time pressure. The CKS exam is 2 hours with ~15-20 complex security tasks. Every saved keystroke compounds into more time for actual problem-solving.

3-Pass Time Management Strategy

The CKS exam has ~15-20 performance-based tasks. Don't solve them in order — use the 3-pass strategy:

⏱️ CKS 3-PASS STRATEGY — 120 Minutes
1️⃣
PASS 1: Quick Wins 0-45 min

Scan ALL tasks. Solve easy ones first (1-3 min each):

  • RBAC: Role + RoleBinding
  • Pod securityContext
  • Namespace with PSS labels
  • kubectl auth can-i
  • NetworkPolicy deny/allow

🎯 Goal: 5-7 tasks done, confidence built

2️⃣
PASS 2: Medium 45-105 min

Tackle tasks needing more config (3-8 min each):

  • Falco rule: write custom rule
  • Seccomp/AppArmor profiles
  • Trivy: scan + fix CVEs
  • Audit policy: configure
  • OPA/Kyverno admission

🎯 Goal: 7-9 more tasks solved

3️⃣
PASS 3: Hard + Verify 105-120 min

Return to skipped hard tasks (8-15 min each):

  • Encryption at rest
  • OPA ConstraintTemplate
  • ImagePolicyWebhook
  • Full incident response
  • RE-VERIFY context!

🎯 Goal: Finish everything, verify all

Domain-by-Domain Strategy

Each CKS domain tests different skills. Here's how to approach each one during the exam:

DomainWeightKey Files/CommandsExam Strategy
Cluster Setup10%/etc/kubernetes/manifests/, kube-bench, NetworkPolicy YAMLQuick wins — do these FIRST. Fix API server flags, apply NetPol, secure Ingress
Cluster Hardening15%RBAC YAML, SA config, kubelet config.yamlMedium difficulty. Always verify with kubectl auth can-i
System Hardening15%/etc/apparmor.d/, seccomp JSON, sshd_configProfile must exist on NODE before pod can use it. Verify with aa-status
Minimize Microservice Vulns20%Pod YAML securityContext, EncryptionConfiguration, RuntimeClassLargest domain — master SecurityContext fields. Know all PSS levels
Supply Chain Security20%trivy, cosign, OPA ConstraintTemplate, Kyverno ClusterPolicyKnow YAML structure for OPA and Kyverno. Practice cosign verify flow
Monitoring & Runtime Security20%/etc/falco/falco.yaml, audit-policy.yaml, /var/log/kubernetes/audit.logFalco rules are YAML-based conditions. Audit policy is YAML. Both need restart after changes

Top 10 Mistakes That Cost Points

❌ COMMON MISTAKES
  • 1. Mixing up AppArmor vs Seccomp (most common mistake)
  • 2. Forgetting to enable PSS on the right namespace
  • 3. Not switching cluster context before starting
  • 4. Creating RBAC but not verifying it works
  • 5. Forgetting to verify NetworkPolicy actually blocks
  • 6. Confusing PSS modes: enforce/audit/warn
  • 7. Skipping audit log configuration flags
  • 8. Not knowing Falco rule syntax
  • 9. Leaving privileged containers untouched
  • 10. Not using docs (kubernetes.io is allowed!)
✅ WHAT TO DO INSTEAD
  • AppArmor = profile on node. Seccomp = syscall filter in pod spec
  • kubectl label ns <name> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
  • ALWAYS: kubectl config current-context first
  • Test: kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=<user>
  • Use: kubectl exec pod -- ping <target> to verify blocks
  • Enforce=blocks, Audit=logs only, Warn=warns but allows
  • Check apiserver manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
  • Know: falco.yaml, output formats, /etc/falco/falco.yaml
  • Always check SecurityContext: runAsNonRoot: true
  • Prep 15+ bookmarks before the exam!

📚 Part 1: Foundation 🟢 Beginner

Chapter 1: Introduction to Kubernetes Security

Before diving into cluster builds and security configs, let's understand why Kubernetes security is fundamentally different from traditional IT security, what the 4Cs model means, and which principles guide every security decision. We'll use our anihpj/jobpost Django app to make every concept concrete.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📖 Concepts 🎯 Foundation

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why Kubernetes security is fundamentally different from traditional IT security
  • ✅ The 4Cs of Cloud Native Security — Cloud, Cluster, Container, Code
  • ✅ Five core security principles: Least Privilege, Defense in Depth, Zero Trust, Immutability, Audit Everything
  • ✅ How each principle applies to the anihpj/jobpost Django application
  • ✅ The "assume breach" mindset — act as if attackers already got in
🎓 CKS Relevance
Foundation ALL DOMAINS
Understanding "Why" Matters on the CKS

The CKS is a performance-based exam (2 hours, ~15-20 tasks in a live terminal). While Chapter 1 isn't directly tested with commands, understanding why Kubernetes security works the way it does helps you reason through unfamiliar scenarios faster. Key concepts to internalize:

  • Defense in Depth — Every CKS task adds a layer. PSS + SecurityContext + NetworkPolicy + Seccomp + AppArmor = layers that complement each other.
  • Least Privilege — RBAC questions are about granting the MINIMUM needed. Always start from zero permissions, add only what's required.
  • The 4Cs Model — When the exam asks "where should this fix be applied?", the 4Cs model tells you: Cloud vs Cluster vs Container vs Code.

1.1 Why Kubernetes Security Is Different

Imagine you've built anihpj — a Django app with a jobpost module where employers list jobs filtered by Skills, Location, and Author. It works perfectly on your laptop. But now it's running on Kubernetes in production. The security rules have completely changed.

📖 Key Concept: The Attack Surface Explosion

In traditional IT, you secured one server with a firewall. In Kubernetes, you have potentially thousands of pods, each a potential entry point. A single misconfigured RBAC rule, one container running as root, or one exposed dashboard can compromise the entire cluster. This guide teaches you to close every door.

🏙️ Why Kubernetes Security Is Uniquely Challenging

The Kubernetes Cluster as a City — Every District Has Its Own Risks

🧠CONTROL PLANEmayor's office
🔴API Server exposedAttackers target it first — port 6443
🔴etcd stores ALL secretsIf accessed, cluster is fully owned
🔴Compromised CP = GAME OVEREntire cluster falls instantly
✅Ch 8, 9, 19API Server, RBAC, etcd encryption
🏘️WORKER NODEScity blocks
🔴Pods run as ROOT by defaultPrivilege escalation possible
🔴Shared OS kernelContainer escape = node takeover
🔴One pod can escape to hostNode compromise from single container
✅Ch 15, 17, 18Seccomp, PSS, SecurityContext
🌐NETWORKINGcity roads
🔴ALL pods talk to ALL podsFlat network — no restrictions
🔴Unrestricted east-west trafficLateral movement is trivial
🔴Reach DBs, secrets, other NSOne pod can access everything
✅Ch 6, 7, 22NetworkPolicy, TLS, mTLS
📦IMAGESdelivery packages
🔴Images from public registriesMalicious code risk
🔴No scanning = blind spotsUnknown vulnerabilities inside
🔴Base images go staleYesterday's security ≠ today's
✅Ch 23, 26, 27Trivy, cosign, SBOM/SLSA
📜 Traditional IT Security vs Kubernetes Security

What Changes When You Move to Kubernetes

❌ Traditional IT Security✅ Kubernetes Security
One server = one firewall rule1000 pods = 1000 targets
Static IPs and hostnamesEphemeral pods, rotating IPs
Update OS once a monthImages rebuilt & deployed daily
Users log in via SSHPods authenticate with SA tokens
Audit logs in /var/log/auth.logAudit logs via K8s API policy
Firewall blocks at edgeNetworkPolicy inside the cluster
Manual security reviewsPolicy-as-code at admission
App runs as its own Linux user🔴 By default: runs as ROOT!
Secret in /etc/app.conf🔴 Secret in etcd (PLAINTEXT!)
Patch = update one binaryPatch = rebuild + redeploy image
� The Cost of a K8s Security Breach — Why This Matters for anihpj

Scenario: anihpj/jobpost is running on Kubernetes without CKS hardening. An attacker finds a path in.

💸
Financial Impact
  • Average cloud data breach cost: $4.45M (IBM 2023)
  • Crypto-mining on stolen compute: immediate resource cost spike
  • GDPR fine for user data leak: up to €20M or 4% annual revenue
🏢
Business Impact
  • jobpost user emails exposed → user trust destroyed
  • Company credentials leaked → all cloud resources at risk
  • Service taken offline → job seekers cannot access listings
⏱️ Time to Detect (without CKS controls)
  • Average: 204 days to DETECT a breach (IBM Ponemon 2023)
  • Average: 73 days to CONTAIN it after detection
  • With Falco + Audit Logs: minutes to hours ✅

✅ Supply chain secured
😰 Managing anihpj WITHOUT CKS Security Knowledge
  • 🔴 Pod runs as root → CVE in Pillow library → attacker writes backdoor to /etc/
  • 🔴 All secrets in plaintext env vars → anyone in namespace can read DATABASE_URL
  • 🔴 No NetworkPolicy → compromised pod reaches postgres, redis, other namespaces
  • 🔴 No audit logging → attacker's API calls leave no trace
  • 🔴 No Falco → shell spawned in container goes completely undetected
🎉 Managing anihpj WITH CKS Security Knowledge (what you'll learn)
  • ✅ Pod runs as non-root (UID 1000) with read-only filesystem
  • ✅ Secrets encrypted at rest in etcd; Vault manages dynamic credentials
  • ✅ Default-deny NetworkPolicy — only explicitly allowed connections work
  • ✅ Audit policy logs every secret access and pod exec
  • ✅ Falco detects shells, file reads, and unexpected network connections instantly
🕐 Day in the Life — What CKS Security Controls Protect 24/7
✅
00:00 — Trivy Scan

Automatic Trivy scan detects new CVE in running images → PagerDuty alert fires. Continuous vulnerability monitoring, 24/7.

❌
07:30 — Dev Push → CI/CD

Dev pushes code → CI/CD gates: kube-linter + kubesec + trivy. Build FAILS: container runs as root! Dev fixes → adds USER 1000.

✅
09:15 — Secure Deploy

New version deployed → Kyverno verifyImages passes → PSS Restricted enforced → OPA registry check → Pod starts fully hardened.

✅
11:45 — Auto-Scale

Traffic spikes → HPA scales anihpj 3→8 replicas. Each new pod: same security context, same policies, auto-applied.

🛡️
14:20 — Attack Blocked

Attacker probes from internet → SSH BLOCKED by firewall → HTTP BLOCKED by NetPol → CVE exploit BLOCKED by Seccomp → Falco logs all 3 attempts.

⚠️
17:00 — Audit Catch

Audit review: intern ran kubectl exec anihpj -- bash → Falco alert: "Shell spawned in anihpj container" → No damage, policy reminder sent.

✅
22:00 — All Checks PASS

Nightly kube-bench CronJob runs → ALL CHECKS PASS. 🛡️ 24 hours. Zero breaches. Every layer held. That's CKS.

1.2 The 4Cs of Cloud Native Security — The Layered Model

Kubernetes security is built on the 4Cs model: Cloud → Cluster → Container → Code. Each layer depends on the security of the layer below it. If the cloud is insecure, no amount of cluster hardening will save you. Every layer must be independently secured.

🎯 The 4Cs — Nested Security Layers
    ╔═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║  ☁️  CLOUD — Cloud Provider Security      ← OUTERMOST layer  ║
    ║  IAM policies, VPC security groups, firewall rules,          ║
    ║  network ACLs, encryption keys management                    ║
    ║   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐       ║
    ║   │  ☸️  CLUSTER — K8s Platform Security              │       ║
    ║   │  RBAC, NetworkPolicy, API server security,       │       ║
    ║   │  etcd encryption, audit logging, admission        │       ║
    ║   │   ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐     │       ║
    ║   │   │  📦 CONTAINER — Workload Security       │     │       ║
    ║   │   │  Image scanning, Seccomp, AppArmor,     │     │       ║
    ║   │   │  non-root user, SecurityContext, PSS    │     │       ║
    ║   │   │   ┌──────────────────────────────┐      │     │       ║
    ║   │   │   │  💻 CODE — Application Sec.   │      │     │       ║
    ║   │   │   │  SAST, dependency scanning,   │      │     │       ║
    ║   │   │   │  secrets in code, TLS, SDLC   │      │     │       ║
    ║   │   │   │  ← INNERMOST layer            │      │     │       ║
    ║   │   │   └──────────────────────────────┘      │     │       ║
    ║   │   └────────────────────────────────────────┘     │       ║
    ║   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘       ║
    ╚═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    🔴 A breach in ANY outer layer compromises ALL inner layers
    ✅ Security is only as strong as its WEAKEST link → layer EVERYTHING
☁️
Cloud Layer

CKS Domain 15%
IAM policies, VPC security groups, firewall rules, encryption keys. If your cloud credentials are exposed, cluster security is meaningless.

☸️
Cluster Layer

CKS Domain 25%
RBAC, NetworkPolicy, API server hardening, etcd encryption, audit logging, admission control. The core of CKS.

📦
Container Layer

CKS Domain 35%
Image scanning, Seccomp, AppArmor, SecurityContext, PSS, sandboxed runtimes. Your last line of defense.

💻
Code Layer

CKS Domain 20%
SAST, dependency scanning, secrets in code, image signing, SBOM, SLSA. Shift security left.

CKS Domain Coverage Per 4C Layer

LayerCKS Topics CoveredCKS Domains
☁️ CloudIAM policies, firewall rules, node OS hardening, network ACLs, encryption keysSystem Hardening (15%)
☸️ ClusterAPI server hardening, RBAC, ServiceAccounts, NetworkPolicy, audit logging, admission controlCluster Setup (10%) + Cluster Hardening (15%)
📦 ContainerSeccomp, AppArmor, SecurityContext, PSS, sandboxed runtimes, mTLSSystem Hardening (15%) + Microservice Vulns (20%)
💻 CodeImage scanning (Trivy), image signing (cosign), SBOM, SLSA, static analysisSupply Chain Security (20%)
🔍 4Cs Applied to anihpj — Real Threats & Controls
Layer🔴 Threat Example✅ CKS Control Applied
☁️ CloudNode has admin IAM role → attacker reads all S3 backupsMinimal IAM role + NodeRestriction plugin
☸️ Clusteranihpj SA has cluster-admin → attacker reads all secrets in all namespacesRBAC: minimal SA with no API perms + automountSAToken: false
📦 Containeranihpj runs as root → CVE in Pillow → write to /etc/ → backdoor persists in podrunAsNonRoot: true + readOnlyRootFS: true + Seccomp + AppArmor

You identify a security concern. Ask:
Is it about cloud infra (VPC, IAM, firewall)?
YES → ☁️ CLOUD layer
Fix at cloud provider levelNO ↓
Is it about K8s API, RBAC, nodes, networking?
YES → ☸️ CLUSTER layer
Fix with RBAC, NetworkPolicy, etc.NO ↓
Is it about how a container runs (user, caps, FS)?
YES → 📦 CONTAINER layer
Fix SecurityContext, Seccomp, AppArmorNO ↓
→ 💻 CODE layer: Fix with scanning, signing, dependency updates

1.3 Security Principles You Will Apply Throughout This Guide

These five principles form the foundation of every security decision you'll make as a Kubernetes security specialist. Memorize them — they guide every CKS exam task.

🎯
Least Privilege

Grant ONLY what is needed. No more, no less. Every RBAC role, ServiceAccount, IAM policy — start from zero, add only what's required.

🧅
Defense in Depth

Many layers, no single point of failure. If NetworkPolicy fails, SecurityContext still protects. If Seccomp misses it, AppArmor catches it.

🚫
Zero Trust

Trust no pod, user, or service by default. Every connection must be explicitly allowed. Default-deny NetworkPolicy — nothing in, nothing out.

🧊
Immutability

Containers should not change once running. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. Changes go through Git → CI/CD → image rebuild → new pod.

📋
Audit Everything

Log every API call, every access, every anomaly. Audit policy + Falco rules = complete visibility of everything happening in your cluster.

🔗 anihpj Security Requirements → CKS Controls Mapping
anihpj RequirementCKS Control That Satisfies ItChapter
jobpost user data not exposedSecrets encryption at restCh 19
Django admin /admin/ restrictedRBAC + NetworkPolicyCh 6, 9
PostgreSQL not reachable from webNetworkPolicy + Ingress TLSCh 6, 7
SECRET_KEY never in git/envK8s Secrets + VaultCh 19, 20
App must not run as rootrunAsNonRoot: trueCh 18
No unnecessary Linux capabilitiescapabilities: drop ALLCh 18
Container should not modify itselfreadOnlyRootFilesystem: trueCh 18, 31
Images only from our registryOPA / Kyverno admissionCh 24
All deployments must be signedcosign + Kyverno verifyImagesCh 26
Know if someone execs into the podAudit logging + FalcoCh 28, 29
Pod-to-pod traffic only as neededNetworkPolicy zero-trustCh 6
🎯
Least Privilege for anihpj

anihpj pod's ServiceAccount → no API permissions (automount=false). CI/CD ServiceAccount → can only update Deployments, nothing else. Every SA starts from zero — permissions are explicitly granted.

🧅
Defense in Depth for anihpj

anihpj is protected by: NetworkPolicy + PSS + SecurityContext + Falco + TLS. If NetworkPolicy fails → SecurityContext still prevents root exec. If image has CVE → Seccomp still blocks dangerous syscalls.

🚫
Zero Trust for anihpj

Default-deny NetworkPolicy in anihpj-prod: nothing in, nothing out by default. Each connection explicitly allowed: ingress→anihpj:8000 for web traffic, anihpj→postgres:5432 for DB queries only.

🧊
Immutability for anihpj

readOnlyRootFilesystem: true on ALL anihpj containers. Changes go through Git → CI/CD → image rebuild → new pod. Attackers cannot persist changes inside a running container — any modification is lost on restart.

📋
Audit Everything for anihpj

Audit policy logs: all secret reads, all pod exec, all deployments. Falco rule: alert on ANY shell spawned in anihpj container. Trivy Operator: continuous CVE scan of all running images, 24/7.

1.4 The anihpj Application Security Context

Throughout this guide, we'll use anihpj — a Django job posting application — as our real-world example. The app has 5 data models (User, Author, Location, Skill, JobPost), serves public job listings, manages user data, and has an admin interface — exactly the kind of application that needs CKS-level security.

📁
Django + Models

5 data models: User, Author, Location, Skill, JobPost. Job seekers browse listings filtered by skills and location. Employers post jobs with salary ranges.

🗄️
Database Layer

Starts with SQLite for development. Migrates to PostgreSQL with encrypted PVCs and StatefulSets for production. Database credentials never in code.

🔐
Security Stack

K8s Secrets for credentials. RBAC for team roles. NetworkPolicy for pod isolation. PSS Restricted for production. Falco for runtime detection.

📈
Observability

Falco runtime detection. Audit logging for API calls. Prometheus metrics. Health probes for self-healing. Trivy Operator for continuous CVE scanning.

💡 Why anihpj Is Your Perfect CKS Training Project

anihpj has user data (emails), company data (job postings), sensitive credentials (SECRET_KEY, DB password), file uploads (media), and an admin interface. It needs EVERY CKS control: RBAC, NetworkPolicy, PSS, SecurityContext, Secrets encryption, image scanning, Falco, and audit logging. Every concept in this guide is demonstrated through hardening this application step by step.

📖 The Dockerfile — Multi-Stage Build for Security

The anihpj Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build: Stage 1 (builder) compiles Python dependencies with build tools, Stage 2 (runtime) copies only the compiled artifacts into a minimal image. The runtime image: runs as non-root user (UID 1000), has no build tools installed (reducing CVEs), uses Gunicorn as production WSGI server, and includes a health check. This is the foundation that all subsequent chapters build upon — every security control from Ch 4 onward applies to this container.

📋 Part 1 Quick Reference — 5 Security Principles = 5 CKS Exam Answers

🧅 Defense in DepthMultiple overlapping layers"Only one security control is in place" — you need layered protectionAdd NetworkPolicy + SecurityContext + PSS + Seccomp (not just one)
🚫 Zero TrustDefault deny everything"Pods in namespace-A can reach pods in namespace-B" — shouldn't by default!Create default-deny NetworkPolicy + explicit allow rules only

📝 Chapter 1 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What are the 4Cs of Cloud Native Security, and in which order should they be applied? Give a one-sentence description of each.
Show Answer
Answer
CLayerDescription
1stCloud/Co-Lo/DatacenterInfrastructure provider security — physical, network, IAM at the cloud level
2ndClusterKubernetes itself — API server auth, RBAC, etcd encryption, NetworkPolicy
3rdContainerImage scanning, non-root users, read-only filesystem, seccomp, AppArmor
4thCodeApplication-level security — input validation, SQL injection prevention, dependency scanning
Explanation

The 4Cs are the CKS exam's core framework. They are layered outermost→innermost. If the Cloud layer is compromised, nothing below matters. CKS focuses on Cluster and Container layers. Learn this order — it's referenced throughout the entire CKS curriculum.

Q2
You're auditing a Kubernetes cluster and discover pods running as root (UID 0). Which of the 4Cs does this violate, and what is the recommended fix?
Show Answer
Answer

This violates the Container layer (3rd C). The fix is to set runAsNonRoot: true in the securityContext:

securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
Explanation

Running as root inside a container is one of the most common CKS findings. Root in the container = root on the node (by default). CKS exam questions often ask you to "find all pods running as root" and "fix them". Use kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsUser==0)'.

Q3
Name the 7 most common Kubernetes misconfigurations found in production clusters, and identify which chapter in this guide addresses each one.
Show Answer
Answer
#MisconfigurationCKS Chapter
1Anonymous auth enabledCh 8 (API Server Hardening)
2AlwaysAllow authorizationCh 8,9 (AuthZ Modes, RBAC)
3Pods running as rootCh 18 (Security Contexts)
4Privileged containersCh 17,18 (PSS, SecurityContexts)
5Dangerous capabilities (SYS_ADMIN)Ch 18 (Capabilities Drop)
6cluster-admin SA for appsCh 9,10 (RBAC + ServiceAccounts)
7hostPath mountsCh 11,15 (NodeRestrict, Seccomp)
Explanation

These 7 misconfigs represent ~70% of CKS exam tasks. Memorize them: you'll fix at least 3-4 of these on exam day. Each maps to a specific static pod manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.

Q4
What is the principle of "defense in depth" as applied to Kubernetes? Give a concrete example using the 4Cs model.
Show Answer
Answer

Defense in depth means layering multiple independent security controls so that if one fails, others still protect the system. Example for a web pod:

  • Cloud: VPC with private subnets, security groups
  • Cluster: NetworkPolicy denying all but allowed ingress, RBAC limiting who can exec into pods
  • Container: non-root user, readOnlyRootFilesystem, seccomp RuntimeDefault, no privileged mode
  • Code: input sanitization, TLS, authentication tokens in Secrets (encrypted at rest)
Explanation

No single layer is sufficient. If an attacker bypasses the NetworkPolicy, the non-root container still limits damage. If they escape the container, seccomp blocks dangerous syscalls. CKS exam tasks often ask you to "apply multiple layers of security" — this is defense in depth in practice.

Q5
In the context of Kubernetes security, what does "least privilege" mean? Provide three concrete examples specific to Kubernetes.
Show Answer
Answer

Least privilege = every subject (user, SA, pod) gets only the minimum permissions needed for its job. Examples:

  1. RBAC: A monitoring SA gets get,list on pods, not delete or *
  2. Capabilities: A web server container drops ALL capabilities; it doesn't need NET_ADMIN
  3. NetworkPolicy: The anihpj Django pod can reach PostgreSQL on port 5432 ONLY — nothing else
Explanation

CKS constantly tests least privilege. On the exam: when asked to create an RBAC role, give exactly the verbs/resources needed — no more. When configuring capabilities, drop ALL then add back only what's needed. When writing NetworkPolicies, allow specific ports/protocols only.

Q6
What is the difference between "shift-left security" and "shift-right security"? Give a Kubernetes-specific example of each.
Show Answer
Answer
ApproachWhenK8s Example
Shift-leftEarly in dev cycle (pre-deploy)Trivy image scan in CI/CD pipeline BEFORE image is pushed to registry
Shift-rightPost-deployment (runtime)Falco monitoring at runtime detecting unexpected shell spawns
Explanation

Shift-left prevents vulnerabilities from reaching production (cheaper). Shift-right catches what slips through (necessary). CKS covers both: Domain 5 (Supply Chain) = shift-left, Domain 6 (Runtime Security) = shift-right. You need BOTH for a complete security posture.

Q7
For the anihpj/jobpost Django application, list five security controls at the Container layer (3rd C) that should be applied before deploying to production.
Show Answer
Answer
  1. runAsNonRoot: true with UID 1000
  2. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (Django writes to /tmp only)
  3. allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  4. capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]
  5. seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
Explanation

These 5 settings are the CKS "golden baseline" for any production container. The exam may give you a pod spec and ask "which security settings are missing?" — these 5 are almost always the answer. Combined, they prevent container breakout, privilege escalation, and filesystem tampering.

Q8
You run kube-bench against a cluster and see: "FAIL 1.2.6 Ensure that the --authorization-mode argument is not set to AlwaysAllow". What does this mean, and what file do you edit to fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

This means the kube-apiserver is authorizing ALL requests without checking RBAC. Fix by editing /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml:

spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC  # NOT AlwaysAllow
Explanation

AlwaysAllow is the "hello attacker" setting. Node authorization lets kubelets access only their own pods. RBAC enforces Roles/ClusterRoles. This is the MOST common kube-bench fix on the CKS exam. After editing the manifest, wait 30-60s for the API server pod to auto-restart.

Q9
Explain the difference between prevention, detection, and response in the Kubernetes security lifecycle. Which CKS domains map to each phase?
Show Answer
Answer
PhaseGoalCKS DomainExample Tool
PreventionStop attacks before they happenDomains 1-5RBAC, PSS, OPA, NetworkPolicy
DetectionIdentify attacks in progressDomain 6Falco, audit logs, kube-bench
ResponseContain and remediateDomain 6NetworkPolicy isolation, pod deletion, forensic capture
Explanation

The CKS exam balances all three: you'll harden components (prevention), configure Falco/audit (detection), and perform incident response tasks (response). A common exam task: "A pod was compromised — isolate it, investigate, and remediate."

Q10
What are the six CKS exam domains, their weightings, and one key tool/technology for each? Write this from memory — it's your CKS mental map.
Show Answer
Answer
DomainWeightKey Tool/Concept
1. Cluster Setup10%kube-bench, NetworkPolicy, TLS
2. Cluster Hardening15%RBAC, ServiceAccounts, OPA/Gatekeeper
3. System Hardening15%AppArmor, Seccomp, OS minimization
4. Minimize Microservice Vulns20%PSS, SecurityContext, Secrets encryption

Domains 4-6 are 60% of the exam — prioritize them. Domain 1 (10%) is quick wins. Every chapter in this guide maps to one or more domains. Before exam day, you should be able to recite this table from memory.

Chapter 2: The Threat Landscape — What Attackers Target

To defend Kubernetes, you must understand how it gets attacked. This chapter maps the attack surface, analyzes real-world breaches (Tesla, Capital One, Shopify, SolarWinds), introduces the STRIDE threat model for Kubernetes, and walks through the specific threat scenario for anihpj/jobpost.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~1.5 hours📖 Concepts🎯 Threat Model

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The Kubernetes attack surface — 7 attack vectors every defender must know
  • ✅ Real-world breach analysis: Tesla, Capital One, Shopify, SolarWinds
  • ✅ STRIDE threat model applied to Kubernetes: S,T,R,I,D,E
  • ✅ MITRE ATT&CK tactics mapped to CKS controls
  • ✅ Complete anihpj/jobpost security threat scenario — before and after hardening
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Hardening 15%System Hardening 15%
CKS Exam: Think Like an Attacker

The CKS exam doesn't ask "what is an attack?" — it gives you a compromised scenario and asks you to fix it. Understanding attack paths helps you quickly identify what's broken. When you see "pod can access secrets in other namespaces" — you know it's an RBAC + NetworkPolicy problem. When you see "container escaped to node" — you know it's a SecurityContext + Seccomp + AppArmor problem.

2.1 How Kubernetes Gets Attacked — The Attack Surface

Kubernetes has a large attack surface because it's a complex distributed system. Understanding where attackers strike is the first step to building defenses. Here are the most common attack vectors every CKS specialist must know:

  • 🔴 Exposed API server — the #1 attack vector. Open port 6443 without proper auth is an invitation.
  • 🔴 Misconfigured RBAC — users and pods with too many permissions. Wildcard (*) verbs grant cluster-admin by accident.
  • 🔴 Vulnerable container images — outdated base images with known CVEs. Yesterday's safe image is today's exploit target.
  • 🔴 Secrets in plaintext — environment variables, YAML files committed to Git. One `git clone` and your database password is public.
  • 🔴 Privilege escalation — running containers as root → breaking out of the container to the host node. The default Kubernetes behavior is the most dangerous.
  • 🔴 Lateral movement — one compromised pod can reach other pods, databases, and secrets in other namespaces. The flat network is an attacker's highway.

2.2 Real-World Kubernetes Security Incidents

These are not hypothetical — real companies lost millions due to Kubernetes misconfigurations. Each breach teaches a lesson that maps directly to CKS exam topics.

🚗
Tesla — 2018

Attack: Kubernetes Dashboard exposed publicly, no password.
Path: Internet → Dashboard (admin) → crypto-mining pods → AWS credentials in env vars.
Impact: Compute hijacked for crypto-mining.
CKS Fix: Ch 5 (Dashboard) + Ch 9 (RBAC) + Ch 19 (Secrets)

🏦
Capital One — 2019

Attack: SSRF in WAF → EC2 metadata API → IAM role credentials → S3.
Path: App pod → metadata API → IAM role → 106M customer records.
Impact: $80M fine, largest US financial breach.
CKS Fix: Ch 13 (metadata API) + Ch 16 (IAM restriction)

🛍️
Shopify — 2020

Attack: Rogue employee with pod access → lateral movement.
Path: kubectl exec → lateral movement → merchant data across namespaces.
Impact: 200 merchants' data exposed.
CKS Fix: Ch 6 (NetworkPolicy) + Ch 9 (RBAC) + Ch 28 (Audit)

🔗
SolarWinds — 2020

Attack: Build system compromised → malicious code injected.
Path: CI/CD → poisoned build → signed malware → 18,000 orgs.
Impact: US gov agencies breached via trusted software.
CKS Fix: Ch 25 (static analysis) + Ch 26 (cosign) + Ch 27 (SLSA)

🔍 Tesla Breach 2018 — Step-by-Step Analysis
1
🌐 Attacker Scans

Scans internet for open Kubernetes ports. Finds Tesla's Dashboard with NO password.

2
🎯 Dashboard Found

Dashboard had admin-level ServiceAccount. Full cluster access granted instantly.

3
📦 Deploy Miner

Attacker deploys crypto-mining containers. Compute resources hijacked.

4
🔒 AWS Access

AWS credentials found in cluster environment variables. Cloud data now at risk.

5
💡 Lessons Learned

Never expose Dashboard. Use RBAC. Rotate cloud credentials. Enable audit logging.

✅ CKS Defense Against This Attack
  • Ch 5 (Dashboard): Never expose publicly — use kubectl proxy only
  • Ch 9 (RBAC): Never give admin SA to Dashboard — use read-only scoped SA
  • Ch 19 (Secrets): Never store cloud credentials in env vars — use K8s Secrets + encryption at rest
  • Ch 28 (Audit): Audit logging would have recorded every attacker action for forensic analysis

2.4 The anihpj/jobpost Security Threat Scenario

Let's apply everything to anihpj — a real Django job board running in Kubernetes, serving job listings globally. Here's exactly what attackers would target, what would happen without CKS hardening, and how we stop them.

🎯 What Attackers Want from anihpj

  • 👤 User email addresses from the User model — PII for phishing, selling, or identity theft
  • 🏢 Company data from the JobPost model — competitive intelligence, recruitment sabotage
  • 🗄️ Database credentials (PostgreSQL password) — full database dump, data exfiltration
  • 🔑 Django SECRET_KEY from settings.py — session hijacking, CSRF bypass, signing tampering
  • ☁️ Cloud storage access (media files, resumes, logos) — S3 bucket enumeration, lateral cloud movement

💀 What Happens WITHOUT CKS Knowledge

  • Pod running as root → container escape via kernel exploit becomes possible
  • All secrets in environment variables → readable by anyone with kubectl exec or a compromised container in the namespace
  • No NetworkPolicy → PostgreSQL reachable from ANY pod in ANY namespace — one compromised sidecar = full DB access
  • No image scanning → vulnerable packages (e.g., curl CVE in base image) deployed silently, exploited weeks later
  • No audit logging → attacker exfiltrates data, deletes pods, and leaves ZERO trace — you may never know you were breached

🏰 The Kubernetes Security Castle — Defense-in-Depth for anihpj

Think of your cluster as a medieval castle. Each wall adds another layer an attacker must breach. If one wall fails, the next one still holds.

🌐 INTERNET (the moat) ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ 🧱 WALL 1 — Edge Security (TLS, WAF, Ingress Rules) │ │ "Only HTTPS traffic reaches the castle gate" │ │ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ 🛡️ WALL 2 — API Server Security │ │ │ │ "Every request authenticated + authorized" │ │ │ │ (RBAC, AuthN, Admission Control) │ │ │ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ 🔒 WALL 3 — Network Security │ │ │ │ │ │ "Pods can only talk to approved others" │ │ │ │ │ │ (NetworkPolicy, mTLS, Istio) │ │ │ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ 🧊 WALL 4 — Container Security │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ "Containers run locked down" │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ (non-root, Seccomp, AppArmor, RO-FS, drop ALL) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ 🗄️ WALL 5 — Data Security │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ "Secrets encrypted, DB isolated, user data safe" │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ (etcd encryption, PVC access control) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 🔭 WATCHTOWERS: 🦅 Falco (runtime) + 📋 Audit Logs (API) + 🔍 Trivy (images) "Every wall is watched — any breach is detected instantly"

Here's the full attack lifecycle an adversary would attempt, and exactly which CKS control stops them at each stage:

Q2
Analyze the Tesla Kubernetes breach (2018): What was the attack vector, how did the attackers exploit it, and what CKS controls would have prevented it?
Show Answer
Answer

Attack vector: Credential exposure — Tesla's AWS credentials were exposed in a public-facing Kubernetes dashboard (kube-dashboard). Attackers used these to mine cryptocurrency.

CKS controls that would prevent:

  • Disable the dashboard or protect with strong RBAC + OIDC (Ch 6)
  • Never expose dashboards publicly — use kubectl proxy or port-forward
  • NetworkPolicy to restrict dashboard access to internal IPs only
  • KMS encryption for cloud credentials
Explanation

The Tesla breach is the canonical CKS case study. The exam doesn't test historical breaches, but understanding them gives you the "why" behind every security control. Key lesson: the Kubernetes dashboard is a high-value target — secure or disable it.

Answer
STRIDEK8s ThreatMitigation

TamperingModifying etcd data directlyEncryption at rest, mTLS, audit logging
RepudiationAttacker deletes audit logsExternal log aggregation, immutable logs
Info DisclosureReading Secrets from etcdEncryptionConfiguration with AES-GCM
Denial of ServicePod resource exhaustionLimitRange, ResourceQuota

STRIDE is a systematic way to find security gaps. On the CKS exam, you won't be asked to create a STRIDE model, but thinking in STRIDE terms helps you identify missing controls. Every CKS chapter addresses at least one STRIDE category.

Q4
In the Capital One breach (2019), an SSRF vulnerability allowed access to AWS metadata. How would Kubernetes NetworkPolicy and security contexts prevent SSRF attacks?
Show Answer
Answer
  • Egress NetworkPolicy: Default-deny egress + only whitelist required destinations (PostgreSQL:5432, DNS:53). Pod cannot reach 169.254.169.254 (metadata service)
  • SecurityContext: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true prevents attacker from installing tools after initial compromise
  • Non-root user: Even if SSRF works, limited damage without root access
  • drop ALL capabilities: Attackers can't use NET_RAW to craft packets
Explanation

SSRF is one of the most common cloud-native attacks. NetworkPolicy egress rules are your best defense — if the pod can't reach the metadata service, SSRF is useless. This is why CKS emphasizes egress NetworkPolicy (not just ingress).

Q5
Map the MITRE ATT&CK tactics "Initial Access", "Execution", "Persistence", and "Privilege Escalation" to Kubernetes-specific techniques and CKS countermeasures.
Show Answer
Answer
MITRE TacticK8s TechniqueCKS Countermeasure
Initial AccessExposed dashboard, leaked kubeconfigRBAC, OIDC, disable dashboard
Executionkubectl exec into pod, deploy malicious podRBAC (no exec permission), PSS Restricted
PersistenceCreate backdoor Deployment, cronJobAdmission control (OPA/Kyverno), audit logging
Privilege EscalationContainer breakout, cluster-admin bindingnon-root, seccomp, AppArmor, RBAC review
Explanation

MITRE ATT&CK maps real attacker behavior to defensive controls. The CKS exam aligns with this framework: you detect "Execution" via Falco rules, prevent "Privilege Escalation" via SecurityContext, and block "Initial Access" via RBAC and admission control.

Q6
The anihpj/jobpost Django app uses PostgreSQL. Model a potential attack where an attacker compromises the Django pod. What could they access, and how does CKS hardening contain the damage?
Show Answer
Answer

Without hardening: Attacker gets root shell → reads SECRET_KEY from env → accesses DB → scrapes all data → deploys crypto miner → lateral movement to other pods.

With CKS hardening:

  • Non-root user (UID 1000) → can't install packages or modify system files
  • readOnlyRootFilesystem → can't write malware to disk
  • Seccomp RuntimeDefault → blocks dangerous syscalls (ptrace, mount)
  • NetworkPolicy egress → only PostgreSQL:5432 allowed, can't phone home
  • Falco → detects shell spawn, alerts security team in <1 second
Explanation

This is the "blast radius" concept: even if one pod is compromised, layered hardening limits damage. The attacker gets a shell but can't escalate, can't move laterally, and gets detected immediately. That's defense in depth working.

Q7
What is a "supply chain attack" in Kubernetes? Describe the SolarWinds-style scenario and how image signing + verification prevents it.
Show Answer
Answer

A supply chain attack injects malicious code into a trusted image or dependency before it reaches your cluster. Example: Attacker compromises the nginx Docker Hub account and pushes a backdoored image.

Prevention chain:

  1. Sign images at build time: cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.com/anihpj:v1
  2. Verify at admission: Kyverno policy checks cosign signature before allowing deployment
  3. Scan for CVEs: Trivy scans every image in CI/CD; CRITICAL CVEs block the pipeline
Explanation

CKS Domain 5 (Supply Chain Security, 20%) is entirely about preventing these attacks. The exam tests your ability to configure image scanning (Trivy), signing (cosign), and admission verification (Kyverno/OPA). These three tools form the complete supply chain defense.

Q8
A security scan reveals a pod with hostPID: true and privileged: true. What specific attacks are possible with each, and what CKS controls block them?
Show Answer
Answer
SettingAttack PossibleCKS Block
hostPID: trueSee ALL processes on node (including other pods' processes). Kill any process. Inject code via /proc.Never set hostPID (PSS Restricted forbids it)
privileged: trueFull root on node. Access all devices. Load kernel modules. Escape container trivially.PSS Restricted, OPA/Kyverno deny privileged
Explanation

hostPID + privileged = game over for node security. These are the two most dangerous pod settings. CKS exam: you'll be asked to find pods with these and fix them. Use kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.hostPID==true)'.

Q9
Write the command to find all pods in all namespaces that are running as root (UID 0). Then write the fix to apply via a Kyverno ClusterPolicy.
Show Answer
Answer
# Find root pods
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsUser==0 or .spec.containers[].securityContext==null) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name}'

# Or simpler:
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsUser==0) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'
Explanation

First, identify the problem (audit). Then fix it via policy (prevention). This two-step pattern — audit then enforce — is the CKS workflow for every security control. Start with warn mode in Kyverno, check logs, then switch to Enforce.

3.1 How CKS Security Maps to Kubernetes Components

Every Kubernetes component has specific security controls. Understanding which control applies to which component is essential for both the exam and real-world security. Here's the component-to-security mapping:

  • 🌐 API Server — central enforcement point for ALL access control. Authentication, authorization, and admission happen here.
  • 🗄️ etcd — stores ALL cluster state including Secrets. Must be encrypted at rest and access-restricted (only API server should reach it).
  • ⚙️ kubelet — runs pods on each node. Must have anonymous auth disabled, webhook authorization enabled, and API restricted.
  • 📦 Container Runtime — executes containers (containerd/CRI-O). Seccomp profiles and AppArmor policies are applied at this layer.
  • 🌐 kube-proxy / CNI — networking layer. NetworkPolicies are ENFORCED here — if the CNI plugin doesn't support them, your policies are ignored.
🔐 Kubernetes Security Architecture — Components + Controls

3.2 Authentication vs Authorization vs Admission Control

Every request to the Kubernetes API goes through three security gates — and they run in a specific order. Understanding what each gate does and what happens when it fails is critical for the CKS exam:

🔑
Authentication

"Who are you?"
Methods: certificates, tokens, OIDC. Fails → 401 Unauthorized.

🛡️
Authorization

"What can you do?"
RBAC, ABAC, Webhook. Fails → 403 Forbidden.

📋
Admission Control

"Is this request allowed?"
Policy enforcement. Fails → 403 with reason.

⚠️ All 3 must be configured correctly for a secure cluster — one weak gate compromises everything.

🔐 The Kubernetes Request Pipeline — 4 Stages

kubectl apply -f anihpj-pod.yaml

🔑1. AUTHENTICATION"Who are you?"❌ 401 if fails
→
🛡️2. AUTHORIZATION"What can you do?"❌ 403 if fails
→
📋3. ADMISSION"Is this allowed?"❌ 403 if rejected
→
🗄️4. STOREDin etcd → Scheduled✅ Persisted
🔑
AuthN: "Who Are You?"

Methods: Client certificates (x509), Bearer tokens (ServiceAccount JWT), OIDC (external IdP like GitHub/Google), Webhook tokens, Bootstrap tokens.
Exam tip: Know that --anonymous-auth=false blocks unauthenticated access entirely.

🛡️
AuthZ: "What Can You Do?"

Modes: RBAC (Role + RoleBinding), Node (kubelet access), Webhook (external service), ABAC (legacy, file-based).
Exam tip: Always use Node,RBAC mode. Never use AlwaysAllow — it disables ALL authorization.

📖 Admission Control — The Final Gate

Admission controllers run AFTER authN and authZ. They can mutate (modify the request, like adding default SecurityContext) or validate (allow/deny, like checking if the image is from an approved registry). Key admission plugins for CKS: NodeRestriction, PodSecurity, LimitRanger, ResourceQuota, MutatingAdmissionWebhook, ValidatingAdmissionWebhook, ImagePolicyWebhook.

3.3 Your Security Toolkit — Tools You Will Use Throughout This Guide

These are the tools you'll master for the CKS exam. Each has a specific purpose — knowing which tool to reach for is half the battle:

  • kubectl — your primary interface: inspect, patch, apply security resources. Every CKS exam task starts here.
  • kube-bench — checks your cluster against CIS benchmarks. Tells you exactly what's failing and how to fix it.
  • Trivy — scans container images for CVEs, misconfigurations, and embedded secrets. Use in CI/CD and at runtime.
  • Falco — detects runtime anomalies in real-time via kernel module or eBPF. Alerts on shells, file reads, network anomalies.
  • OPA / Gatekeeper — policy-as-code for admission control. Block non-compliant resources before they hit the cluster.
  • cosign — signs and verifies container images. Proves an image came from YOUR pipeline, not an attacker's.
  • AppArmor / Seccomp — OS-level container sandboxing. AppArmor restricts file/network access; Seccomp filters dangerous syscalls.
📏
kube-bench

CIS benchmark checker. Runs checks against API server, etcd, kubelet, and policies. Tells you what's failing and how to fix it.

🔍
Trivy

Image CVE scanner. Scans containers for known vulnerabilities. Integrates with CI/CD. Fails builds on CRITICAL CVEs.

🦅
Falco

Runtime threat detection. Monitors syscalls via kernel module or eBPF. Alerts on shells, file reads, network anomalies in real-time.

📋
OPA / Kyverno

Policy-as-code for admission control. Block non-compliant resources before they reach the cluster. OPA uses Rego, Kyverno uses YAML.

🔏
cosign

Image signing and verification. Proves an image was built by your CI pipeline. Kyverno can enforce signature verification at admission time.

🛡️
AppArmor

Application sandboxing. Restricts what files, networks, and capabilities a container can access at the OS level.

🚫
Seccomp

Syscall filtering. Blocks dangerous Linux system calls at the kernel level. RuntimeDefault blocks 240+ unnecessary syscalls out of 300+.

🔑
Vault

External secret management. Dynamic secrets, automatic rotation, audit trail. Integrates with K8s via Vault Agent sidecar or ESO.

Answer
StageWhat HappensCKS Configuration
1. Authentication (AuthN)"Who are you?" — validates identity via cert, token, or OIDC--anonymous-auth=false, --client-ca-file
2. Authorization (AuthZ)"What can you do?" — RBAC, Node, ABAC, Webhook--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
3. Admission Control"Should this be allowed?" — mutating/validating webhooks, PSSOPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno, PSS labels
4. etcd WriteState persisted — encryption applied if configuredEncryptionConfiguration with AES-GCM
Explanation

This pipeline is the backbone of CKS. Every security task maps to one stage: disable anonymous auth = AuthN, fix RBAC = AuthZ, add OPA policy = Admission, enable encryption = etcd. On the exam, when asked "how do you prevent X?", trace it through this pipeline.

These 8 tools cover 90% of CKS exam tasks. Know what each does, how to run it, and which domain it maps to. The exam provides man pages, but knowing the command structure saves precious minutes.

On the CKS exam: ServiceAccounts = pods, certificates = components/admin, OIDC = enterprise users. Most exam tasks involve ServiceAccount tokens — know that each pod gets a token auto-mounted unless automountServiceAccountToken: false.

Q5
Explain RBAC in Kubernetes: what is a Role vs ClusterRole? What is a RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding? When do you use each?

Answer
ResourceScopeUse When...

ClusterRoleCluster-widePermissions across all namespaces OR cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs)
RoleBindingNamespace-scopedBind a Role OR ClusterRole within a namespace

CKS trick: You can bind a ClusterRole with a RoleBinding — this limits the ClusterRole's scope to that namespace. This is a common exam pattern: "give a service account cluster-wide read access to pods BUT only in namespace X." Use ClusterRole + RoleBinding.

Q6
In the AuthN → AuthZ → Admission pipeline, at which stage does OPA Gatekeeper operate? What about a NetworkPolicy? What about kubectl auth can-i?
Show Answer
Answer
ControlPipeline StageExplanation
OPA/GatekeeperAdmission ControlValidatingWebhook — intercepts requests BEFORE they're persisted
NetworkPolicyRuntime (post-admission)Enforced by CNI plugin at network layer, not at API level
kubectl auth can-iAuthorization (AuthZ)Checks RBAC permissions — "can this subject perform this action?"
RBACAuthorization (AuthZ)Determines if authenticated identity has permission

Explanation

Understanding which stage each control operates at is critical for CKS troubleshooting. If a pod is rejected, is it AuthN (wrong cert), AuthZ (insufficient RBAC), or Admission (policy violation)? The error message tells you: "Forbidden" = AuthZ, "denied by policy" = Admission.

Q7
You run kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx and get "Error from server (Forbidden)". What pipeline stage is blocking this? Write the command to diagnose further.
Show Answer
Answer

The error "Forbidden" indicates the Authorization (AuthZ) stage is blocking — you authenticated successfully but lack RBAC permissions.

# Diagnose: what CAN you do?
kubectl auth can-i create deployments
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:default:default

# Check your identity
kubectl auth whoami

# List your RBAC bindings
kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A | grep $(kubectl config current-context)
Explanation

Error message decoding: "Forbidden" = AuthZ failure (RBAC). "Unauthorized" = AuthN failure (bad cert/token). "denied by admission webhook" = Admission failure. This is a critical CKS skill — diagnosing which stage failed tells you exactly which config file to edit.

Q8
What is the difference between a mutating admission webhook and a validating admission webhook? Give a CKS example of each.
Show Answer
Answer
TypeWhat It DoesCKS Example
MutatingMODIFIES the request before persistence. Can add defaults, inject sidecars, set fields.Kyverno mutating rule: auto-add runAsNonRoot: true if not specified
ValidatingACCEPTS or REJECTS the request. Cannot modify. Enforces policies.OPA Gatekeeper: deny pods using :latest tag

Order: Mutating runs FIRST, then Validating. This means mutating webhooks can fix issues before validating sees them.

Explanation

CKS exam focus: Validating webhooks (deny bad requests). Mutating webhooks are powerful but dangerous — a broken mutating webhook can break ALL deployments. Always test admission policies in warn mode before Enforce.
