Chapter 4: CIS Benchmarks & kube-bench — Measuring Your Security Baseline

Every CKS exam hardening task traces back to a CIS Benchmark check. This chapter teaches you to run kube-bench audits, interpret FAIL/WARN/PASS outputs, fix API server and kubelet misconfigurations, and verify your fixes — the exact workflow you'll repeat on exam day and in production.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~2 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 CIS Benchmarks

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What CIS Benchmarks are and why they're the foundation of CKS hardening
  • ✅ How to run kube-bench against control plane and worker nodes
  • ✅ How to interpret kube-bench output: PASS, FAIL, WARN
  • ✅ How to fix the top 5 most common CIS failures on the API server
  • ✅ How to harden the kubelet configuration for node-level security
  • ✅ Hands-on CIS fix workflow: audit → fix → verify for anihpj cluster
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Setup 10%Cluster Hardening 15%
CKS Exam: kube-bench Is Your Diagnostic Tool

On the CKS exam, you'll be given a cluster with security issues. Run kube-bench first — it tells you exactly what's broken. Every FAIL item maps to a specific flag you need to add/remove from a manifest file. The exam isn't testing your memorization of CIS checks — it's testing your ability to read kube-bench output and apply fixes. Know these file paths cold: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.

4.1 What Are CIS Benchmarks?

The Center for Internet Security (CIS) publishes the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark — a comprehensive list of over 200 security configuration checks covering every Kubernetes component. It's the industry standard for answering one question: "How secure is my cluster?"

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark — 5 Check Areas

🧠Control PlaneAPI + Scheduler + CM
🔐API Server flagsAuthN, AuthZ, TLS, Admission
📋Controller/SchedulerProfiling, binding, ports
🗄️etcdCluster Brain
🔒TLS configurationPeer + client certs
📁File permissionsData dir, cert files
⚙️Worker Nodeskubelet
🚫Anonymous authMust be disabled
🔌Read-only portMust be 0
📦PoliciesK8s Resources
🌐NetworkPolicyZero-trust networking
🔑RBAC + SecretsLeast privilege access
🛡️Pod SecurityPSS, SecurityContext
📖 Why CIS Benchmarks Matter for CKS

The CKS exam doesn't ask you to memorize CIS check numbers. But every hardening task — securing the API server, locking down the kubelet, enabling audit logging — corresponds directly to a CIS check. When kube-bench reports [FAIL] 1.2.6, you know: the --authorization-mode flag needs RBAC. This chapter builds that mental mapping.

How CIS Scoring Works — PASS, FAIL, WARN Explained

ResultWhat It MeansExampleYour Action
PASSYour cluster already meets this security standard[PASS] 1.2.1 --anonymous-auth=false is setNothing — move to next check
FAILYour cluster does NOT meet this standard — vulnerability exists[FAIL] 1.2.6 --authorization-mode does not include RBACFix immediately: edit manifest, add flag, restart
WARNCheck may or may not apply to your setup[WARN] 1.2.32 --service-account-lookup=true not setEvaluate: is this relevant to my cluster? If yes, fix. If no, document why.
INFOInformational — not scored[INFO] 1.2 — API Server checks startingRead for context, no action needed
💡 CKS Exam Strategy: Prioritize FAILs

On the exam, fix all FAIL items first — these are guaranteed vulnerabilities. WARN items are lower priority. If you're running out of time, focus on FAILs. A FAIL on --anonymous-auth=false is more critical than a WARN on --service-account-lookup. Use kube-bench's output to prioritize your exam time efficiently.

4.2 Running kube-bench — Your Security Audit Tool

kube-bench automates CIS Benchmark checks. You run it against control plane nodes and worker nodes separately. The output tells you exactly what to fix — with remediation advice for every FAIL.

Installation & Basic Usage

Terminal: Install & Run kube-bench
# Install kube-bench (one command)
curl -L https://github.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/releases/download/v0.9.0/kube-bench_0.9.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz | tar xz
sudo mv kube-bench /usr/local/bin/

# Run all checks on master node
kube-bench run --targets=master

# Run all checks on worker node
kube-bench run --targets=node

# Run a specific CIS check (1.2 = API Server section)
kube-bench run --check 1.2

# Run a single specific check
kube-bench run --check 1.2.6

# Output in JSON (for pipelines)
kube-bench run --json --targets=master
🔴 Reading kube-bench Output — What Failed
kube-bench --check 1.2 output
[INFO] 1 Master Node Security Configuration
[INFO] 1.2 API Server
[PASS] 1.2.1 Ensure --anonymous-auth=false
[FAIL] 1.2.2 Ensure --token-auth-file is not set
[WARN] 1.2.6 Ensure --authorization-mode includes RBAC
[PASS] 1.2.9 Ensure --enable-admission-plugins
              includes NodeRestriction

== Remediations master ==
1.2.2 Edit the API server pod specification file
      /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
      Remove --token-auth-file parameter
✅ How to Interpret Each Result
ResultMeaningYour Action
PASSConfiguration is already secureNothing — move to next check
FAILConfiguration is insecure — must fixRead remediation, edit manifest, restart
WARNCheck if applicable — may be optionalAssess: is this relevant to my cluster?
Exam Speed Tip

On the CKS exam, run kube-bench run --targets=master FIRST THING after your terminal setup. It diagnoses the cluster in under 30 seconds and gives you a prioritized fix list. Every FAIL is a potential exam task waiting for you to solve it.

Why kube-bench Is Your First Command on Exam Day

Think of kube-bench as your diagnostic tool — like a doctor running blood tests before prescribing medication. The CKS exam gives you a cluster with security problems, but it doesn't tell you what those problems are. kube-bench tells you exactly:

  • What's broken: Each [FAIL] line maps to a specific security control that's misconfigured
  • Where to fix it: The remediation section tells you which file to edit (kube-apiserver.yaml, config.yaml, etc.)
  • How to verify: After fixing, re-run kube-bench on that specific check to confirm [PASS]
  • Priority order: Fix the FAIL items first, then address WARN items if they apply to your cluster
📖 Understanding kube-bench Exit Codes

Exit code 0 = all checks PASS (rare on an unhardened cluster). Exit code 1 = one or more FAIL items (this is expected — it shows you what to fix). Exit code >1 = kube-bench itself encountered an error (check your command syntax). On the CKS exam, you'll see exit code 1 — that's normal and expected.

4.3 Fixing Common CIS Failures — The API Server Manifest

The API server is configured via a static pod manifest at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Changes take effect immediately — the kubelet detects the file change and restarts the API server pod. Most CKS fixes involve adding or removing flags from this manifest.

The Hardened API Server Manifest

/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml — Hardened Configuration
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: kube-apiserver
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --anonymous-auth=false                    # CIS 1.2.1
    - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC            # CIS 1.2.6 (NEVER AlwaysAllow!)
    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity # CIS 1.2.9
    - --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml  # CIS 1.2.22
    - --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log         # CIS 1.2.14
    - --audit-log-maxage=30
    - --audit-log-maxbackup=10
    - --audit-log-maxsize=100
    - --tls-cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt      # CIS 1.2.20
    - --tls-private-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.key
    - --client-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
    - --etcd-certfile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.crt
    - --etcd-keyfile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.key
    - --service-account-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/sa.pub
    - --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
    image: registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.31.0
CIS CheckFlagSecure ValueWhy It Matters
1.2.1--anonymous-authfalseAnonymous users can't access ANY API — blocks the most common recon attack
1.2.6--authorization-modeNode,RBACNEVER AlwaysAllow — that disables ALL authorization checks!
1.2.7--admission-control-config-fileSet to audit policy pathConfigures admission plugin behavior
1.2.9--enable-admission-pluginsMust include NodeRestrictionLimits what kubelets can modify — prevents node-based attacks
1.2.14--audit-log-path/var/log/kubernetes/audit.logCreates forensic record of ALL API activity
1.2.20--tls-cert-file + keyValid certificate pathsEncrypts all API server communication
1.2.22--audit-policy-filePath to audit policy YAMLDefines WHAT gets audited — not just IF

Why Each Flag Matters — The Attack It Prevents

  • --anonymous-auth=false: Without this, anyone who can reach port 6443 can make API calls as system:anonymous. Even with no RBAC permissions, they can discover what's running — the first step in any targeted attack.
  • --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC: If set to AlwaysAllow, any authenticated user can do anything — delete all pods, read all secrets, create backdoor accounts. AlwaysAllow disables ALL authorization checks.
  • --enable-admission-plugins=...,NodeRestriction: Without NodeRestriction, a compromised kubelet on one worker node can modify labels on other nodes, evict their pods, and impersonate other nodes — cluster-wide attack from a single worker.
  • --audit-log-path + --audit-policy-file: Without these, there's no record of who did what. When a security incident occurs, you have no forensic evidence — no way to determine what the attacker accessed, when, or how.
  • --tls-cert-file + --tls-private-key-file: Without valid TLS certificates, all traffic to the API server is unencrypted — credentials, secrets, and pod data travel in plaintext across the network.

4.4 kubelet Hardening — CIS Node Checks

The kubelet runs on every node and manages pod lifecycle. An insecure kubelet means an attacker can control pods on that node. Configuration lives at /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.

Before vs After — kubelet Configuration

🔴 INSECURE KUBELET
/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml — BROKEN
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: true          # 🔴 ANYONE can query kubelet!
  webhook:
    enabled: false         # 🔴 No API server auth check!
authorization:
  mode: AlwaysAllow        # 🔴 ALL requests authorized!
readOnlyPort: 10255        # 🔴 Unauthenticated read access!
✅ HARDENED KUBELET
/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml — SECURE
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false         # ✅ No unauthenticated access
  webhook:
    enabled: true          # ✅ API server validates tokens
authorization:
  mode: Webhook            # ✅ API server checks RBAC
readOnlyPort: 0            # ✅ Read-only port DISABLED
protectKernelDefaults: true # ✅ Kernel tuning protected
💡 After Editing kubelet Config

Edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, then restart: sudo systemctl restart kubelet. Verify with sudo systemctl status kubelet. Re-run kube-bench run --targets=node to confirm fixes.

4.5 Applying CIS Benchmark Fixes — Hands-On with anihpj

Scenario: your anihpj cluster fails 12 CIS checks. You'll walk through the 5 most impactful fixes using the kube-bench workflow.

CIS FIX WORKFLOW — The Cycle You Repeat for Every FAIL
1
RUN kube-bench

kube-bench run --targets=master,node
Produces: PASS ✅ FAIL ❌ WARN ⚠️

2
READ the FAIL

Read remediation advice
"Edit kube-apiserver.yaml, remove --token-auth-file"

3
LOCATE the file

vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
(or /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml)

4
APPLY the fix

Add/remove the flag
Static pods: auto-restart on save
kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet

5
VERIFY the fix

kube-bench run --check 1.2.2
→ Should now show [PASS] ✅

#FixImpactFile to EditVerify
1--anonymous-auth=false on API serverPrevents unauthenticated API access/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yamlkube-bench --check 1.2.1
2Enable audit loggingCreates forensic record of all API activitykube-apiserver.yaml + create audit-policy.yamlkube-bench --check 1.2.22
3Disable kubelet read-only portPrevents unauthenticated kubelet data reads/var/lib/kubelet/config.yamlkube-bench --targets=node
4Enable NodeRestriction admission pluginLimits what compromised kubelets can dokube-apiserver.yaml --enable-admission-plugins=...kube-bench --check 1.2.9
5Enable encryption at rest for SecretsSecrets unreadable even if etcd is accessedCreate EncryptionConfiguration + add API server flagkube-bench --check 1.3.6

📝 Chapter 4 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
You run kube-bench run --targets=master and see FAIL for check 1.2.6. What specific flag needs to be modified, in which file, and what should the new value be?
Show Answer
Answer

Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Find the --authorization-mode flag and set it to:

- --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC

Remove AlwaysAllow if present. Wait 30-60s for the API server pod to restart, then re-run kube-bench to verify PASS.

Explanation

CIS check 1.2.6 is the most commonly failed check on the CKS exam. AlwaysAllow means NO authorization at all — every request is accepted. Node authorization is essential for kubelet access. RBAC enforces your Roles and ClusterRoles. Always include BOTH: Node,RBAC.

Q2
kube-bench reports FAIL for check 4.2.6 about kubelet --read-only-port. What is the read-only port, why is it dangerous, and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

The read-only port (default 10255) exposes kubelet metrics and pod information WITHOUT authentication. Fix in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml:

readOnlyPort: 0

Then restart kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet. Verify: ss -tlnp | grep 10255 should return nothing.

Explanation

The read-only port was deprecated in Kubernetes 1.10 and finally removed in 1.27. Setting it to 0 disables it completely. An attacker who can reach port 10255 can enumerate all pods on that node without any authentication — a serious information disclosure risk.

Q3
After fixing all kube-bench FAIL items on the API server, how do you verify the fixes took effect? Write the verification commands.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Re-run kube-bench
kube-bench run --targets=master --check 1.2.6
# Should show PASS

# 2. Verify the API server pod restarted with new flags
kubectl get pod -n kube-system kube-apiserver-<node> -o yaml | grep authorization-mode

# 3. Test that unauthorized requests are denied
kubectl get pods --as=system:anonymous
# Expected: Error from server (Forbidden)

# 4. Verify RBAC still works
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:default
# Expected: yes or no (RBAC is working)
Explanation

The CKS exam requires verification after every change. Always: (1) re-run kube-bench, (2) check the pod manifest, (3) test with an actual request. A common pitfall: the API server pod says "Running" but is using old flags because the YAML has a syntax error. Check pod age with kubectl get pod -n kube-system kube-apiserver-* --show-labels.

Q4
What is the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark? Who publishes it, how often is it updated, and what do PASS/FAIL/WARN mean in kube-bench output?
Show Answer
Answer
ResultMeaningAction Required
PASSConfiguration matches the CIS recommendationNone — compliant
FAILConfiguration does NOT match CIS recommendationFIX IMMEDIATELY — this is a security gap
WARNkube-bench couldn't definitively determine statusManual review required — check the component

The CIS Benchmark is published by the Center for Internet Security (CIS), updated with each Kubernetes minor release. kube-bench is an Aqua Security open-source tool that automates CIS checking.

Explanation

On the CKS exam: focus on FAIL items first — they're explicit security gaps. WARN items may or may not be issues; use judgment. Don't waste time on PASS items unless asked to verify a specific setting.

Q5
kube-bench check 1.1.1 tests that the API server manifest has proper file permissions (644 or more restrictive). Write the commands to check and fix this.
Show Answer
Answer
# Check current permissions
stat -c "%a %n" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Fix if too permissive (e.g., 777)
chmod 644 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Verify
stat -c "%a %n" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Expected output: 644 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Also check ownership
ls -la /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# Should be owned by root:root
Explanation

File permissions are an often-overlooked CKS exam task. If the manifest files are world-writable (777), any process on the node can modify them — leading to API server compromise on next restart. 644 = owner read/write, group read, others read. Check ALL manifests: find /etc/kubernetes/manifests -type f -perm /o+w.

Q6
Write the command to run kube-bench against a worker node. What's the difference between --targets=master and --targets=node?
Show Answer
Answer
# Worker node check
kube-bench run --targets=node

# Master node check (control plane)
kube-bench run --targets=master

# Check everything
kube-bench run --targets=master,node

Difference: --targets=master checks control plane components (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager). --targets=node checks kubelet configuration, container runtime, and kube-proxy.

Explanation

On the CKS exam, you'll likely be given access to a control plane node. Run --targets=master first. The node target checks are relevant if you also have worker node access. Know which CIS sections apply to which target: Sections 1-3 = master, Section 4 = node.

Q7
CIS check 1.2.10 requires that --enable-admission-plugins includes NodeRestriction. What does NodeRestriction do, and how do you add it?
Show Answer
Answer

NodeRestriction limits kubelets to ONLY modify their own Node object and ONLY their own pods. Without it, a compromised kubelet could modify any node or pod in the cluster.

# In /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
- --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,AlwaysPullImages,...
Explanation

NodeRestriction is a critical defense against kubelet compromise. Even with Node authorization, without NodeRestriction, a kubelet could label its node to attract pods from other namespaces. CKS exam tip: NodeRestriction should ALWAYS be in the admission plugins list alongside Node authorization mode.

Q8
CIS check 4.2.1 requires kubelet --anonymous-auth=false. Where is this configured, and how do you verify anonymous requests are actually blocked?
Show Answer
Answer
# Configure in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false
  webhook:
    enabled: true

# Restart kubelet
systemctl restart kubelet

# Verify: anonymous request should FAIL
curl -k https://localhost:10250/pods
# Expected: Unauthorized

# Authorized request should work
curl -k https://localhost:10250/pods --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"
Explanation

Kubelet anonymous auth is separate from API server anonymous auth — you must disable BOTH. The kubelet's anonymous mode allows unauthenticated access to pod specs, container logs, and exec. This is a CRITICAL finding — fix it immediately on all nodes.

Q9
After fixing 5 CIS failures, you re-run kube-bench and still see FAIL for check 1.2.8. The API server pod is Running. What might be wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

Possible causes:

  1. YAML syntax error: The API server is running but using OLD flags. Check: kubectl get pod -n kube-system kube-apiserver-* -o yaml | grep <flag-name>
  2. Wrong file path: Edited the wrong manifest file. Double-check /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  3. Flag duplicate: The flag appears twice in the command list. The last occurrence wins. Search: grep -c 'flag-name' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  4. Indentation error: YAML is whitespace-sensitive. Ensure flag is at correct indentation level under command:
Explanation

This is THE most common CKS exam pitfall. When the API server manifest has a YAML error, kubelet silently ignores it and keeps the old pod running. Always check docker ps or crictl ps to see which API server container is actually running. Check pod age — if it didn't restart, your changes didn't take effect.

Q10
Write a complete CIS hardening workflow for a new cluster: from initial kube-bench run to final verification. Include all commands.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. AUDIT — Run baseline scan
kube-bench run --targets=master > /tmp/kube-bench-report.txt

# 2. IDENTIFY — Filter for FAIL items only
grep FAIL /tmp/kube-bench-report.txt

# 3. FIX — For each FAIL, edit the corresponding manifest
# API server: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Kubelet: /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# etcd: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml

# 4. VERIFY — Wait for restart, then re-scan
sleep 30
kube-bench run --targets=master --check <check-number>
# Each should now show PASS

# 5. DOCUMENT — Save final report
kube-bench run --targets=master > /tmp/kube-bench-final.txt
Explanation

This Audit→Identify→Fix→Verify→Document workflow is the CKS exam pattern for all hardening tasks. Practice it until it's muscle memory. Time management: allocate 5 minutes per CIS fix on the exam. Don't spend 15 minutes on one check — move on and come back.

Chapter 5: Securing the Kubernetes Dashboard & Web UIs

The Tesla breach started with an exposed Kubernetes Dashboard. A web UI that gives visual access to pods, secrets, and exec shells must never face the public internet. This chapter teaches you to deploy Dashboard securely, restrict access, and remove unnecessary components — exactly what the CKS exam tests.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~1 hour🔧 Hands-On🎯 Dashboard Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why an exposed Dashboard is a CRITICAL security risk (Tesla case study)
  • ✅ How to deploy Dashboard with read-only RBAC and token authentication
  • ✅ The secure access workflow: kubectl proxy instead of LoadBalancer/NodePort
  • ✅ How to audit your cluster for unnecessary exposed components
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Setup 10%

5.1 Why the Dashboard Is Dangerous

The Kubernetes Dashboard provides a graphical interface to your entire cluster — pods, deployments, secrets, config maps, and even a web-based exec terminal. If exposed without authentication, anyone who finds it owns your cluster.

How Dashboard Is ExposedRisk LevelWhat Attacker Can Do
Public Internet, no auth (LoadBalancer / NodePort)🔴 CRITICALFull cluster access — create pods, read secrets, exec shells. Same as Tesla breach.
Public Internet, with token (no extra network controls)🟠 HIGHIf token is stolen or brute-forced: full access. Token in URL = logged in browser history.
Internal only, with RBAC (read-only SA, no public exposure)🟡 MEDIUMLimited if RBAC is correctly scoped. Still a target if network perimeter is breached.
kubectl proxy only (local) + strong RBAC + no public exposure🟢 LOWOnly the person running proxy can access. Traffic goes through API server authN/authZ.
🚗 Tesla Breach (2018) — The Dashboard Lesson
  • 🔴 Kubernetes Dashboard exposed publicly on the internet with NO password
  • 🔴 Dashboard had admin-level ServiceAccount — full cluster access
  • 🔴 Attackers created crypto-mining pods, found AWS credentials in environment variables
  • 🔴 Compute hijacked for cryptocurrency mining; cloud credentials at risk of exfiltration
  • ✅ Lesson: Never expose Dashboard publicly. Always use kubectl proxy + scoped RBAC.
📖 Why This Breach Changed Kubernetes Security Forever

The Tesla incident was a watershed moment for Kubernetes security. Before this, many operators assumed "it's just a dashboard — what's the worst that could happen?" After Tesla, the industry realized: a dashboard with admin access is identical to giving attackers a kubectl terminal with cluster-admin privileges. The CNCF responded by creating the CKS certification later that same year (2019), and CIS Benchmark checks for Dashboard security became mandatory. Every CKS exam question about Dashboard security traces back to lessons learned from this single breach.

5.2 Deploying Dashboard Securely

The secure deployment pattern: Dashboard gets a ClusterIP service only, access is through kubectl proxy (which enforces API server authentication), and a scoped ServiceAccount limits what the Dashboard user can see and do.

🔴 INSECURE — Never Do This
❌ Exposing Dashboard publicly
# NEVER do this!
kubectl expose deploy kubernetes-dashboard \
  --type=LoadBalancer --port=443 -n kubernetes-dashboard
# → Dashboard now has a PUBLIC IP — anyone can reach it!
✅ SECURE — The Right Way
✅ kubectl proxy workflow
# Step 1: Dashboard has ClusterIP only (internal)
# Step 2: Start proxy (runs locally)
kubectl proxy --port=8443

# Step 3: Access at localhost only
open https://localhost:8443/api/v1/namespaces/\
kubernetes-dashboard/services/https:\
kubernetes-dashboard:/proxy/

# Step 4: Login with scoped SA token (NOT admin!)
kubectl -n kubernetes-dashboard create token \
  dashboard-readonly-user
💡 The kubectl proxy Advantage

kubectl proxy handles all authentication and authorization through the API server. The Dashboard inherits whatever RBAC permissions the token you provide has. Use a read-only ServiceAccount for Dashboard — never the default admin token. This way, even if someone accesses Dashboard, they can't modify anything.

Why kubectl proxy Is Secure — The Complete Flow

1
kubectl proxy starts

Opens localhost:8443. Uses YOUR kubeconfig credentials. No network exposure.

2
Browser → localhost

You open https://localhost:8443. Traffic never leaves your machine.

3
Proxy → API Server

kubectl proxy forwards to API server with YOUR credentials. API server authenticates and authorizes normally.

4
Dashboard renders

Dashboard shows only what YOUR RBAC permissions allow. No extra network ports opened.

⚠️ Common Dashboard Security Mistakes
  • Mistake 1: Using kubectl expose --type=LoadBalancer — this creates a public IP for Dashboard. Anyone on the internet can try to access it.
  • Mistake 2: Using the admin kubernetes-dashboard ServiceAccount token — this SA often has cluster-admin. Use a dedicated read-only SA instead.
  • Mistake 3: Skipping RBAC — Dashboard without RBAC shows everything to everyone. Always configure RBAC before deploying.
  • Mistake 4: Leaving the skip-login flag enabled — --enable-skip-login allows access without any token at all. Never use in production.

5.3 Removing Unnecessary Components

CIS Benchmarks emphasize removing unused components to reduce attack surface. Before deploying to production, audit your cluster for unnecessary exposure.

📋 Pre-Production Cluster Component Audit Checklist
  • □ Is Kubernetes Dashboard installed? → If yes, is it only accessible via port-forward?
  • □ Are there any services of type LoadBalancer that shouldn't be publicly exposed?
  • □ Are there any services of type NodePort exposing internal apps?
  • □ Is --insecure-port=0 set on the API server? (REMOVED in 1.20+)
  • □ Is the kubelet read-only port (10255) disabled? readOnlyPort: 0
  • □ Are any pods using hostNetwork: true unnecessarily?
  • □ Are any pods using hostPID: true unnecessarily?
  • □ Are any pods using privileged: true unnecessarily?
  • □ Is there a wildcard (*) RBAC binding anywhere? kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -A5 '*'
  • □ Are there any Services with externalIPs set?

📝 Chapter 5 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What was the Tesla Kubernetes breach (2018), and what specific Kubernetes component was the attack vector?
Show Answer
Answer

The Kubernetes Dashboard was exposed to the internet without authentication. Attackers discovered it, found AWS cloud credentials accessible through the dashboard, and used Tesla's compute resources to mine cryptocurrency. The dashboard was the single point of entry.

Explanation

This breach is the #1 reason CKS tests dashboard security. Key lesson: NEVER expose the Kubernetes Dashboard publicly. Use kubectl proxy for temporary local access, or require strong authentication + RBAC + NetworkPolicy if dashboard must be deployed. The CKS exam may ask you to "secure a dashboard deployment" — this is why.

Q2
Write the command to create a ServiceAccount for dashboard access, bind it to the cluster-admin ClusterRole, and retrieve the token for login.
Show Answer
Answer
# Create SA and binding
kubectl create sa dashboard-admin -n kubernetes-dashboard
kubectl create clusterrolebinding dashboard-admin-binding \
  --clusterrole=cluster-admin \
  --serviceaccount=kubernetes-dashboard:dashboard-admin

# Get the token (Kubernetes 1.24+)
kubectl create token dashboard-admin -n kubernetes-dashboard

# Or get long-lived token (older versions)
kubectl get secret -n kubernetes-dashboard \
  $(kubectl get sa dashboard-admin -n kubernetes-dashboard -o jsonpath='{.secrets[0].name}') \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d
Explanation

CKS best practice: Never use cluster-admin for dashboard access. Create a read-only ClusterRole instead. On the exam, use the least-privilege principle: if the task says "view only", create a role with get,list,watch — not cluster-admin.

Q3
What is the secure way to access the Kubernetes Dashboard? Compare kubectl proxy with NodePort/LoadBalancer/Ingress approaches.
Show Answer
Answer
MethodSecurityUse Case
kubectl proxy✅ SAFEST — localhost only, uses kubeconfig authAdmin debugging, one-off access
NodePort❌ DANGEROUS — exposes on node IPNEVER use for production
LoadBalancer❌ VERY DANGEROUS — public IP unless restrictedNEVER without IP whitelist + auth
Ingress + OIDC⚠️ Acceptable IF OIDC + TLS + IP restrictionsEnterprise with SSO integration
Explanation

kubectl proxy is the CKS-recommended approach: it runs locally (127.0.0.1:8001), uses your kubeconfig credentials, and adds no new attack surface. On the exam, if asked "how should a user access the dashboard?", the answer is ALWAYS kubectl proxy + browser to http://localhost:8001/api/v1/namespaces/kubernetes-dashboard/services/https:kubernetes-dashboard:/proxy/.

Q4
How do you audit your cluster to find all exposed web UIs and dashboards? Write the kubectl commands to discover them.
Show Answer
Answer
# Find all Services with type LoadBalancer or NodePort
kubectl get svc -A -o wide | grep -E 'LoadBalancer|NodePort'

# Find all Ingresses
kubectl get ingress -A

# Check for dashboard namespaces
kubectl get ns | grep -i dashboard

# Find pods with web UI labels
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.labels.app=="dashboard" or .metadata.labels["k8s-app"]=="kubernetes-dashboard") | {ns: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name}'
Explanation

The CKS exam might give you a cluster with a dashboard already deployed and ask you to "find and secure the exposed dashboard." First, discover what's running. Then check if it's exposed (LoadBalancer/NodePort = exposed). Then secure it with RBAC or delete it.

Q5
Deploy the Kubernetes Dashboard with a read-only ServiceAccount that can view resources in ALL namespaces but cannot modify anything.
Show Answer
Answer
# ClusterRole: read-only across all namespaces
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata: {name: dashboard-readonly}
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods","services","deployments","configmaps","secrets","nodes","namespaces"]
  verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata: {name: dashboard-readonly-binding}
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: dashboard-viewer
  namespace: kubernetes-dashboard
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: dashboard-readonly
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
Explanation

Notice: read-only but still includes "secrets" in the list. The CKS exam may ask you to EXCLUDE secrets from the read-only view for extra security. Always think: "what's the minimum this role truly needs?" Remove secrets if not explicitly required.

Q6
You discover the Kubernetes Dashboard deployed in namespace kubernetes-dashboard exposed via a LoadBalancer Service. What commands do you run to secure it immediately?
Show Answer
Answer
# IMMEDIATE: Remove LoadBalancer exposure
kubectl patch svc kubernetes-dashboard -n kubernetes-dashboard \
  -p '{"spec":{"type":"ClusterIP"}}'

# Alternative: Delete the service entirely
kubectl delete svc kubernetes-dashboard -n kubernetes-dashboard

# Verify no external exposure
kubectl get svc -A | grep -E 'LoadBalancer|NodePort'

# Use kubectl proxy for secure access instead
kubectl proxy &
Explanation

This is an emergency response task. The CKS exam may simulate a security incident: "a dashboard was found exposed publicly — secure it." Priority order: (1) remove exposure (patch to ClusterIP), (2) verify no other exposure, (3) set up proper authentication, (4) document the incident.

Q7
For the anihpj project, should the Kubernetes Dashboard be deployed? Justify your answer with CKS security principles.
Show Answer
Answer

Recommended: NO Dashboard for anihpj production. Reasons:

  • Least privilege: Dashboard adds unnecessary attack surface
  • Minimal attack surface: Every extra component is a potential vulnerability
  • Defense in depth: kubectl + RBAC already provides all needed management capabilities
  • If dashboard is needed for dev: Deploy in dev namespace only, use ClusterIP, access via kubectl proxy
Explanation

CKS thinking: "Default deny" applies to components too — if you don't need it, don't deploy it. The dashboard is a convenience tool, not a production requirement. kubectl provides all the same capabilities with better security.

Q8
What other web UIs or components might be exposed in a Kubernetes cluster besides the Dashboard? List at least 4 and how to check for each.
Show Answer
Answer
ComponentDetection CommandRisk
Grafanakubectl get svc -A | grep grafanaMonitoring data exposure
Prometheuskubectl get svc -A | grep prometheusMetrics + target enumeration
Jenkinskubectl get svc -A | grep jenkinsCI/CD pipeline control
ArgoCDkubectl get svc -A | grep argocdGitOps deployment control
Kiali/Jaegerkubectl get svc -A | grep -E 'kiali|jaeger'Service mesh visualization
Explanation

Any web UI is a potential entry point. The CKS exam may ask you to "audit the cluster for exposed services." The universal answer: check for LoadBalancer/NodePort services, then verify each one is intentionally exposed with proper authentication.

Q9
How do you COMPLETELY remove the Kubernetes Dashboard from a cluster? Write all commands to ensure no leftovers remain.
Show Answer
Answer
# Remove dashboard deployment and service
kubectl delete -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/dashboard/v2.7.0/aist/recommended.yaml

# Or namespace-scoped cleanup
kubectl delete ns kubernetes-dashboard

# Remove any remaining RBAC
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding kubernetes-dashboard
kubectl delete clusterrole kubernetes-dashboard

# Remove any SA tokens/secrets
kubectl delete sa dashboard-admin -n kube-system 2>/dev/null

# Verify nothing remains
kubectl get all -n kubernetes-dashboard 2>/dev/null
# Expected: No resources found
Explanation

Deleting the namespace is the cleanest approach — it cascades to all resources. But be careful: if other resources share the namespace, use targeted deletion. The CKS exam values clean, complete removal — no dangling ClusterRoleBindings or ServiceAccounts.

Q10
You must deploy a web UI (like ArgoCD) for the anihpj team. Write the complete security requirements checklist before deployment.
Show Answer
Answer
  1. ☑ Deploy in dedicated namespace with ResourceQuota
  2. ☑ Use ClusterIP Service only — NO NodePort/LoadBalancer
  3. ☑ Configure Ingress with TLS termination
  4. ☑ Integrate OIDC authentication (Azure AD, Google, Okta)
  5. ☑ Create dedicated ServiceAccount with least-privilege RBAC
  6. ☑ Apply NetworkPolicy: allow ingress only from specific IPs/namespaces
  7. ☑ Enable audit logging for all dashboard access
  8. ☑ Run container as non-root with readOnlyRootFilesystem
  9. ☑ Scan the dashboard image with Trivy before deployment
  10. ☑ Set up Falco rules to alert on dashboard exec/shell activity
Explanation

This checklist applies to ANY web UI deployed in Kubernetes. It covers all 6 CKS domains: Cluster Setup (TLS, Ingress), Cluster Hardening (RBAC), System Hardening (non-root), Microservice Vulns (NetworkPolicy), Supply Chain (Trivy scan), Runtime Security (Falco).

Chapter 6: Network Policies — Zero-Trust Pod Networking

By default, every pod can talk to every other pod in a Kubernetes cluster. This flat network means one compromised pod can reach databases, secrets, and other namespaces. NetworkPolicy is your firewall inside the cluster — it enforces zero-trust networking where only explicitly allowed connections work.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~2 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 NetworkPolicy

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why the default flat network is a catastrophic security risk
  • ✅ NetworkPolicy fundamentals: podSelector, policyTypes, ingress, egress
  • ✅ 5 common NetworkPolicy patterns you MUST know for the CKS exam
  • ✅ How to test and verify NetworkPolicy with busybox probes
  • ✅ Full zero-trust NetworkPolicy implementation for anihpj (6 policies)
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Setup 10%Minimize Vulns 20%
CKS Exam: NetworkPolicy Is a Must-Know

NetworkPolicy questions appear on virtually every CKS exam. You'll be asked to: create a default-deny policy, allow specific pod-to-pod traffic on specific ports, allow ingress from specific namespaces, and allow DNS egress. Critical tip: always allow DNS (UDP port 53) in your egress rules — without it, pods can't resolve service names and everything breaks. Also: ensure your CNI plugin supports NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, Weave = yes; Flannel alone = no).

6.1 The Default: All Pods Can Talk to All Pods

Without NetworkPolicy, Kubernetes operates on a flat network model: every pod in the cluster can reach every other pod, regardless of namespace. This is the "one breach = lateral movement everywhere" problem. Zero-trust networking flips this: default-deny everything, then allow only what's needed.

🔴 FLAT NETWORK (Default) — One Breach = Full Access
anihpj ←──────────────→ postgres
   ↕                        ↕
 redis ←──────────────→ monitoring
   ↕                        ↕
other-ns ←───────────→ everything-else

Attacker in ANY pod:
can reach EVERYTHING 🔴
✅ ZERO TRUST + NetworkPolicies — Only Allowed Paths
anihpj ──────→ postgres (5432)
anihpj ──────→ redis (6379)
anihpj ──────→ DNS (53)
ingress ────→ anihpj (8000)
monitoring → all pods (9090)

ALL OTHER TRAFFIC: BLOCKED ✅
⚠️ CNI Plugin Dependency

NetworkPolicy objects are IGNORED if your CNI plugin doesn't support them. Flannel and Kindnet do NOT support NetworkPolicy. You need Calico, Cilium, or Weave Net. Always verify: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave'

CNI PluginNetworkPolicy SupporteBPFFQDN Egress FilteringProduction Ready
Calico✅ Full✅✅ Yes✅ Yes
Cilium✅ Full✅✅ Yes✅ Yes
Weave Net✅ Full❌❌ No✅ Yes
Flannel❌ None❌❌ No⚠️ No NetPol
Kindnet❌ None❌❌ No⚠️ Testing Only
🔴 If Your Cluster Uses Flannel

NetworkPolicy objects you create will be silently ignored. Your pods will continue to communicate freely. Before implementing zero-trust policies, you must switch to Calico or Cilium. This is a critical architectural dependency that the CKS exam expects you to understand.

6.2 NetworkPolicy Fundamentals

A NetworkPolicy uses label selectors to identify target pods, then defines allowed ingress (incoming) and egress (outgoing) traffic. Empty ingress rules = deny all incoming; empty egress rules = deny all outgoing.

Field-by-Field Anatomy

NetworkPolicy Anatomy — anihpj → PostgreSQL Example

🔍 Field-by-Field Breakdown

🎯podSelector
Which pods this policy protects. matchLabels: {app: postgres} means this policy applies to PostgreSQL pods only.
📋policyTypes
Ingress controls incoming traffic to the selected pods. Egress controls outgoing traffic from the selected pods. You can specify one or both.
⬇️ingress.from
Who can send traffic TO the selected pods. Can use podSelector, namespaceSelector, or ipBlock (CIDR). Multiple entries = OR logic.
🔌ports
Which ports and protocols are allowed. port: 5432, protocol: TCP. Without a port specified, ALL ports are allowed — be specific!
⬆️egress.to
Where the selected pods can send traffic TO. Critical for DNS: always allow egress to UDP port 53 on kube-dns.
postgres-netpol.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: postgres-netpol
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector:                 # ← which pods this PROTECTS
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress                    # ← control INCOMING traffic to postgres
  ingress:
  - from:                      # ← allow traffic FROM:
    - podSelector:             #   pods with label app=anihpj
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj
    ports:                     #   on this port only
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432

6.3 Common NetworkPolicy Patterns You Must Know

These 5 patterns cover 90% of CKS exam NetworkPolicy questions. Memorize the YAML structure for each.

PatternUse CaseExam FrequencyKey YAML
Default deny all ingressIsolate a namespace completelyVery HighpolicyTypes: [Ingress] + empty ingress: []
Default deny all egressPrevent data exfiltrationHighpolicyTypes: [Egress] + empty egress: []
Allow same-namespaceTeam isolationHighfrom: [podSelector: {}] (empty = all in NS)
Allow pod→pod on specific portDatabase access controlVery Highfrom: [podSelector: {app: frontend}] + ports: [{port: 5432}]
Allow DNS egressApps need name resolutionMediumegress: [{to: [{namespaceSelector: {}}], ports: [{port: 53, protocol: UDP}]}]
Allow from specific namespaceCross-namespace accessHighfrom: [namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: monitoring}}]
Allow specific CIDR blockExternal IP ranges onlyMediumfrom: [ipBlock: {cidr: 10.0.0.0/8}]

Ready-to-Use YAML — Copy, Edit, Apply

5 common NetworkPolicy patterns
# Pattern 1: Default deny ALL ingress in a namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny-ingress, namespace: my-ns}
spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress]}
# Empty ingress: [] means deny ALL incoming traffic
---
# Pattern 2: Default deny ALL egress (prevent data exfiltration)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny-egress, namespace: my-ns}
spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Egress]}
# Empty egress: [] means deny ALL outgoing traffic
---
# Pattern 3: Allow pod-to-pod on a specific port (app → database)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-db-access, namespace: my-ns}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: postgres}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: frontend}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
---
# Pattern 4: Allow ingress from a specific namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-from-monitoring, namespace: my-ns}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: monitoring}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 9090}]
---
# Pattern 5: Allow DNS egress (CRITICAL — apps need DNS!)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns, namespace: my-ns}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}, {protocol: TCP, port: 53}]
⚠️ Always Include DNS Egress

The most common NetworkPolicy mistake: creating a default-deny egress policy without also allowing DNS (UDP port 53). Pods suddenly can't resolve service names — everything breaks. Always add a DNS egress rule whenever you implement egress restrictions.

6.4 Testing and Verifying NetworkPolicy — Does It Actually Work?

Always verify your policies with test probes. A policy that looks correct in YAML may not behave as expected.

Testing NetworkPolicy with busybox probes
# Create a test pod in the same namespace
kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never -n anihpj-prod -- sh

# From inside the test pod, probe connections:
# Test ALLOWED: anihpj → postgres (should succeed)
nc -zv postgres-service 5432 -w 3
# → Connection to postgres-service 5432 port [tcp/postgresql] succeeded! ✅

# Test BLOCKED: test pod → postgres (should fail)
nc -zv postgres-service 5432 -w 3
# → nc: connect to postgres-service port 5432 (tcp) timed out ❌

# Test BLOCKED: anihpj → internet (should fail)
wget -q --timeout=5 http://google.com
# → wget: download timed out ❌ (egress blocked!)
FROMTOPortExpected
ingress-nginxanihpj pod8000✅ ALLOWED
anihpj podpostgres pod5432✅ ALLOWED
anihpj podredis pod6379✅ ALLOWED
any podkube-dns53/UDP✅ ALLOWED
postgres podanihpj pod8000❌ BLOCKED
attacker podpostgres pod5432❌ BLOCKED
anihpj podinternet IPsany❌ BLOCKED

Why Testing Is Critical — The "Looks Right but Doesn't Work" Problem

NetworkPolicy errors are silent — Kubernetes accepts the YAML even if the policy doesn't do what you intended:

  • Wrong label selectors: You wrote app: postgres but the actual pod label is app: postgresql. The policy applies to zero pods — no error, no warning.
  • Missing DNS egress: You denied all egress without allowing port 53. Pods suddenly can't resolve service names. Connections just hang.
  • CNI doesn't support NetworkPolicy: You created perfect YAML on a Flannel cluster. NetworkPolicy objects are silently ignored — pods communicate freely.
  • Ingress vs Egress confusion: You created an Ingress policy thinking it controls both directions. Outgoing traffic from the pod is still completely unrestricted.
💡 The 30-Second NetworkPolicy Sanity Check

After applying any NetworkPolicy, immediately run: kubectl run netpol-test --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never -n <ns> -- sh and test both ALLOWED and BLOCKED connections. If a connection that should be BLOCKED succeeds — your policy has a bug. On the CKS exam, this 30-second verification can save you from losing points.

6.5 Securing anihpj with NetworkPolicies — Full Implementation

Here is the complete zero-trust NetworkPolicy set for the anihpj production namespace. Six policies that together create a hardened network topology with 5 security zones.

anihpj Network Security Zones — Post-NetworkPolicy Topology

5 Security Zones — Each Isolated by NetworkPolicy

🔀ZONE 1: DMZ
🌐Ingress ControllerCan reach anihpj:8000 only
🚫Cannot reach DB/RedisIsolated from data tier
📦ZONE 2: App
🐍anihpj DjangoCan reach: pg:5432, redis:6379, DNS:53
🚫No external egressCannot reach internet
🗄️ZONE 3: Data
🐘PostgreSQL + RedisOnly reachable by anihpj + monitoring
🔒No outboundEgress fully denied
📊ZONE 4: Monitor
📈Prometheus + FalcoCan reach all pods:9090
🔒Not reachable by appsOne-way monitoring access

🔒 Default-deny: ALL other traffic is BLOCKED

anihpj-full-netpol-set.yaml — All 6 Policies
# Policy 1: Default deny all ingress in anihpj-prod
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny-ingress, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress]}
---
# Policy 2: Allow anihpj → PostgreSQL (port 5432)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-anihpj-to-postgres, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: postgres}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
---
# Policy 3: Allow Ingress Controller → anihpj (port 8000)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-ingress-to-anihpj, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: ingress-nginx}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 8000}]
---
# Policy 4: Allow anihpj → Redis (port 6379)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-anihpj-to-redis, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: redis}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 6379}]
---
# Policy 5: Allow all pods → DNS (port 53)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns-egress, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to: [{namespaceSelector: {}}]
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}, {protocol: TCP, port: 53}]
---
# Policy 6: Allow monitoring → all pods (port 9090)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-monitoring, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: monitoring}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 9090}]

📝 Chapter 6 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What is the default network behavior in Kubernetes? Why is this a security risk, and what is the first NetworkPolicy you should ALWAYS apply?
Show Answer
Answer

By default, all pods can communicate with all other pods across all namespaces. This is a flat, open network. The first policy to apply is a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny-all, namespace: prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
Explanation

Without default-deny, your namespace is wide open. Even if you add allow rules later, the default-deny ensures only explicitly allowed traffic passes. CKS exam pattern: apply default-deny FIRST, then add allow rules for specific needs (DNS, database, ingress).

Q2
Create a NetworkPolicy for the anihpj namespace that: (a) denies all ingress by default, (b) allows ingress from the ingress-controller namespace on port 8000, (c) allows egress to PostgreSQL on port 5432, (d) allows egress DNS (UDP 53).
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: anihpj-network-policy, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: ingress-nginx}}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 8000}]
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: postgres}}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]
Explanation

DNS egress is critical — without it, pods can't resolve service names. This is the #1 reason NetworkPolicy seems "broken" on the CKS exam. Always check: can the pod resolve kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local? If not, DNS egress is missing.

Q3
After applying a default-deny NetworkPolicy to namespace prod, pods can no longer resolve DNS names. Why? Write the fix.
Show Answer
Answer

Default-deny blocks ALL egress, including DNS queries to CoreDNS (UDP port 53). Fix: add a DNS egress rule:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns, namespace: prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}, {protocol: TCP, port: 53}]
Explanation

TCP port 53 is also needed for DNS responses exceeding 512 bytes. Always include both UDP:53 AND TCP:53 in DNS egress rules. Use namespaceSelector: {} to match CoreDNS which typically runs in kube-system. Test: kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup kubernetes.default.

Q4
What are the 5 most common NetworkPolicy patterns tested on CKS? Write a one-line description and example YAML snippet for each.
Show Answer
Answer
#PatternKey Selector
1Default-deny-allpodSelector: {}, both policyTypes
2Allow from namespacenamespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: ns}}
3Allow from specific podpodSelector: {matchLabels: {app: x}}
4Allow DNS egresskube-dns podSelector + UDP:53 + TCP:53
5Allow on specific portports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
Explanation

Master these 5 patterns and you can compose any NetworkPolicy on the exam. Most CKS NetworkPolicy questions combine 2-3 of these patterns: "block all, allow from monitoring namespace, on port 9090 only."

Q5
How do you test and verify that a NetworkPolicy is working correctly? Write the complete verification workflow with busybox.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Create a temporary test pod
kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never -- sh

# 2. Test allowed connection (should succeed)
wget -qO- --timeout=2 http://anihpj-svc.anihpj:8000

# 3. Test blocked connection (should timeout/fail)
wget -qO- --timeout=2 http://postgres-svc.prod:5432

# 4. Test DNS (should work if DNS allow rule exists)
nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local

# 5. Clean up
exit  # pod auto-deletes with --rm
Explanation

Always test from a pod in the SAME namespace with SAME labels. A common mistake: testing from the wrong namespace and thinking the policy works when it doesn't. Use --rm -it for ephemeral test pods — they clean up automatically.

Q6
What CNI plugins support NetworkPolicy? What happens if you apply a NetworkPolicy with a CNI that doesn't support it?
Show Answer
Answer
CNI PluginNetworkPolicy Support
Calico✅ Full support + extra Calico-specific policies
Cilium✅ Full support + L7 policies
Weave✅ Full support
Flannel (alone)❌ NO support — policies are ignored
Canal (Flannel+Calico)✅ Calico adds NetworkPolicy support

If you apply a NetworkPolicy with Flannel alone, the policy is silently ignored — all traffic flows as if no policy exists. No error is thrown.

Explanation

CKS exam tip: always verify the CNI plugin before writing NetworkPolicies. kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave|flannel'. If you see only Flannel pods, your NetworkPolicies won't work — you need to deploy a compatible CNI or switch.

Q7
Write a NetworkPolicy that isolates a compromised pod: blocks ALL ingress and ALL egress except DNS. This is emergency incident response.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: emergency-isolate, namespace: prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: compromised-app}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  # No ingress rules = deny all ingress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]
Explanation

This is a CKS incident response task. When a pod is compromised, you need to isolate it FAST: (1) apply this policy, (2) the pod can't talk to anything except DNS (needed for minimal functionality), (3) attackers can't move laterally or exfiltrate data. DNS access is kept so you can still diagnose the pod.

Q8
What is the difference between podSelector: {} and podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: nginx}} in a NetworkPolicy?
Show Answer
Answer
SelectorApplies ToUse Case
podSelector: {}ALL pods in the namespaceDefault-deny policy, namespace-wide rules
podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: nginx}}Only pods with label app=nginxTargeted policy for specific application
Explanation

The empty podSelector: {} is the "select all" wildcard — it matches every pod in the namespace. Use it for namespace-wide default-deny. Use specific selectors for application-specific rules. A common CKS mistake: creating a default-deny with a specific podSelector — it won't protect other pods.

Q9
For the anihpj/jobpost application, write a complete set of 6 NetworkPolicies implementing zero-trust networking. Consider Django, PostgreSQL, Redis, monitoring, and ingress.
Show Answer
Answer
  1. Default-deny: Block all ingress/egress for anihpj namespace
  2. DNS allow: UDP+TCP 53 to kube-dns
  3. Django→PostgreSQL: TCP 5432, podSelector app=postgres
  4. Django→Redis: TCP 6379, podSelector app=redis
  5. Ingress→Django: TCP 8000 from ingress-nginx namespace
  6. Monitoring→All: TCP 9090 from monitoring namespace (Prometheus scraping)
Explanation

This is the CKS zero-trust model applied to a real app. Each policy is independent and minimal. Every connection is explicitly whitelisted. If you can write these 6 policies from memory, you can handle any CKS NetworkPolicy question.

Q10
What happens when you have TWO NetworkPolicies selecting the same pod? How are conflicts resolved?
Show Answer
Answer

NetworkPolicies are additive — they UNION. If two policies select the same pod, traffic is allowed if ANY policy permits it. Example:

Policy A AllowsPolicy B AllowsEffective Result
Port 80 from ns-aPort 443 from ns-bPort 80 from ns-a AND Port 443 from ns-b

There are no "deny" rules in NetworkPolicy — only allow rules. A default-deny works by having NO rules (nothing is allowed).

Explanation

This additive behavior is powerful but can be confusing. If you have default-deny + allow-DNS, the effective policy is: deny everything EXCEPT DNS. If you add allow-PostgreSQL, now DNS AND PostgreSQL are allowed. There's no way to create a "deny specifically port 443" rule — you just don't include it in any allow rule.

Chapter 7: Ingress with TLS — Encrypted External Traffic

Without TLS, traffic between users and your cluster travels in plaintext — passwords, session tokens, and personal data visible to anyone on the network path. TLS encrypts this traffic. This chapter covers TLS certificates in Kubernetes, the cert-manager automation tool, and enforcing HTTPS for anihpj.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 TLS

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why TLS is non-negotiable for production Kubernetes ingress
  • ✅ TLS certificate types: self-signed, Let's Encrypt, private CA, wildcard
  • ✅ How cert-manager automates certificate issuance and renewal
  • ✅ How to enforce HTTPS by redirecting all HTTP traffic
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Setup 10%

7.1 Why TLS Matters for Kubernetes Ingress

Encryption is the first line of defense for external traffic. Without it, every request — including authentication credentials — is transmitted in plaintext across the network.

🔴 WITHOUT TLS — Plaintext Danger
👤 User ─── HTTP (plaintext) ─── anihpj pod
     "password=secret" visible on
     EVERY network hop between
     user and cluster 🔴
✅ WITH TLS — Terminated at Ingress
               🔒 Ingress
👤 User ─── HTTPS ─── [decrypt] ─── HTTP ─── anihpj
   encrypted          TLS cert         internal
   on internet        stored here      (inside cluster)

Understanding TLS Termination — Step by Step

When a user visits https://anihpj.com, here's what happens behind the scenes:

1
TLS Handshake

Browser connects to Ingress on port 443. Ingress presents TLS certificate. Browser verifies it's valid and trusted.

2
Encrypted Tunnel

Browser and Ingress negotiate encryption keys. All subsequent data is encrypted end-to-end across the internet.

3
Decrypt at Ingress

Ingress decrypts the HTTPS request using its private key. The plaintext HTTP request is extracted.

4
Forward to Pod

Ingress forwards the plaintext HTTP request to the anihpj pod on port 8000 inside the cluster.

📖 TLS Termination Explained

TLS termination means the Ingress Controller decrypts HTTPS traffic and forwards it as HTTP to your pods. This is the most common pattern because it centralizes certificate management at the Ingress. For even stronger security, use end-to-end TLS with mTLS (see Chapter 22) where pod-to-pod traffic is also encrypted.

7.2 TLS Certificates in Kubernetes

Kubernetes stores TLS certificates as Secret objects of type kubernetes.io/tls. The Ingress references these Secrets to enable HTTPS.

Certificate Types Compared

Certificate TypeUse CaseBrowser Trust
Self-signed openssl req -x509Local dev, testing only⚠️ "Not secure" warning
Let's Encrypt via cert-managerProduction public domains✅ Trusted by all browsers
Private CA (internal)Internal services, air-gapped⚠️ Only org devices trust it
Wildcard *.anihpj.comCovers all subdomains✅ If from trusted CA
tls-secret.yaml + ingress.yaml
# Step 1: Create TLS Secret (or let cert-manager create it)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-tls
  namespace: anihpj-prod
type: kubernetes.io/tls
data:
  tls.crt: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi...   # base64-encoded certificate
  tls.key: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi...   # base64-encoded private key

---
# Step 2: Reference in Ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - anihpj.com
    secretName: anihpj-tls       # ← references the TLS Secret
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj-service
            port:
              number: 8000

7.3 cert-manager — Automated Certificate Management

cert-manager automates the entire TLS certificate lifecycle: issuance, renewal, and revocation. It integrates with Let's Encrypt to provide free, auto-renewing TLS certificates trusted by all browsers.

The 4-Step cert-manager Workflow

1
Install cert-manager

kubectl apply -f cert-manager.yaml
Creates CRDs, controller, webhook

2
Create Issuer

ClusterIssuer or Issuer
Configures Let's Encrypt endpoint
ACME challenge type (HTTP-01/DNS-01)

3
Annotate Ingress

cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
cert-manager detects annotation

4
Auto-Issue + Renew

Certificate automatically requested, validated, issued, stored as Secret, and renewed before expiry

CKS Exam: cert-manager Awareness

You won't install cert-manager on the CKS exam, but you should know: it uses CRDs (Certificate, Issuer, ClusterIssuer), it handles Let's Encrypt ACME challenges, and it auto-renews certificates 30 days before expiry. Know that cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer annotation on Ingress triggers automatic TLS.

7.4 Enforcing HTTPS — Redirecting HTTP to HTTPS

Having a TLS certificate isn't enough — you must enforce that all traffic uses HTTPS. Configure your Ingress to redirect HTTP (port 80) to HTTPS (port 443).

Ingress with HTTP→HTTPS redirect
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  annotations:
    # nginx ingress: force HTTPS redirect
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    # cert-manager: auto-provision TLS
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - anihpj.com
    secretName: anihpj-tls
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj-service
            port:
              number: 8000
✅ HTTPS Enforcement Checklist for anihpj
  • ✅ TLS Secret exists and is valid (not expired)
  • ✅ Ingress references correct secretName
  • ✅ force-ssl-redirect annotation set to "true"
  • ✅ cert-manager annotation present for auto-renewal
  • ✅ Verify: curl -I https://anihpj.com returns 200 OK
  • ✅ Verify: curl -I http://anihpj.com returns 301 redirect to HTTPS

Beyond HTTPS — Essential Ingress Security Annotations

AnnotationEffectWhy It Matters
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"Forces HTTP→HTTPS redirectUsers who type http:// get automatically upgraded to https://
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts: "true"HTTP Strict Transport Security — browser remembers to always use HTTPSPrevents SSL-stripping attacks for return visitors
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts-max-age: "31536000"HSTS duration: 1 year in secondsBrowser won't even try HTTP for a full year after first HTTPS visit
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-protocols: "TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3"Only allow modern TLS versionsBlocks old TLS 1.0/1.1 which have known vulnerabilities
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "10"Rate limiting: 10 requests per second per IPPrevents brute-force attacks and DoS attempts
📖 Production-Grade Ingress Security

A TLS certificate alone is the minimum — not the goal. A production-grade Ingress should include: TLS with modern protocols only, HSTS to prevent downgrade attacks, rate limiting to prevent abuse, and the X-Frame-Options and X-Content-Type-Options headers to prevent clickjacking and MIME sniffing. These annotations take 2 minutes to add and protect against entire categories of web attacks.

⏱️ Target: 8 minutes
🔐 CKS Drill: Lock Down the anihpj Network

Scenario: The anihpj-prod namespace currently has NO NetworkPolicies. All pods can reach each other freely. An attacker who compromises the monitoring pod could reach the PostgreSQL database directly.

Your Tasks:

  1. Create a default-deny NetworkPolicy that blocks all ingress traffic in the anihpj-prod namespace.
  2. Create a policy that allows the anihpj pod (label app: anihpj) to reach PostgreSQL (label app: postgres) on port 5432.
  3. Create a policy that allows the ingress controller (namespace label name: ingress-nginx) to reach the anihpj pod on port 8000.
  4. Allow DNS egress (UDP port 53) for all pods so they can resolve service names.
  5. Verify your policies: can the monitoring pod still reach PostgreSQL? (It should NOT be able to.)

📝 Chapter 7 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
Create a TLS Secret named anihpj-tls from a certificate and key file. Then write an Ingress that uses it for TLS termination on host anihpj.com.
Show Answer
Answer
# Create TLS secret
kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls \
  --cert=/path/to/tls.crt \
  --key=/path/to/tls.key \
  -n anihpj

# Verify
kubectl describe secret anihpj-tls -n anihpj
# Should show: tls.crt, tls.key
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: anihpj-ingress, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts: [anihpj.com]
    secretName: anihpj-tls
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service: {name: anihpj-svc, port: {number: 8000}}
Explanation

The TLS secret MUST contain tls.crt and tls.key as data keys — these are the exact names Ingress looks for. Using kubectl create secret tls ensures correct key names. Common error: using wrong key names (cert/key instead of tls.crt/tls.key) — the Ingress silently ignores the secret.

Q2
What is cert-manager? How does it automate TLS certificate lifecycle? Write the key resources it manages.
Show Answer
Answer

cert-manager automates TLS certificate issuance, renewal, and rotation. Key resources:

ResourcePurpose
IssuerNamespace-scoped CA (self-signed, Let's Encrypt, private CA)
ClusterIssuerCluster-wide CA — any namespace can reference
CertificateRequests a certificate from an Issuer — auto-renews before expiry
Explanation

cert-manager solves the "expired TLS certificate" problem — it auto-renews 30 days before expiry. On the CKS exam, you may be asked to troubleshoot TLS issues. Check: kubectl get certificaterequests and kubectl get orders to see the cert-manager workflow state.

Q3
How do you enforce HTTPS by redirecting all HTTP (port 80) traffic to HTTPS (port 443)? Write the Ingress configuration.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts: [anihpj.com]
    secretName: anihpj-tls
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service: {name: anihpj-svc, port: {number: 8000}}
Explanation

The force-ssl-redirect annotation is specific to nginx-ingress. For other ingress controllers, the annotation name differs. If the exam asks "enforce HTTPS", always add this annotation. Test with: curl -I http://anihpj.com — you should get a 301/308 redirect to HTTPS.

Q4
What are the differences between self-signed, Let's Encrypt, private CA, and wildcard certificates? When would you use each for the anihpj application?
Show Answer
Answer
TypeTrustUse Case
Self-signedNot trusted by browsersInternal testing, dev environments ONLY
Let's EncryptPublicly trusted (free)Public-facing anihpj.com production
Private CATrusted within organizationInternal services, mTLS between microservices
Wildcard (*.anihpj.com)Depends on issuerMultiple subdomains (api, admin, www)
Explanation

For the CKS exam: production public-facing = Let's Encrypt (via cert-manager). Internal service-to-service = private CA with cert-manager. Never use self-signed in production — browsers show "Your connection is not private" warnings.

Q5
A user reports "NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID" when visiting anihpj.com. What is the likely cause, and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

This error means the TLS certificate is not signed by a trusted CA. Likely causes:

  1. Self-signed certificate in production → Replace with Let's Encrypt via cert-manager
  2. Wrong secret referenced → Check Ingress tls.secretName matches actual Secret
  3. Certificate expired → kubectl get certificate -A to check status
  4. Missing intermediate cert → Recreate TLS secret with full chain
Explanation

On the CKS exam, check the TLS secret first: kubectl describe secret anihpj-tls -n anihpj. Verify both tls.crt and tls.key exist. Then check cert expiration: openssl x509 -in <(kubectl get secret anihpj-tls -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d) -noout -dates.

Q6
How do you configure HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) for the anihpj Ingress? Write the annotation and explain what it does.
Show Answer
Answer
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts-max-age: "31536000"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts-include-subdomains: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts-preload: "false"

What HSTS does: Tells browsers "always use HTTPS for this domain for the next 1 year (31536000 seconds)." Prevents SSL stripping attacks and accidental HTTP access.

Explanation

HSTS is a critical security header. On the CKS exam, enabling HSTS is often part of a "harden the Ingress" task. Combine with force-ssl-redirect: true for complete HTTPS enforcement. Note: hsts-preload: true is irreversible — don't enable unless you're certain.

Q7
What is mTLS (mutual TLS) and when would you use it in Kubernetes? How is it different from standard TLS?
Show Answer
Answer
FeatureStandard TLSmTLS
Server verified?✅ Yes✅ Yes
Client verified?❌ No✅ Yes (client presents certificate)
Use in K8sIngress → userPod ↔ Pod, Pod ↔ etcd, service mesh

In Kubernetes, mTLS is used by service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) for pod-to-pod communication and by the API server ↔ etcd connection.

Explanation

On the CKS exam, mTLS is most relevant for etcd security (Domain 2). The etcd cluster uses mTLS: both the API server AND etcd verify each other's certificates. The flags are --etcd-certfile, --etcd-keyfile, and --etcd-cafile on the API server side.

Q8
Write the commands to verify that TLS is correctly configured on anihpj.com Ingress. Include certificate chain, expiration date, and protocol check.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Check TLS handshake and certificate
openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -servername anihpj.com

# 2. Check certificate expiration
openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -servername anihpj.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates

# 3. Check certificate chain
openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -servername anihpj.com -showcerts

# 4. Verify HSTS header
curl -I https://anihpj.com 2>/dev/null | grep -i strict-transport

# 5. Test HTTP → HTTPS redirect
curl -I http://anihpj.com 2>/dev/null | grep -i location
# Expected: Location: https://anihpj.com
Explanation

CKS exam verification: always test TLS from outside the cluster. If you can't reach the cluster externally, use port-forward: kubectl port-forward -n ingress-nginx svc/ingress-nginx-controller 8443:443 then test against localhost:8443.

Q9
The anihpj Ingress has TLS but users can still access the site via HTTP. What three things should you configure to completely enforce HTTPS?
Show Answer
Answer
  1. SSL Redirect: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
  2. HSTS Header: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts: "true" with max-age
  3. Force SSL: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect: "true"
Explanation

These three annotations together create defense-in-depth for HTTPS: redirect catches the first HTTP request, HSTS tells browsers to never try HTTP again, and force-ssl ensures even misconfigured clients get redirected. Without all three, there's still a way to access via HTTP.

Q10
Create a cert-manager ClusterIssuer using Let's Encrypt with HTTP-01 challenge. Then create a Certificate resource for anihpj.com that references this issuer.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata: {name: letsencrypt-prod}
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: admin@anihpj.com
    privateKeySecretRef: {name: letsencrypt-prod-key}
    solvers:
    - http01:
        ingress: {class: nginx}
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata: {name: anihpj-com, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  secretName: anihpj-tls
  issuerRef: {name: letsencrypt-prod, kind: ClusterIssuer}
  dnsNames: [anihpj.com, www.anihpj.com]
Explanation

The ACME server URL differs between staging and production. For testing, use https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory to avoid rate limits. Once verified, switch to prod. cert-manager auto-renews 30 days before expiry — no manual intervention needed.

🟡 Part 3: Cluster HardeningChapters 8-12

Chapter 8: Restricting API Server Access

Every kubectl command, every controller action, every pod communication — everything flows through the API server. It is the single entry point to your cluster. Compromise it, and you own the entire cluster. This chapter teaches you to lock it down: disable anonymous access, enable audit logging, restrict IP ranges, remove the insecure port, and understand every authentication method.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 API Server

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why the API server is the most critical security component in Kubernetes
  • ✅ How to disable anonymous authentication and enforce credential-based access
  • ✅ How to configure audit logging with proper levels and policies
  • ✅ How to restrict API server access using layered IP restrictions
  • ✅ All 6 authentication methods and when to use each
  • ✅ How to identify and remove the insecure port (CIS 1.2.5)
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Hardening 15%
CKS Exam: API Server Hardening Is Always Tested

On the CKS exam, expect at least one task involving the API server manifest at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. You'll add or remove flags to fix CIS failures. The most common tasks: disable anonymous-auth, set authorization-mode to Node,RBAC, enable audit logging, and configure admission plugins. Always verify your changes: after editing the manifest, the kubelet auto-restarts the API server pod. Wait 30 seconds, then test with kubectl or curl.

8.1 The API Server Is the Crown Jewel

The API server sits at the center of every Kubernetes operation. Every kubectl command, every controller reconciliation, every admission webhook — they all pass through this single component. The CIS Benchmark devotes more checks to the API server than any other component.

Everything Flows Through the API Server
🌐
API SERVER
port 6443
👤
kubectl Users

Human admins & developers

↑ x509 certs ↑
🤖
Service Accounts

Pods authenticating to API

↑ JWT tokens ↑
🔄
Controllers

Deployment, ReplicaSet, etc.

↑ watch + reconcile ↑
⚙️
kubelets

Node agents reporting status

↑ node status ↑
📋
Admission Webhooks

OPA, Kyverno, custom

↑ validate/mutate ↑
📊
Monitoring

Prometheus, metrics-server

↑ metrics scrape ↑
📖 Key Insight: Single Point of Entry = Single Point of Defense

Because everything flows through the API server, securing it gives you maximum leverage. A single flag change — like --anonymous-auth=false — instantly blocks an entire category of attacks. Conversely, a single misconfiguration exposes everything. This chapter focuses on making the API server impenetrable.

🏗️ The Seaport Analogy — Why the API Server Is Everything

Think of Your Cluster as a Busy Seaport
   🌊 OUTSIDE WORLD (Internet)              🏗️ INSIDE THE PORT (Cluster)
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   
   🚢 Ships (kubectl users) ──→ ┌──────────────────────────┐
                                 │  🛃 CUSTOMS & GATE       │
   📦 Cargo (pod specs)    ──→  │  ──────────────────      │
                                 │  AUTHENTICATION:         │
   📋 Manifests (YAML)     ──→  │  "Who are you?"          │
                                 │  → Check ID (certs)      │
   🤖 Auto-systems (CICD)  ──→  │                          │
                                 │  AUTHORIZATION:          │
   🏗️ Cranes (kubelets)    ──→  │  "What can you do?"      │
                                 │  → Check permit (RBAC)   │
   📊 Inspectors (monitor) ──→  │                          │
                                 │  ADMISSION:              │
   🔄 Schedulers (controllers)→ │  "Is this cargo safe?"   │
                                 │  → Final check (PSS/OPA) │
                                 └──────────┬───────────────┘
                                            │
                         ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐
                         │  🗄️  WAREHOUSE (etcd)                │
                         │  All cargo manifests stored here     │
                         │  🔒 Must be locked + surveilled      │
                         └──────────────────────────────────────┘
   
   💡 If the customs gate is left UNGUARDED:
      → Anyone can dock any ship
      → Anyone can unload any cargo
      → Anyone can access the warehouse
      → The ENTIRE port is compromised
   
   🛡️  This chapter LOCKS every gate, checks every ID,
       and inspects every cargo before it enters the port.

What Happens When the API Server Is Compromised?

Understanding the blast radius of an API server compromise explains why hardening it is the highest priority in Kubernetes security:

🔴 Attacker Gains API Server Access
  • 🔴 Can list all secrets in every namespace — database passwords, API keys, TLS certs — everything stored in Secrets
  • 🔴 Can create privileged pods running as root with hostPath mounts — giving them access to the underlying node filesystem
  • 🔴 Can delete or modify any resource — Deployments, ConfigMaps, NetworkPolicies, RBAC rules
  • 🔴 Can exec into any running pod — getting a shell inside production containers
  • 🔴 Can create new RBAC bindings — creating persistent backdoor access that survives restarts
  • 🔴 Can exfiltrate data by creating pods that send data to external servers
✅ What a Hardened API Server Blocks
  • ✅ --anonymous-auth=false → attacker cannot even make unauthenticated requests to discover what's running
  • ✅ --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC → even with valid credentials, RBAC limits what they can do to only their assigned roles
  • ✅ NodeRestriction admission plugin → compromised kubelet cannot modify other nodes or their pods
  • ✅ Audit logging enabled → every API call is recorded — you'll know exactly what the attacker accessed and when
  • ✅ IP restriction → attacker cannot even reach the API server port from outside allowed networks
  • ✅ Encryption at rest → even if attacker reads etcd directly, secrets are encrypted and unreadable

8.2 Disabling Anonymous Authentication

By default, unauthenticated requests to the API server are assigned the system:anonymous user and system:unauthenticated group. While these have minimal permissions by default, some misconfigured clusters grant them access. CIS Benchmark 1.2.1 requires disabling anonymous auth entirely.

Disable Anonymous Auth

🔴 INSECURE — Anonymous Auth Enabled
kube-apiserver.yaml — BROKEN
spec:
  containers:
