  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    # Missing --anonymous-auth=false
    # Anyone can make unauthenticated calls!
✅ SECURE — Anonymous Auth Disabled
kube-apiserver.yaml — SECURE
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --anonymous-auth=false
    # ALL requests must carry valid credentials
Testing anonymous auth is disabled
# Test 1: Anonymous request (should FAIL)
curl -k https://localhost:6443/api/v1/pods
# → {"message": "forbidden: User \"system:anonymous\" cannot get..."}

# Test 2: With valid credentials (should SUCCEED)
curl -k https://localhost:6443/api/v1/pods \
  --cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/admin.crt \
  --key /etc/kubernetes/pki/admin.key
# → {"kind": "PodList", "items": [...]}  ← ✅ Works with valid cert!
⚠️ What Anonymous Auth Actually Means in Practice

When anonymous auth is enabled (the default in some older setups), anyone who can reach port 6443 can issue kubectl commands as system:anonymous. While this user has no RBAC permissions by default, the attacker can still discover what's running — they can probe API endpoints to learn about pods, namespaces, and versions. This reconnaissance is often the first step in a targeted attack. Even worse, some cluster administrators accidentally bind roles to system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated, granting real access to anyone. Never rely on "default no-permissions" — disable anonymous access entirely.

8.3 Enabling Audit Logging on the API Server

Audit logging records every request to the API server — who made it, what resource they accessed, what action they performed, and when. It's required for compliance (PCI-DSS, SOC2, HIPAA) and essential for forensic investigation. On the CKS exam, you'll be asked to configure an audit policy.

Audit Levels: None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse

LevelWhat Gets LoggedWhen to Use
NoneNothing — the event is not loggedHigh-volume, low-value events (e.g., events, endpoints)
MetadataWho, what resource, what verb, when — NOT request/response bodySecrets, ConfigMaps (don't log values)
RequestMetadata + full request bodyPod creation, Deployment changes
RequestResponseMetadata + request body + response body (most verbose)Critical operations only — fills disk fast!

Audit Policy YAML Structure

/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
# Don't log noisy event updates
- level: None
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["events"]
# Log who accessed secrets (but not the values!)
- level: Metadata
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
# Log full pod operations
- level: RequestResponse
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["pods"]
# Log everything else at metadata level
- level: Metadata
  omitStages:
  - "RequestReceived"

API Server Flags for Audit

kube-apiserver.yaml — audit flags
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
    - --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
    - --audit-log-maxage=30       # days to retain
    - --audit-log-maxbackup=10    # max rotated files
    - --audit-log-maxsize=100     # MB per file
📖 Real-World Audit Log Use Case

Imagine a security incident: someone deleted a critical Deployment at 3:14 AM. Without audit logging, you have no idea who did it — was it a malicious insider, a compromised credential, or an automated script? With audit logging enabled at RequestResponse level for Deployments, you can search the audit log: cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="deployments" and .verb=="delete")'. You'll find the exact user, their IP, the timestamp, and the full request body — giving you everything you need for your incident report and remediation.

8.4 Restricting API Server to Specific IP Ranges

Even with strong authentication, the API server shouldn't be reachable from the entire internet. Layer IP-based restrictions with Kubernetes-native controls for defense in depth.

Auth Methods: Cert, Token, OIDC, Webhook, Bootstrap

MethodHow It WorksBest Used For
Client Certificate (x509)kubectl uses cert from kubeconfig; API verifies against cluster CAHuman admins, kubeadm default
Bearer Token (SA)SA token in Authorization header; signed by K8sPods → API, in-cluster apps
OIDC (OpenID Connect)External IdP (GitHub, Google, Dex) issues JWTSSO for humans, enterprise auth
Webhook Token AuthExternal server validates token via HTTP callbackCustom auth systems
Bootstrap TokensShort-lived tokens for new nodes joining clusterkubeadm join
Static Token FileTokens in CSV file on control plane disk❌ NEVER in production!

Layered IP Restriction

🔥LAYER 1Cloud Firewall
✅Allow 6443 from admin CIDRe.g. 10.0.0.0/8 only
🚫Deny 6443 from 0.0.0.0/0Block all internet traffic
🔑LAYER 2RBAC
🛡️What authenticated callers can doEven if past firewall, RBAC blocks
📋LAYER 3Admission
🚪OPA/PSS can still rejectEven if RBAC allows it
📝LAYER 4Audit
👁️Every access recordedEven successful ones logged

8.5 Insecure Port — Removing the Back Door

Older Kubernetes versions had --insecure-port=8080 — a port with NO authentication and NO TLS. Removed in 1.20+, but some clusters still have it. CIS 1.2.5 requires ensuring it's gone.

PortPurposeSecurity Status
6443Secure API port (TLS + auth required)✅ Only port to expose
8080Insecure port (NO TLS, NO auth)❌ Must be 0 or absent (removed in 1.20)
10250kubelet API (should be locked down)⚠️ Auth required, not public
10255kubelet read-only (unauthenticated!)❌ Must be 0 (disabled)
2379etcd client (only API server)⚠️ Control plane IPs only
2380etcd peer (only etcd members)⚠️ etcd cluster only
Verify insecure port is disabled
# Check if anything is listening on 8080
ss -tlnp | grep 8080
# → Should return NOTHING. If it shows kube-apiserver, FIX IMMEDIATELY!

# Also verify in the API server manifest
grep "insecure-port" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# → Should NOT find anything (flag removed entirely in 1.20+)

📝 Chapter 8 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
You run curl -k https://api-server:6443/api without any credentials and get a successful response. What security issue exists, and how do you fix it in the API server manifest?
Show Answer
Answer

Issue: Anonymous authentication is enabled (--anonymous-auth=true, the default). Fix in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml:

- --anonymous-auth=false
Explanation

When anonymous auth is enabled, requests without credentials get system:anonymous identity with system:unauthenticated group. With RBAC this is usually harmless — but it's a foothold. CKS exam always expects you to disable it: --anonymous-auth=false.

Q2
Configure audit logging for the API server: (a) policy file at /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml, (b) log to /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log, (c) max age 30 days, (d) max size 100MB. Write all required flags and volume mounts.
Show Answer
Answer
# API server flags
- --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
- --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
- --audit-log-maxage=30
- --audit-log-maxsize=100

# Volume mounts (required!)
volumeMounts:
- name: audit-policy
  mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
  readOnly: true
- name: audit-log
  mountPath: /var/log/kubernetes

# Volumes
volumes:
- name: audit-policy
  hostPath: {path: /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml, type: File}
- name: audit-log
  hostPath: {path: /var/log/kubernetes, type: DirectoryOrCreate}
Explanation

The volume mounts are as important as the flags. Without them, the API server pod cannot access the policy file or write logs — and it will crash. This is a common CKS exam pitfall: candidates add the flags but forget the volume mounts.

Q3
What is the insecure port (--insecure-port) on the API server? Why was it removed, and how do you verify it's not accessible?
Show Answer
Answer

The insecure port (default 8080) allowed unauthenticated, unauthorized access to the API server — a massive security hole. It was removed in Kubernetes 1.20. Verify it's not present:

# Check port isn't listening
ss -tlnp | grep 8080
# Expected: no output

# Verify flag not in manifest
grep 'insecure-port' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Expected: no matches
Explanation

In older Kubernetes versions (pre-1.20), the insecure port was a massive security risk — anyone who could reach port 8080 had cluster-admin access with NO authentication. Modern K8s doesn't have this flag. If you see it on the CKS exam, removing it is a priority fix.

Q4
List all 6 Kubernetes authentication methods. For each, state when it's appropriate to use and one security consideration.
Show Answer
Answer
MethodUse CaseSecurity Note
X.509 CertsCluster components (kubelet, scheduler)Hard to revoke — use short-lived certs
Bearer TokensServiceAccounts (pod→API)Bound tokens (1.24+) preferred over static
OIDCHuman users, enterprise clustersDelegates auth to external IdP
WebhookCustom auth integrationExternal service — must be highly available
Static Token FileBootstrap, emergency accessTokens NEVER expire — use sparingly
Bootstrap TokensNode bootstrap (kubeadm join)Auto-expire after 24h by default
Explanation

CKS exam focus: X.509 certs (API server flags like --client-ca-file) and Bearer Tokens (ServiceAccounts). OIDC is mentioned in CKS but not deeply tested. Know that static token files are a last resort — tokens are stored in plaintext and never expire.

Q5
What admission plugins MUST be enabled for a secure CKS-compliant cluster? List at least 5 and explain what each enforces.
Show Answer
Answer
PluginWhat It Enforces
NodeRestrictionKubelets can only modify their own Node + pods
AlwaysPullImagesEvery pod start pulls fresh image (prevents cached backdoored images)
DenyServiceExternalIPsPrevents Services from using external IPs for MITM
PodSecurityEnforces PSS (privileged/baseline/restricted) at namespace level
EventRateLimitPrevents DoS via event flooding
Explanation

Add these to --enable-admission-plugins in the API server manifest. The CKS exam specifically tests NodeRestriction and PodSecurity (PSS). AlwaysPullImages prevents a clever attack where an attacker pushes a malicious image with the same tag to bypass admission.

Q6
How do you restrict API server access to specific IP ranges? Write the flag and explain the security benefit.
Show Answer
Answer
# In kube-apiserver.yaml
- --advertise-address=10.0.0.1

Combine with network-level controls (firewall/security groups) to restrict which IPs can reach port 6443. The API server itself doesn't have built-in IP filtering — use cloud firewalls (AWS Security Groups, Azure NSG) or iptables/nftables on the node.

Explanation

Layered IP restriction: (1) cloud firewall limits source IP ranges, (2) --advertise-address ensures API server only binds to internal IP, (3) RBAC limits what authenticated users can do. Defense in depth — each layer catches what the previous layer misses.

Q7
Write an audit policy that logs: pod creation/deletion at RequestResponse, secret access at Metadata, and ignores kubelet read requests. Apply it to the API server.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
- level: None
  users: ["system:kube-proxy"]
  verbs: ["watch"]
  resources: [{group: "", resources: ["endpoints","services"]}]
- level: RequestResponse
  verbs: ["create","delete"]
  resources: [{group: "", resources: ["pods"]}]
- level: Metadata
  resources: [{group: "", resources: ["secrets","configmaps"]}]
- level: Metadata
Explanation

Audit levels: None (skip), Metadata (log who/what/when but not body), Request (log request body), RequestResponse (log both request and response). Use None for noisy components (kubelet watches). Use RequestResponse for critical operations (pod deletion).

Q8
After editing /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, the API server pod is CrashLoopBackOff. What commands do you run to diagnose and fix?
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Check pod logs (if available)
kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-<node>
# OR check container logs directly
crictl logs <container-id>

# 2. Check for YAML syntax errors
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | python3 -c "import sys,yaml; yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin)"

# 3. Fix the error, save, wait 30s
# 4. If still crashing, restore from backup
cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.bak /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
Explanation

ALWAYS backup the manifest before editing: cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.bak. If the API server crashes and you can't fix it quickly, restore the backup. On the CKS exam, you may need to SSH directly to the node to fix this.

Q9
What is the difference between --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC and --authorization-mode=RBAC,Node? Why does order matter?
Show Answer
Answer

Authorization modes are evaluated in order — first match wins. With Node,RBAC: Node authorizer checks first, then RBAC. With RBAC,Node: RBAC checks first. The recommended order is Node,RBAC because Node is more specific (only kubelets) and more performant.

Explanation

The CKS exam expects Node,RBAC specifically (CIS 1.2.6). Node authorization handles kubelet requests efficiently (only its own pods). RBAC handles everything else. If you reverse the order, RBAC would check kubelet requests first (unnecessary overhead, and potentially allowing broader access).

Q10
Audit the API server security for the anihpj cluster: write a script that checks anonymous-auth, authorization-mode, insecure-port, admission plugins, and TLS configuration.
Show Answer
Answer
#!/bin/bash
echo "=== API Server Security Audit ==="

# Check anonymous auth
grep anonymous-auth /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
echo "Expect: --anonymous-auth=false"

# Check authorization mode
grep authorization-mode /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
echo "Expect: Node,RBAC"

# Check admission plugins
grep enable-admission-plugins /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
echo "Expect: includes NodeRestriction"

# Check TLS
grep tls-cert-file /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
echo "Expect: --tls-cert-file and --tls-private-key-file set"

# Check insecure port (should NOT exist)
if grep -q insecure-port /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml; then
  echo "WARNING: insecure-port found!"
fi
echo "=== Audit Complete ==="
Explanation

Automate your audits. On the CKS exam, you might run similar checks manually with grep. The most common findings: anonymous-auth=true, authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow, missing NodeRestriction, insecure-port present. Fix all four for a PASS.

Chapter 9: RBAC — Role-Based Access Control for Security

RBAC controls what authenticated users and pods can do in your cluster. It's the principle of least privilege implemented as code. A single wildcard (*) in the wrong place can grant cluster-admin to everyone. This chapter teaches you to design, implement, verify, and audit RBAC for security.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 RBAC

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The 4 RBAC resources: Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding
  • ✅ How to identify and fix dangerous RBAC misconfigurations
  • ✅ Complete RBAC design for the anihpj team (developer, CI/CD, ops, security)
  • ✅ How to verify RBAC with kubectl auth can-i
  • ✅ How to audit RBAC for overpermitted subjects
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Hardening 15%
CKS Exam: RBAC Is a Quick Win

RBAC tasks are the fastest to solve on the CKS exam. You'll typically create a Role/ClusterRole + RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding for a specific scenario. Always use kubectl auth can-i --as=<user> to verify before moving on. Common mistakes: using ClusterRole when a namespaced Role would suffice, forgetting to create the RoleBinding, and mixing up subjects (User vs ServiceAccount vs Group).

9.1 RBAC Refresher — The Security Lens

RBAC connects who (subjects: users, groups, ServiceAccounts) to what they can do (roles: verbs on resources) through bindings. Namespace-scoped roles use Role + RoleBinding. Cluster-wide roles use ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.

RBAC 4-Resource Anatomy — How They Connect
Namespace-Scoped
👤 User: alice
🤖 SA: anihpj-sa ──── RoleBinding ──── Role
👥 Group: devs    (in one namespace)  (verbs + resources)
                                        in one namespace
Cluster-Wide
👤 User: bob
🤖 SA: monitoring  ── ClusterRoleBinding ── ClusterRole
👥 Group: ops      (across ALL namespaces)  (cluster-wide verbs
                                             + resources)
📖 Key Rule

A RoleBinding can bind either a Role OR a ClusterRole — but only within one namespace. A ClusterRoleBinding binds a ClusterRole cluster-wide. If you need namespace-scoped permissions, use a Role. If you need cluster-wide or cluster-object access (nodes, namespaces, PVs), use a ClusterRole.

🔢 RBAC Verb × Resource Permission Matrix — anihpj Team

This matrix shows exactly what each anihpj team role can do — and, critically, what they cannot do. The last row is the one you must never grant:

Rolecreategetupdatedeleteexec/logs
anihpj-dev
Developer (Alice)		podspods
logs		——pods/log
pods/exec
anihpj-deployer
CI/CD Pipeline		—deploy
pods		deploy——
cluster-viewer
Ops (Bob) — Read-Only		—all———
security-audit
Security (Carol) — Read-Only		—roles
secrets		———
cluster-admin
⚠️ NEVER GRANT!		ALLALLALLALLALL
⚠️ How to Read This Matrix

Each cell shows which resources the role can act on with that verb. A dash (—) means the role cannot perform that action on any resource. Notice how every role has the minimum permissions needed — nobody has delete access except cluster-admin, and cluster-admin should never be granted. This is the principle of least privilege in action.

🧭 RBAC Decision Flowchart — Role or ClusterRole?

One of the most common CKS exam mistakes: using a ClusterRole when a namespaced Role would do. Use this flowchart to decide:

Does this permission apply to a SINGLE namespace?
YES → Use Role + RoleBinding
Example: "Alice can get pods in anihpj-dev"NO ↓
Does it involve cluster-scoped resources (nodes, namespaces, PVs)?
YES → Use ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding
Example: "Bob can view all nodes"NO ↓
Do you need the SAME permissions across ALL namespaces?
YES → Use ClusterRole + RoleBinding
Example: "Carol can read secrets in EVERY namespace"
Bind ClusterRole to each namespace via RoleBindingNO → Re-evaluate: do you really need this permission?

9.2 RBAC Misconfigurations — The Top Security Risks

🔴 DANGEROUS — Never Use in Production
❌ Wildcard RBAC = cluster-admin
rules:
- apiGroups: ["*"]     # 🔴 ALL API groups
  resources: ["*"]     # 🔴 ALL resources
  verbs: ["*"]         # 🔴 ALL actions
# This IS cluster-admin!
# Never use in production.
✅ SECURE — Specific, Minimal Permissions
✅ Minimal RBAC for anihpj dev
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
# Only what's needed.
# Nothing more.
🔴 Dangerous Pattern✅ Secure Alternative
verbs: ["*"] — all actions including deleteverbs: ["get","list","watch"] — read-only
resources: ["*"] — all resource typesresources: ["pods","services"] — specific only
apiGroups: ["*"] — all API groupsapiGroups: [""] — core group only
Binding to system:masters groupNever bind to system:masters — it's permanent cluster-admin
Granting escalate, bind, impersonate verbsThese allow privilege escalation — audit them carefully
⚠️ The Most Common RBAC Mistakes Beginners Make
  • Mistake 1: Using ClusterRole when a namespaced Role would suffice. Rule: if working within one namespace, use Role + RoleBinding.
  • Mistake 2: Forgetting to create the RoleBinding. A Role alone does nothing — you must bind it to a subject.
  • Mistake 3: Confusing User, Group, and ServiceAccount in subjects. Users are strings ("alice"), Groups are strings, ServiceAccounts are namespaced ("default:my-sa").
  • Mistake 4: Using verbs: ["*"] "just to get it working." This grants ALL actions including delete. Specify only needed verbs.
  • Mistake 5: Not testing with kubectl auth can-i --as=<user> before deploying. Always verify!

9.3 RBAC for the anihpj Application

👨‍💻DeveloperAlice
📦anihpj-dev NS onlyget, list pods/logs
🚫No delete, no secretsCannot access prod
🤖CI/CDPipeline
🔄anihpj-prod NS onlyget, update deployments
🚫No delete, no secretsCannot delete anything
🔧OpsBob
👁️Cluster-wide readget, list, watch nodes/NS
🛡️SecurityCarol
🔍Read-only auditget, list roles, secrets
anihpj-complete-rbac.yaml — All 4 Team Roles
# === DEVELOPER ROLE: alice in anihpj-dev ===
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {name: anihpj-developer, namespace: anihpj-dev}
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log", "pods/portforward"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: {name: anihpj-developer-binding, namespace: anihpj-dev}
subjects:
- kind: User; name: alice; apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef: {kind: Role, name: anihpj-developer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io}
---
# === CI/CD ROLE: pipeline in anihpj-prod ===
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {name: anihpj-deployer, namespace: anihpj-prod}
rules:
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "update", "patch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: {name: anihpj-deployer-binding, namespace: anihpj-prod}
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount; name: ci-deployer-sa; namespace: anihpj-prod
roleRef: {kind: Role, name: anihpj-deployer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io}
---
# === OPS ROLE: bob cluster-wide read-only ===
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata: {name: cluster-viewer}
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["nodes", "namespaces", "pods", "services"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata: {name: cluster-viewer-binding}
subjects:
- kind: User; name: bob; apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef: {kind: ClusterRole, name: cluster-viewer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io}
---
# === SECURITY AUDITOR: carol read-only across all NS ===
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata: {name: security-auditor}
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
- apiGroups: ["rbac.authorization.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["roles", "rolebindings", "clusterroles", "clusterrolebindings"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]

9.4 Verifying RBAC — kubectl auth can-i

Always verify RBAC before applying to real users. Use kubectl auth can-i with impersonation flags.

RBAC verification commands
# Test as alice (developer)
kubectl auth can-i get pods -n anihpj-dev --as=alice           # → yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n anihpj-dev --as=alice        # → no
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n anihpj-dev --as=alice        # → no
kubectl auth can-i get pods -n anihpj-prod --as=alice          # → no

# Test as ci-pipeline (deployer)
kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n anihpj-prod --as=ci   # → yes
kubectl auth can-i delete deployments -n anihpj-prod --as=ci   # → no
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n anihpj-prod --as=ci          # → no

# Test anihpj ServiceAccount (should have NO access!)
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-sa  # → no
kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-sa  # → no
💡 Understanding the kubectl auth can-i Pattern

The command structure is: kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> [-n namespace] --as=<user>. It asks the API server: "If this user made this request, would RBAC allow it?" — without actually performing the action. The --as flag impersonates the user. For ServiceAccounts, use the full identifier: system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<sa-name>. This is the most important CKS exam verification tool — use it after every RBAC change to confirm the permissions are exactly what you intended.

9.5 Automatic RBAC Audit — Finding Overpermitted Subjects

Before production deployment, scan your cluster for RBAC misconfigurations.

RBAC audit commands
# Find all subjects with cluster-admin rights
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | .subjects'

# Find all subjects that can access secrets in any namespace
kubectl get clusterrole,role --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.rules[]?.resources[]?=="secrets") | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace}'

# Find wildcard (*) verbs (dangerous!)
kubectl get clusterrole,role --all-namespaces -o yaml | grep -B5 'verbs:.*\*'

# Find bindings to system:masters (permanent cluster-admin!)
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="system:masters")'
⏱️ Target: 6 minutes
🔐 CKS Drill: Lock Down anihpj Team Permissions

Scenario: A new developer, Dave, needs read-only access to pods and logs in the anihpj-dev namespace. The CI/CD pipeline needs permission to update Deployments in anihpj-prod only. A security auditor needs to list roles and secrets across all namespaces (read-only).

Your Tasks:

  1. Create a Role (anihpj-developer) in anihpj-dev with get, list, watch on pods, pods/log.
  2. Create a RoleBinding binding the developer Role to user "dave" in anihpj-dev.
  3. Create a Role (anihpj-deployer) in anihpj-prod with get, list, update on deployments.
  4. Create a ClusterRole (security-auditor) with get, list on roles, secrets cluster-wide.
  5. Verify all permissions with kubectl auth can-i --as=<user>.
  6. Verify Dave cannot delete pods or access secrets.

📝 Chapter 9 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
Create a Role pod-reader in namespace anihpj that allows get, list, and watch on pods only. Bind it to user jane. Verify with kubectl auth can-i.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n anihpj
kubectl create rolebinding pod-reader-binding --role=pod-reader --user=jane -n anihpj

# Verify
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=jane -n anihpj  # → yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=jane -n anihpj  # → no
kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=jane -n anihpj  # → no
Explanation

This is the most fundamental CKS RBAC task. Always verify with kubectl auth can-i --as=<subject> — both what they CAN do and what they CANNOT do. The CKS exam values least privilege: if the task says "view pods", give ONLY get,list,watch on pods — nothing more.

Q2
What's the difference between a Role (namespace-scoped) and ClusterRole (cluster-wide)? When would you use a ClusterRole with a RoleBinding instead of ClusterRoleBinding?
Show Answer
Answer

Use ClusterRole + RoleBinding when you want to grant cluster-wide resource permissions (like "read all pods") but limit the scope to ONE namespace. The RoleBinding scopes the ClusterRole down.

# ClusterRole: read pods cluster-wide
kubectl create clusterrole pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
# RoleBinding: but only in namespace anihpj
kubectl create rolebinding pod-reader-ns --clusterrole=pod-reader --user=jane -n anihpj
Explanation

This ClusterRole+RoleBinding pattern is a CKS exam favorite. It lets you define permissions once (ClusterRole) and scope them per namespace (RoleBinding). Without it, you'd need to recreate the same Role in every namespace.

Q3
Audit this RBAC configuration for security issues: ClusterRole: {rules: [{apiGroups: ["*"], resources: ["*"], verbs: ["*"]}]} bound with ClusterRoleBinding to group system:authenticated. What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

This gives every authenticated user cluster-admin access. The wildcards (*) on apiGroups, resources, and verbs grant unlimited power. Binding to system:authenticated means anyone who can log in has full control.

# Find this dangerous configuration
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o yaml | grep -A10 'system:authenticated'

# Fix: Delete and recreate with proper scoping
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding dangerous-binding
Explanation

This is the #1 RBAC anti-pattern. The CKS exam may present you with a cluster and ask "find and fix dangerous RBAC configurations." Look for: (1) wildcard * in verbs or resources, (2) bindings to system:authenticated or system:unauthenticated, (3) cluster-admin bindings to non-admin subjects.

Q4
Design complete RBAC for the anihpj team: developers (read logs, exec into pods in dev), CI/CD (update deployments in all namespaces), security auditors (read all resources, no modifications). Write all Roles and Bindings.
Show Answer
Answer
# Developer (namespace: anihpj-dev)
kubectl create role developer --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods,pods/log -n anihpj-dev
kubectl create role developer-exec --verb=create --resource=pods/exec -n anihpj-dev
kubectl create rolebinding dev-binding --role=developer --group=developers -n anihpj-dev

# CI/CD (cluster-wide deployer)
kubectl create clusterrole cicd-deployer --verb=get,list,update,patch --resource=deployments,services
kubectl create clusterrolebinding cicd-binding --clusterrole=cicd-deployer --group=cicd

# Security auditor (read-only across cluster)
kubectl create clusterrole auditor --verb=get,list,watch --resource='*'
kubectl create clusterrolebinding auditor-binding --clusterrole=auditor --group=auditors
Explanation

Notice: developers get pods/exec (subresource) as a separate role — exec is dangerous and should be explicitly granted. CI/CD gets update but NOT delete. Auditors get * resources but only get,list,watch (read-only). This is least privilege in practice.

Q5
How do you check which users/groups have cluster-admin access? Write the command and explain the output.
Show Answer
Answer
# Find all cluster-admin bindings
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | {name: .metadata.name, subjects: .subjects}'

# Also check for wildcard ClusterRoles
kubectl get clusterrole -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.rules[].verbs[]=="*") | .metadata.name'
Explanation

Regular RBAC auditing is a CKS requirement. The cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding is the most powerful — anyone bound to it can do anything. Audit this regularly: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin")'.

Q6
What subresources exist for pods, and why is controlling access to pods/exec and pods/log separately important for CKS?
Show Answer
Answer
SubresourceWhat It AllowsSecurity Risk
pods/execkubectl exec into containerHIGH — full shell access to container
pods/logRead container logsMEDIUM — may leak secrets in logs
pods/portforwardPort forward to podHIGH — bypasses NetworkPolicy
pods/attachAttach to running containerHIGH — interactive access
Explanation

Subresources are controlled independently from the parent resource. Granting get pods does NOT automatically grant pods/exec. The CKS exam tests this: a developer may need to view pods but should NOT be able to exec into production pods. Create separate Roles for subresources.

Q7
How do you temporarily impersonate a ServiceAccount to test its RBAC permissions? Write the kubectl command.
Show Answer
Answer
# Test as a ServiceAccount
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-sa -n anihpj

# Test as a user
kubectl auth can-i delete secrets --as=jane -n anihpj

# Test as a group
kubectl auth can-i list deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:default:default --as-group=developers

# Full impersonation (requires impersonate privileges)
kubectl get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-sa -n anihpj
Explanation

kubectl auth can-i --as= is your RBAC testing tool. The format for ServiceAccounts is system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<sa-name>. Always verify BOTH positive and negative cases: "can the SA get pods?" AND "can the SA delete pods?"

Q8
You create a RoleBinding but the user still gets "Forbidden". What are 4 possible reasons the RBAC isn't working?
Show Answer
Answer
  1. Wrong namespace: RoleBinding created in ns-a, user trying to access ns-b
  2. Wrong apiGroup: Deployments are in apps/v1 (apiGroups: ["apps"]), not core (apiGroups: [""])
  3. Resource name mismatch: Used pods instead of pods (or deployment vs deployments)
  4. Subject mismatch: Bound to user "jane" but user authenticates as "jane@company.com"
Explanation

RBAC debugging is a common CKS exam task. Use kubectl auth can-i --as=<user> -n <ns> to isolate the issue. Then check: kubectl describe rolebinding <name> -n <ns> to verify subjects and roleRef. The apiGroups field is the most common gotcha — it's case-sensitive and version-specific.

Q9
How do you find all RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings that reference a specific user or ServiceAccount? Write the command.
Show Answer
Answer
# Find all bindings for user "jane"
kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="jane") | {kind: .kind, name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace}'

# Find all bindings for SA "anihpj-sa" in namespace "anihpj"
kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name=="anihpj-sa" and .subjects[]?.namespace=="anihpj")'
Explanation

This is essential for access review and incident response. If a ServiceAccount is compromised, you need to immediately know what it has access to. The jq filter on .subjects[] is your forensic tool — practice this command until it's automatic.

Q10
For the anihpj production namespace, design a complete RBAC policy that follows least privilege: Django SA (read secrets, no exec), monitoring SA (read metrics endpoints), CI/CD SA (update deployments). Write all manifests.
Show Answer
Answer
# Django SA: reads its own secret
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {name: django-role, namespace: anihpj-prod}
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets"]
  resourceNames: ["anihpj-secret"]
  verbs: ["get"]
---
# Monitoring SA: get pods (for Prometheus)
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {name: monitoring-role, namespace: anihpj-prod}
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods","services","endpoints"]
  verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
Explanation

Note the resourceNames field — Django can read ONLY the "anihpj-secret" Secret, not all secrets. This is granular least privilege: even if the Django pod is compromised, it can't read other secrets in the namespace (like PostgreSQL credentials if stored separately).

Chapter 10: Service Accounts — Securing Pod Identity

Every pod gets a Service Account that defines its identity when talking to the Kubernetes API. A misconfigured Service Account can give a compromised pod cluster-admin access. This chapter teaches you to create dedicated, minimal-permission Service Accounts and disable API access for pods that don't need it.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 SA

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ How pods authenticate to the API server using ServiceAccount tokens
  • ✅ Why the default ServiceAccount is dangerous — and how to replace it
  • ✅ Old static tokens vs new bound/projected tokens — security comparison
  • ✅ How to disable automountServiceAccountToken for pods that don't need API access
  • ✅ Securing anihpj Service Accounts with dedicated, minimal-permission SAs
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Hardening 15%

10.1 How Pods Authenticate to the API Server

Every pod gets a ServiceAccount token mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/. The pod uses this JWT token to authenticate to the API server. If the SA has RBAC permissions, the pod inherits them.

1
Pod Starts

kubelet creates projected volume at /var/run/secrets/

2
Read Token

App reads JWT token from mounted file

3
Call API

App sends Authorization: Bearer <token>

4
RBAC Check

API server validates token → checks RBAC → responds

📖 If automountServiceAccountToken: false

Step 1 never happens. The /var/run/secrets/ directory is empty. The pod cannot call the Kubernetes API at all — which is exactly what you want for a pure web application like anihpj Django.

🔑 Service Account Token Lifecycle — From Creation to Expiry

How a Pod Gets and Uses Its Identity Token
  ⏰ TIME    │  ACTION
  ───────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
             │
  Pod Start  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │       │  │  kubelet creates projected volume            │
     │       │  │  Mount: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/      │
     │       │  │         serviceaccount/                      │
     │       │  │  Files: token (JWT), ca.crt, namespace       │
     │       │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │       │
     ▼       │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  App Reads │  │  $ cat /var/run/secrets/.../token            │
     │       │  │  → eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs... (JWT token)      │
     │       │  │  Token contains: SA name, namespace, expiry  │
     │       │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │       │
     ▼       │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  API Call  │  │  curl https://kubernetes.default.svc/api     │
     │       │  │    -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"        │
     │       │  │  API server validates:                       │
     │       │  │  ① Is the token signed by K8s?              │
     │       │  │  ② Has the token expired? (<1 hour)         │
     │       │  │  ③ Is the audience correct?                 │
     │       │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │       │
     ▼       │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  RBAC      │  │  API server checks RBAC:                      │
  Check     │  │  "Can 'anihpj-sa' in 'anihpj-prod'           │
     │       │  │   get pods in this namespace?"               │
     │       │  │  YES → respond with data ✅                  │
     │       │  │  NO  → 403 Forbidden ❌                      │
     │       │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │       │
     ▼       │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  Token     │  │  ~60 minutes later: token expires             │
  Expires   │  │  kubelet automatically rotates token          │
             │  │  New token appears at same mount path        │
             │  │  App doesn't need to restart! 🔄            │
             │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why This Matters: The Compromised Pod Scenario

Imagine an attacker exploits a vulnerability in your Django application (CVE in Pillow library, SQL injection, etc.) and gains code execution inside the anihpj container. What can they do next?

🔴 Pod Has API Access (automount=true)
  • Attacker reads the mounted SA token
  • Uses it to call the Kubernetes API
  • If SA has permissions → lists pods, secrets, deployments
  • If SA has create permissions → creates new privileged pods
  • If SA has exec permissions → shells into other containers
  • The attacker pivots from one compromised container to the entire cluster
✅ Pod Has NO API Access (automount=false)
  • Attacker reads /var/run/secrets/ → directory is EMPTY
  • No token, no API access, no way to pivot
  • Attacker is trapped inside that single container
  • NetworkPolicy blocks lateral movement to other pods
  • Seccomp + AppArmor block dangerous syscalls
  • The blast radius is limited to ONE container
⚠️ The Default ServiceAccount Trap

Here's a real scenario that happens too often: An admin grants the default ServiceAccount permission to read ConfigMaps (seems harmless). But every pod — including a compromised one — is now a default SA. The attacker reads ConfigMaps, finds database credentials stored there (another common mistake), and now has access to your production database. Lesson: never grant permissions to the default SA, and never store secrets in ConfigMaps.

10.2 The Dangers of the Default Service Account

🔴 DEFAULT ServiceAccount
  • All pods share the "default" SA
  • Grant permissions to default → ALL pods get them
  • Compromised pod can access API as default
  • May reach secrets across namespace
✅ DEDICATED ServiceAccounts
  • anihpj pod → anihpj-sa
  • postgres pod → postgres-sa
  • Each SA → minimal permissions
  • Compromised anihpj pod → only anihpj-sa permissions

Disabling automountServiceAccountToken

anihpj-sa.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: anihpj-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
automountServiceAccountToken: false  # ← No API access needed!

10.3 Bound Service Account Tokens (Projected Tokens)

Feature🔴 Old Static Token✅ New Bound Token (1.21+)
StorageK8s Secret (auto-created)Projected volume
ExpiryNever expires!1 hour (default)
RotationManual onlyAutomatic ✅
If stolenPersistent access!Expires soon

Token Flow: Pod → Mount → JWT → API Call → RBAC

Reading the mounted token from inside a pod
# From inside any pod:
cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
# → eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6ImtXSj...  (JWT token)

# Use it to call the API
curl https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace)/pods \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" \
  --cacert /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt

10.4 Securing anihpj Service Accounts

ServiceAccountAPI Access?NamespacePermissions
anihpj-sa❌ No (automount=false)anihpj-prodNone — pure web app
postgres-sa❌ No (automount=false)anihpj-prodNone — database only
anihpj-operator-sa✅ Yesanihpj-prodget, list ConfigMaps only
ci-deployer-sa✅ Yesanihpj-prodget, update Deployments only

📝 Chapter 10 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What is the default ServiceAccount in every namespace, and why is it dangerous to use it for application pods?
Show Answer
Answer

Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount that is automatically mounted to every pod unless specified otherwise. It's dangerous because: (1) ALL pods in the namespace share the same identity, (2) it may have unintended RBAC permissions, (3) a compromised pod can use it to access the API server.

Explanation

Best practice: create a dedicated ServiceAccount per application with only the permissions it needs. Never use the default SA for production workloads. The CKS exam will ask you to "create a dedicated SA and ensure pods use it."

Q2
Create a ServiceAccount anihpj-sa with a token that never expires (pre-1.24 method). Then create a pod that uses this SA and verifies the mounted token.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl create sa anihpj-sa -n anihpj
kubectl create token anihpj-sa -n anihpj  # 1.24+ bound token

# Pod using the SA
kubectl run test --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml | sed 's/serviceAccount: .*/serviceAccount: anihpj-sa/' | kubectl apply -f -

# Verify mounted token
kubectl exec test -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null
Explanation

In Kubernetes 1.24+, tokens are bound (time-limited, audience-scoped) by default. The old static token method required creating a Secret manually. CKS exam: use kubectl create token for 1.24+ clusters. The token is auto-mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/.

Q3
What is the difference between static (legacy) tokens and bound (projected) ServiceAccount tokens? Which is more secure and why?
Show Answer
Answer
FeatureStatic Token (Legacy)Bound Token (1.24+)
ExpiryNEVER expires1 hour by default
StorageStored in Secret (etcd)Not stored — signed JWT
RevocationDelete Secret manuallyAuto-expires
AudienceNoneSpecific audience binding
Explanation

Bound tokens are significantly more secure: auto-expiry means a leaked token is useless after 1 hour, audience binding prevents token reuse, and no etcd storage reduces attack surface. The CKS exam tests awareness of this difference. For 1.24+, always use bound tokens.

Q4
How do you disable the automatic mounting of a ServiceAccount token for a pod that doesn't need API access? Write the pod spec.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: no-api-access}
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx

Or on the ServiceAccount itself to apply to all pods using it:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: restricted-sa}
automountServiceAccountToken: false
Explanation

Most application pods (web servers, workers, databases) don't need to talk to the Kubernetes API. Disabling the token mount removes a potential attack vector — if the pod is compromised, there's no API token to steal. Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the SA for defense in depth.

Q5
A pod uses the default ServiceAccount. You discover it has cluster-admin via a ClusterRoleBinding. How did this happen, and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer
# Find the offending binding
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.kind=="ServiceAccount" and .subjects[]?.name=="default")'

# Remove it
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding <bad-binding-name>

# Create a dedicated SA with minimal permissions
kubectl create sa anihpj-sa -n anihpj
kubectl create role anihpj-role --verb=get --resource=pods -n anihpj
kubectl create rolebinding anihpj-rb --role=anihpj-role --serviceaccount=anihpj:anihpj-sa -n anihpj
Explanation

This is a real-world misconfiguration: someone ran kubectl create clusterrolebinding all-default --clusterrole=cluster-admin --serviceaccount=default:default. Now every pod in the default namespace has cluster-admin. The CKS exam may present you with such a scenario — find and fix it immediately.

Q6
Write the command to list all ServiceAccounts in a namespace, then for each one, show which pods are currently using it.
Show Answer
Answer
# List all SAs
kubectl get sa -n anihpj

# Show which SA each pod uses
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq -r '.items[] | "\(.metadata.name): \(.spec.serviceAccount // "default")"'

# Find pods using default SA (dangerous)
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.serviceAccount==null or .spec.serviceAccount=="default") | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'
Explanation

Regular SA auditing is essential. The last command finds all pods using the default SA cluster-wide — these are your priority targets for migration to dedicated SAs. A pod with serviceAccount field null also uses the default SA.

Q7
What is TokenRequest API and how does it differ from the old ServiceAccount Secret approach? Write the command to create a time-limited token.
Show Answer
Answer
# Create a 30-minute token (1.24+)
kubectl create token anihpj-sa -n anihpj --duration=30m

# Create a token with specific audience
kubectl create token anihpj-sa -n anihpj --audience=vault

# TokenRequest API: tokens are NOT stored in etcd, auto-expire, audience-bound
Explanation

TokenRequest API (GA since 1.22) generates short-lived, audience-bound, non-persisted tokens. They're never stored in etcd (unlike old Secrets). The kubelet handles rotation automatically for projected volumes. CKS exam: use kubectl create token for 1.24+ clusters.

Q8
Design ServiceAccounts for the anihpj application: Django needs to read its Secret and nothing else. PostgreSQL needs no API access. Redis needs no API access. Create all SAs with appropriate settings.
Show Answer
Answer
# Django SA — minimal API access (read one secret)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: anihpj-django, namespace: anihpj-prod}
---
# PostgreSQL SA — no API access
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: anihpj-postgres, namespace: anihpj-prod}
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
# Redis SA — no API access
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: anihpj-redis, namespace: anihpj-prod}
automountServiceAccountToken: false
Explanation

Only Django needs API access (to read its Secret via the API). PostgreSQL and Redis are pure data stores — they never need to talk to the Kubernetes API. Disabling token mount for them eliminates an entire attack vector. This is CKS least privilege applied to ServiceAccounts.

Q9
How do you check what permissions a ServiceAccount has? Write the complete verification workflow.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Check direct RoleBindings
kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.kind=="ServiceAccount" and .subjects[]?.name=="anihpj-sa")'

# 2. Test specific permissions
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-sa -n anihpj

# 3. Test what they CANNOT do (equally important)
kubectl auth can-i delete secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-sa -n anihpj

# 4. List all permissions in readable format
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-sa
Explanation

kubectl auth can-i --list --as= is the most comprehensive RBAC audit command. It shows every resource and verb the subject can access. Use this before deploying any pod — verify the SA has exactly the permissions it needs and nothing more.

Q10
What security risks come from long-lived, never-expiring ServiceAccount tokens? How does the CKS exam expect you to mitigate this?
Show Answer
Answer

Risks: Token leaked in logs/backup/repo → attacker has permanent API access. No rotation → breach goes unnoticed indefinitely. No audience restriction → token usable anywhere.

CKS mitigation:

  • Use bound tokens (auto-expire, audience-scoped)
  • Set automountServiceAccountToken: false for pods that don't need API access
  • Use projected volumes with short expiry
  • Audit SA permissions regularly
Explanation

Static tokens are the Kubernetes equivalent of hardcoded passwords that never change. The CKS exam expects you to: (1) prefer bound tokens, (2) disable token mount where unnecessary, (3) use dedicated SAs with least privilege. These three practices eliminate the token persistence risk.

Chapter 11: Node Restriction & Hardening Authorization

The NodeRestriction admission plugin limits what a compromised kubelet can do — without it, a single breached worker node can modify labels on any other node or evict pods cluster-wide. Combined with proper authorization modes, this chapter locks down node-level access.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1 hour🔧 Hands-On🎯 Node Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What NodeRestriction does and why it's required by CIS Benchmark 1.2.17
  • ✅ How authorization modes chain together (Node,RBAC is the secure default)
  • ✅ How to protect node-level access with SSH hardening and IAM

11.1 The NodeRestriction Admission Plugin

NodeRestriction limits what kubelets can modify via the API. Without it, a compromised kubelet on node-worker-2 can modify labels on node-worker-1 or evict pods from node-worker-3 — enabling cluster-wide privilege escalation.

Before vs After — The Blast Radius Difference

🔴 WITHOUT NodeRestriction

Compromised kubelet on worker-2 CAN:

  • Modify labels on worker-1
  • Evict pods from worker-3
  • Modify labels on pods it doesn't run
  • Impersonate other nodes
✅ WITH NodeRestriction

Compromised kubelet on worker-2 CAN ONLY:

  • Read its own node object
  • Modify its own node status/labels
  • Read/write pods ON worker-2 only
  • Cannot touch worker-1 or worker-3
Enable NodeRestriction
# In /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity

11.2 Authorization Modes — Understanding the Chain

Kubernetes supports multiple authorization modes simultaneously. Modes are checked in order; the first ALLOW stops the chain. The secure configuration is --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC.

Authorization Modes Compared

ModeHow It WorksSecurity Level
AlwaysAllowAllow everything, no checks🔴 NEVER use
AlwaysDenyDeny everything (testing only)⚠️ Testing
RBACRoles + Bindings✅ Use this
NodeKubelet access control✅ Required
WebhookExternal authorization service✅ Advanced
ABACAttribute-based, file-based (legacy)⚠️ Legacy
💡 Secure Configuration

--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC — Modes are checked in order. The first ALLOW stops the chain. Always include both Node and RBAC. Never include AlwaysAllow.

11.3 Protecting Node-Level Access

Beyond Kubernetes-native controls, the underlying node operating system must be hardened against direct access. SSH configuration is a critical part of the defense.

Node Access Hardening Checklist

📋 Node Access Hardening Checklist
  • □ SSH access: use SSO, audit keys, remove stale users
  • □ Disable root SSH login: PermitRootLogin no in sshd_config
  • □ Use SSH key-based auth only — disable password login
  • □ Use node groups and IAM roles for cloud-managed nodes
  • □ Never expose kubelet API (port 10250) to the internet
  • □ Rotate SSH keys regularly; remove keys for departed team members

📝 Chapter 11 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What does the NodeRestriction admission plugin do? What specific attacks does it prevent?
Show Answer
Answer

NodeRestriction limits kubelets to ONLY modify: (1) their own Node object, (2) pods bound to their node. Without it, a compromised kubelet could: modify labels on other nodes (attracting sensitive pods), evict pods from other nodes (DoS), or modify its own node's taints to prevent scheduling.

Explanation

NodeRestriction is required by CIS 1.2.17. Combined with Node authorization mode, it creates a tight sandbox: kubelets can only work with their own resources. Add it to --enable-admission-plugins in the API server manifest.

Q2
Explain the authorization mode chain: Node,RBAC. In what order are they evaluated? What happens when Node authorizer denies a request?
Show Answer
Answer

Evaluation order: Node first, then RBAC. Node authorizer handles kubelet requests specifically (pod listing, node status updates, etc.). If Node authorizer DENIES, the request passes to RBAC. If Node authorizer ALLOWS, the request succeeds immediately (RBAC is skipped).

Explanation

The chain is "first match wins" — once an authorizer says ALLOW, no further authorizers are checked. This is why Node must come before RBAC: Node is more restrictive for kubelet requests (only own pods), while RBAC might accidentally grant broader access.

Q3
How do you enable NodeRestriction? Where is it configured, and how do you verify it's working?
Show Answer
Answer
# In /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
- --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,...
# Also ensure authorization mode includes Node
- --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC

# Verify: kubelet should only see its own pods
kubectl get pods -A --as=system:node:worker-1
# Should only show pods on worker-1
Explanation

NodeRestriction alone isn't enough — you need BOTH --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction AND --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC. The admission plugin enforces the restriction; the authorization mode gives kubelets the Node identity. Run kube-bench check 1.2.17 to verify.

Q4
What specific labels and taints could a malicious kubelet modify on another node, and what would be the security impact?
Show Answer
Answer
ModificationImpact
Add label env=production to attacker's nodeProduction pods scheduled on compromised node
Remove taint NoSchedule from critical nodeNon-critical pods land on sensitive infrastructure
Change node-role.kubernetes.io/master labelDisrupt control plane scheduling
Modify topology.kubernetes.io/zoneBreak anti-affinity rules, cause availability issues
Explanation

Without NodeRestriction, a compromised kubelet can manipulate the scheduler by modifying node metadata on ANY node. This enables sophisticated attacks: attract sensitive pods to compromised nodes, or push critical pods off healthy nodes. NodeRestriction blocks all of these.

Q5
How do you secure SSH access to Kubernetes nodes? List 5 SSH hardening measures relevant to CKS.
Show Answer
Answer
  1. Disable root SSH login: PermitRootLogin no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  2. Key-based auth only: PasswordAuthentication no
  3. Restrict users: AllowUsers admin@10.0.0.0/8
  4. Change default port: Port 2222 (security by obscurity, but reduces noise)
  5. Use SSH bastion/jump host: No direct SSH from internet to nodes
Explanation

CKS Domain 3 (System Hardening) includes SSH hardening. After editing sshd_config, restart SSH: systemctl restart sshd. Always test from a NEW session before closing your current one — a bad SSH config can lock you out.

Q6
What is the difference between Node authorization mode and RBAC? Why do you need both?
Show Answer
Answer
FeatureNode AuthorizationRBAC
ScopeKubelets onlyAll subjects (users, SAs, groups)
GranularityFixed: own node + podsFully customizable
ConfigurationBuilt-in, no YAML neededRole/ClusterRole YAML required

You need BOTH because: Node handles kubelet access (efficient, hardcoded rules), RBAC handles everything else (users, SAs, custom policies). Without Node, kubelets would need complex RBAC rules. Without RBAC, there's no access control for users.

Explanation

The CKS exam expects --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC on every cluster. Never use just RBAC alone — kubelets need Node authorization for proper scoping. Never use AlwaysAllow — it's a massive security hole.

Q7
How can you verify that a kubelet can only see its own pods? Write the test commands.
Show Answer
Answer
# Get kubelet client certificate
KUBELET_CERT=/var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem

# Test: list pods as kubelet
curl -k --cert $KUBELET_CERT --key /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem https://localhost:6443/api/v1/pods

# Or with kubectl
kubectl get pods -A --as=system:node:<node-name>
# Should show ONLY pods running on <node-name>

# Verify CANNOT see pods on another node
kubectl get pods -A --as=system:node:worker-1 --field-selector spec.nodeName=worker-2
# Should return: No resources found
Explanation

This verification confirms NodeRestriction and Node authorization are working. A kubelet should see its own pods but NOT pods on other nodes. If it can see all pods, Node authorization is misconfigured — likely --authorization-mode=RBAC without Node.

Q8
What is the Node authorizer's "escalation prevention" feature? Give a concrete example of what it blocks.
Show Answer
Answer

The Node authorizer prevents a kubelet from modifying its own Node object in a way that escalates privileges. Example: a kubelet CANNOT change its own node-role.kubernetes.io/master label to become a control plane node, or modify its own taints to prevent eviction of critical pods.

Explanation

Without escalation prevention, a compromised kubelet could promote its node to a master role, gaining access to control plane pod specs. Node authorizer specifically blocks modifications to labels prefixed with node-role.kubernetes.io/ and node-restriction.kubernetes.io/.

Q9
Write the kubelet configuration that enables Webhook authorization and disables anonymous auth. Where is this file located?
Show Answer
Answer
# File: /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false
  webhook:
    enabled: true
    cacheTTL: 2m
authorization:
  mode: Webhook
Explanation

Kubelet webhook auth delegates authorization decisions to the API server. This ensures the API server's RBAC rules apply to kubelet API requests too. The config file path /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml is a CKS exam must-know. After editing, restart kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet.

Q10
Create a comprehensive node security checklist for the anihpj production cluster covering: NodeRestriction, authorization, kubelet config, SSH, firewall, and kernel hardening.
Show Answer
Answer
  1. ☑ API server: --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
  2. ☑ API server: --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction
  3. ☑ Kubelet: authentication.anonymous.enabled: false
  4. ☑ Kubelet: authorization.mode: Webhook
  5. ☑ SSH: PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no
  6. ☑ Firewall: only 6443 (API), 10250 (kubelet), 22 (SSH)
  7. ☑ Remove unused packages: apt remove --purge <pkg>
  8. ☑ Kernel: apply seccomp profiles to all pods
  9. ☑ Audit: run kube-bench --targets=node weekly
Explanation

This checklist maps to CKS Domain 3 (System Hardening). Each item directly addresses a CIS Benchmark check or a CKS exam objective. Print this and use it as your node hardening reference before the exam.

Chapter 12: Kubernetes Version Management for Security

Running outdated Kubernetes versions means running known, published vulnerabilities. CVEs like CVE-2018-1002105 (CVSS 9.8) allow privilege escalation to cluster-admin. This chapter covers the upgrade strategy, the K8s support matrix, and when to apply security patches vs minor upgrades.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1 hour📖 Concepts🎯 Version Mgmt

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why running outdated K8s versions is a critical security risk
  • ✅ Notable CVEs and their impact on cluster security
  • ✅ The 3-phase safe upgrade strategy (prepare → control plane → workers)
  • ✅ When to apply patches immediately vs plan minor upgrades

12.1 Why Keeping Kubernetes Updated Is a Security Requirement

CVESeverityAffectedImpact
CVE-2018-1002105 "The Big Bird"CRITICAL 9.8<1.10.11, <1.11.5, <1.12.3Privilege escalation to cluster-admin via API server proxy
CVE-2019-11247HIGH 8.1<1.13.9, <1.14.5RBAC bypass: access cluster-scoped resources as namespace-scoped
CVE-2021-25741HIGH 8.1<1.19.15, <1.20.11, <1.21.5Symlink attack: hostPath volume escapes restriction
CVE-2022-3294HIGH 7.6<1.25.4, <1.24.8Node address type confusion → man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack possible
⚠️ How Attackers Exploit Known CVEs

When a CVE is published, attackers immediately begin scanning the internet for vulnerable clusters. CVE-2018-1002105 (the "Big Bird" vulnerability) was particularly dangerous: an attacker could send a specially crafted request through the API server's proxy functionality to escalate from any authenticated user to full cluster-admin. The fix was released within days — but clusters that didn't upgrade remained vulnerable for months or years. The lesson: when a critical CVE is announced, treat the patch as an emergency. Attackers are already looking for you.

📅 Kubernetes Version Release Lifecycle — How to Stay Ahead

The K8s Version Support Window — Plan Your Upgrades
  2024                    2025                    2026
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  
  v1.29  ████████████████░░░░  (EOL ~Feb 2025)
         │   supported   │  EOL │
  
  v1.30     ████████████████░░░░  (EOL ~Jun 2025)
            │   supported   │  EOL │
  
  v1.31        ████████████████░░░░  (EOL ~Oct 2025)
               │   supported   │  EOL │
  
  v1.32           ████████████████████████  (CURRENT)
                  │       supported         │
  
  📏 RULE: Only 3 minor versions supported at any time
     → Run N, N-1, or N-2 ONLY
     → N-3 is UNSAFE — no patches, even for CRITICAL CVEs
  
  ⏱️  PATCH RELEASES: Every 4-6 weeks → APPLY IMMEDIATELY
  ⏱️  MINOR RELEASES: Every 4 months → PLAN within 6-8 months
  ⏱️  EOL DEADLINE:   ~14 months after release → UPGRADE BEFORE

K8s Support Matrix

VersionStatusAction
1.31 (latest)✅ Fully supportedSafe to run
1.30✅ SupportedSafe to run
1.29✅ SupportedSafe to run
1.28❌ End of LifeURGENT upgrade — no more patches!

12.2 Upgrade Strategy for a Running Cluster

1
PREPARE

kubeadm upgrade plan
Backup etcd
Check addon compat

2
UPGRADE CP

apt-get install kubeadm
kubeadm upgrade apply
restart kubelet

3
UPGRADE WORKERS

kubectl drain worker
upgrade + restart
kubectl uncordon

Complete upgrade commands
# Phase 1: PREPARE
kubeadm upgrade plan                    # See available versions
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-pre-upgrade.db  # Backup etcd
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running   # Check for unhealthy pods

# Phase 2: UPGRADE CONTROL PLANE
apt-get update && apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.29.x-00
kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.x
apt-get install -y kubelet=1.29.x-00 kubectl=1.29.x-00
systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get nodes  # → control plane shows new version

# Phase 3: UPGRADE WORKER NODES (repeat for each worker)
kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
# SSH to worker-1:
apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.29.x-00 kubelet=1.29.x-00
kubeadm upgrade node
systemctl restart kubelet
# Back on control plane:
kubectl uncordon worker-1
kubectl get nodes  # → all nodes show v1.29.x ✅

12.3 Security Patches vs Minor Upgrades

🔴 PATCH (1.29.0→1.29.5)

Security fixes only. Apply IMMEDIATELY when CVE is in release notes.

🟡 MINOR (1.29→1.30)

New features. Test in staging, upgrade within 6-8 months.

🔴 EOL: Running N-3 or Older

No more security patches, even for CRITICAL CVEs. You are running known, published vulnerabilities that attackers actively scan for. Upgrade is URGENT — this is not a "plan for next sprint" situation.

How to Decide: Patch Now or Plan Later?

Did a new CVE get published affecting your version?
YES → Apply patch IMMEDIATELYNO ↓
Are you running N-3 (End of Life)?
YES → URGENT: plan upgrade this weekNO ↓
Are you 2 minor versions behind (N-2)?
YES → Schedule upgrade within 2 monthsNO ↓
→ You're on a supported version with no active CVEs. Continue monitoring release notes monthly.

ChapterYou Should Now Know...Quick Self-Test
Ch 8: API ServerDisable anonymous auth, enable audit logging, restrict IPs, remove insecure portWhat flag disables unauthenticated access? → --anonymous-auth=false
Ch 9: RBAC4 resources, least privilege, wildcard dangers, kubectl auth can-i verificationWhich verb grants ALL actions? → * (wildcard — never use)
Ch 10: Service AccountsPod→API auth flow, default SA dangers, bound tokens, automount disableHow to prevent pod from calling K8s API? → automountServiceAccountToken: false
Ch 11: Node RestrictionNodeRestriction limits, authz modes chain, node SSH hardeningWhich 2 authz modes are required? → Node,RBAC
