Chapter 37: Mock Scenarios & Practice Labs

Practice makes perfect. This chapter provides domain-specific practice tasks and a full 17-task mock exam that simulates the real CKS experience. Time yourself. Score yourself. Repeat until you pass.

🔴 Exam Prep⏱️ ~3 hours🔧 Practice🎯 Mock Exam

37.1 Domain 1: Cluster Setup

Task A Run kube-bench on control plane, fix top 3 FAIL items
# 1. Run kube-bench on the control plane
kube-bench run --targets=master

# 2. Review the output — look for [FAIL] items
# Common FAILs: anonymous-auth enabled, audit logging disabled,
#               insecure-port not disabled, AlwaysAllow authz mode

# 3. Edit the API server manifest
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# 4. Add/change these flags:
# --anonymous-auth=false
# --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
# --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
# --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC

# 5. Wait for API server to restart (kubelet auto-detects changes)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep apiserver

# 6. Re-run kube-bench to verify fixes
kube-bench run --targets=master --check 1.1.1,1.1.2,1.2.1
# Expected: ALL PASS ✅
Task B Apply NetworkPolicy set to isolate a namespace
# Step 1: Default deny all ingress + egress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
# Step 2: Allow inbound from ingress controller
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-ingress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: ingress-nginx
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8000
---
# Step 3: Allow DNS egress (essential!)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53

# Apply all policies
kubectl apply -f default-deny.yaml
kubectl apply -f allow-ingress.yaml
kubectl apply -f allow-dns.yaml

# Verify: test pod should NOT reach anything except DNS
kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh -n anihpj-prod
# nslookup kubernetes.default → ✅ works (DNS allowed)
# wget -O- http://anihpj:8000 → ❌ blocked (no egress to pods)
Task C Configure Ingress with TLS for a test service
# 1. Create TLS secret (cert-manager would automate this in production)
kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls \
  --cert=tls.crt \
  --key=tls.key \
  -n anihpj-prod

# Verify the secret
kubectl get secret anihpj-tls -n anihpj-prod
kubectl describe secret anihpj-tls -n anihpj-prod
# 2. Create Ingress resource with TLS
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - anihpj.example.com
    secretName: anihpj-tls
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj-service
            port:
              number: 8000

# 3. Apply and verify
kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml
kubectl get ingress -n anihpj-prod

# 4. Test TLS
curl -k https://anihpj.example.com
# Verify cert: openssl s_client -connect anihpj.example.com:443
Task D Secure Kubernetes Dashboard with token + NetworkPolicy
# 1. Create Service Account and ClusterRoleBinding
kubectl create sa dashboard-admin -n kubernetes-dashboard
kubectl create clusterrolebinding dashboard-admin \
  --clusterrole=cluster-admin \
  --serviceaccount=kubernetes-dashboard:dashboard-admin

# 2. Generate a token (never use the default SA token)
kubectl create token dashboard-admin -n kubernetes-dashboard
# Copy this token — you'll use it to log in

# 3. Apply NetworkPolicy to restrict dashboard access
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: dashboard-restrict
  namespace: kubernetes-dashboard
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      k8s-app: kubernetes-dashboard
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.0/8  # Only internal network
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8443
EOF

# 4. Access dashboard via kubectl proxy (most secure)
kubectl proxy
# Now visit: http://localhost:8001/api/v1/namespaces/kubernetes-dashboard/services/https:kubernetes-dashboard:/proxy/
# Enter the token you generated in step 2

37.2 Domain 2: Cluster Hardening

Task A Disable anonymous auth on API server, verify
# 1. Edit the kube-apiserver static pod manifest
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# 2. Add this flag (or ensure it exists):
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --anonymous-auth=false          # <-- Add this

# 3. Wait for API server to restart (~30 seconds)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep apiserver

# 4. VERIFY — anonymous requests should be REJECTED
kubectl get pods --as=system:anonymous
# Expected: Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden

# 5. Also verify on the API server directly
kubectl get --raw /api --as=system:anonymous
# Expected: {"kind":"Status","reason":"Unauthorized"...}

# ✅ Anonymous auth is now disabled
Task B Create audit policy + enable logging
# 1. Create audit policy file on control plane node
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
# Content:
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
  # Don't log node status updates (noisy)
  - level: None
    users: ["system:nodes"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  # Log pod changes fully
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["create", "update", "delete"]
  # Log secret access at metadata level
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
  # Default: log metadata
  - level: Metadata
# 2. Configure API server to use audit policy
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add these flags + volume mounts:
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
    - --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
    - --audit-log-maxage=30
    - --audit-log-maxbackup=10
    - --audit-log-maxsize=100
    volumeMounts:
    - name: audit-policy
      mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
      readOnly: true
    - name: audit-log
      mountPath: /var/log/kubernetes
  volumes:
  - name: audit-policy
    hostPath:
      path: /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
      type: File
  - name: audit-log
    hostPath:
      path: /var/log/kubernetes
      type: DirectoryOrCreate

# 3. Wait for restart and verify
sudo tail -f /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq .
# You should see JSON audit events streaming
Task C Create minimal RBAC for a ServiceAccount
# 1. Create the ServiceAccount
kubectl create sa anihpj-sa -n anihpj-prod

# 2. Create a minimal Role (only what's needed)
kubectl create role anihpj-role \
  --verb=get,list \
  --resource=pods,services,configmaps \
  -n anihpj-prod

# 3. Bind the Role to the ServiceAccount
kubectl create rolebinding anihpj-binding \
  --role=anihpj-role \
  --serviceaccount=anihpj-prod:anihpj-sa \
  -n anihpj-prod

# 4. VERIFY least privilege
kubectl auth can-i get pods \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-sa \
  -n anihpj-prod
# Expected: yes

kubectl auth can-i delete secrets \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-sa \
  -n anihpj-prod
# Expected: no ✅ (least privilege enforced)
Task D Configure SA with automount disabled
# Method 1: Patch the default SA in a namespace
kubectl patch sa default \
  -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken":false}' \
  -n anihpj-prod

# Method 2: Create a new SA with automount disabled
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: no-api-access
  namespace: anihpj-prod
automountServiceAccountToken: false
EOF

# Verify — new pods using this SA will have NO mounted token
kubectl run test --image=busybox --restart=Never \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"no-api-access"}}' \
  -n anihpj-prod -- sleep 3600

kubectl exec test -n anihpj-prod -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
# Expected: ls: cannot access: No such file or directory ✅

37.3 Domain 3: System Hardening

Task A Load AppArmor profile and apply to a pod
# 1. Create an AppArmor profile on the node
sudo vi /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-profile
# Content: deny writes to /etc/, allow everything else
#include <tunables/global>
profile anihpj-profile flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  #include <abstractions/python>
  # Deny writes to /etc/
  deny /etc/** w,
  # Allow everything else
  /** rwkl,
}

# 2. Load the profile
sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-profile

# 3. Verify it's loaded
sudo aa-status | grep anihpj-profile
# Expected: anihpj-profile (enforce)

# 4. Apply to a pod (annotation-based in K8s < 1.30)
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-secure
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj: localhost/anihpj-profile
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: anihpj:v2
EOF

# 5. Verify enforcement
kubectl exec anihpj-secure -n anihpj-prod -- touch /etc/test
# Expected: touch: cannot touch '/etc/test': Permission denied ✅
Task B Apply seccomp RuntimeDefault to a pod
# Pod YAML with RuntimeDefault seccomp profile
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: seccomp-pod
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault  # blocks ~300 dangerous syscalls
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
# Verify seccomp is active
kubectl get pod seccomp-pod -n anihpj-prod \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type}'
# Expected: RuntimeDefault

# The pod can still function normally, but dangerous syscalls
# (like mount, ptrace, create_module) are blocked by the kernel
Task C Harden kubelet config
# Edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml on each node
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false    # Block unauthenticated requests
  webhook:
    enabled: true     # Use API server token review
authorization:
  mode: Webhook       # Always check RBAC
readOnlyPort: 0       # Disable read-only port (10255)
protectKernelDefaults: true  # Prevent kernel tuning changes
# After editing, restart kubelet
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
sudo systemctl status kubelet

# Verify anonymous auth is blocked on kubelet
curl -k https://localhost:10250/pods --header "Authorization: Bearer fake"
# Expected: Unauthorized

# Verify read-only port is disabled
curl http://localhost:10255/healthz
# Expected: Connection refused
Task D Remove unnecessary services from a node
# 1. List all running services
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running

# 2. Identify unnecessary services (examples):
# - cups (printing) - not needed on K8s nodes
# - avahi-daemon (mDNS) - security risk
# - rpcbind (RPC) - legacy, not needed
# - bluetooth - not needed on servers

# 3. Stop and disable each
sudo systemctl stop cups avahi-daemon rpcbind bluetooth
sudo systemctl disable cups avahi-daemon rpcbind bluetooth

# 4. Verify they're stopped
systemctl is-active cups avahi-daemon
# Expected: inactive

# 5. Remove unnecessary packages (optional, for security)
sudo apt-get remove --purge cups avahi-daemon -y
# This also removes potential CVE-bearing binaries

37.4 Domain 4: Microservice Vulnerabilities

Task A Apply PSS Restricted to namespace + fix violating pods
# 1. Label the namespace for PSS Restricted enforcement
kubectl label ns anihpj-prod \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted

# 2. Check for existing violating pods
kubectl get events -n anihpj-prod --field-selector reason=FailedCreate
# Look for "violates PodSecurity" messages

# 3. Fix a violating pod (example: running as root)
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-pss-fixed
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: anihpj:v2
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
EOF
# ✅ Now compliant with Restricted PSS
Task B Add full security context to anihpj pod
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-hardened
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  # Pod-level securityContext
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 1000
    fsGroup: 1000
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
    # Container-level securityContext (overrides pod-level)
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
      runAsNonRoot: true
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
    - name: media
      mountPath: /app/media
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: media
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: anihpj-media-pvc

# Run kubesec to score:
kubectl apply -f anihpj-hardened.yaml --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubesec scan -
# Expected score: ≥ 8/10
Task C Enable encryption at rest for Secrets
# 1. Create EncryptionConfiguration (on control plane)
# File: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources:
  - secrets
  providers:
  - aescbc:
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: $(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)
  - identity: {}  # fallback for reading old plaintext secrets
# 2. Configure API server to use encryption
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add: --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
# Add volumeMount + volume for the file

# 3. Rotate all existing secrets (rewrite them encrypted)
kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -

# 4. VERIFY encryption is working
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/anihpj-prod/anihpj-secret \
  | hexdump -C
# Look for "k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:key1:" prefix → encrypted ✅
# If you see plaintext values → NOT encrypted ❌
Task D Apply RuntimeClass gVisor to untrusted workload
# 1. Create RuntimeClass resource
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc  # gVisor's OCI runtime handler
# 2. Apply RuntimeClass to a pod
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: untrusted-upload-handler
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor  # <-- This pod gets sandboxed!
  containers:
  - name: processor
    image: anihpj-media-processor:v1
    securityContext:
      runAsNonRoot: true
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault

# 3. Verify gVisor is active
kubectl exec untrusted-upload-handler -n anihpj-prod -- dmesg
# Expected: dmesg: read kernel buffer failed: Operation not permitted
# (gVisor's sentry blocks raw kernel access)

37.5 Domain 5: Supply Chain Security

Task A Scan image with Trivy, report CRITICAL CVEs
# 1. Scan the image (local or remote)
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v1

# Output example:
# anihpj:v1 (debian 11.6)
# Total: 23 (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 8, MEDIUM: 13)
#
# CVE-2023-38545 (CRITICAL) curl 7.74.0 → Fixed in 7.88.1
# CVE-2023-4911  (CRITICAL) glibc 2.31 → Fixed in 2.36

# 2. Document findings and fix
echo "CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 8" > scan-report.txt

# 3. Rebuild image with patched base
docker build -t registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 \
  --build-arg BASE_IMAGE=python:3.12-slim .

# 4. Re-scan to verify fixes
trivy image --severity CRITICAL \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
# Expected: CRITICAL: 0 ✅

# 5. Gate in CI/CD (exit code 1 = fail build)
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 || exit 1
Task B Create OPA ConstraintTemplate for approved registries
# ConstraintTemplate: K8sAllowedRegistries
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sallowedregistries
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sAllowedRegistries
      validation:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            registries:
              type: array
              items:
                type: string
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8sallowedregistries
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        satisfied := [good |
          registry := input.parameters.registries[_]
          good := startswith(container.image, registry)
        ]
        not any(satisfied)
        msg := sprintf("image %v not from approved registry", [container.image])
      }
# Constraint: enforce the policy
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sAllowedRegistries
metadata:
  name: allowed-registries
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      kinds: ["Pod"]
    namespaces: ["anihpj-prod"]
  parameters:
    registries:
    - registry.anihpj.com/
    - gcr.io/anihpj-project/

# Apply and test
kubectl apply -f constraint-template.yaml
kubectl apply -f constraint.yaml

# Test: try deploying from Docker Hub (should be DENIED)
kubectl run test --image=nginx -n anihpj-prod
# Expected: admission webhook "validation.gatekeeper.sh" denied
Task C Sign image with cosign + configure Kyverno to verify
# 1. Generate cosign key pair (store securely!)
cosign generate-key-pair
# Creates: cosign.key (private), cosign.pub (public)

# 2. Sign the image
cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
# Signature stored alongside image in registry

# 3. Verify manually (optional pre-flight check)
cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
# Expected: Verification for registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 --
#           The following checks were performed...
#           ✅ The signature is valid
# 4. Create Kyverno ClusterPolicy to enforce verification
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: verify-anihpj-images
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: verify-cosign-signature
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences:
      - "registry.anihpj.com/*"
      attestors:
      - count: 1
        entries:
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |-
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              ...cosign.pub content...
              -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

# 5. Apply and test
kubectl apply -f kyverno-verify.yaml
# Try deploying unsigned image → DENIED
# Deploy signed v2 → ALLOWED ✅
Task D Deploy ImagePolicyWebhook + test rejection
# 1. ImagePolicyWebhook admission config (on control plane)
# File: /etc/kubernetes/admission-config.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: AdmissionConfiguration
plugins:
- name: ImagePolicyWebhook
  configuration:
    imagePolicy:
      kubeConfigFile: /etc/kubernetes/imagepolicy-kubeconfig.yaml
      allowTTL: 300
      denyTTL: 300
      retryBackoff: 500
      defaultAllow: false  # Default DENY if webhook unreachable
# 2. Configure API server to use admission config
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add flags:
# --admission-control-config-file=/etc/kubernetes/admission-config.yaml
# --enable-admission-plugins=...,ImagePolicyWebhook

# 3. Test: try deploying an image the webhook denies
kubectl run test --image=untrusted-registry.com/bad:latest
# Expected: Error from server (Forbidden): admission webhook denied

# 4. Verify rejection log on webhook server side
# The external webhook server logs should show the denied request

37.6 Domain 6: Runtime Security

Task A Configure Falco to log secret reads
# 1. Add custom rule to /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml
- rule: Read Secret Files in Container
  desc: Detect any process reading files under /var/run/secrets/
  condition: >
    open_read and
    container and
    fd.name startswith /var/run/secrets/ and
    not proc.name in (known_binaries)
  output: >
    Secret file read! (user=%user.name
    command=%proc.cmdline file=%fd.name
    container=%container.name
    k8s_ns=%k8s.ns.name k8s_pod=%k8s.pod.name)
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [filesystem, secrets, CKS]
# 2. Restart Falco to load new rules
kubectl rollout restart daemonset falco -n falco

# 3. Test the rule
kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -n anihpj-prod -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token

# 4. Check Falco logs for the alert
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=50 | grep "Secret file read"
# Expected alert should appear within seconds
Task B Write Falco rule to detect shell in specific container
# 1. Define shell_binaries list (at top of rules file)
- list: shell_binaries
  items: [bash, sh, zsh, dash, ksh]

# 2. Define a macro for the target container
- macro: anihpj_container
  condition: container.name = "anihpj"

# 3. Create the detection rule
- rule: Shell Spawned in anihpj Container
  desc: >
    Detect any shell being spawned inside the anihpj container.
    Django apps should NEVER spawn shells at runtime.
  condition: >
    spawned_process and
    anihpj_container and
    proc.name in (shell_binaries)
  output: >
    🚨 Shell spawned in anihpj!
    (user=%user.name cmd=%proc.cmdline
    container=%container.name
    pod=%k8s.pod.name ns=%k8s.ns.name)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [anihpj, shell, CKS, runtime]
# 4. Apply and restart Falco
sudo vi /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml  # add above rules
kubectl rollout restart daemonset falco -n falco

# 5. Test by exec'ing into the container
kubectl exec -it anihpj-xxx -n anihpj-prod -- /bin/bash
# Falco should immediately trigger the CRITICAL alert
Task C Investigate a Falco alert
# SCENARIO: You receive a Falco alert:
# "Shell spawned in anihpj! (user=root cmd=bash container=anihpj)"

# 1. Check Falco logs for full context
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=200 | grep "Shell spawned"

# 2. Identify which pod triggered the alert
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=200 \
  | jq 'select(.output | contains("Shell")) | {time: .time, pod: .output_fields["k8s.pod.name"], cmd: .output_fields["proc.cmdline"]}'

# 3. Investigate the pod
POD_NAME=$(kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=200 \
  | grep "Shell spawned" | jq -r '.output_fields["k8s.pod.name"]')

kubectl describe pod $POD_NAME -n anihpj-prod
kubectl logs $POD_NAME -n anihpj-prod --tail=100

# 4. Check if this is a legitimate operation
# Look at: who ran it? when? from where?
kubectl get events -n anihpj-prod --field-selector involvedObject.name=$POD_NAME

# 5. Check audit logs for exec events on this pod
tail -1000 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | jq 'select(.objectRef.name=="'$POD_NAME'" and .objectRef.subresource=="exec")'
Task D Find suspicious kubectl exec from audit logs
# 1. Query audit logs for exec subresource access
tail -1000 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | jq 'select(.verb=="create" and .objectRef.subresource=="exec")'

# 2. Extract key fields for investigation
tail -2000 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | jq 'select(.verb=="create" and .objectRef.subresource=="exec") | {
    time: .requestReceivedTimestamp,
    user: .user.username,
    pod: .objectRef.name,
    namespace: .objectRef.namespace,
    source_ip: .sourceIPs[0],
    user_agent: .userAgent
  }'

# 3. Filter for non-CI/CD users (suspicious execs)
tail -2000 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | jq 'select(
    .verb=="create" and
    .objectRef.subresource=="exec" and
    (.user.username | startswith("system:serviceaccount:ci") | not)
  )'

# 4. Look for execs in production at unusual hours
tail -5000 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | jq 'select(
    .verb=="create" and
    .objectRef.subresource=="exec" and
    .objectRef.namespace=="anihpj-prod" and
    (.requestReceivedTimestamp | fromdateiso8601 | strftime("%H") | tonumber) < 7
  )'
# Finds execs between midnight and 7 AM — highly suspicious!

38.3 Security Context Quick Reference

securityContext:                    # Pod-level
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  runAsGroup: 1000
  fsGroup: 1000
  seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
containers:
- name: app
  securityContext:                  # Container-level
    allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}
    appArmorProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: profile-name}

38.4 NetworkPolicy Quick Reference

# Default deny all ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny, namespace: ns}
spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress]}
---
# Allow pod→pod on specific port
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: db}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: frontend}}}]
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
---
# Allow DNS egress (always needed!)
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to: [{namespaceSelector: {}}]
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]

38.5 Falco Rule Quick Reference

- rule: Shell in Container
  condition: spawned_process and container.name="app" and proc.name in (shell_binaries)
  output: Shell in app! (user=%user.name cmd=%proc.cmdline)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [shell, app]
# Key fields: spawned_process, container.name, proc.name, proc.cmdline, fd.name
# Macros: - macro: app_container; condition: container.name = "app"
# Lists:  - list: shell_binaries; items: [bash, sh, zsh]
# Config: /etc/falco/falco.yaml → json_output: true for SIEM

⚠️ Context Switching — The #1 CKS Exam Killer

The CKS exam uses multiple clusters. Each task specifies which cluster context to use. If you forget to switch, you'll solve the right problem on the wrong cluster and get zero points. Run the context command FIRST for every single task:

Terminal — context switching (EVERY task!)
# The exam says: "Use context: cks-cluster-1"
kubectl config use-context cks-cluster-1

# Verify you're on the right cluster
kubectl config current-context

# List all available contexts (shows which is CURRENT)
kubectl config get-contexts

# Set default namespace (saves typing -n every time)
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=anihpj-prod

💡 A.1 Pro Tips
  • Impersonation is your friend: Use --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:sa to verify RBAC without creating actual pods. No pod needed — just check permissions from the API.
  • ClusterRole vs Role: If the exam says "across all namespaces" → use ClusterRole. If it says "in namespace X" → use Role. Watch for this keyword in task descriptions.
  • SA tokens: After disabling automount, existing pods still have tokens. You must delete and recreate the pod for the change to take effect.

ActionCommand
Check seccomp on podkubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type}'
Check AppArmor on podkubectl get pod <name> -o yaml | grep apparmor

⚠️ A.2 Pro Tips
  • kubelet config changes require restart: systemctl restart kubelet. Check status after: systemctl status kubelet. A bad config can prevent nodes from joining.
  • AppArmor profiles must exist on EVERY node: The pod gets scheduled to a node that may not have the profile loaded. Use ssh <node> aa-status to verify before applying pods.
  • Seccomp RuntimeDefault vs Unconfined: RuntimeDefault blocks ~300 syscalls but can break apps using clone, mount, or ptrace. If a pod fails after adding seccomp, check kubectl describe pod for the blocked syscall.

🔍 A.3 Pro Tips
  • PSS labels are additive: You can set all three modes (enforce + audit + warn) on the same namespace. Audit mode logs violations without blocking — useful for testing before enforcing.
  • Test NetworkPolicy with busybox: kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh — then use wget, nslookup, nc to test connectivity. Always verify DNS works first!
  • jsonpath is your secret weapon: kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext}' gives you a clean view of security settings without grepping through full YAML.

🚨 A.4 Pro Tips
  • Audit log jq is essential: tail -f /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.verb=="create" and .objectRef.subresource=="exec")' finds exec events. Practice jq queries before the exam — they save minutes.
  • Falco restart after rule changes: kubectl rollout restart ds falco -n falco. Always verify with kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=20 that the new rules loaded.
  • etcd encryption verification: The encrypted data will show k8s:enc:aescbc:v1: prefix. Plaintext secrets will show readable JSON. If you see both, rotation is incomplete — run kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -.
  • Trivy --exit-code 1: This flag makes Trivy fail the CI pipeline when CRITICAL CVEs are found. Without it, Trivy just reports and succeeds — useless as a gate.

B.1 Hardened Pod Template — Full Security Context

A production-ready pod spec with every security field set. Start here, then remove what you don't need for the exam task. Covers cks.txt templates B.4 (Pod Security Context), B.7 (SA automount), and B.11 (AppArmor).

📦 Complete Hardened Pod — All Security Fields
anihpj-hardened-pod.yaml — Every security field in one manifest
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-hardened
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  labels:
    app: anihpj
    version: v2
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj: localhost/anihpj-profile
spec:
  # ─── POD-LEVEL SECURITY ───
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true        # 🚫 Never run as UID 0
    runAsUser: 1000           # 👤 Specific non-root user
    runAsGroup: 1000          # 👥 Specific group
    fsGroup: 1000             # 📁 Volume ownership
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault    # 🔒 Block ~300 dangerous syscalls
  # ─── SERVICE ACCOUNT ───
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa
  automountServiceAccountToken: false  # 🔐 No API access by default
  # ─── CONTAINERS ───
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2@sha256:abc123...
    imagePullPolicy: Always
    # ─── CONTAINER-LEVEL SECURITY ───
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false   # 🚫 No setuid binaries
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true      # 🛡️ Immutable filesystem
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]                   # 🚫 Drop ALL Linux capabilities
      runAsNonRoot: true                # 👤 Double-enforce
    # ─── RESOURCES ───
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: "100m"
        memory: "128Mi"
      limits:
        cpu: "500m"
        memory: "512Mi"
    # ─── VOLUMES ───
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp        # Writable scratch space
    - name: media
      mountPath: /app/media  # User uploads (PVC-backed)
    - name: apparmor-socket
      mountPath: /var/run/apparmor
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: media
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: anihpj-media-pvc
🔧 ServiceAccount — Disabled Automount
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: no-api-access
  namespace: anihpj-prod
automountServiceAccountToken: false  # ⭐ The key field
---
# Pod using this SA:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: no-api-pod
spec:
  serviceAccountName: no-api-access
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
💡 When to disable automount

Disable for any pod that doesn't need to call the Kubernetes API. Django apps, databases, caches, and static file servers typically never need API access. This prevents token theft and reduces your attack surface significantly.

B.2 Hardened Deployment Template

Production-ready Deployment with rolling update strategy, health probes, resource limits, and all security fields. Uses the hardened pod spec from B.1 as its template — combine them for a complete production manifest.

💡 Deployment vs Pod — When to Use Which

Use a Pod when the exam task says "create a pod with security context X." Use a Deployment when the task says "deploy an application" or "ensure 3 replicas." The Deployment wraps the Pod template — all security fields go inside spec.template.spec.

🚀 Complete Hardened Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  labels:
    app: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1     # Zero-downtime deploys
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          protocol: TCP
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
        resources:
          requests: {cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi"}
          limits:   {cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi"}
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}

B.3 NetworkPolicy Templates — The Complete Set

Three essential NetworkPolicy templates covering B.1 (Default Deny), B.2 (Pod-to-Pod Allow), and B.3 (DNS Egress) from the cks.txt curriculum. Combine them to build zero-trust networking in any namespace.

⚠️ NetworkPolicy Ordering on the Exam

Always apply in this order: ① Default Deny first → ② DNS Egress (or nothing resolves!) → ③ Specific Allow rules. If you apply Deny last, you'll lock yourself out. If DNS isn't allowed, pods can't resolve service names — and connecting to the API server or any pod by name will fail.

🌐 Template 1: Default Deny All (Ingress + Egress)
# ALWAYS apply this FIRST — then add allow rules
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}              # Applies to ALL pods
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress                    # Block all incoming
  - Egress                     # Block all outgoing
# ⚠️ After applying, NOTHING works until you add allow rules
🌐 Template 2: Allow Specific Pod-to-Pod (with port)
# Allow anihpj pods to reach postgres on TCP 5432
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-anihpj-to-postgres
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres           # TARGET: postgres pods
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj         # SOURCE: only anihpj pods
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
  # Also allow from monitoring namespace
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: monitoring
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
🌐 Template 3: Allow DNS Egress (Always Needed!)
# Without this, pods can't resolve ANY hostname
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}             # All pods need DNS
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}   # Any namespace
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns   # CoreDNS pods
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53                # DNS uses UDP 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53                # Some DNS queries use TCP

B.4 RBAC Templates — Role, RoleBinding, ClusterRole

Least-privilege RBAC manifests covering B.5 (Role + RoleBinding) and B.6 (ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding) from the cks.txt curriculum. Always verify with kubectl auth can-i after applying.

👤 Role + RoleBinding — Namespace-Scoped Read-Only
# Role: read-only access to pods and services in one namespace
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: anihpj-prod
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]               # Core API group
  resources: ["pods", "services"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]  # Read-only — no create/update/delete
---
# RoleBinding: bind Role to ServiceAccount
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-pods
  namespace: anihpj-prod
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: monitoring-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
🌐 ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding — Cross-Namespace Viewer
# ClusterRole: read pods across ALL namespaces
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: cluster-pod-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "nodes"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
# ClusterRoleBinding: grant to a specific user
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-cluster-pods
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: security-auditor
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cluster-pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

B.5 Security Templates — Audit, Encryption, Admission, PSS

Critical security resource YAMLs covering B.8 (Audit Policy), B.9 (EncryptionConfiguration), B.12 (OPA ConstraintTemplate), B.13 (Kyverno non-root), B.14 (Kyverno verifyImages), and B.15 (PSS Labels) from the cks.txt curriculum — 6 templates in one section.

📋 Audit Policy — CKS Exam Ready (Medium Coverage)
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
# Omit stages that are not matching
omitStages:
- "RequestReceived"
rules:
# Don't log system node status updates (very noisy)
- level: None
  users: ["system:nodes"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
# Log pod lifecycle fully (who created/updated/deleted pods)
- level: RequestResponse
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["create", "update", "delete", "patch"]
# Log secret access at metadata (don't log values!)
- level: Metadata
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
# Log RBAC changes fully
- level: RequestResponse
  resources:
  - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
    resources: ["roles", "rolebindings", "clusterroles", "clusterrolebindings"]
# Default: log everything else at metadata level
- level: Metadata
🔐 EncryptionConfiguration — AES-GCM for Secrets
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources:
  - secrets
  providers:
  # PRIMARY: AES-GCM (stronger, authenticated encryption)
  - aesgcm:
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: YWJjZGVmZ2hpamtsbW5vcHFyc3R1dnd4eXowMTIzNDU=
  # SECONDARY: AES-CBC (fallback compatibility)
  - aescbc:
      keys:
      - name: key2
        secret: MTIzNDU2Nzg5MGFiY2RlZmdoaWprbG1ub3BxcnN0dQ==
  # TERTIARY: identity (plaintext) for reading old unencrypted secrets
  - identity: {}
# API server flag: --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
# After applying: kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
⚖️ OPA Gatekeeper — Approved Registry ConstraintTemplate
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sallowedregistries
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sAllowedRegistries
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8sallowedregistries
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        satisfied := [good |
          registry := input.parameters.registries[_]
          good := startswith(container.image, registry)
        ]
        not any(satisfied)
        msg := sprintf("image %v not from approved registry", [container.image])
      }
🟢 Kyverno — Require Non-Root (ClusterPolicy)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-non-root
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-runasnonroot
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "Running as root is not allowed. Set runAsNonRoot: true."
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - securityContext:
              runAsNonRoot: true
🔏 Kyverno — verifyImages with Cosign
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: verify-anihpj-images
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-image-signature
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences:
      - "registry.anihpj.com/*"
      attestors:
      - count: 1
        entries:
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |-
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              MFkwEwYHKoZI...
              -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
🏷️ PSS Labels — All Three Enforcement Modes
# PSS Restricted (maximum security — production)
kubectl label ns anihpj-prod \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted

# PSS Baseline (moderate security — development)
kubectl label ns anihpj-dev \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline

# PSS Privileged (no restrictions — system namespaces only)
kubectl label ns kube-system \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged \
  --overwrite

B.6 Falco Rule Template — Complete with Macros & Lists

A fully commented Falco rule covering B.10 from the cks.txt curriculum. Includes lists, macros, and two detection rules (shell spawn + sensitive file read). Adapt the condition for any exam task that asks you to write a Falco rule.

🦅 Complete Falco Rule — Shell Detection in anihpj
# ─── LISTS (define reusable value sets) ───
- list: shell_binaries
  items: [bash, sh, zsh, dash, ksh, fish]

- list: sensitive_files
  items: [/etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, /etc/sudoers]

# ─── MACROS (reusable condition fragments) ───
- macro: anihpj_container
  condition: container.name = "anihpj"

- macro: is_shell
  condition: proc.name in (shell_binaries)

# ─── RULES ───
- rule: Shell Spawned in anihpj
  desc: Detect shell execution in the anihpj container
  condition: >
    spawned_process and
    anihpj_container and
    is_shell
  output: >
    🚨 Shell spawned in anihpj!
    user=%user.name cmd=%proc.cmdline
    container=%container.name
    pod=%k8s.pod.name ns=%k8s.ns.name
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [anihpj, shell, CKS, runtime]

- rule: Sensitive File Read in anihpj
  desc: Detect reads of shadow/passwd files
  condition: >
    open_read and
    anihpj_container and
    fd.name in (sensitive_files)
  output: >
    🔐 Sensitive file read!
    user=%user.name file=%fd.name
    container=%container.name
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [anihpj, filesystem, CKS]
💡 CKS Exam Falco Tips
  • Lists: define allowed/blocked values — proc.name in (shell_binaries)
  • Macros: reusable conditions — condition: anihpj_container and is_shell
  • Key fields: spawned_process, container.name, proc.name, proc.cmdline, fd.name, user.name, k8s.ns.name, k8s.pod.name
  • Priority: CRITICAL > WARNING > NOTICE — exam usually asks for WARNING or CRITICAL
  • After editing: kubectl rollout restart ds falco -n falco
🎯 CKS Exam Day — Template Usage Strategy
🟢 Quick Tasks

For RBAC, PSS labels, or simple pod security — use the templates as-is, just change names/namespaces. Don't overthink — copy, paste, adapt, apply.

🟡 Medium Tasks

For NetworkPolicy or audit policy — use the structure but customize rules. Remember to test with busybox and verify with kubectl describe.

🔴 Complex Tasks

For OPA/Kyverno policies or Falco rules — understand the structure first, then adapt. Test with intentional violations to confirm enforcement works.

Every CKS candidate hits these errors. This appendix gives you the Error → Cause → Fix for each one — so you spend less time debugging and more time solving. All 14 errors from the CKS curriculum, organized by exam domain.

⚡ CKS Exam Debugging Shortcuts
  • kubectl describe pod <name> -n <ns> — Always start here; the Events section at the bottom tells you WHY a pod was rejected (PSS violation, AppArmor missing, etc.)
  • kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=<sa> -n <ns> — RBAC test without creating pods; faster than deploying a test pod
  • kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' — Timeline of all issues in a namespace
  • tail -f /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.responseStatus.code >= 400)' — See all denied API requests in real-time
  • kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=20 — Quick Falco health check after rule changes
🗺️ Error Categories — What's Breaking?
🔒 Pod Security
PSS, SecurityContext,
Seccomp, AppArmor
🌐 Network
NetworkPolicy,
CNI, connectivity
🛡️ Auth & RBAC
Anonymous auth, SA tokens,
kubectl exec denied
🔍 Runtime & Supply
Falco, Audit, etcd,
Trivy, cosign, OPA

🔒 Pod Security Errors

Errors related to Pod Security Standards, security contexts, Seccomp, and AppArmor — the most common failures when hardening workloads. These account for ~35% of CKS exam tasks.

🔴 Error 1: Pod Rejected — Violates PodSecurity
🐛 Symptom

Error: pods "my-pod" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest"

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: The namespace has PSS Restricted enforced, but your pod runs as root or lacks required security fields.

Fix: Add runAsNonRoot: true, seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]} to the pod's securityContext.

# Quick fix — add to your pod spec:
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: app
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
Error 2: AppArmor Profile Not Found
🐛 Symptom

Cannot enforce AppArmor: profile "my-profile" not found

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: The AppArmor profile exists on your workstation but not on the node where the pod was scheduled.

Fix: apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/<profile> on every node. Verify with: ssh node01 aa-status | grep <profile>

Error 3: Seccomp RuntimeDefault Breaks Application
🐛 Symptom

Pod starts but crashes with Operation not permitted or invalid argument.

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: RuntimeDefault blocks ~300 syscalls. Your app uses an unusual syscall (like clone, mount, ptrace) that RuntimeDefault denies.

Fix: Create a custom seccomp profile that allows the needed syscall. Check which syscall is blocked via kubectl describe pod or dmesg on the node.

🌐 Network & NetworkPolicy Errors

🔴 Error 4: NetworkPolicy Not Blocking Traffic
🐛 Symptom

You applied a default-deny NetworkPolicy but pods can still reach each other.

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: Your CNI plugin (Flannel, default kubenet) does not support NetworkPolicy enforcement. Only Calico, Cilium, Weave Net, and Antrea enforce NetworkPolicies.

Fix: Switch to a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy. For the CKS exam, the cluster should already have a compatible CNI — check with kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave'.

# Check which CNI is running
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave|flannel'

# Quick NetPol connectivity test
kubectl run test-src --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh -n <ns>
# Inside the pod:
wget -O- --timeout=3 http://<target-svc>:<port>
# If it connects despite default-deny → CNI issue
💡 CKS Exam Context

On the CKS exam, the cluster will have a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy. If your NetPol isn't working, don't waste time checking the CNI — instead verify: (1) labels match between NetPol selector and target pod, (2) namespace labels match if using namespaceSelector, (3) you're in the right namespace. 90% of exam NetPol issues are label mismatches.

🛡️ Authentication & RBAC Errors

Error 5: Anonymous Auth Still Works After Disabling
🐛 Symptom

kubectl get pods --as=system:anonymous still returns results after adding --anonymous-auth=false.

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: The API server manifest was edited but either: (1) the kubelet hasn't restarted the static pod yet, or (2) there's a syntax error in the YAML and the old config is still running.

Fix: Wait 30-60 seconds for the kubelet to detect the change. Verify: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep apiserver — the AGE should be recent. Check ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep anonymous on the control plane to confirm the flag is active.

Error 6: SA Token Still Automounts After Disabling
🐛 Symptom

You patched the SA with automountServiceAccountToken: false but the pod still has a mounted token.

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: The patch only affects new pods. Existing pods still have their token because the token was mounted at pod creation time.

Fix: Delete the existing pod — the Deployment/ReplicaSet will recreate it with the new SA settings. kubectl delete pod <name> -n <ns>. Verify: kubectl exec <new-pod> -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ should return "No such file or directory".

Error 7: kubectl exec Denied
🐛 Symptom

Error from server (Forbidden): pods "my-pod" is forbidden: User cannot create resource "pods/exec"

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: The Role/ClusterRole does not include the pods/exec subresource. pods and pods/exec are separate resources in RBAC.

Fix: Add pods/exec to the Role's resources list: resources: ["pods", "pods/exec", "pods/log"]. Then verify: kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec --as=<user> -n <ns>.

🔍 Runtime Security & Supply Chain Errors

Error 8: Falco Not Detecting Events
🐛 Symptom

Falco is running but not generating alerts when you trigger the rule condition.

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: (1) Rule condition is syntactically wrong, (2) Falco hasn't been restarted after editing rules, or (3) the rule targets a different container name.

Fix: ① Run Falco in debug mode: edit /etc/falco/falco.yaml set log_level: debug. ② Restart: kubectl rollout restart ds falco -n falco. ③ Check logs: kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=50.

Error 9: etcd Data Not Encrypted
🐛 Symptom

ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/ns/name | hexdump -C shows readable JSON (plaintext).

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: (1) EncryptionConfiguration has identity: {} as the first provider (should be last as fallback), or (2) the API server wasn't configured with --encryption-provider-config, or (3) existing secrets weren't rotated.

Fix: Ensure aescbc or aesgcm is the FIRST provider in EncryptionConfiguration. Then rotate: kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -. Verify the output shows k8s:enc:aescbc:v1: prefix.

Error 10: cosign verify Fails
🐛 Symptom

Error: no matching signatures or Error: unable to verify signature

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: The public key (cosign.pub) used for verification doesn't match the private key (cosign.key) used for signing. Or the image wasn't signed at all.

Fix: ① Regenerate keys: cosign generate-key-pair. ② Re-sign: cosign sign --key cosign.key image@sha256:.... ③ Re-verify: cosign verify --key cosign.pub image@sha256:.... ④ If using Kyverno, update the publicKeys field in the ClusterPolicy.

Error 11: Audit Log Not Created
🐛 Symptom

/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log doesn't exist or is empty despite configuring audit policy.

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: (1) The directory /var/log/kubernetes/ doesn't exist or isn't writable by the API server. (2) The audit policy file path or volume mount is incorrect.

Fix: Create the directory: sudo mkdir -p /var/log/kubernetes && sudo chmod 755 /var/log/kubernetes. Verify the API server manifest has both --audit-log-path and the correct hostPath volume mount. Check: ls -la /var/log/kubernetes/.

Error 12: OPA Policy Not Enforcing
🐛 Symptom

You applied a ConstraintTemplate and Constraint, but pods with unapproved images are still created.

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: The Constraint's match.namespaces or namespaceSelector doesn't target the right namespace. The policy is being applied to a different namespace than where you're testing.

Fix: Check the Constraint: kubectl get constraint -o yaml | grep -A10 match. Ensure it targets your test namespace. Test with: kubectl run test --image=nginx -n <target-ns> — should be denied.

Error 13: ImagePolicyWebhook Blocks ALL Images
🐛 Symptom

Every pod creation fails with admission webhook denied the request, even for approved images.

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: The defaultAllow: false setting combined with an unreachable webhook server means ALL requests are denied. The webhook server at the configured endpoint is down.

Fix: ① Verify the webhook server is running: kubectl get pods -n <webhook-ns>. ② Check connectivity from API server to webhook. ③ Temporarily set defaultAllow: true to let pods through while fixing. ④ Check webhook server logs for certificate/authentication errors.

Error 14: Trivy — Too Many False Positives
🐛 Symptom

Trivy reports dozens of CVEs, including ones already patched in your base image.

🔍 Cause → ✅ Fix

Cause: Trivy's vulnerability database is stale. It's comparing your image against an outdated CVE list, flagging vulnerabilities that are already fixed in newer package versions you have.

Fix: Update the DB before scanning: trivy image --update-db or run trivy image --refresh. For CI/CD: run trivy image --cache-dir /tmp/trivy-cache --update-db at the start of every pipeline run.

🔄 CKS Troubleshooting Workflow — When Something Breaks
1
Read the Error

What resource? What namespace? What verb? kubectl describe <resource> <name> -n <ns>

2
Check Events

kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp — events tell you WHY something was denied.

3
Check RBAC

kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=<user> -n <ns> — is it a permissions issue?

4
Check Logs

kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> --tail=50 or tail /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq

💡 CKS Exam Terminology Tip

You won't be asked definitions directly, but understanding these terms precisely helps you parse CKS question wording correctly. The exam uses exact terminology — knowing the difference between Role vs ClusterRole, Seccomp vs AppArmor, AuthN vs AuthZ, and mTLS vs TLS saves critical seconds. Terms marked with ⭐ CKS EXAM appear in exam tasks most frequently.

🏗️ CKS Security Object Hierarchy — How Resources Relate
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                        CLUSTER (most restrictive wins)                     │
 │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
 │  │  RBAC: ClusterRoleBinding → ClusterRole (cluster-wide permissions)  │  │
 │  │  Admission: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration → OPA/Kyverno policies   │  │
 │  │  Audit: Policy → API Server flags → log file / webhook             │  │
 │  │  Encryption: EncryptionConfiguration → API Server flag              │  │
 │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
 │                                                                           │
 │  ┌──────────────── NAMESPACE ─────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
 │  │  RBAC: RoleBinding → Role (namespace-scoped permissions)           │  │
 │  │  NetworkPolicy: podSelector → ingress/egress rules                 │  │
 │  │  PSS: namespace label → pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce         │  │
 │  │  ┌──────────────── POD ───────────────────────────────────────┐   │  │
 │  │  │  ServiceAccount → automountServiceAccountToken             │   │  │
 │  │  │  SecurityContext: seccompProfile, appArmorProfile,         │   │  │
 │  │  │    runAsNonRoot, capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem      │   │  │
 │  │  │  ┌─────────── CONTAINER ───────────────────────────────┐  │   │  │
 │  │  │  │  Container SecurityContext (overrides pod-level)     │  │   │  │
 │  │  │  │  Image: digest > tag, cosign-verified, Trivy-scanned │  │   │  │
 │  │  │  │  Runtime: gVisor/Kata (RuntimeClass)                 │  │   │  │
 │  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │   │  │
 │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │  │
 │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A

Admission Controller — A plugin that intercepts API requests after authentication/authorization and can mutate (modify) or validate (allow/deny) them. Examples: PodSecurity, NodeRestriction, ImagePolicyWebhook. ⭐ CKS EXAM

AppArmor — A Linux Security Module (LSM) that restricts what a program can do via profiles. In Kubernetes, applied via pod annotations or the securityContext.appArmorProfile field. Profiles define file access, network, and capability rules. ⭐ CKS EXAM

Attack Surface — The sum of all possible points where an attacker can attempt to breach a system. Reducing attack surface means removing unnecessary ports, services, packages, and permissions.

Audit Log — A chronological record of every request made to the Kubernetes API server. Records who did what, when, from where, and with what result. Essential for incident investigation and compliance. ⭐ CKS EXAM

Authentication (AuthN) — Verifying the identity of a user or service. Answers "Who are you?" In Kubernetes: certificates, bearer tokens, OIDC, ServiceAccount tokens.

Authorization (AuthZ) — Determining what an authenticated entity is allowed to do. Answers "What can you do?" In Kubernetes: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), Node authorization, Webhook.

B

Base Image — The foundational image layer your Dockerfile builds upon (e.g., python:3.12-slim). Choosing a minimal base image (distroless, alpine, slim) reduces the attack surface by removing unnecessary packages.

Baseline (PSS) — A Pod Security Standard level that prevents known privilege escalations while allowing minimally specified pods. Allows: standard Linux capabilities, hostPath volumes, non-root users. Blocks: hostNetwork, hostPID, privileged containers.

C

CA (Certificate Authority) — An entity that issues and signs digital certificates. In Kubernetes: the cluster CA signs API server, kubelet, and component certificates for mutual TLS.

Capabilities (Linux) — Fine-grained privileges split from the traditional root superuser. Instead of "all or nothing" root, capabilities allow specific powers: CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, CAP_SYS_ADMIN, etc. In Kubernetes: securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"].

CIS Benchmark — Center for Internet Security's configuration security standards. kube-bench automates CIS Benchmark checks for Kubernetes clusters, testing ~100+ controls.

ClusterRole — An RBAC role that grants permissions across all namespaces or to cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs, namespaces). Combine with ClusterRoleBinding to grant cluster-wide access.

Container Escape — Exploiting a vulnerability to break out of container isolation and access the host system. Mitigated by: non-root users, seccomp, AppArmor, gVisor/Kata, readOnlyRootFilesystem.

cosign — A tool for signing and verifying container images. Part of the Sigstore project. cosign sign --key cosign.key image creates a cryptographic signature stored in the registry.

CVE — Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a public database of known security flaws. Each CVE has a unique ID (e.g., CVE-2023-38545) and a severity score (CVSS 0-10). Trivy scans images against the CVE database.

D

Defense in Depth — A security strategy using multiple, independent layers of protection. If one layer fails, others still hold. In Kubernetes: RBAC → NetworkPolicy → PSS → SecurityContext → Seccomp/AppArmor → Falco → Audit — each a layer.

distroless — A type of minimal container image containing only the application and its runtime dependencies. No shell, no package manager, no utilities. Maximum security: an attacker who gets code execution can't even run ls.

Dynamic Secret — A secret generated on-demand with a limited lifetime (hours/days). Vault creates dynamic database credentials: each pod gets a unique, time-limited username/password that auto-expires. Prevents credential reuse.

E

eBPF — extended Berkeley Packet Filter. A kernel technology that allows running sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. Falco uses eBPF probes to capture system call events without loading a kernel module. Safer and more modern than kernel modules.

Encryption at Rest — Encrypting data where it is stored (disk). In Kubernetes: encrypting Secrets in etcd so that anyone who reads the etcd data directly sees ciphertext, not plaintext. Configured via EncryptionConfiguration.

Encryption in Transit — Encrypting data while it moves over the network. In Kubernetes: TLS for API server communication, mTLS for pod-to-pod traffic (via Istio/Linkerd). Prevents eavesdropping on network traffic.

F

Falco — An open-source, CNCF-graduated runtime security tool. Monitors Linux system calls in real-time to detect anomalous container behavior. Rules define conditions (e.g., "shell spawned in container X") that trigger alerts. CKS-critical: you will write Falco rules on the exam. ⭐ CKS EXAM

4Cs — The four layers of cloud-native security: Cloud (provider IAM, firewalls), Cluster (RBAC, NetPol, API server), Container (image scanning, SecurityContext, PSS), Code (SAST, dependency scanning, secrets). Defense must span all four.

G

gVisor — A sandboxed container runtime by Google. Intercepts system calls in userspace (via the Sentry component) instead of passing them directly to the Linux kernel. Provides stronger isolation than traditional containers. Applied via RuntimeClass with handler: runsc.

GitOps — An operational model where Git is the single source of truth for infrastructure and application configuration. Security benefit: every change has a commit history, author, PR review, and audit trail. ArgoCD/Flux sync Git state to the cluster.

H

HSTS — HTTP Strict Transport Security. A web security policy that tells browsers to always use HTTPS when connecting to a domain. Prevents SSL stripping attacks. Configured via Ingress annotations or response headers.

hostNetwork — A pod setting (spec.hostNetwork: true) that uses the node's network namespace instead of an isolated pod network. Dangerous: the pod can see all node network interfaces and bypass NetworkPolicy. Blocked by PSS Restricted.

hostPID — A pod setting (spec.hostPID: true) that uses the node's PID namespace. Dangerous: the pod can see (and potentially signal) all processes on the node. Blocked by PSS Restricted.

I

Image Digest — A SHA256 hash uniquely identifying an exact image version (e.g., sha256:abc123...). Unlike tags, digests are immutable — the same digest always points to the same image content. Best practice: use image@sha256:... in production.

Image Tag — A mutable label on an image (e.g., :latest, :v1). Tags can be moved to point to different image content — :latest today may be different from :latest tomorrow. Use tags in development, digests in production.

Immutable Container — A container whose filesystem cannot be modified after startup (readOnlyRootFilesystem: true). Changes must go through the CI/CD pipeline (rebuild image, redeploy). Blocks attackers from writing malware or modifying configurations.

IRSA — IAM Roles for Service Accounts (AWS). Maps Kubernetes ServiceAccounts to AWS IAM roles, giving pods fine-grained cloud permissions without storing AWS credentials in Secrets. Every pod gets unique, time-limited credentials.

J

JWT (JSON Web Token) — A compact, URL-safe token format used for authentication. Kubernetes ServiceAccount tokens are JWTs containing: the SA name, namespace, expiry time, and a cryptographic signature. The API server validates JWT tokens via the TokenReview API. ⭐ CKS EXAM

K

Kata Containers — A sandboxed container runtime using lightweight VMs per container. Provides hardware-level isolation (each container gets its own kernel). Stronger than gVisor, with slightly more overhead. Applied via RuntimeClass with handler: kata.

kube-bench — A tool that checks Kubernetes clusters against the CIS Benchmark. Runs as a binary or container. Outputs PASS/FAIL/WARN for each CIS control with remediation advice. Run against master and worker nodes separately. ⭐ CKS EXAM

Kyverno — A Kubernetes-native policy engine. Policies are written in YAML (no Rego needed). Supports: validate, mutate, generate, and verifyImages (image signature verification). Easier learning curve than OPA Gatekeeper. ⭐ CKS EXAM

L

Lateral Movement — After breaching one system (e.g., anihpj pod), an attacker attempts to move to other systems (e.g., postgres database, redis cache) within the same network. Blocked by: NetworkPolicy (only allows anihpj → postgres on port 5432).

Least Privilege — The security principle of granting only the minimum permissions required to perform a task. In Kubernetes: RBAC roles with specific verbs/resources, non-root users, dropped Linux capabilities, restricted NetworkPolicies.

M

mTLS (Mutual TLS) — TLS where both client and server verify each other's certificates. Unlike regular TLS (server-only verification), mTLS ensures unauthorized pods cannot connect. Istio/Linkerd automate mTLS between pods via sidecar proxies.

Multi-stage Build — A Dockerfile pattern that compiles/builds in one stage (with full toolchain) and copies only the final artifact to a minimal runtime stage. Result: a tiny production image with no build tools, reducing attack surface and CVE count.

N

NetworkPolicy — A Kubernetes resource that defines allowed pod-to-pod network traffic. Acts as a firewall at the pod level. Requires a CNI plugin that supports NetworkPolicy enforcement (Calico, Cilium, Weave Net). Default behavior: all traffic allowed; apply default-deny to lock down. ⭐ CKS EXAM

NodeRestriction — An admission plugin that limits what each kubelet can modify via the API server. A kubelet can only modify its own Node object and pods scheduled to it. Prevents a compromised kubelet from affecting other nodes.

Non-root Container — A container running as a non-root Linux user (UID > 0). Configured via securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true and runAsUser: 1000. If an attacker compromises the app, they have user-level (not root) access — limiting damage.

O

OIDC (OpenID Connect) — An identity protocol built on OAuth 2.0. Used for Kubernetes authentication: users authenticate with an external identity provider (Google, Azure AD, Okta), and the API server validates the OIDC token.

OPA (Open Policy Agent) — A general-purpose policy engine. Uses the Rego language for policy definition. Can be used for Kubernetes admission control (via Gatekeeper), infrastructure-as-code validation (conftest), and API authorization.

OPA Gatekeeper — The Kubernetes-specific integration of OPA. Deployed as an admission webhook. Policies are defined as ConstraintTemplates (Rego) and enforced via Constraints. More powerful but steeper learning curve than Kyverno.

P

Pod Security Admission (PSA) — The built-in Kubernetes admission controller that enforces Pod Security Standards. Replaces the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy (PSP). Configured via namespace labels: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted.

Pod Security Standards (PSS) — Three built-in security policy profiles: Privileged (unrestricted), Baseline (blocks known privilege escalations), and Restricted (maximum security — enforces best practices). Applied at the namespace level. ⭐ CKS EXAM

Privileged Container — A container running with securityContext.privileged: true, granting full host root access. Can access all host devices, bypass seccomp/AppArmor, and load kernel modules. Never run in production. Blocked by PSS Restricted.

Privilege Escalation — Gaining more permissions than originally granted. In Linux: a process elevating from user to root. In Kubernetes: a pod escaping its namespace or gaining cluster-admin. Controlled by allowPrivilegeEscalation: false.

R

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) — The primary Kubernetes authorization system. Defines who (subjects: users, groups, SAs) can do what (verbs: get, create, delete) on which resources (pods, secrets, nodes). Roles are namespace-scoped; ClusterRoles are cluster-scoped. ⭐ CKS EXAM

readOnlyRootFilesystem — A securityContext field that makes the container's root filesystem read-only. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true blocks writes to /, /etc/, /bin/ — critical for preventing attackers from installing malware or modifying configurations.

Rego — OPA's policy language. A declarative, functional language for writing policy rules. Example: violation[msg] { input.review.object.spec.containers[_].securityContext.runAsNonRoot != true }. Used in OPA Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplates.

Restricted (PSS) — The most secure Pod Security Standard level. Enforces: non-root, seccomp RuntimeDefault, drop ALL capabilities, no hostPath/hostNetwork/hostPID, readOnlyRootFilesystem recommended. Use for production namespaces.

S

SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) — A complete list of every component in a software artifact. Like a nutrition label for software: lists all packages, versions, and dependencies. Generated by Syft or Trivy. Enables rapid CVE impact assessment: "Are we affected by this new vulnerability?"

Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) — A Linux kernel feature that filters which system calls a process can make. RuntimeDefault blocks ~300 dangerous syscalls. Custom profiles can be even stricter or allow specific needed syscalls. Applied via securityContext.seccompProfile. ⭐ CKS EXAM

SecurityContext — A pod/container field defining security settings. Pod-level: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, fsGroup, seccompProfile. Container-level: allowPrivilegeEscalation, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities, appArmorProfile. ⭐ CKS EXAM

ServiceAccount — A Kubernetes identity assigned to pods. Pods use SA tokens to authenticate to the API server. Disable automount (automountServiceAccountToken: false) for pods that don't need API access. SAs are the subject of RBAC RoleBindings. ⭐ CKS EXAM

Sigstore — An ecosystem of open-source tools for supply chain security: cosign (image signing), Fulcio (certificate authority for keyless signing), Rekor (transparency log). Enables verifying who built an image and that it hasn't been tampered with.

SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) — A framework for build provenance and integrity. Levels 0-3 provide increasing guarantees about how software was built. Prevents supply chain attacks like SolarWinds: verifies that the code you wrote is what was actually built and deployed.

Static Pod — A pod defined by a YAML file on a node's filesystem (/etc/kubernetes/manifests/) and managed directly by the kubelet. The API server, etcd, and controller manager run as static pods. Changes to the YAML file are auto-detected and applied by kubelet.

T

TLS (Transport Layer Security) — A cryptographic protocol for securing network connections. Provides: encryption (data can't be read), authentication (server identity verified), and integrity (data can't be modified in transit). Used in Kubernetes for all API server communication.

TokenReview — An API endpoint that validates a ServiceAccount JWT token. The API server checks: is the token valid? Has it expired? Which SA does it belong to? Used by webhook authenticators and external services to verify pod identities.

Trivy — An open-source vulnerability scanner by Aqua Security. Scans container images, filesystems, Git repositories, and Kubernetes clusters for CVEs, misconfigurations, and secrets. CKS exam tool: trivy image --severity CRITICAL image:tag.

U

Unconfined (Seccomp) — The default seccomp profile that allows ALL system calls. Equivalent to no seccomp enforcement. seccompProfile.type: Unconfined — only use for system/privileged pods that need full kernel access. PSS Restricted blocks Unconfined. ⭐ CKS EXAM

V

Vault (HashiCorp) — An enterprise secret management platform. Provides: dynamic secrets (auto-generated, time-limited), encryption as a service, audit logging of secret access, and Kubernetes auth method (pods authenticate via SA token). Stores Django SECRET_KEY, DB passwords, API keys.

ValidatingWebhookConfiguration — A Kubernetes resource that defines an external validating admission webhook. The API server calls the webhook with the request; the webhook returns allow/deny. Used by OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno to enforce policies.

W

Webhook (Admission) — An HTTP callback that the API server calls during admission. Mutating webhooks can modify resources before they're saved. Validating webhooks can accept or reject requests. OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno implement validating webhooks. ⭐ CKS EXAM

Z

Zero Trust — A security model that assumes no implicit trust. Every request must be authenticated, authorized, and encrypted — regardless of whether it originates inside or outside the network. In Kubernetes: mTLS between all pods, RBAC for every API call, NetworkPolicy default-deny.

Complete production-ready, CKS-hardened Kubernetes manifests for the anihpj/jobpost Django application. Every manifest is annotated with security comments — copy, adapt, apply. All 15 manifests from the cks.txt curriculum in one place.

📖 How to Use These Manifests

Apply in order (E.1→E.8). Each manifest depends on the previous ones. Or apply all at once: kubectl apply -f anihpj-manifests/ (place all YAML in one directory). Critical: Apply NetworkPolicies after creating the namespace, or your kubectl connection may be blocked. Always verify with kubectl get all -n anihpj-prod after applying.

🔢 Manifest Deployment Order — Apply in This Sequence
1
Namespace + PSS

kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml
Foundation layer — creates the anihpj-prod namespace with Restricted PSS enforcement.

2
RBAC

kubectl apply -f rbac.yaml
ServiceAccounts, Roles, RoleBindings — identity and permissions before workloads.

3
Config + Secrets

kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml secret.yaml
Configuration must exist before pods reference it.

4
NetworkPolicy

kubectl apply -f networkpolicies.yaml
Default-deny FIRST, then allow rules — or you'll lock yourself out.

5
Deployment + Service

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml service.yaml
Workloads go last — everything they need (RBAC, secrets, network rules) is ready.

6
Ingress + Runtime

kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml falco.yaml policies.yaml
External access + runtime monitoring — final polish.
