E.1 Namespace with PSS Labels

🎯 Purpose — Why First

Every other manifest references namespace: anihpj-prod. PSS Restricted labels enforce non-root, seccomp, and capabilities restrictions at admission time. Create this before anything else.

The foundation of anihpj security. PSS Restricted enforces non-root, seccomp, and capabilities restrictions at admission time — pods that violate these standards are rejected before they're created.

📁 Namespace + PSS Enforcement
anihpj-namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
  labels:
    # Pod Security Standards — Restricted (maximum security)
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
    # Environment label
    environment: production
---
# Development namespace (less strict — Baseline)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: anihpj-dev
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    environment: development

E.2 ConfigMap + Secret — Django Configuration

🎯 Purpose

Non-sensitive settings (DB host, debug mode) in ConfigMap. Sensitive data (SECRET_KEY, DB password) in Secret — encrypted at rest via EncryptionConfiguration in etcd. Referenced by pods via envFrom.

Non-sensitive settings in ConfigMap, sensitive data (SECRET_KEY, DB password) in Secret — encrypted at rest via EncryptionConfiguration.

⚙️ ConfigMap — Non-Sensitive Django Settings
anihpj-configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: anihpj-config
  namespace: anihpj-prod
data:
  DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "jobpost.settings.production"
  DJANGO_DEBUG: "false"
  DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS: "anihpj.com,www.anihpj.com"
  DJANGO_LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"
  DATABASE_HOST: "postgres-service"
  DATABASE_PORT: "5432"
  DATABASE_NAME: "anihpj"
🔐 Secret — Sensitive Credentials (Encrypted at Rest)
anihpj-secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-secret
  namespace: anihpj-prod
type: Opaque
data:
  # Base64-encoded — encrypted at rest in etcd via EncryptionConfiguration
  DJANGO_SECRET_KEY: <base64>
  DATABASE_USER: <base64>
  DATABASE_PASSWORD: <base64>

E.3 Hardened Django Deployment + PostgreSQL StatefulSet

Production-grade Deployment and StatefulSet with full security contexts, health probes, resource limits, and immutability.

🚀 Hardened Django Deployment
anihpj-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        runAsGroup: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2@sha256:abc123...
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: anihpj-config
        - secretRef:
            name: anihpj-secret
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
        resources:
          requests: {cpu: "200m", memory: "256Mi"}
          limits:   {cpu: "1000m", memory: "512Mi"}
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
        - name: media
          mountPath: /app/media
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: media
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: anihpj-media-pvc
🗄️ Hardened PostgreSQL StatefulSet
postgres-statefulset.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  serviceName: postgres-service
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgres
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 999
        fsGroup: 999
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:16-alpine
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: anihpj-config
              key: DATABASE_NAME
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: anihpj-secret
              key: DATABASE_USER
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: anihpj-secret
              key: DATABASE_PASSWORD
        volumeMounts:
        - name: postgres-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: postgres-data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi

E.4 Service + Ingress with TLS

Internal-only ClusterIP Service (no external exposure) + TLS-terminated Ingress for secure external access.

🔌 ClusterIP Service (Internal Only)
anihpj-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-service
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  type: ClusterIP  # No external exposure
  selector:
    app: anihpj
  ports:
  - name: http
    protocol: TCP
    port: 8000
    targetPort: 8000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgres-service
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: postgres
  ports:
  - name: postgres
    protocol: TCP
    port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
🌐 Ingress with TLS
anihpj-ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts: "true"
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - anihpj.com
    - www.anihpj.com
    secretName: anihpj-tls
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj-service
            port:
              number: 8000

E.5 NetworkPolicy Set — Zero-Trust Networking

⚠️ Critical — Apply Order Matters!

Always apply in this order: ① Default Deny → ② DNS Egress → ③ Specific Allow rules. If you apply Deny last, you'll lock yourself out. DNS must be allowed or pods can't resolve service names.

The complete NetworkPolicy set: default-deny, specific pod-to-pod allows, DNS egress. Apply in this order.

🌐 anihpj Zero-Trust Network Policy Set
anihpj-networkpolicies.yaml
# 1. DEFAULT DENY ALL
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
# 2. ALLOW INGRESS → ANIHPJ
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-to-anihpj
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: ingress-nginx
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8000
---
# 3. ALLOW ANIHPJ → POSTGRES
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-anihpj-to-postgres
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
---
# 4. ALLOW DNS EGRESS
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53

E.6 RBAC — ServiceAccounts, Roles, RoleBindings

Dedicated SAs with least-privilege RBAC. No pod uses the default ServiceAccount.

👤 anihpj RBAC Manifests
anihpj-rbac.yaml
# ServiceAccount for anihpj pods
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: anihpj-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
# ServiceAccount for monitoring
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: monitoring-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
---
# Role: read-only access to pods and services
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: anihpj-prod
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "services"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
# RoleBinding: bind monitoring-sa to pod-reader
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: monitoring-pod-reader
  namespace: anihpj-prod
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: monitoring-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

E.7 Runtime Security — Falco Rules, OPA, Kyverno

Custom Falco rules for anihpj-specific threat detection, OPA image registry policy, and Kyverno image verification.

🦅 Falco Custom Rules — anihpj Detection
falco-rules-configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: falco-rules
  namespace: falco
data:
  falco_rules.local.yaml: |
    - list: shell_binaries
      items: [bash, sh, zsh, dash]
    - macro: anihpj_container
      condition: container.name = "anihpj"
    - rule: Shell in anihpj
      desc: Detect shell spawn in Django container
      condition: >
        spawned_process and anihpj_container
        and proc.name in (shell_binaries)
      output: "🚨 Shell in anihpj! cmd=%proc.cmdline pod=%k8s.pod.name"
      priority: CRITICAL
      tags: [anihpj, shell, CKS]
    - rule: Unexpected Outbound from anihpj
      desc: Detect connections not to postgres or DNS
      condition: >
        outbound and anihpj_container
        and not fd.sport in (5432, 53)
      output: "Unexpected connection from anihpj to %fd.name"
      priority: WARNING
      tags: [anihpj, network, CKS]
⚖️ OPA + Kyverno Admission Policies
admission-policies.yaml
# Kyverno: verifyImages with cosign
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: verify-anihpj-images
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-signature
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
          namespaces: ["anihpj-prod"]
    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences:
      - "registry.anihpj.com/*"
      attestors:
      - count: 1
        entries:
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |-
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              MFkwEwYHKoZI...
              -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
---
# Kyverno: require securityContext
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-security-context
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-runasnonroot
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "runAsNonRoot must be true"
      pattern:
        spec:
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true

E.8 Audit Policy + Encryption Configuration

Production-grade audit policy and encryption configuration — the final layer of anihpj security.

📋 Audit Policy — Production-Grade
audit-policy.yaml
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages:
- "RequestReceived"
rules:
- level: None
  users: ["system:nodes"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- level: RequestResponse
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["create", "update", "delete", "patch"]
- level: Metadata
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
- level: RequestResponse
  resources:
  - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
    resources: ["roles", "rolebindings", "clusterroles", "clusterrolebindings"]
- level: Request
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["pods/exec", "pods/portforward"]
- level: Metadata
🔐 EncryptionConfiguration — AES-GCM for anihpj Secrets
encryption-config.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources:
  - secrets
  providers:
  - aesgcm:
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: <32-byte-base64-key>
  - aescbc:
      keys:
      - name: key2
        secret: <32-byte-base64-key>
  - identity: {}
# Apply with: --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
# Rotate: kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -

F.3 Tips, Tricks & Time Management

⏱️ 10 Essential CKS Exam Tips
1. Context First

kubectl config use-context before every task. The #1 reason candidates fail — solving correctly on wrong cluster = 0 points.

2. Copy-Paste from Docs

YAML templates from kubernetes.io save minutes. Don't write YAML from scratch — copy, paste, adapt.

3. Read ALL Tasks First

2-minute initial scan. Identify easy tasks (RBAC, PSS labels) — do them first for quick points and confidence.

4. Skip, Don't Struggle

If stuck >3 min on quick task, skip. Return in Pass 3. Partial credit on all tasks beats perfect on 5.

5. Verify Everything

After applying: run kubectl describe, kubectl auth can-i, or kubectl exec to confirm it works as expected.

6. Use Dry-Run

--dry-run=client -o yaml generates YAML templates. Faster than manual writing and no syntax errors.

7. Bookmark Search Skill

Practice finding YAML examples fast on kubernetes.io. Use the docs search — it's your biggest time-saver.

8. Set Aliases Early

alias k=kubectl, export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml" — first 30 seconds of the exam.

9. Know Your Files

/etc/kubernetes/manifests/, /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, /etc/falco/ — no internet needed.

10. Stay Calm

You have 2 hours. 67% passes. That's roughly 10-13 correct out of 15-20. You can miss 5-7 tasks and still pass.

📅 Appendix G: 10-Week CKS Learning Path

📅 APPENDIX 📖 Reference 🗓️ 10 Weeks

A structured 10-week study roadmap from beginner to CKS-certified. Each week has clear objectives, daily tasks, checkpoint assessments, and chapter references. Recommended pace: 6-9 hours per week (2-3 h reading + 4-6 h hands-on lab).

🟢 Week 2: Cluster Setup Security
🎯 GOAL: Understand WHY and WHERE K8s is vulnerable. Run kube-bench and see real FAIL items.

🟢 Week 2: Cluster Setup Security
📖 Reading: Chapters 4-7

CIS benchmarks, kube-bench mastery, Kubernetes Dashboard security, NetworkPolicy fundamentals, Ingress with TLS.

🔧 Lab

Fix kube-bench failures. Apply NetworkPolicy set to anihpj namespace. Configure Ingress with TLS secret and cert-manager annotation.

🎯 GOAL: Zero-trust networking in one namespace. TLS on Ingress. All kube-bench master checks PASS.
⏱️ 7-9 hours
🟡 Week 3: Cluster Hardening — API Server & RBAC
📖 Reading: Chapters 8-10

API server hardening: disable anonymous auth, enable Node authorizer. RBAC deep dive: Roles, ClusterRoles, Bindings. ServiceAccounts and token management.

🔧 Lab

Disable anonymous auth, verify. Create RBAC for anihpj team (SA + Role + RoleBinding). Test with kubectl auth can-i. Disable SA automount for web pods.

🎯 GOAL: kubectl auth can-i returns expected yes/no for every role. No anonymous API access.
⏱️ 7-9 hours
🟡 Week 4: Cluster Hardening II — Authorization & Versions
📖 Reading: Chapters 11-12

NodeRestriction admission plugin, authorization modes (Node, RBAC, ABAC, Webhook), Kubernetes version management for security patches.

🔧 Lab

Enable NodeRestriction, verify kubelet hardening. Check version lifecycle. Run kube-bench on both master and node — aim for all PASS.

🎯 GOAL: All CIS checks PASS. Understand authorization flow. Know which version to upgrade to.
⏱️ 6-8 hours
🟡 Week 5: System Hardening — OS, AppArmor, Seccomp
📖 Reading: Chapters 13-16

OS hardening: remove unnecessary services/packages. AppArmor: profiles, enforcement, K8s integration. Seccomp: RuntimeDefault vs custom profiles. Port/IAM minimization. etcd security.

🔧 Lab

Create custom AppArmor profile for anihpj. Apply Seccomp RuntimeDefault. Harden kubelet config. Remove unnecessary services from worker node.

🎯 GOAL: Pod runs with AppArmor + Seccomp enforced. No unnecessary services on nodes.
⏱️ 7-9 hours
🟡 Week 6: Microservice Vulnerabilities
📖 Reading: Chapters 17-22

Pod Security Standards (PSS): Privileged/Baseline/Restricted. SecurityContext deep dive. Secrets encryption at rest. Vault integration. gVisor/Kata sandboxing. mTLS with Istio.

🔧 Lab

Apply PSS Restricted to anihpj-prod. Add full securityContext (non-root, drop ALL, RO-FS). Enable encryption at rest, verify with etcdctl. Apply RuntimeClass gVisor.

🎯 GOAL: kubesec score ≥ 8 for your pod spec. Secrets encrypted in etcd. PSS enforced.
⏱️ 8-10 hours
🔴 Week 7: Supply Chain Security
📖 Reading: Chapters 23-27

Image scanning with Trivy. Admission controllers: OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno, ImagePolicyWebhook. Image signing with cosign. SBOM generation. SLSA framework. Static analysis with kube-linter/kubesec.

🔧 Lab

Scan anihpj image with Trivy, fix all CRITICAL CVEs. Write OPA ConstraintTemplate for registry approval. Sign image with cosign. Configure Kyverno verifyImages.

🎯 GOAL: CRITICAL CVE = 0. Image signed. Kyverno enforces signature verification. SBOM generated.
⏱️ 8-10 hours
🔴 Week 8: Runtime Security & Incident Response
📖 Reading: Chapters 28-32

Audit logging: policy, configuration, log analysis with jq. Falco: architecture, rules, alerts. Incident response lifecycle. Immutable containers. Continuous compliance monitoring.

🔧 Lab

Configure audit policy, enable logging, analyze with jq. Write 3 custom Falco rules, test alerts. Run incident response simulation. Apply readOnlyRootFilesystem.

🎯 GOAL: Falco detects shell spawn + file read in anihpj. Audit logs capture all exec events. IR process memorized.
⏱️ 8-10 hours
🔴 Week 9: End-to-End Hardening + Full Mock Exam
📖 Reading: Chapters 33-37

Complete anihpj hardening (7-step workflow). Security automation & GitOps. Incident response simulation. CKS exam strategy, mock scenarios, and full mock exam.

🔧 Lab

Run full mock exam (17 tasks in 120 min). Score yourself. Identify weak areas. Practice speed drills on weak domains. Repeat mock until 70%+.

🎯 GOAL: Score ≥ 70% on mock exam. Complete full hardening in < 90 min. Know exactly what to improve.
⏱️ 8-10 hours
🔴 Week 10: Final Review + Exam 🎓

Last-mile review: cheat sheet, mental model, critical commands. Review Appendices for command reference, YAML templates, error fixes, glossary, exam prep guide.

📋 Study Tips
  • Consistency beats cramming: 60-90 min daily is better than 8-hour weekend marathons.
  • Check off each week: Don't move to the next week until you've achieved the checkpoint goal.
  • Use killer.sh early: Take the first session at Week 5 to gauge progress, not just at Week 9.
  • Hands-on > reading: For every hour of reading, spend 2 hours in the terminal. The CKS is performance-based.
  • Bookmark this path: Return to this page each Monday to plan your week.

Harden API server, kubelet, RBAC. Run and fix kube-bench. Disable anonymous access. Configure audit logging.

Apply AppArmor and Seccomp profiles. Harden nodes. Minimize attack surface. Restrict etcd access.

📦 Workload Security

Enforce PSS. Configure SecurityContext. Encrypt Secrets at rest. Deploy sandboxed runtimes. Set up mTLS.

🔗 Supply Chain

Scan images with Trivy. Write OPA/Kyverno policies. Sign images with cosign. Generate SBOMs. Implement SLSA.

🦅 Runtime Security

Write custom Falco rules. Analyze audit logs with jq. Run incident response. Deploy immutable containers.

🎯 Exam Mastery

3-pass time management. Context switching discipline. Speed aliases. Documentation search mastery. Mock exam confidence.

🧪 Appendix H: CKS Exam Simulator

  • Pass score: 67/100 points (67%). Track your score honestly — you're only cheating yourself.

Task 1 — Fix 3 kube-bench FAIL items [5 pts / 8 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Run kube-bench on the control plane. Identify the top 3 FAIL items and fix them. Re-run kube-bench to verify all 3 now show PASS.

Answer Click to reveal solution
# 1. Run kube-bench
kubectl config use-context cks-cluster-1
kube-bench run --targets=master

# 2. Identify FAIL items (example: 1.1.1, 1.2.6, 1.2.16)
# 3. Fix in API server manifest:
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add: --anonymous-auth=false
# Add: --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
# Add: --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log

# 4. Wait for restart, re-run:
kube-bench run --targets=master --check 1.1.1,1.2.6,1.2.16
# Expected: ALL PASS ✅

Task 2 — Apply NetworkPolicy Set [7 pts / 10 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1, namespace: anihpj-prod | Task: Apply default-deny-all NetworkPolicy. Then allow: ingress from ingress-nginx namespace to anihpj pods on port 8000. Allow DNS egress for all pods.

Answer Click to reveal solution
# 1. Default deny all
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny-all, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
# 2. Allow ingress from nginx to anihpj
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-ingress, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: ingress-nginx}}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 8000}]
---
# 3. Allow DNS
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}, {protocol: TCP, port: 53}]
---
kubectl apply -f netpol.yaml

Task 3 — Disable Anonymous Auth [4 pts / 4 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Disable anonymous authentication on the API server. Verify by attempting an anonymous request — it should fail with 401/403.

Answer Click to reveal solution
kubectl config use-context cks-cluster-1
# Edit manifest:
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add flag: --anonymous-auth=false
# Wait 30-60s for kubelet restart
# Verify:
kubectl get pods --as=system:anonymous
# Expected: Error from server (Forbidden)

Task 4 — Configure Audit Policy [6 pts / 8 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Create audit policy at /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml. Log pod changes at RequestResponse, secret access at Metadata, RBAC changes at RequestResponse. Enable audit logging to /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log.

Answer Click to reveal solution
kubectl config use-context cks-cluster-1
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
# (write the policy — see Appendix E.8 for full template)
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add flags: --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
#             --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
# Add volumeMount + hostPath volume for both files
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/kubernetes
# Verify: tail -f /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq .

Task 5 — Create Minimal RBAC [5 pts / 5 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1, namespace: anihpj-prod | Task: Create SA "monitor-sa". Create Role with get/list/watch on pods and services. Bind Role to SA. Verify SA can get pods but cannot delete secrets.

Answer Click to reveal solution
kubectl config use-context cks-cluster-1
kubectl create sa monitor-sa -n anihpj-prod
kubectl create role monitor-role --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods,services -n anihpj-prod
kubectl create rolebinding monitor-rb --role=monitor-role --serviceaccount=anihpj-prod:monitor-sa -n anihpj-prod
# Verify CAN:
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:monitor-sa -n anihpj-prod
# → yes
# Verify CANNOT:
kubectl auth can-i delete secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:monitor-sa -n anihpj-prod
# → no ✅

Task 6 — Apply AppArmor [6 pts / 8 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Create AppArmor profile at /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-deny-etc. Load it. Create pod "secure-app" in anihpj-prod with the profile applied.

Answer Click to reveal solution
kubectl config use-context cks-cluster-1
sudo vi /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-deny-etc
# profile anihpj-deny-etc flags=(attach_disconnected) {
#   #include 
#   deny /etc/** w,
#   /** rwkl,
# }
sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-deny-etc
kubectl run secure-app --image=nginx -n anihpj-prod --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml
# Edit pod.yaml, add annotation:
# container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/secure-app: localhost/anihpj-deny-etc
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml

Task 7 — Apply Seccomp RuntimeDefault [4 pts / 5 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Create pod "seccomp-pod" in ns "anihpj-prod" with seccompProfile type RuntimeDefault. Verify it's applied.

Answer Click to reveal solution
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: seccomp-pod, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx
---
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
kubectl get pod seccomp-pod -n anihpj-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type}'
# → RuntimeDefault ✅

Task 8 — Harden Kubelet [5 pts / 7 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1, node: worker01 | Task: Edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml: disable anonymous auth, set authorization mode to Webhook, disable readOnlyPort. Restart kubelet.

Answer Click to reveal solution
ssh worker01
sudo vi /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# Set: authentication.anonymous.enabled: false
#      authorization.mode: Webhook
#      readOnlyPort: 0
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
sudo systemctl status kubelet  # verify running

Task 9 — Apply PSS Restricted [5 pts / 6 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Label namespace "secure-ns" with PSS Restricted enforcement. Create a pod with full securityContext that complies.

Answer Click to reveal solution
kubectl config use-context cks-cluster-1
kubectl create ns secure-ns
kubectl label ns secure-ns pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
# Create compliant pod:
kubectl run secure-pod --image=nginx -n secure-ns --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml
# Edit: add securityContext.runAsNonRoot:true, seccompProfile.type:RuntimeDefault, containers[].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation:false, capabilities.drop:["ALL"]
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml

Task 10 — Full Security Context [7 pts / 8 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Create pod "anihpj-hardened" in anihpj-prod with: runAsNonRoot:true, runAsUser:1000, drop ALL caps, allowPrivilegeEscalation:false, readOnlyRootFilesystem:true, seccompProfile RuntimeDefault.

Answer Click to reveal solution
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: anihpj-hardened, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 1000
    fsGroup: 1000
    seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: nginx
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}

Task 11 — Secrets Encryption at Rest [8 pts / 12 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Configure encryption at rest using AES-GCM. Verify encrypted data in etcd shows "k8s:enc:" prefix. Rotate existing secrets.

Answer Click to reveal solution
# 1. Create EncryptionConfiguration
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
# (see Appendix B.5 for full template — aesgcm as first provider)

# 2. Configure API server
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add: --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
# Add volumeMount + hostPath volume

# 3. Rotate existing secrets
kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -

# 4. Verify
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/anihpj-prod/anihpj-secret | hexdump -C
# Look for: k8s:enc:aesgcm:v1: → encrypted ✅

Task 12 — Trivy Image Scan [6 pts / 8 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Scan container image "anihpj:v1" with Trivy. Document CRITICAL CVEs. Rebuild with patched base and verify 0 CRITICAL.

Answer Click to reveal solution
trivy image --severity CRITICAL anihpj:v1
# Document findings, rebuild:
docker build -t anihpj:v2 --build-arg BASE_IMAGE=python:3.12-slim .
trivy image --severity CRITICAL anihpj:v2
# Expected: CRITICAL: 0 ✅
# CI gate: trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 anihpj:v2

Task 13 — OPA ConstraintTemplate [7 pts / 10 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Create OPA Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate that only allows images from "registry.anihpj.com/". Apply Constraint enforcing this on namespace anihpj-prod.

Answer Click to reveal solution
# ConstraintTemplate — see Appendix B.5 for full template
# Key Rego:
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
  container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
  not startswith(container.image, "registry.anihpj.com/")
  msg := sprintf("image %v not from approved registry", [container.image])
}
# Apply Constraint targeting anihpj-prod namespace
# Test: kubectl run test --image=nginx -n anihpj-prod → DENIED ❌

Task 14 — Kyverno verifyImages [6 pts / 8 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Create Kyverno ClusterPolicy that verifies cosign signatures for images from "registry.anihpj.com/*". Use the provided cosign.pub key.

Answer Click to reveal solution
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: {name: verify-anihpj}
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-signature
    match:
      any:
      - resources: {kinds: ["Pod"]}
    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences: ["registry.anihpj.com/*"]
      attestors:
      - count: 1
        entries:
        - keys: {publicKeys: "-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----\n...\n-----END PUBLIC KEY-----"}
# Apply: kubectl apply -f policy.yaml
# Test: deploy unsigned image → DENIED ✅

Task 15 — Configure Falco Audit Logging [5 pts / 7 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Edit /etc/falco/falco.yaml to enable JSON output. Restart Falco. Verify alerts appear in JSON format.

Answer Click to reveal solution
kubectl config use-context cks-cluster-1
sudo vi /etc/falco/falco.yaml
# Set: json_output: true
kubectl rollout restart ds falco -n falco
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=5
# Expected: JSON formatted output containing "output", "priority", "rule" fields ✅

Task 16 — Write Custom Falco Rule [7 pts / 8 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: Write Falco rule to detect any shell spawn in container "anihpj". Rule name: "Shell in anihpj". Priority: CRITICAL. Output must include container name, command, and pod name.

Answer Click to reveal solution
# Add to /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml:
- list: shell_binaries
  items: [bash, sh, zsh, dash]
- macro: anihpj_container
  condition: container.name = "anihpj"
- rule: Shell in anihpj
  desc: Detect shell spawn in anihpj container
  condition: spawned_process and anihpj_container and proc.name in (shell_binaries)
  output: "Shell in anihpj! cmd=%proc.cmdline pod=%k8s.pod.name"
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [anihpj, shell, CKS]
# Restart: kubectl rollout restart ds falco -n falco
# Test: kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -n anihpj-prod -- sh → should trigger alert ✅

Task 17 — Investigate Falco Alert + Audit Log [7 pts / 8 min]

Context: cks-cluster-1 | Task: A Falco alert fired: "Shell in anihpj! cmd=bash pod=anihpj-7d8f9-abc". Find the pod. Check audit logs for any kubectl exec on this pod in the last hour. Report the user who executed it.

Answer Click to reveal solution
kubectl config use-context cks-cluster-1
# 1. Identify pod
kubectl get pods -n anihpj-prod | grep anihpj-7d8f9-abc

# 2. Check audit logs for exec
tail -2000 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | jq 'select(.objectRef.name=="anihpj-7d8f9-abc" and .objectRef.subresource=="exec")'

# 3. Extract user who ran exec
tail -2000 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | jq 'select(.objectRef.name=="anihpj-7d8f9-abc" and .objectRef.subresource=="exec") | .user.username'
# → "system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:operator-sa" ← Report this!

🏷️ Appendix I: Well-Known Security Labels, Annotations & Taints

🏷️ APPENDIX 📖 Reference 📋 Quick Lookup

Quick-reference for all well-known security labels, annotations, and taints used in Kubernetes security. Bookmark this page for the exam — you'll use these frequently.

🏷️ Pod Security Standards (PSS) Labels
LabelValuesPurpose
pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforceprivileged, baseline, restrictedEnforce PSS level — pods violating are rejected
pod-security.kubernetes.io/auditprivileged, baseline, restrictedLog violations without blocking (audit mode)
pod-security.kubernetes.io/warnprivileged, baseline, restrictedWarn user about violations without blocking
pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-versionlatest, v1.29, v1.30, etc.Target specific K8s version policies
🔧 RBAC-Related Labels & Annotations
Label/AnnotationUse
kubernetes.io/enforce-rbacEnforce RBAC on namespace level
rbac.authorization.kubernetes.io/autoupdateAuto-update ClusterRole bindings (true/false)
kubernetes.io/bootstrappingMark bootstrap RBAC resources
🔒 Security-Related Taints
TaintEffectUsage
node.kubernetes.io/unschedulableNoScheduleNode is cordoned
node.kubernetes.io/not-readyNoExecuteNode is not ready — evict pods
node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressureNoScheduleNode has low disk space
📦 Image Security Annotations
AnnotationUse
container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<ctr>Apply AppArmor profile to container
seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/podApply Seccomp profile (pod-level, deprecated)
cosign.sigstore.dev/signatureStores cosign signature in registry
🦅 Falco & Audit Annotations
Label/AnnotationUse
app: falcoFalco pod selector label
audit.kubernetes.io/policyReference to audit policy resource
audit.k8s.io/v1Audit policy API version
🔒 Additional Security Taints & Toleration Examples
TaintEffectUsage / Toleration Example
node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressureNoScheduleNode low on memory — toleration: key="node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure", operator="Exists"
node.kubernetes.io/pid-pressureNoScheduleToo many PIDs on node
node.kubernetes.io/network-unavailableNoScheduleNetwork plugin not ready
security=restricted:NoScheduleNoScheduleCustom: only hardened pods — kubectl taint node worker1 security=restricted:NoSchedule
📋 NetworkPolicy Label Reference
LabelTypical ValueUsed By
appanihpj, postgres, redisMost common pod selector for NetPol rules
k8s-app: kube-dnsCoreDNS podsDNS egress rules — always needed with default-deny
name: ingress-nginxIngress controller namespaceAllow ingress traffic to workloads
name: monitoringMonitoring namespaceAllow Prometheus/Grafana to scrape metrics
⚡ Quick Usage Examples — Copy-Paste for the Exam
# PSS: Label namespace for restricted security
kubectl label ns anihpj-prod \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted

# Taint: Only allow hardened pods on a node
kubectl taint node worker1 security=restricted:NoSchedule

# AppArmor: Apply profile to a container
# Pod annotation:
# container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj: localhost/anihpj-profile

# NetPol: Allow DNS egress (critical with default-deny!)
# podSelector.matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}
💡 CKS Exam Tip — Labels vs Annotations

Labels are used for selection and grouping (podSelectors, service selectors, NetPol selectors). Annotations are for metadata and configuration (AppArmor profiles, Ingress settings). The CKS exam often tests your ability to use the right one — know the difference!

📝 CKS Exam Practice QuestionsExam Prep

16 exam-style questions across all 6 CKS domains. Each question is modeled after real exam tasks. Click "Show Answer" to reveal the solution and explanation. Time yourself — aim for 5-8 minutes per question.

🔵 Domain 1: Cluster Setup (10% of exam)

Q1Domain 1

You run kube-bench run --targets=master and see FAIL for check 1.2.6. What does this check verify, and how do you fix it?

Check 1.2.6 verifies that the --authorization-mode argument is not set to AlwaysAllow. The fix is to edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml and set:

--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC

This ensures all API requests go through RBAC authorization rather than being allowed by default. Node authorization is needed for kubelet access. Wait 30-60s for the API server to restart, then re-run kube-bench to verify PASS.

Q2Domain 1

You need to apply a NetworkPolicy to namespace secure-app that blocks ALL ingress and egress traffic by default, then allows pods to reach kube-dns on UDP port 53. Write the YAML.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny, namespace: secure-app}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns, namespace: secure-app}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]

Explanation: Always apply default-deny FIRST, then add DNS egress. Without DNS, pods can't resolve service names — the most common mistake candidates make.

🟡 Domain 2: Cluster Hardening (15% of exam)

Q3Domain 2

After disabling anonymous auth with --anonymous-auth=false, how do you verify it's actually working? Write the verification commands.

# Test 1: Anonymous request should FAIL
kubectl get pods --as=system:anonymous
# Expected: Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden

# Test 2: Raw API request should FAIL
kubectl get --raw /api --as=system:anonymous
# Expected: {"kind":"Status","reason":"Unauthorized"...}

# Test 3: Verify the flag is active
ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep anonymous-auth
# Should show: --anonymous-auth=false
Q4Domain 2

Create a ServiceAccount monitor-sa in namespace prod. Grant it ONLY permission to get and list pods. Verify it cannot delete configmaps.

kubectl create sa monitor-sa -n prod
kubectl create role monitor-role --verb=get,list --resource=pods -n prod
kubectl create rolebinding monitor-rb --role=monitor-role --serviceaccount=prod:monitor-sa -n prod

# Verify CAN:
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:monitor-sa -n prod
# → yes

# Verify CANNOT:
kubectl auth can-i delete configmaps --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:monitor-sa -n prod
# → no ✅

🟡 Domain 3: System Hardening (15% of exam)

Q5Domain 3

Create an AppArmor profile that prevents writing to /etc/ and apply it to a pod named secure-nginx. Write all commands.

# 1. Create profile
sudo tee /etc/apparmor.d/deny-etc-write << 'EOF'
#include <tunables/global>
profile deny-etc-write flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  deny /etc/** w,
  /** rwkl,
}
EOF

# 2. Load profile
sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/deny-etc-write

# 3. Create pod with annotation
kubectl run secure-nginx --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml
# Edit: add annotation
# container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/secure-nginx: localhost/deny-etc-write
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml

# 4. Verify: should fail
kubectl exec secure-nginx -- touch /etc/test
# → Permission denied
Q6Domain 3

A pod crashes after applying seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}. The app uses the clone syscall. How do you fix this?

RuntimeDefault blocks ~300 syscalls, including clone. To fix: create a custom seccomp profile that allows the needed syscall:

{
  "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",
  "architectures": ["SCMP_ARCH_X86_64"],
  "syscalls": [
    {"names": ["clone","read","write","open","close","mmap","futex","exit","exit_group"],"action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"}
  ]
}

Save as /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/custom.json, then reference in pod: seccompProfile: {type: Localhost, localhostProfile: custom.json}. Alternative: downgrade to Unconfined temporarily to confirm seccomp is the cause.

🟠 Domain 4: Microservice Vulnerabilities (20% of exam)

Q7Domain 4

Namespace production has PSS Restricted enforced. A pod fails to create with error "violates PodSecurity". Write the minimum pod YAML that will work.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: compliant-pod, namespace: production}
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true           # Required by Restricted
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault       # Required by Restricted
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # Required by Restricted
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]            # Required by Restricted

PSS Restricted requires: runAsNonRoot, seccomp RuntimeDefault, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, drop ALL capabilities. Missing any of these = rejected.

Q8Domain 4

You need to enable encryption at rest for Secrets. After configuring EncryptionConfiguration with AES-GCM, how do you verify existing secrets are now encrypted?

# 1. After adding --encryption-provider-config flag and restarting API server:
kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -

# 2. Verify encryption:
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/default/my-secret | hexdump -C
# Look for: k8s:enc:aesgcm:v1:key1: → encrypted ✅
# If you see plain text JSON → NOT encrypted ❌

# 3. Also verify plaintext is rejected:
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/default/my-secret
# Should show binary/unreadable output, not JSON
Q9Domain 4

Create a RuntimeClass named gvisor with handler runsc. Then create a pod that uses this RuntimeClass.

# RuntimeClass
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata: {name: gvisor}
handler: runsc
---
# Pod using gVisor
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: sandboxed-app}
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx

🔴 Domain 5: Supply Chain Security (20% of exam)

Q10Domain 5

You scan an image with Trivy and find 2 CRITICAL CVEs. Write the command to scan and explain how to fix them.

# Scan
trivy image --severity CRITICAL myapp:v1

# Fix: Rebuild with updated base image
docker build -t myapp:v2 --build-arg BASE_IMAGE=python:3.12-slim .
trivy image --severity CRITICAL myapp:v2
# Expected: CRITICAL: 0 ✅

# CI/CD gate:
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:v2 || exit 1
Q11Domain 5

Write an OPA Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate that only allows images from registry.company.com/. Apply a Constraint enforcing this on namespace prod.

# ConstraintTemplate
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata: {name: k8sapprovedregistry}
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names: {kind: K8sApprovedRegistry}
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8sapprovedregistry
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        not startswith(container.image, "registry.company.com/")
        msg := sprintf("image %v not approved", [container.image])
      }
---
# Constraint
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sApprovedRegistry
metadata: {name: prod-registry}
spec:
  match:
    kinds: [{apiGroups: [""], kinds: ["Pod"]}]
    namespaces: ["prod"]
Q12Domain 5

Write a Kyverno ClusterPolicy that verifies images from registry.company.com/* must be signed with a specific public key.

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: {name: verify-company-images}
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-signature
    match:
      any:
      - resources: {kinds: ["Pod"]}
    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences: ["registry.company.com/*"]
      attestors:
      - count: 1
        entries:
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |-
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              MFkwEwYHKoZI...
              -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

🔴 Domain 6: Monitoring, Logging & Runtime Security (20% of exam)

Q13Domain 6

Write a complete Falco rule that detects any shell (bash, sh, zsh) spawned in a container named web-app. Priority: CRITICAL. Output must include the command and pod name.

- list: shell_binaries
  items: [bash, sh, zsh, dash]
- macro: web_app_container
  condition: container.name = "web-app"
- rule: Shell in web-app
  desc: Detect shell execution in web-app container
  condition: >
    spawned_process and
    web_app_container and
    proc.name in (shell_binaries)
  output: >
    Shell spawned in web-app!
    cmd=%proc.cmdline pod=%k8s.pod.name
    ns=%k8s.ns.name
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [shell, web-app, CKS]

Add to /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml. Restart: kubectl rollout restart ds falco -n falco. Test: kubectl exec web-app-xxx -- sh.

Q14Domain 6

A Falco alert fired. Write the commands to investigate: find which pod triggered it, check if there was a kubectl exec on that pod, and identify which user executed it.

# 1. Find the pod from Falco logs
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco --tail=200 | grep "Shell"
# Extract pod name from output

# 2. Check audit logs for kubectl exec
tail -2000 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | jq 'select(.objectRef.name=="<pod-name>" and .objectRef.subresource=="exec")'

# 3. Identify the user
tail -2000 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | jq 'select(.objectRef.name=="<pod-name>" and .objectRef.subresource=="exec") | .user.username'
# → system:serviceaccount:namespace:sa-name

# 4. Check what else this user did
tail -2000 /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | jq 'select(.user.username=="<user>")'
Q15Domain 6

Configure an audit policy that logs pod creation/deletion at RequestResponse level, secret access at Metadata level, and ignores node status updates. Enable audit logging to file.

apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]
rules:
- level: None
  users: ["system:nodes"]
  verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- level: RequestResponse
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["create","delete"]
- level: Metadata
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["secrets","configmaps"]
- level: Metadata

Enable in API server: --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log. Mount volumes for both paths.

Q16Domain 6

A pod in namespace anihpj-prod has been compromised. Write the step-by-step commands to: isolate the pod, capture forensic evidence, eradicate it, and verify the replacement is clean.

# 1. ISOLATE — Remove from Service, apply emergency NetPol
kubectl label pod <pod> app- -n anihpj-prod
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: emergency-deny, namespace: anihpj-prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: null}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
EOF

# 2. INVESTIGATE — Capture forensic evidence
kubectl get pod <pod> -n anihpj-prod -o yaml > forensic.yaml
kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj-prod -- ps aux > processes.txt
kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj-prod -- netstat -tlnp > connections.txt

# 3. ERADICATE
kubectl delete pod <pod> -n anihpj-prod --force --grace-period=0
# Deployment/replicaset auto-creates clean replacement

# 4. VERIFY
kubectl get pods -n anihpj-prod -l app=anihpj
kubectl describe pod <new-pod> -n anihpj-prod
# Check image, securityContext, runtime
